the hero who has hurt her and the woman who still softens toward him

act: the boar joins its mate
sense: the beast of his hill unites with its own mate, while the man leaves the woman he loves to grow pale, so he should come and marry her

act: the boar rears and protects the striped young whose mother the tiger killed

the lord who has had his joy of the girl and gone off unchanged

the guarded girl and the man who comes for her by night
the guarded girl and the man who comes for her by night

act: the tusker embraces his mate and, though starving, does not leave for other lands but suffers the hunger with her
sense: even the beast in drought will not leave his mate for a richer land, so the man who would leave her for wealth falls below it

act: the hen kite, alone on the bare fork, calls out for its mate
sense: the lonely call on his road is the call of the woman he has left behind, which is why her nature does not leave him however far he goes

act: the male wild dog, keeping to its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go unharmed

act: the bull elephants keep to their herd as they roam the grove
sense: even the elephants on her road stay with their herd, while the girl has left her own band of companions and their wedding for one man

act: the hen dove croons to give her mate pleasure
sense: the man, hearing a mate call to her partner, knows his wife waits calling for him, and so hurries home

act: the doe, with her fawn beside her, frolics in the newly rained land

act: the male vulture flies out hungry to bring food to its mate, who has laid and lies weak in the nest

act: the nectar birds sleep in the flowering boughs together with their mates

act: the stag holds its young doe close and leaps as it grazes beside her
sense: in this season even the stag keeps to its mate, yet the husband has not come home to his

act: the male wild dog attacks a boar because his mate, weak after whelping, is hungry
sense: the road itself shows a male who fights to feed the mate he provides for, the very task the heart has abandoned halfway

act: the stag, done with grazing, embraces his loving doe, drinks with her and rests beside her
sense: the season has brought even the stag to his mate's side, which is where the man who named this season should now be

act: the male kite on the bare yaa tree keeps calling his hooked-beaked mate to come to him
sense: even the kite on this dry road calls its mate to its side, while the man has left his wife and may not even turn back to her

act: the stag feeds tender grass to his young doe and guards her back while she sleeps
sense: the stag's care is the care the man is hurrying home to give his wife

the woman's heart and her absent husband

act: the cow elephant, worn by the summer heat, goes into the flood to bathe together with her bull

act: the tiger kills a great elephant to end the craving hunger of his pregnant mate

the hero's wife and the young women around her husband, as the courtesan sees them

sense: the man on that road will hear a parted creature crying for its mate and so feel his own parting and come back

act: the milch cows go back to their calves at dusk

act: the wild cow sleeps unafraid on the man's slope
sense: as the creatures of his hill rest secure there, the girl who has no one but him should rest secure in his kindness

note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common pond (பழனம்). Kural 1311: the wife refuses her husband's chest because all women feast on it in common with their eyes.
teaches: The fear the Ainkurunuru girls voice before marriage, that his chest may become common property, is the very charge the Kural's wife brings in a sulk after it, so the two show the marutham husband's straying anticipated as a danger and then turned into a reason to refuse him.

note: Ainkurunuru 9: the girls wish that their bond with the lover not become town gossip (அம்பல்). Kural 1143: the man welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, since it feels like having her already.
teaches: The same talk of the town that the women pray to escape is a pleasure the man savours, so read together the two show that in secret love gossip threatened the woman's standing while it flattered the man's hopes.

note: Ainkurunuru 8: the mother wishes that the king rule justly and there be no theft (and in poem 10, that the rains come). Kural 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The mother's prayers for just rule and for timely rain stand as separate wishes in the decade, while the Kural makes the second follow from the first, so a household's prayer list shows the belief that the Kural later states as a law of kingship.

note: Ainkurunuru 8: the girls wish that the lover's oath sworn here may prove true. Kuruntokai 53: the friend tells the man of the fields that what afflicts them is the oath he swore at the broad ford of their town, holding the girl's forearm.
teaches: The oath the Ainkurunuru girls hope will come true is, in the Kuruntokai, already the cause of their suffering, so the pair shows the kalavu vow of the field country both as the girl's only security and as the wound when it lags.

note: Ainkurunuru 5: the girls wish that the lover's chariot stand at their front gate. Akananuru 160: the friend tells the girl that his chariot, which used to come by night, has now come by day, loudly, for the whole village to see.
teaches: The Akananuru scene shows what the Ainkurunuru wish means: a chariot that comes by day to the gate, seen by the village, is a suitor's public claim, so the single wish for 'the chariot at our gate' is a request for marriage.

note: Ainkurunuru 6: may he marry her and our father give her. Ainkurunuru 7: may he take her and go to his own town.
teaches: Read in order, the decade's wishes walk through the rite step by step, the father's giving (6) and then the bride's leaving for the husband's town (7), so the series records the sequence of a Sangam marriage that no single poem states.

note: In both the wife's shoulders waste and she will not call him cruel; in Ainkurunuru 11 she says he is good while her own shoulders say he is not, in Kural 1236 she is pained that others call him cruel because her shoulders and bangles slacken.
teaches: The Sangam poem sets the accusation inside her own body, against her own words, while Valluvar moves it to other people reading her body, so the couplet's defence of him against outsiders presupposes the older poem's private split between what she says and what her shoulders show.

note: The two poems share the refrain துறைகேழ் ஊரன் கொடுமை ... யாமே ... என் தடமென் தோளே; in 11 she calls him good and the shoulders contradict her, in 12 she lets him keep his cruelty and lets the shoulders lose.
teaches: Read in order, the shared refrain moves the wife from denial, where her body overrules her words, to surrender, where she grants him the cruelty and her body the defeat, so the decade builds a progression out of near-identical lines.

note: Ainkurunuru 15 has the wife say that the man whose town's reed is a float to the bathing women is no husband of hers; in Akananuru 186 the courtesan says their bond was only as far as bathing together on a float of reed (வேழத்துப் புணைதுணை யாகப் புனல்ஆடு கேண்மை).
teaches: The same reed float is the wife's proof that he belongs to other women and the courtesan's plea that the affair was mere water-play, so the pair shows the marutham reed raft as a contested sign whose meaning depends on which woman speaks.

note: Ainkurunuru 14 praises the chest of the ford-town lord for its softness that gives cool sleep; Naladiyar 389's wife of the field-town lord looks at the same chest smeared with sandal by other women's breasts.
teaches: The marutham husband's chest is the wife's place of rest in the Sangam poem and the evidence of his other women in the Naladiyar, so the later moralist turns the older image of comfort into the record of its betrayal.

note: In both the wife recalls that he promised not to leave (பிரியலென், அஞ்சல்) and then left; Ainkurunuru 18 ends on her weeping eyes and the question, Kural 1154 asks whether those who believed his assuring words are at fault.
teaches: The Sangam wife quotes his broken promise as an accusation, while Valluvar's wife turns it into a question of blame for having believed, so the couplet adds to the older scene a moral reckoning about trust that the poem leaves unasked.

note: In both the wife's bangles slip from her wrist because of the man; in Ainkurunuru 20 they loosen as she thinks of him, in Kural 1157 they broadcast that he has left.
teaches: The Sangam poem treats the slipping bangle as the private effect of memory, while Valluvar makes the same bangle a gossip that announces his desertion to everyone, so the couplet turns an inner sign into public scandal.

note: Both turn on assurance (தெளிப்பவும், தெளித்தசொல்): in Ainkurunuru 21 the friend sets the man's assurances against the girl's paling eyes; in Kural 1154 the woman asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The Kural asks who bears the blame once a trusted promise fails, while the Ainkurunuru shows the body already failing while the promise is still being spoken, so the couplet's moral question comes after a doubt that the older poem places in the girl's eyes before any leaving.

note: Ainkurunuru 24 says he takes the beauty (நலங்கொண்டு) of the women he embraced and abandons them; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns the friend's accusation of plain taking into an exchange in which pallor is the payment, so the same loss that the Sangam friend calls the act of a kin-destroying creature becomes, in the couplet, the woman's own bitter bookkeeping.

note: Both use the belief that the crab is killed by its own young: Ainkurunuru 24 names the crab born at its mother's death (தாய்சாப் பிறக்கும்), Sirupanchamoolam 10 lists its own brood as death to the crab (ஞெண்டிற்குத் தன்பார்ப்பு).
teaches: The pairing shows a piece of field lore surviving from the akam landscape into the didactic list: the Sangam friend uses it to charge a man with destroying his own, while the later moralist uses it to say a thing's own offspring or speech is its death, so the same belief turned from accusation of another into warning to oneself.

note: Both say the man's chest belongs to many women: Ainkurunuru 25's friend says the ooran's chest (மார்புபலர்க்கு) brings grief to many; Kural 1311's wife refuses his chest (மார்பு) because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The friend counts the cost to the many women his chest has harmed, while the Kural wife refuses that chest because it is shared even by looks, so held together they show the same charge of a common chest used first as report to the mother and then as the wife's own ground for refusal.

note: Both mark the loss in the shoulders and the slipping bangle: Ainkurunuru 28 has the bright bangle loosening as the soft shoulders pale (ஒண்டொடி நெகிழ, மென் தோள் பசப்பது); Kural 1234 has the bangle slipping from shoulders that have lost their old beauty.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru friend uses the paled shoulders to tell the mother that a man, not the ford goddess, is the cause, while the Kural keeps only the signs, so the couplet's portrait of wasting shoulders was in the older poem a piece of evidence in a disclosure.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 28 line 1's conditional is compressed; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Both open on the neem-bud-eyed crab of the marutham field and its earthen hole (வேப்புநனை யன்ன நெடுங்கள் களவன், வேப்புநனை அன்ன நெடுங்கண் நீர்ஞெண்டு, மண்அளை): in Ainkurunuru 30 it fills its hole with paddy blossom while the girl loses her beauty; in Akananuru 176 it flees the heron into its hole in a poem refusing the husband at the door.
teaches: The neem-bud simile and the crab's earthen hole are a shared marutham formula, and the two poems make it mean opposite things by the act they give it, hoarding in the four-line poem and fearful hiding in the long one, so in this stock image the sense lies in what the crab does, not in how it looks.

note: Both end on the same words, உற்ற சூளே, an oath sworn at the broad ford of 'our town'; in Kuruntokai 53 the friend says it was sworn holding the girl's forearm with the hill goddesses as witness and now afflicts them, in Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman says it was sworn before the bathing companions and asks whether he will call it no debt.
teaches: The witness decides what a broken ford-oath costs: sworn before goddesses it turns into a danger that falls on the women, sworn before human bathers it shrinks to a debt the man can simply disown, so the courtesan's oath is the weaker for lacking a god.

note: In Ainkurunuru 31 the other woman holds the lord to an oath he swore her at the bathing ford; in Akananuru 166 the same kind of lord swears to his wife by the god of Velur that he never bathed with the other woman, and the courtesan asks who then held the float with her yesterday.
teaches: Held together, the two show the marutham lord's oaths cancelling each other: the bathing he swore by to the courtesan is the bathing he forswears to his wife, so one of the two oaths must be false and each woman is left holding an oath the other's makes worthless.

note: Both put the courtesan's report of the wives in the same formula: அழுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women weep) in Ainkurunuru 32, கழறுப என்ப அவன் பெண்டிர் (they say his women rail) in Akananuru 76.
teaches: The one formula frames the wives two ways, as melting in tears like wax or as clamouring like a bard's drum, and the courtesan's answer scales with it, from a mocking count of days in the short poem to an open vow to hold him by force in the long one.

note: Ainkurunuru 36 says that if he forgets them, they too could forget and be content, were it not that her eyes go pale; Kural 1207 has the woman say she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
teaches: The Sangam speaker claims forgetting is in her power and lays the failure on her paling eyes, while the Kural woman denies she can forget at all, so the older poem places love's hold in the body against the will and the couplet moves it into the mind itself.

note: Ainkurunuru 37 has நயந்தோர் உண்கண் பசந்துபனி மல்க, the eyes of those who loved him pale and brimming; Kural 1232 has நயந்தவர் ... பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண், pale eyes streaming that seem to tell of the beloved's unkindness.
teaches: Valluvar keeps the Ainkurunuru's very words for the pale, wet eyes but changes their office: in the Sangam poem they are evidence the wronged woman cites against his lying oath, in the couplet they become speakers that publish his unkindness to others, so the image moves from accusation to involuntary gossip.

note: Ainkurunuru 41 says the lord turns gold-pale the bodies of those who trusted his word; Akananuru 146 has the wife foresee that the next woman who believes the deceiver's word (வாய்மொழி நம்பி) will weep and go pale as she did.
teaches: Held together, the two show that pallor from a trusted word was a fixed charge against the marutham husband: the Ainkurunuru states it as a habit of his town in four lines, and the Akananuru turns the same charge into a forecast for the rival, so the wronged wife becomes the proof of what awaits the other woman.
audit_text_issue: akananuru:146 line 8 அனியள் is likely a misprint for அளியள்.

note: In both the wife refuses the straying husband's chest: in Ainkurunuru 42 the friend reports it to him as if it were joy-drunk folly; in Kural 1311 the wife herself refuses it because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The refusal of the chest was a recognised act of the sulking wife before Valluvar; the Sangam friend presents it with mock surprise to shame the man, while the Kural gives the wife her own reason, so the couplet supplies the motive that the older poem leaves to irony.

note: Ainkurunuru 43 calls the husband's bard a bigger liar than the husband, full of oaths; Akananuru 56 shows that bard on the street hurrying to bring new brides to the lord, scared into the wife's own house by a cow, and laughed at.
teaches: The two give the bard's double role in marutham: the Ainkurunuru names the charge (he lies and swears for his master) and the Akananuru shows why the wife can mock him openly, since attacking the go-between lets her shame the husband without naming him.

note: Ainkurunuru 44 says the tortoise's young grow by looking at the mother's face; Siddhar 176 says the sea tortoise's eggs take form as the mother thinks of them, and asks when the poet will so reach God.
teaches: The same belief, that the tortoise nurtures without touch, serves the Sangam friend to argue that a wife needs only her husband's presence and the later siddhar to describe grace given by attention alone, so a piece of animal lore carried a model of care at a distance from household love into devotion.

note: In Ainkurunuru 49 the bard-woman pours a few fish and gets much paddy; in Akananuru 126 the bard's daughter in Evvi's Kaviri land will not even take old red paddy for her brothers' vaalai fish and is given pearls.
teaches: The barter of the bard's women was a stock picture of the bard family getting more than it gives; the Akananuru uses it as praise of a patron's wealth, while the Ainkurunuru turns the same profit into an accusation, since the bard who gets much for little also gets much for his lies.

note: Kural 1303 says that not embracing the one who sulks is like adding pain to those already in distress; Ainkurunuru 50 tells the husband who gives no refuge that the household and they suffer, and his wife weeps too.
teaches: The Kural states the cost of withheld grace for one sulking woman, while the Ainkurunuru friend counts it across the whole household, its wealth and its people, so the older poem makes the husband's refusal a failure of the house and not only of love.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 (துணையோர் செல்வமும்) is of uncertain sense.

note: Kuruntokai 53 names what afflicts them as the oath he swore at their town's ford, holding her forearm before the water goddesses; Ainkurunuru 53 has the friend ask why the ford should be blamed for their sickness when the cause is his oath.
teaches: Read together they show that the ford was both where the oath was sworn and where the household looked for the spirit that seized the girl, so the friend's correction turns the family's diagnosis of possession into a charge of perjury against the man.

note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Ainkurunuru 55 the friend tells the man that because he desired her beauty and left her, her brow has paled for many to see.
teaches: The Kural keeps the exchange of beauty for pallor as the woman's private complaint, while the Ainkurunuru friend turns the same exchange into public evidence held up to the man, so the pallor that is a lament in the couplet becomes an accusation in the town.

note: Both measure a woman's beauty by Iruppai of the generous Viraan: in Natrinai 350 the wife says she would let that old beauty perish rather than accept the straying man; in Ainkurunuru 58 the friend says he seems possessed by it yet keeps house for others.
teaches: The same rich town names the wife's beauty both as what the straying husband pretends to be captured by and as what the wife herself is ready to lose rather than take him back, so the marutham quarrel is fought over who holds that beauty as a claim.

note: Kural 1102 says the woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes the man; in Ainkurunuru 59 the friend says she was once the cure for his love-sick heart but can be no cure for the girl now.
teaches: The couplet makes the beloved the only remedy for the man's love-sickness, but the Sangam friend shows a third person who served as that remedy by bringing them together, and who has none for the woman once he strays, so the cure flows only toward the man.

note: In Akananuru 162 the man tells his heart that he stood in a midnight storm at a corner of her father's tall house until the strict guards slackened; in Ainkurunuru 60 the friend tells the man that he comes to the tall house while all sleep and asks whether he does not fear her father's spear.
teaches: The danger at the father's tall house that the lover recounts to himself as proof of his devotion is the very thing the friend names to him as a reason to stop coming by night, so the same risk is a boast in his mouth and a demand for marriage in hers.

note: Both open with the ripe sweet mango that falls of itself into the water below; in Kuruntokai 8 the courtesan has the vaalai fish snatch it, in Ainkurunuru 61 it drops into the deep pond of Kazhar, the town the wife uses to measure his new women.
teaches: Held together, the formula shows the falling fruit as the man who drops to whoever waits below, used by the courtesan to boast she caught him and by the wife to say he keeps falling into new marriages.

note: Akananuru 226 sets the husband's scandalous bathing with another woman at Matti's Kazhar ford; Ainkurunuru 61 makes Matti's Kazhar the standard for the women he courts.
teaches: For the marutham wife the patron's rich ford had become shorthand for the husband's other women, so a chief's town entered akam as a place of the hero's pleasures, not only of the patron's fame.

note: Both are the wife in oodal refusing the husband's chest; Ainkurunuru 63 because other women have lain on it, Kural 1311 because all women consume him with their eyes.
teaches: The couplet raises the bar of the older refusal: where the Sangam wife needs the touch of other women to refuse him, Valluvar's wife refuses for their looks alone, so the Kural turns a grievance about deeds into a jealousy of glances.

note: The same line, the otter getting a vaalai fish as its daily food, addresses the husband in both; in Kuruntokai 364 it is spoken by the household concubine answering the wife's slander, in Ainkurunuru 63 by the wife refusing him.
teaches: Because rival women use the identical otter line, the image belongs to the husband, a daily hunter in his own pond, and each woman fits it to her side of the quarrel.

note: Both have the wife charging the husband with bathing in the new flood with other women; Ainkurunuru 64 rests on the many who saw it, Akananuru 266 says the talk is loud as a feast and then that this is no grief to her compared with the oath he swore before Murugan.
teaches: The long poem moves the offence the short one names: in Ainkurunuru 64 the wound is that many saw, while Akananuru 266 dismisses the gossip and fixes on his broken oath, so publicity was the first charge but perjury the deeper one.
audit_text_issue: akananuru:266 colophon reads தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது, likely a misprint for தலைமகள்

note: Kuruntokai 80 has the other woman announce she will bathe with lilies in her hair at the flooded ford and dare the wife to guard her husband; Ainkurunuru 64 has the wife report that many saw him bathing there with his beloved.
teaches: Read together, the public bathing that the wife cites as proof of his fault is the very display the rival intends as her victory, so the same act counts as scandal in one voice and as triumph in the other.

note: Both refuse the husband by pointing to the body of a nursing mother: Ainkurunuru 65 says her son-bearing body would spoil his chest; in Natrinai 380 the friend lists the ghee, smoke, milk and birth-smell that make them no match for the man of the courtesans' street.
teaches: Natrinai 380 itemises the household marks that Ainkurunuru 65 leaves as one sarcastic phrase, showing that 'it would spoil your chest' means the labour of the home set against the adorned women of the street.

note: In Ainkurunuru 66 the wife asks who the woman is who stole his homecoming to his toddling son; in Akananuru 16 the wife tells how a young courtesan found that son alone in the chariot street and hugged him as her own.
teaches: The son is the wife's claim on the husband, and the pair shows the rival reaching for it from both ends: diverting the father on his way to the child, and taking the child into her own arms.
audit_text_issue: line 1 not in one source

note: Kuruntokai 8 has the courtesan boast that the husband talks big at her house but dances like a mirror puppet to his son's mother; Ainkurunuru 67 has the wife call the new woman naive for matching herself against her, since the women who have drawn him off outnumber bees. On one reading each woman claims the other holds no power over him.
teaches: Each side belittles the other through the man's nature, the courtesan by making him the wife's puppet and the wife by making him a bee of countless flowers, so neither woman's speech can be taken as the truth of the household.

note: Natrinai 300 has the water-lily bend to the lotus in the wind as attendants bow to an angry princess; Ainkurunuru 68 has the lily open at dawn like the lotus, while the wife complains that the other woman will not hold herself in.
teaches: The pairing shows that lily and lotus were a shared code of rank in marutham: in Natrinai the lesser flower bows and order holds, in Ainkurunuru it apes the greater flower, which is exactly the other woman's offence.

note: The line 'she stood crying till her kohl eyes went red' closes both; in 69 the river flood sweeps away the rival's sand-play at the bathing ford, in 125, a neythal poem, the clear wave snatches her doll.
teaches: The mockery of the rival as a crying child was a stock retort carried across landscapes by changing only the water and the toy, river flood and sand-play for marutham, sea wave and doll for neythal.

note: Both set the wife who has borne a son against the women he prefers: in Ainkurunuru 70 his women are clean and fragrant while she is like a ghoul; in Akananuru 26 she turns to the boy saying 'you suit the good women; I suit this rich one' after the husband shrank from her milk.
teaches: Akananuru 26 shows the scene behind the four-line retort, the husband's flinch from the nursing body, so the Ainkurunuru 'ghoul' reads as the wife's bitter echo of his own recoil.

note: Ainkurunuru 71: the wife says people report he bathed yesterday with his beloved (நெருநை ... ஆடினை என்ப), and the gossip can no more be hidden than sunlight. Akananuru 266: the wife opens with the same report (ஆடினை என்ப மகிழ்ந, நெருநை), compares the uproar to a victory feast, then says the gossip is no grief to her beside his broken oath.
teaches: The same reported charge, that he bathed with her yesterday, is the whole case in the Ainkurunuru but only the preface in the Akananuru, whose wife sets the gossip aside for the oath he broke, so the pair shows the bathing formula as a fixed opening of marutham complaint that a longer poem could push past to a deeper wrong.

note: Ainkurunuru 74: a young woman climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water, her hair spreading like a descending peacock. Purananuru 243: an old man recalls how in youth he climbed the low marutham branch at the ford and leapt into the deep pool to the wonder of those on the bank.
teaches: The leap from the riverside marutham was a common game of youth in the field towns, and the two books use it oppositely: the akam poet freezes it as the height of a woman's beauty seen by a lover, while the puram poet, leaning on his staff, makes the same leap the measure of what age has taken.

note: Ainkurunuru 77: the other woman asks the husband to bathe with her so that gossip rises in the town, and not to go home. Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan says she will go to bathe at the flooded ford, and if the wife is afraid, let her guard her husband's chest with her kin like Ezhini's herds.
teaches: The Kuruntokai courtesan aims her dare at the wife, while the Ainkurunuru rival speaks to the man and names the gossip itself as her goal, so together they show the flood-bath as a public move in the rivalry, staged to be talked about and to pull him from his house, not a pleasure she hides.
audit_text_issue: The infinitive அலர்எழ in Ainkurunuru 77 may be circumstantial rather than purposive.

note: Ainkurunuru 78: a woman asks the man to bathe in the dam-breaking flood, likened to Killi's wall-breaking elephant, and take her shoulders as his raft. Akananuru 312: the friend says that if the hill lord means to marry, they will bathe in the flood with his chest as their raft, and the lightning is likened to Vazhuthi's spear.
teaches: The raft of the lover's body runs in both directions: in the kurinji poem the girls take the man's chest as their float as the reward of a promised marriage, while in the marutham poem a woman offers her shoulders as his float to draw him away, and both dress the flood in a king's weapon, so the same intimate game and the same borrowed war image serve the making of a marriage in one land and its straining in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are so red after he bathed in the first-rain flood as the shoulder-companion of fine women. Naladiyar 387: the wife complains that the man who embraced other women comes to embrace her too without bathing.
teaches: In the Naladiyar the husband's fault is that he comes to his wife unwashed from other women, while in the Ainkurunuru the bath itself is the scene of his straying and its red eyes the evidence, so the pair shows bathing in the field country as both the cleansing a wife expects after his absence and the occasion of the absence.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife asks why his eyes are red after bathing in the first-rain flood with fine women. Kalittokai 98: the husband says he was delayed bathing in the new flood of the Vaigai, and the wife turns the flood, point by point, into the woman he bathed with.
teaches: The Kalittokai shows the flood-bath as the husband's ready alibi and the wife unpicking it at length, while the Ainkurunuru wife grants the bath in a word and reads his red eyes as the trace of the women in it, so the pair shows the new flood as the standard excuse of the marutham husband and its marks on his body as the wife's standard proof.

note: Ainkurunuru 80: the wife, saying she is not sulking, reads his reddened eyes after the flood-bath as a sign of the women he bathed with. Kural 1313: the husband says that even if he wears a wreath of branch flowers, she grows angry, saying he wore it to show another woman.
teaches: Both turn the husband's body into evidence in a love-quarrel, but the Kural's husband protests that the sign is innocent and the suspicion hers, while the Ainkurunuru sign comes from a bath with women he did take, so together they show that the oodal's reading of marks on the man can be either jealous fancy or plain proof, and the couplet's comedy depends on the scene being the first.

note: Ainkurunuru 81: the other woman says his wife would grieve if she heard him say he desired her. Natrinai 100: the other woman laughs at how the man trembled when she said she would go and tell his wife.
teaches: In both the other woman's hold on the man is the wife's knowledge: the Ainkurunuru voices it as mock pity for the wife, the Natrinai as a threat that sets him shaking, so together they show that the courtesan's power in marutham rests on what the wife may hear.

note: Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman calls his chest a Thai bathing pond that many plunge into. Kural 1311: the wife refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes.
teaches: The Kural wife's complaint that his chest is common property is made, in the Ainkurunuru, by one of the women who share it, who boasts of it rather than complains, so the same image of the common chest serves as reproach from the house and as triumph from outside it.

note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common field-pond (பழனம்). Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman says his chest is a pond where many bathe.
teaches: The decade of wishes prays against exactly the outcome this decade reports, his chest as a pond for all, so the anthology's own order sets the bride's fear and the courtesan's taunt in one image eight decades apart.

note: Ainkurunuru 87: the other woman says the wife sulks at everyone, so why at her. Akananuru 186: the courtesan says the wife quarrels with her (எம்மொடு புலக்கும்), but she is not the enemy; the husband who leaves women pale is.
teaches: The four-line protest that the wife's sulk is aimless becomes in the Akananuru a full defence that redirects the blame to the husband, so the pair shows the courtesan's answer to the wife's anger as a set speech with two steps: she is not singled out, and the fault lives in the wife's own house.

note: Ainkurunuru 89: the other woman tells the bard the wife is greatly graced, only because she wants the name of wife. Naladiyar 390: the wife tells the bard not to lie that he will be kind; she is the dry end of the cane and the others its sweet middle. On a plain reading each woman says the other has his favour.
teaches: Each woman tells the same messenger that the other is the favoured one, so the bard meets the identical complaint at both doors and the triangle has no one who admits to being loved; the Naladiyar files that voice under the chaste wife, the Ainkurunuru gives it to the rival.

note: Ainkurunuru 90: the other woman says the husband has the bee's nature, and his son's mother wrongly sulks with her. Kuruntokai 8: the other woman says the man boasts in her house but at home moves like a mirror image to whatever his son's mother wants.
teaches: Both courtesans name the wife only as his son's mother, but one says he roves like a bee and the other that he obeys his wife like a puppet, so together they show the other woman claiming no hold on him at all: he belongs to every flower and, at home, to the mother of his son.

note: Both set a newly calved buffalo cow beside her calf in the marutham town: in Ainkurunuru 92 the suitor names it as he promises to come for the girl, in Kuruntokai 181 the wife names the same cow, grazing near the calf the ploughman tied, as she speaks of matrons worn by the great house's duties.
teaches: The suitor's emblem of the home he offers becomes, in the wife's mouth, the emblem of the home that has used her up, so the one buffalo image measures how courtship's promise of motherhood reads after years of karpu.

note: Kuruntokai 2 has the man ask the bee whether any flower it knows is more fragrant than the girl's hair; Ainkurunuru 93 shows bees, already fed full in many groves, coming to hum at her flowered crown.
teaches: What Kuruntokai 2 leaves as a question to the bee, Ainkurunuru 93 answers from the bee's own conduct, since a bee sated on every grove that still seeks her hair has given the verdict the lover asked for.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 93 line 3 is hard to construe (marker flag).

note: Both liken the marutham bull buffalo to field warriors (மள்ளர் அன்ன, மள்ளரின்): in Ainkurunuru 94 it rests with its mate in the shaded pool of the girl's father's fields, in Natrinai 260 it leaves the lotus it is tired of and sleeps alone on the sand, in the wife's refusal of the lord.
teaches: The same warrior-like bull stands for the husband to come when it stays beside its mate and for the husband who strays when it wanders off sated, so the image's sense in marutham is fixed by whether the beast keeps to its partner, not by its strength.

note: Both open on a buffalo that breaks its tether (கயிறுபரிந்து; நோன் தளை பரிந்து) and grazes the town's crops; Akananuru 46 anchors the image in a second marriage over sixteen lines, Ainkurunuru 95 only in 'he gave us a hard sickness even by day'.
teaches: That a four-line poem can rest the whole charge on the rope-breaking buffalo, with no wedding named, shows the image was already a fixed sign of the straying lord, which the longer Akananuru poem spells out rather than invents.

note: Ainkurunuru 98 has the friend tell the lover that the girl's parents guard her more strictly than she guards herself; Kural 57 asks what use guarding a woman by confinement is, since the guard of her own steadfastness is the best.
teaches: The Kural's rule ranks a woman's own guard above confinement, but the Sangam friend relies on the confinement exactly because in courtship the girl's own guard has already given way, so the household's watch the couplet finds useless is what turns a lover into a husband.

note: Both say the woman is the cure of the love sickness: Kural 1102 says every other illness has a different cure but hers is cured by herself; Ainkurunuru 99 says the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for his sickness.
teaches: The couplet's paradox that the cause is the cure is put by the Sangam poem as something that has already happened (ஆகிய), placing the claim after the first meeting, which is where the Kural sets it too, under the joy of union.

note: Natrinai 80 has the man, kept away, say there is no medicine but the broad-shouldered girl for his sickness; Ainkurunuru 99 has him say the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for it.
teaches: The one formula of the girl as the only medicine marks the two ends of courtship, a remedy denied while the friend keeps him off in Natrinai 80 and a remedy received in Ainkurunuru 99, so the tense of the line tells where in the affair the man stands.

note: Both make the cause of love-sickness its cure; in Kural 1102 the man says the girl is the medicine for the sickness she gives, in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother the lord's chariot is the medicine for the sickness the girl's eyes caught.
teaches: Valluvar states the paradox as the lover's private wonder, while the Sangam friend uses the same paradox as evidence before the mother, so the idea that only the beloved can cure love began as an argument for marriage before it was a maxim of delight.

note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs inwardly that the velan's rite was wasted when her lover, the true cure, came by night; in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother outright that the coming chariot is the cure.
teaches: Held together, the two show the same diagnosis moving from the girl's secret mockery of the mother's remedy to the friend's open correction of it, which is the step the disclosure to the mother exists to take.

note: In Natrinai 145 the friend tells the girl that the unjust mother suspects them and still the chariot bell comes softly down their street at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 102 the friend tells the mother herself that the chariot bell rings sweetly to end the girl's grief.
teaches: The chariot bell is the sound of stealth to be hidden from a suspicious mother in one poem and the sound announced to that mother as relief in the other, so the pair shows the disclosure changing the meaning of the lover's signal from danger to remedy.

note: In Akananuru 156 the mother, not knowing the cause, weeps and offers toddy and a goat to the god of the ford while the girl's gem-dark skin turns gold; in Ainkurunuru 105 the friend tells the mother that the girl's brow has gone more golden than gold since the lord came.
teaches: The golden pallor that sends the mother to the god in the Akananuru is given its human cause in the Ainkurunuru, so reading them together shows that the friend's disclosure is the answer to the mother's misdirected rite.

note: In Natrinai 61 the mother asks the sleepless girl 'don't you sleep, my little one?' and the girl keeps the reason in her heart; in Ainkurunuru 107 the friend tells the mother that the girl does not sleep whenever she hears the waves.
teaches: The question the girl will not answer in the Natrinai is answered for her by the friend in the Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend speaking the very secret the girl's modesty withholds from the mother.

note: Both open on எந்தோள் துறந்த and ask எவன்கொல்: 108 sets the abandoned shoulders against the shoulders he desired, 109 against the many days of his grace.
teaches: Read as a pair, the near-identical poems move the friend's charge from the body he wanted to the time he spent, so the decade builds the case against the lord in two steps, desire then history, before the mother.

note: In Kural 1130 the woman says he lives in her heart while this town (இவ் வூர்) says he is loveless and far; in Ainkurunuru 110 the friend says we call him ours while this town (இவ்வூர்) says otherwise, and asks fate to make it so.
teaches: Both set the lovers' word against the town's, but Valluvar's woman rests in her inner certainty while the Sangam friend turns to fate to make the bond public, so the couplet's private comfort appears in the older poem as a demand for marriage.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 110 line 5 was repaired and the marker flagged its sense.

note: In Kural 1209 the woman's life fails as she dwells on the lack of grace of one who said they were not apart; in Ainkurunuru 109 the friend asks what the many days of his grace were worth now that he has left.
teaches: Valluvar turns the memory of past grace into a slow inward death, while the Sangam friend turns it into a reproach spoken to the mother, so the same memory serves as private lament in the couplet and as public evidence in the decade.

note: Ainkurunuru 111 says she cannot live parted because she cannot do hard penance (அருந்தவம் முயறல் ஆற்றாதேமே); Kuruntokai 344 says those who see their lovers return must have done penance (நோற்றோர் மன்ற).
teaches: In one poem penance is the endurance a woman would need to survive separation, in the other the merit that earns the lover's return, so Sangam akam uses tapas both as a power to bear absence and as the price of its ending.

note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Ainkurunuru 111's woman says she is no performer of hard penance and so could not live apart from him.
teaches: The heroine's disclaimer assumes exactly the Kural's definition of penance as the bearing of suffering, so the pair shows that the endurance of separation was already counted as an ascetic feat, and that the lover's refusal of it is a refusal of tapas.

note: Both are the woman's own words: Kural 1257 says she knows nothing called modesty when the beloved does what love wants; Ainkurunuru 112 tells her modest heart they have forgotten, as they wait to see him come.
teaches: The Kural's general claim that shame vanishes before love is shown in the poem as a single moment, the heroine speaking to the heart that owns modesty just as she gives it up to watch him arrive.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 112 line 4 was repaired from a damaged reading.

note: Both pair the town's gossip with the mother's word: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and mother's words water to this sickness; in Ainkurunuru 113 the town names her the lord's woman, mother calls her, and she says it is only a fever (வெம்மை).
teaches: The Kural calls the love a sickness that gossip and the mother feed, and the poem shows the girl turning that very likeness into her alibi, naming the fever and hiding its cause, so the couplet's metaphor began as the lover's cover story.

note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.
audit_text_issue: 116 line 4 is uncertain. | Ainkurunuru 116 line 4 is obscure (repeated காலை). | line 4 repeated காலை is uncertain

note: Kural 1235 has the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel man (கொடியார் கொடுமை); in Ainkurunuru 117 the woman says it is cruel (கொடிதே) that beauty comes to this in those who do not forget him.
teaches: The friend in the Kural lays the cruelty on the man, while the heroine in the poem lays it on the condition of loving him, so the same lost beauty is a charge against him from outside and a lament without an accused from within.

note: Kural 1284: she went to sulk, but her heart forgot it and went to unite; Ainkurunuru 118: she went meaning to rage at the unjust man and hold him back, but thought again, relented and came away.
teaches: Both women set out angry and lose the anger on the way, but the Kural's anger turns into union while the Sangam heroine's turns into retreat, so a failed quarrel need not end in an embrace: it can end in pity and silence.

note: Kural 1265 wishes to see the கொண்கன் with full eyes so that the pallor of her soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) may leave; Ainkurunuru 120 reports that her soft shoulders (மெல் தோளே) have become beautiful because the lord has come.
teaches: The Kural states as a hope that the sight of the shore lord will cure the shoulders, and the Ainkurunuru records the cure as done, so the couplet's optative has an older poem in which the wish was already fulfilled.

note: Both answer a husband who denies the other woman with the same verb, கண்டிகும் (we saw): Natrinai 20's heroine describes a woman leaving his bed with crushed garland and loosened hair, Ainkurunuru 121's friend a girl leaping into the sea with her garland soaked.
teaches: The one retort to a denial can be built two opposite ways, by showing the rival as a spent lover whose body carries his marks or as a child at play, so the 'we saw her' formula's sting lies in how the witness chooses to portray the woman, not in the seeing.

note: In Natrinai 30 the friend tells the denying husband கண்டனென் ... கண்டு எவன்செய்கோ, I saw, and what can I do having seen; in Ainkurunuru 122 the friend's having seen becomes a mocking portrait of a girl asking a heron for her jewel.
teaches: Natrinai 30 admits that the friend's witness gives her no power over the husband, and the Ainkurunuru decade shows what she does with that powerless witness instead: she turns it into ridicule, the one weapon left to a go-between who cannot compel.
audit_text_issue: Ain 122 line 3 வினைவுவோளே gives no sense as written; read வினவுவோளே.

note: Purananuru 243's old man remembers garlanding a doll of packed sand and leaping into deep water as the untaught youth he has lost; Ainkurunuru 124 shows a girl with a sand doll punishing the sea that took it.
teaches: The same shore games of sand dolls and leaps into water are, in the puram elegy, the innocence age mourns, and in the akam barb, the proof that a man has taken up with a child, so the scene of youth carries nostalgia or contempt according to who recalls it and for what end.

note: Both have the wife's side describe the rival by her dress: in Natrinai 170 the girl in a leaf skirt who comes alone to the festival is a danger the wives must rise against, while in Ainkurunuru 127 the garland across budding breasts marks her as a child of no account.
teaches: On a defensible reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what a young rival's youth means, a strength that may overwhelm the household or a weakness that makes her laughable, showing that the wife's party had no settled verdict on the young courtesan and chose the one their moment needed.

note: In Ainkurunuru 131 the woman says the lord's friendship is good only while no gossip rises in the town; in Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is the manure on which her love-sickness grows.
teaches: Valluvar's woman turns the gossip into nourishment for her love, while the Sangam woman, speaking to the man's bard, treats the same gossip as the limit the bond cannot outlive, so the couplet's paradox rewrites a fear the older poem left plain.

note: 131 makes the friendship good only so long as gossip does not rise; 132 says the town has now made gossip of the lord's very grace.
teaches: Read in sequence the decade's first two poems pass from the condition to its breach: the gossip that 131 named as the bond's limit has arisen in 132, and it has risen not from his neglect but from his kindness.

note: Both have the woman's bangled shoulders lose their beauty when her partner leaves (Kural: துணைநீங்கித் தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்; Ainkurunuru: பிரிந்தெனப் புல்லென்றன என் புரிவளைத் தோளே).
teaches: The couplet describes the wasted shoulders as a fact, while the poem puts them as a helpless question to the absent man's own bard, so the same bodily sign becomes in the older poem a complaint lodged with his side of the household.

note: In Kural 1265 the woman wishes to see her husband (கொண்கனை) and says the pallor of her shoulders will then leave; in Ainkurunuru 134 she tells the bard her dark-gold beauty has come back with the chariot of the shore lord (கொண்க).
teaches: Valluvar states as a wish that only the sight of the husband will cure the pallor; the Sangam poem shows the cure already happened, the beauty arriving in his chariot, so the couplet's claim that news is not enough rests on the older scene of the bodily return.

note: 134 says the woman's beauty came back by itself with the shore lord; 137 asks whether the women who loved the lord ever get back their former beauty, implying they do not.
teaches: Within one decade the same speaker holds both that beauty returns with the lord and that those who loved him never regain it, so the decade shows the restored beauty of 134 as one turn of a cycle that 137 suspects will not last.

note: Both refuse the bard who comes with the shore lord's words: Natrinai 167 says his humble words will not remove the pallor of the bangled girl, Ainkurunuru 136 calls him shameless for pouring out words for the lord who made her bangles slip.
teaches: The Natrinai friend grants the bard's skill and denies only its effect, while the Ainkurunuru woman denies him decency itself, so set together they show the refusal of the go-between ranging from courtesy to contempt within the same neythal situation.

note: 136 (நாணிலை மன்ற பாண) blames the bard for spilling words for the lord; 138 (பண்பிலை மன்ற பாண) blames him for harsh words in the town and for not bringing the lord.
teaches: The paired rebukes show the bard condemned from both sides, for speaking on the lord's behalf and for failing to deliver the lord, so what the woman rejects is his offering words where only the man's presence would do.

note: In Akananuru 146 the wife, refusing the bard, says the woman who trusts the deceiving philanderer's word (மாயப் பரத்தன் வாய்மொழி) will lose her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 139 she tells the lord that his bard ruins good women's beauty more than he does.
teaches: The longer poem lays the ruin of beauty on the husband's own lying word, the short one shifts it to the bard who carries that word, so the pair shows the go-between counted as an agent of the harm and not merely its messenger.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 139 prints as 2 lines; line 1 looks like two lines run together.

note: In both the bard who came for the shore lord is told to report what he has seen of the woman: Natrinai 291 கண்டாங்கு உரையாய், Ainkurunuru 140 காண்மதி பாண நீ உரைத்தற்கு உரியை.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 140 names the message only as the state of her slipped bangles, while Natrinai 291 fills the same eyewitness report with a puram image of cattle raided at night, so the pair shows the three-line convention of the bard as witness expanded by borrowing from war poetry.

note: In Kural 1157 the woman says her slipping bangles spread the news that the shore lord (துறைவன்) has left her; in Ainkurunuru 140 she asks the bard to tell the lord of the ford (துறைகெழு கொண்கன்) the state of her bangles since he left.
teaches: Valluvar makes the bangles themselves the gossips who publish his departure, while the Sangam woman needs the bard to carry that sign to the man, so the couplet's bangles that speak for themselves compress a scene in which the body's testimony still had to be delivered.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 of Ainkurunuru 140 is a repaired reading.

note: Ainkurunuru 142's heroine resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep; in Kural 1207 the woman says she does not know how to forget and asks what would become of her if she did.
teaches: The Sangam heroine treats not-thinking as a cure she can choose for her sleeplessness, while Valluvar's woman declares forgetting impossible and fatal, so the couplet denies exactly the resolve the older poem lets her voice.

note: Both close on the same line, உள்ளேன் தோழி படீஇயர் என் கண்ணே, after a bird-loud shore; Kuruntokai 243 fills the shore with girls playing at sand houses, Ainkurunuru 142 with birds settling to roost.
teaches: The refusal to think of him was a stock closing formula, and each poet earns it with a different shore picture, the girls' play recalling her past in one and the roosting birds setting her sleeplessness against their rest in the other.

note: The two poems end on the same words, என் மாமைக் கவினே, for the same shore lord: in 144 the beauty has turned pale, in 146 it is surely sweet to him.
teaches: Read together, the decade measures the whole state of the love by one phrase about her complexion, which can stand for neglect or for delight with nothing changed but the verb.

note: In Kural 1188 people say only that she has grown pale and never that he has left; in Ainkurunuru 145 the friend says the shore lord has now taken her pallor away.
teaches: The friend names the man as the one who can remove the pallor, which makes him its cause, so the Sangam poem supplies the very attribution that the couplet's woman complains no one makes.

note: In Natrinai 359 the hill lord's gift of a leaf skirt is a danger, since wearing it will alarm the mother; in Ainkurunuru 147 the shore lord gives his country as the price of the leaf skirt.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the leaf skirt moving from a secret courting gift that cannot be worn openly to the token for which a bride price is paid, so the same object marks both ends of secret love.

note: Both are spoken to the man about to leave, by the friend on one reading of the Kural: Ainkurunuru 149 asks him not to become able to go after causing her affliction, Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return only to those who will survive it.
teaches: The Sangam friend still appeals to the man's character, asking him not to be the kind who can leave, whereas the couplet has given up persuasion and answers his promise with the threat of her death.

note: Ainkurunuru 150's heroine calls the shore lord bitter in union (புணர்வின் இன்னான்) and hard to unite with; in Kural 1152 the woman says union now holds pain for fear of parting.
teaches: Valluvar gives the reason the Sangam poem leaves implicit, that union turns bitter because parting is foreseen, while the poem's pun of the ever-embracing wave (புணரி) shows what that bitterness is measured against.

note: Both are the woman speaking of her heart against the man in oodal: the couplet says the heart's anger is false because it yields at the sight of him; Ainkurunuru 151 grants that the heart has already melted and refuses all the same.
teaches: The couplet treats a heart that yields as proof the quarrel was never real, while the poem keeps the refusal standing after the heart has gone over, so the Sangam woman's oodal is a decision of will against her own feeling rather than a mood that the man's presence dissolves.

note: Ainkurunuru 154's woman can only call the town a liar and ask what she can do; in Kuruntokai 34 the friend says the town would not believe their denials (மறுப்பத் தேறலர்) and is silenced only by the sweet news that the lord will marry her.
teaches: Read together they show that in the neythal love story gossip cannot be ended by calling it false, since the town does not believe denials, and the only cure the poets allow is marriage, which turns the lying town into one that rejoices.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 154 sense flagged uncertain by the marker. | ainkurunuru:154 பொய்க்கும் is ambiguous (the town lies, or the man will prove false) | AK154 flagged uncertain

note: Ainkurunuru 159's friend demands that the lord give back her friend's beauty and go, insisting she is not begging; Kuruntokai 349's heroine refuses her friend's proposal to take back their beauty, saying that asking for it back is like demanding the return of what was given to those who begged, and worse than losing life.
teaches: On a defensible reading the two make incompatible claims about the demand 'give back her beauty', a just reclaiming of what was taken or a shameful asking-back of a gift, which shows the formula belonged to the friend's voice and that the heroine could reject it as beneath her.

note: Both are Ammuvanar's and end on the same demand, தந்தனை சென்மோ ... நலனே and நலம் தந்து சென்மே; Natrinai 395's colophon says the friend uses it to press the lover to marry.
teaches: The same poet's colophoned use of the formula supplies the occasion that this decade's colophons leave out, so 159's demand for the beauty back can be read as a push to marriage (வரைவு கடாயது) rather than a farewell.

note: Same situation and speaker: the woman of the shore says the lord of the ford (துறைவன்) has left her and her bangles slip from her forearm; the Kural keeps the Ainkurunuru's words துறைவன், துற, முன்கை, இறை and வளை.
teaches: The couplet lifts a neythal formula whole, but gives the bangles a new office: in the Ainkurunuru they imitate his desertion, in the Kural they broadcast it like gossip, so the later poet turned the body from mirror of the man into witness to the town.

note: The Kural tells friends to read a painful act of an old friend as folly or deep intimacy; the heroine of 167 calls the man who promised grace and gave none an old companion, தொல் கேள்.
teaches: The heroine applies the ethics book's rule of old friendship inside love, and the poem shows its cost: the same rule that keeps a long bond alive lets a broken promise go unanswered, so the wronged side carries the whole duty of forbearance.

note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why her daughter will not drink milk (பாலும் உண்ணாள்) and has paled; in 168 the friend tells the man that the girl will drink milk again if he shows grace.
teaches: Refusing milk is a fixed sign of secret love that the friend can turn two ways: toward the household, as the symptom she explains in disclosing the affair, and toward the lover, as the cure only he can give, so one sign drives both halves of the push toward marriage.

note: On the plain reading the claims are incompatible: in 170 the woman holds up her pallid eyes as evidence against the friend's word that he is good, while in Kural 1190 she would rather be called pallid than have the friend blame his unkindness.
teaches: Read together, the two show the heroine taking the side opposite to whoever speaks to her, so her pallor is not a fixed verdict on the man but an argument she turns against his praise or for his defence as the friend's stance requires.

note: In both the woman has accepted the man's part with her mind, in Kural 1181 by consenting to his absence, in 169 by knowing the truth of his heart, and still the pallor spreads on her.
teaches: The couplet makes her consent the reason she cannot complain of her pallor, and the Ainkurunuru adds that even trust in his heart does not stop it, so pallor in this tradition is a bodily fact beyond the will rather than a charge against the man.

note: Both set a wing-worn heron at the ford of Thondi: Kuruntokai 128's பறைதபு நாரை on the eastern sea longs in vain for the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, as the man's heart longs for a distant girl; Ainkurunuru 180's பறைதபு முதுகுருகு sits fed on the rich fish the netters bring.
teaches: The flightless heron of Thondi is hopeless longing when it must reach the fish itself and secure dependence when the fishermen bring the fish to it, so the friend's version answers the lover's lament: the helpless are fed only when someone provides, which is what she asks the man to do by marrying.

note: Both liken the girl to Kuttuvan's Thondi: in Ainkurunuru 178 the courting man calls her like Thondi of Kuttuvan of the just sceptre, while in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that likeness and turned pale while he delays marriage.
teaches: The Thondi likeness is the lover's praise in courtship and becomes the heroine's own measure of loss when marriage is delayed, so the beauty the man praises to win her is the very thing his delay spends, and the friend of 179 and 180 is right to press him.

note: Both have the man name the girl's power with the word அணங்கு: in Kural 1081 he cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Ainkurunuru 173 her fragrant hair is the அணங்கு and those it seizes lose their sleep.
teaches: The Kural leaves the smitten man's question open, and the Sangam poem answers it not by settling what she is but by the symptom, sleepless nights and a cutting pain, so that in the tradition the afflicting goddess is known by what she does to the one who sees her.

note: Both have the man in secret love say the girl keeps his eyes from sleep at night: Ainkurunuru 172 likens his wakefulness to the never-resting waves of Thondi; Kural 1136 has him, sleepless at midnight, think of riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 172 stops at the sleepless night and gives it the image of the restless sea, while the Kural shows where that night leads, to the threat of the madal, so the pair marks sleeplessness as the stage of love just before shame is given up.

note: Kural 1150 says the town raises the very talk we want and the lover will grant (நல்குவர்) if he wishes; Ainkurunuru 181 says if the shore lord grants (நல்கின்), this clamouring town will be sweet to live in.
teaches: The Kural names the town's clamour as a lever that can push the lover to grant marriage, and the Ainkurunuru poem shows the far side of that lever: once he grants, the same noise becomes the festive kuravai of a town she can live in happily, so gossip and celebration are one sound judged before and after his word.

note: In Akananuru 272 the mother, seeing the garlanded lover at night, takes him for Murugu and worships; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend points to a garlanded chest and says he is no god of power.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the misreading the friend's disclosure has to undo: the household's habit of turning a garlanded young man into a god, which in Akananuru 272 leads to worship and in Ainkurunuru 182 is corrected by naming the garland as a shore man's hand-woven wreath.

note: In Natrinai 155 the hero on the neythal shore asks the girl whether she is a goddess of the sea; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend says the one who struck the girl at the great ford is no god.
teaches: The belief that a beloved seen at the shore must be a divine power runs both ways, the man thinking her a sea goddess and the household thinking her stricken by a god, and in both the cure of the error is the same: the striker turns out to be a human lover who must be named.

note: Kural 1225's woman asks what good she has done the morning and what wrong the evening, so morning is the friendly hour; Ainkurunuru 183 ends that even if morning comes there is no one to clear her pain.
teaches: The Kural's separated woman still has a kind hour in the morning, while the Ainkurunuru heroine denies even that, so the pair shows two degrees of the same grief: one that rises and falls with the day, and one that the day's turn no longer touches.

note: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and blooms at evening; in Ainkurunuru 183 evening arrives early in the harsh day while the neythal of the backwater closes.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for evening pain gains a real flower in the Sangam poem, and the two move in opposite directions: as the shore's neythal closes at evening, the sickness opens, so the landscape's hour of rest is the lover's hour of full bloom of pain.

note: Kuruntokai 3's woman says her love for the hill man is larger than the earth, higher than the sky and deeper than the sea; Ainkurunuru 184's says the friendship with the man whose town the sea adorns is greater than the sea.
teaches: Each heroine measures love against her own lover's world: the hill woman needs the whole cosmos, while the shore woman takes the one thing that crowns his town and sets it below their bond, so the boast of measureless love takes its scale from the land of the man loved.

note: Ainkurunuru 185's man is taken by the Korkai girl's teeth bright as pearls; in Akananuru 27 the friend says the girl's red mouth with teeth like Korkai pearls may not hold the man who means to leave for wealth.
teaches: The pearl-toothed mouth of Korkai is what draws the man at first sight in Ainkurunuru 185 and what the friend in Akananuru 27 fears is not enough to keep him, so the same harbour formula marks both the start of the beauty's power and its limit against the call of wealth.

note: In Akananuru 20 the friend says mother, on the word of spiteful women, has confined the girl because a chariot circles the great ford day and night; in Ainkurunuru 186 the friend quotes mother herself saying a chariot comes often to this ford, so do not go.
teaches: In the long poem the confinement rests on the town's report, in the short one on the mother's own sight of the chariot, so the friend's warning to the lover can come in two strengths, and the second leaves him no excuse that it is only gossip.

note: Ainkurunuru 188's man compares his love's eyes to the neythal blooming at dawn at Korkai's great ford; in Natrinai 23 the friend says the girl's eyes have faded like the small-leaved neythal of Korkai's harbour.
teaches: The same Korkai neythal serves for the eyes in bloom when the lover praises them and for the eyes faded when the friend presses for marriage, so the flower's daily opening and closing lets one image carry both the courtship's first wonder and its later cost.

note: In 189 the lord of the gentle shore has come and her eyes have become good; in 190 the same மெல்லம் புலம்பன் is the one who made her many-petalled eyes weep.
teaches: Placed side by side in the decade with the same name for the man, the two poems make the heroine's eyes a gauge wholly in his hands, healed by his coming and wet by his absence, and the neythal image follows them, dusted with gold in one and cut down in the other.

note: In 170 a small white gull tears the neythal of the backwater, and the friend is asked why the eyes of one with such a good man grow pale; in 190 reapers cut down the neythal flower while harvesting white paddy, and the man has made her eyes weep.
teaches: Both hide the spoiled eyes in a destroyed neythal, but the destroyers differ: the gull tears it to feed, the reapers fell it only because it stands among the grain they want, so the decade offers two kinds of blame, appetite and indifference, for the same harm.

note: Kural 1171's woman asks why her eyes weep when it was they who showed him to her; Ainkurunuru 190's woman says the lord of the shore surely is the one who made her eyes weep.
teaches: For the same tears the Kural's woman blames her own eyes for having looked, while the Ainkurunuru woman blames the man with an emphatic மன்ற, so the pair shows the two directions in which the abandoned lover can turn the fault, inward on her own seeing or outward on him.

note: The Kural man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Ainkurunuru man knows she is a shore girl and says she is harder to win than the mountain nymphs (வரையர மகளிரின் அரியள்).
teaches: The likeness to a goddess can carry two different fears: in the couplet it is bewilderment at what she is, in the shore poem it is despair of reaching her, so the divine comparison in akam measures distance as often as beauty.

note: Both have the woman of the shore say her bangles registered the lord's leaving (தணந்தமை ... உணர்ந்த வளை; பிரிந்தென நெகிழ்ந்தன); Ainkurunuru 192 adds that they have grown tight again (வீங்கின).
teaches: The Kural treats the bangle only as an early witness of separation, while the Ainkurunuru poem shows it registering his return as well, so the convention is a two-way gauge of the man's presence and not merely a sign of wasting.

note: Natrinai 282's friend, the hero within hearing, describes the slipping bangles, faded brow and the old diviner misreading the illness; Ainkurunuru 194's friend tells the hero directly that the mother has suspected a wrong cause (கொன் ஒன்று கடுத்தனள்).
teaches: Set beside Natrinai's full scene of pebbles and diviner, the Ainkurunuru friend's two words show the misread illness was familiar enough to be invoked in a half-line, and that in both its use is the same: to press the man to marry before a wrong cure exposes the girl.

note: Both men say the bangled girl has given them suffering, with the verb of a gift (துயரம் நல்கி; தந்தாள் ... துயர்); in the Kural the gift is the palmyra horse and the evening's pain, in Ainkurunuru 195 a grief that will not pass and lost sleep.
teaches: Read together they show the stages of the same plea to the friend: the Ainkurunuru man stops at sleeplessness, and the couplet shows where his complaint goes next if no one answers it, to the threat of riding the palmyra horse.

note: In Akananuru 380 the shore lord leaves his chariot far off and asks the girls the name of their town; in Ainkurunuru 198 the tall-shouldered man stands asking about the small ford where girls play.
teaches: The question about a ford or a town is the fixed first move of the shore courtship: Ainkurunuru 198 catches it as it is asked, and Akananuru 380 shows the friend later reading the same pretext as the start of a suit that ends in his shame and her consent.

note: In the Kural the slipping bangles spread the news (தூற்றா) that the lord of the shore has left; in Ainkurunuru 199 the woman names him by the bangles he loosened and asks to climb the high dune to gaze at his land.
teaches: The couplet's woman fears her bangles will publish the loss to the town, while the Ainkurunuru woman makes the loss her name for him and climbs where all can see her looking, so the same token can be suffered as exposure or claimed in the open.

note: In Natrinai 359 the friend says the hill lord gave them a leaf skirt (உடுக்கும் தழை) that they dare not wear for fear of the mother nor return for fear of hurting him; in Ainkurunuru 201 the leaves have become their skirts (எமக்கும் தழையாயின) and the friend asks the mother what tree on his slope they come from.
teaches: The leaf skirt that in Natrinai is a gift too dangerous to wear before the mother becomes in the Ainkurunuru the very thing the friend shows her, so the pair traces one courtship token from the secret it endangers to the disclosure it carries.

note: In Natrinai 53 the mother herself says the new stream water coming down from the high hill is medicine and sends the girl to drink and bathe in it; in Ainkurunuru 203 the friend tells the mother that the muddy water of his land is sweeter than their honeyed milk.
teaches: The mother who prescribes the water of the far hill without knowing whose hill it is, and the friend who tells her that the water of his land is sweeter than home's milk, together show that in kurinji the lover's water stands for the lover, so the disclosure turns the mother's innocent remedy into a confession.

note: In Kuruntokai 356 the foster mother grieves that the girl who refused milk mixed with puffed rice must now gulp scalding muddy water (கலுழி) by a dried spring; in Ainkurunuru 203 the girl's side says the muddy water (கலிழி) of his land is sweeter than honeyed milk.
teaches: The two poems make opposite claims about the same exchange of home's milk for the forest's muddy water, a pitiable loss to the foster mother and a gain to the girl's side, which shows that the pathos of the elopement poems is the mother's view and not the girl's.

note: In Akananuru 272 the mother sees the night visitor wet from the hill, garlanded with koothalam, and takes him for Murugu, scattering millet in worship; in Ainkurunuru 206 the friend shows the mother a man wet with spray and dew and likens him to a watchman of the rainy hill.
teaches: Where the mother left to herself reads the drenched visitor from the hill as a god, the friend who discloses the love names him as a man like their own field watchmen, so the disclosure works by bringing the stranger down from the sacred to the familiar.

note: In Akananuru 378 the deserted girl says she lives only because the peak of his hill, crowned with a waterfall, is in sight (வான்தோய் சிமையம் தோன்றலானே); in Ainkurunuru 209 she says she cannot forget him because his cloud-crowned hill never stops appearing (தோன்றல் அனாது).
teaches: The same visible peak is what keeps the girl alive in the Akananuru and what defeats any demand that she forget in the Ainkurunuru, so together they show the hill working as a bond that neither absence nor counsel can loosen.

note: In Kuruntokai 367 the friend tells the girl that her shoulders may regain their beauty now that his hill with its cool boulders (துறுகல்) shows after the rain; in Ainkurunuru 210 the friend tells the mother the girl's sickness may abate if she climbs their boulder (துறுகல்) and looks at his hill.
teaches: The sight of his hill, offered privately as comfort to the girl in the Kuruntokai, becomes in the Ainkurunuru a cure the friend asks the mother to allow, so the pair shows a consolation turned into an open request that names its source.

note: In 208 the girl's eyes fill with tears whenever his mountain is hidden; in 210 the friend says her sickness may abate if she stands looking at his hill.
teaches: Read together the two poems make the girl's state a function of the hill's visibility, tears when it is hidden and healing when it is seen, which is the argument the friend needs before the mother for letting the girl climb and look.

note: Both open on the same refrain to the mother and point to the lover's mount: in the neythal decade the shore lord's chariot is the medicine for the girl's sickness, in the kurinji decade the hill lord's horses have tufted heads like the town's Brahmin boy.
teaches: The two disclosure decades present the lover's mount to the mother as evidence in opposite tones, the neythal friend solemnly as a cure and the kurinji friend comically through a homely likeness, so the same act of disclosure could be made by gravity or by disarming laughter.

note: Ainkurunuru 212: the girl asks why they should be parted from a man of virtue (அறவன்). Kural 1154: the woman asks whether those who trusted the assurances of the one who said 'do not fear' are at fault if he leaves.
teaches: The girl rests her whole security on the man's being virtuous, while the Kural imagines that very assurer leaving and moves the blame onto him, so the pair shows that in secret love the only guarantee was his character and the Kural tests it to the point of failure.

note: Ainkurunuru 213: the girl says she can live only if he comes. Kural 1263: the wife says she still lives on the longing for her husband's return from war.
teaches: For the wife the longing for return is already enough to keep her alive, while the unmarried girl says life itself waits on his coming, so the pair grades the same dependence: hope sustains in marriage, only presence sustains in secret love.

note: Ainkurunuru 215: at evening the bee hums sweeter than the musicians' flute, and those who leave then will do worse. Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon.
teaches: The Kural makes the evening flute itself the weapon, while the Ainkurunuru keeps the music sweet and turns its sweetness into the measure of the leaver's cruelty, so together they show evening music wounding the parted woman not by harshness but by sweetness heard alone.

note: Ainkurunuru 217: the friend asks why the girl pales even though the man keeps coming. Kural 1187: the woman says pallor came on her thickly the moment she turned a little in his embrace.
teaches: The friend's puzzle, pallor despite his visits, finds its answer in the Kural's hyperbole that the least gap in union breeds pallor, so the pair shows that secret visits, each ending in parting, feed the pallor rather than cure it.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 is a repaired reading.

note: Ainkurunuru 218: the girl's eyes throb and her bangles tighten, and she asks if he will come. Akananuru 141: answering the anxious friend, the wife says her dreams are sweet and the house birds give good signs, so may he come for the festival.
teaches: The Akananuru wife reads hope in dreams and household birds while the Ainkurunuru girl reads it in her own eyes and bangles, so the pair shows the omen-reading of akam reaching from the house to the body, and always voiced by the one who waits, against the friend's fear.

note: Ainkurunuru 218: throbbing eyes and tightening bangles promise his coming. Kural 1203: a sneeze that starts and dies away makes the woman fear he began to think of her and stopped.
teaches: Both women read the absent man in involuntary signs of their own bodies, but the girl's signs come to completion and promise him while the Kural's sneeze aborts and suggests his forgetting, so the pair shows the same bodily sign-language turned to hope or doubt.

note: Ainkurunuru 219: the friend asks why the girl's forehead pales since the hill man went away. Kural 1188: the woman complains that people say she has grown pale, and no one says that he left her.
teaches: The friend's question names the man's leaving together with the pallor, which is exactly the acknowledgement the Kural's woman says the world withholds, so the pair shows the friend as the one voice that ties the girl's pallor to the man who caused it.

note: Kural 1156 says that a man who can speak of leaving leaves no hope; Ainkurunuru 221 shows the heroine's beauty fading at the quoted word செல்வல், before any journey begins.
teaches: The couplet judges the announcement as a moral sign of hardness, while the poem shows it working on the body at once, so together they make the spoken intention, not the absence, the first wound of parting in Tamil love poetry.

note: In Ainkurunuru 224 the heroine says bathing in the falls with them has become hard for him; in Akananuru 38 the friend imagines him finding the pool clear because the girls no longer leap in and bathe there.
teaches: The same lost bathing in the hill pool is blamed on his growing distance by the heroine and traced by the friend to the girls' own absence, so the end of shared play reads as neglect from inside the house and as confinement from the friend's wider view.
audit_text_issue: 38 line 15 (ஐ.தேங்கு) looks corrupt. | Akananuru 38 line 15 (ஐ.தேங்கு) looks corrupt.

note: Kural 1188 says people call her pale but no one says he left her; Ainkurunuru 225 asks whether the lover himself does not perceive the paling of her brow.
teaches: Held together they show the pallor seen by the whole town yet unread by the one man it concerns, so the symptom that exposes her to gossip fails at the only task she wants of it, reaching him.

note: Both heroines face a lover who swore assurances to the friend and stays apart while her beauty fades; Natrinai 358's heroine goes to pray that the oath's god not harm him, Ainkurunuru 227's asks the friend whether she has released him from it.
