teaches: An oath sworn before the friend binds the lover through a god's punishment, so the heroine is caught between wanting it held and fearing what holding it would do to him, and the two poems show the two halves of that bind.

note: Kural 1155 asks the friend to prevent the departure of the man fit for her, since union is hard once he goes; Ainkurunuru 228 asks what becomes of their life if he leaves without having pleaded for favour.
teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: in secret love the man's suit must pass through the friend, so the heroine's plea that the friend stop his leaving is a plea that she accept his pleading.

note: Kural 1265 says the pallor of her shoulders will leave once she has seen her husband her eyes' fill; in Ainkurunuru 229 the friend sees the brow's golden beauty returned and asks whether he came in the night.
teaches: The couplet makes the lover's presence the cure for pallor, and the poem turns that rule into a means of detection, so the cure that the heroine longs for is also what betrays her secret meeting to the friend.

note: In Natrinai 386 the friend recalls the hill-lord coming humbly with the word வதுவை so that the village shone; in Ainkurunuru 230 the friend announces the wedding for the hill-lord who once guarded millet with them and wasted the heroine's beauty.
teaches: Both friends mark the wedding as the end of kalavu, but one remembers the suitor's humility and the other his damage, so the go-between's announcement of marriage could be told as the lover's submission or as payment of what he owed.

note: Kural 1213's woman says she lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; in Ainkurunuru 234 the friend tells the lover that the girl sees his chest in dreams and not awake, and that is why she pales.
teaches: The same split between dream and waking presence is the woman's own comfort in the Kural and the friend's evidence of harm in the Sangam poem, so the couplet's consolation is shown to be what an onlooker reads as wasting, and the dream becomes a lever for marriage rather than a way to live.

note: Both close on எழுகமோ, shall we rise; 235 sets it against holding him and saying 'we will not part', 236 gives the destination, நும்மூர்ச் செல்கம், we will go to your town.
teaches: Read alone, 235's 'shall we rise' could mean only leaving the tryst; the next poem fixes it as setting out for his town and names what forced the choice, the mother's knowing and the gossip, so the decade moves from weighing elopement to proposing it.

note: In both the friend tells the lover that the girl will go with him: in Akananuru 107 because she cannot bear his repeated departures, in Ainkurunuru 236 because the mother knows, gossip has spread and the house is desolate.
teaches: The friend's offer of elopement is made from two opposite pressures, the grief of his going in the Akananuru and exposure at home in the Ainkurunuru, so udanpokku appears in the anthologies as the answer both to separation and to discovery.

note: Ainkurunuru 236's friend says the north wind leaves the good house's tall mansion desolate (நன்மனை நெடுநகர் புலம்புகொள) as a reason to leave; Akananuru 35's mother says the girl left the high-walled good house desolate (நன்னகர் புலம்ப) by going.
teaches: The same desolation of the great house is the cause of the girl's going in the friend's plea and its effect in the mother's lament, so the two speakers each blame the empty house on the other side and the elopement is seen whole only from both.

note: Both are a friend's reproach to the hill lord for his absences in courtship, with a tusker's embrace in the same words (இரும்பிணர் ... தழு): in Akananuru 78 he clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his rough trunk, in Ainkurunuru 239 he clasps a rough boulder, taking it for his mate.
teaches: The one image of a tusker's embrace serves the friend two ways, as the care the man owes the girl when the mate is there and as the blind longing of a beast whose mate is gone, so the reproach can shame the lover either by what the beast does for its mate or by what it suffers without her.

note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the pollen-seeking bee whether any flower is more fragrant than his woman's hair; in Ainkurunuru 240 the friend says bee swarms crowd his chest because it smells of the fragrant girl's hair.
teaches: The scent of her hair that the lover praises in private to the bee is the very thing that betrays the secret union to the friend, so the bees that witness his boast in one poem become the witnesses against him in the other.

note: Ainkurunuru 241 doubts that the velan can know the girl's bond with the hill man; Natrinai 34 tells Murugu himself that he came to the veri house knowing the sickness was not his seizure (நின் அணங்கு அன்மை அறிந்தும்).
teaches: Ainkurunuru blames the rite's error on the diviner's ignorance, while Natrinai charges the god, who knows the truth, with folly for coming anyway, so the pair shows the friend's protest against veri aimed either at the man who performs it or at the deity who accepts it.

note: In both the mother acts out of not knowing (அறியாமையின் / அறிந்தனள் அல்லள்) and calls the rite; Akananuru 98 fears that if the rite fails the secret will become gossip, Ainkurunuru 242 says it is cruel to leave the mother in her grief.
teaches: Akananuru 98 counts the cost of the rite to the girl, the secret turning into gossip, and Ainkurunuru 242 its cost to the mother, a grief spent on a wrong cause, so the case for disclosure in the veri situation rests on two separate harms.

note: Kuruntokai 263 protests to the girl that the mother's offerings to strange gods are no cure and brand her possessed; Ainkurunuru 243 says to the mother herself that she will believe the ignorant diviner.
teaches: The same protest against the rite is spoken between the girls in Kuruntokai and turned on the mother in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend's objection to veri moving from private complaint to the first step of telling the household.

note: In Akananuru 98 the velan sings the god's great name (செல்வன் பெரும்பெயர் ஏத்தி) at the veri ground; in Ainkurunuru 244 the girl says the veri is useless unless the velan sings the hill of her man.
teaches: Akananuru 98 shows what the diviner's song praises in the rite, the god's name, and Ainkurunuru 244 asks for the same song turned to the man's hill, so the girl imagines the only working cure as the rite itself with her lover in the god's place.

note: Both turn on the same line, முருகென மொழியும் ஆயின்: 245 asks whether naming Murugu is a kindness to the girl's afflicter, 247 whether Murugu is the hill man's name.
teaches: The decade gives the one conditional two opposite ironies: in 245 the wrong name shields the man by hiding him, in 247 it names him by accident, so the misdiagnosis is shown as both the secret's cover and its leak.

note: Both set the hill tiger with its mate beside the velan's rite: in Natrinai 322 the tiger lurks to ease its hungry female, in Ainkurunuru 246 it ends its distress by joining her.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the kurinji tiger used as the counter-image to the veri rite: what relieves a creature of the hill, by hunting for its mate or by joining her, is the partner and never the offering.

note: Natrinai 282 says it would be fine indeed (நன்றுமன்) if the old diviner's word could calm the bond; Ainkurunuru 248 says fine indeed (நன்றால் அம்ம) will be her beauty if his beads find the cause.
teaches: The same mock approval of the diviner is aimed in Natrinai at his cure and in Ainkurunuru at his diagnosis, so the friend's ironic நன்று is shown as a set turn of the veri situation that can be pointed at either half of the rite.

note: 241 asks whether the velan can know the hill man's bond; 249 blesses the velan because he does not know the hill man.
teaches: The decade's first poem raises the diviner's ignorance as a doubt and its ninth turns it into a blessing, so across the sequence the friend comes to see his ignorance as the secret's safety and not only as the rite's failure.

note: Akananuru 388 would ask the velan whether his god goes hunting with blood-smeared arrows; Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that Vel, lord of the valli forest, is not the afflicter.
teaches: Akananuru separates god from lover by asking about the lover's hunt, Ainkurunuru by naming the god's own peacock and valli, so together they show the girls answering the rite by setting the two lords side by side in each other's emblems.

note: Both have the man, on seeing the girl, take her for an அணங்கு (Kural: அணங்குகொல்; Ainkurunuru: ஆர் அணங்கினளே).
teaches: Valluvar's man hesitates between goddess, peahen and woman, while the Sangam man has settled the question and pins it on her youth (இளையள் ஆயினும்), so the couplet's doubt is a refinement of an older certainty that a hill girl can be a striking power.
audit_text_issue: 256 lines repaired

note: 255 says the girl's grace resembles the mountain goddesses (வரையர மகளிர்ப் புரையும்); 256 says she herself is a great அணங்கு.
teaches: Two consecutive poems on the same opening line move from likeness to identity, so the decade itself shows a comparison with the hill goddesses hardening into the claim that the girl is one.

note: In both the friend (on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural) speaks to the man who is about to leave, to hold him back.
teaches: The couplet holds the man back with a threat that she will not live, while the Sangam friend holds him back with the girl's worth, a daughter begged from the god, so the pair shows two arguments for the same refusal: her death against her value.

note: In 257 the father worshipped the god and begged for the daughter; in 259 the daughter herself worships the clan god of the hill.
teaches: Read together the two poems pass the rite from father to daughter: the god who gave her in answer to the father's begging now receives her own offering, made when she has a love of her own to pray for.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 259's sense is flagged uncertain.

note: Akananuru 178's friend rejoices that marriage is settled (வரைவு மலிந்து); Ainkurunuru 258's friend says the household has agreed to give her if he weds, yet her grief has not ceased.
teaches: Against the friend's joy in Akananuru 178, Ainkurunuru 258 shows that the household's consent alone ends nothing for the girl, so the akam sequence separates the family's yes from the man's coming as two steps.

note: Akananuru 28 warns that if the girl does not keep scaring parrots from the millet, mother will set others in her place and his chest will be hard to reach (உறற்கு அரிது); Ainkurunuru 260 says the millet has ripened and the girl is hard to win (பெறற்கரிது).
teaches: Akananuru 28 spells out the custom that the Ainkurunuru poem only implies: the girl's freedom lasts exactly as long as the field needs guarding, so 'the millet has ripened' in four lines carries the whole threat of her being kept at home.

note: 258 says the household will give the girl if the lord of the hill weds her; 254 says the wealthy ones have taken her to their hill country.
teaches: Read against 258's conditional promise, 254 is its fulfilment, so within one decade the hill man's daughter passes from being offered to being carried off to the man's country.

note: In Natrinai 386 the great-tempered boar that gorges on the hunters' millet and sleeps unafraid of the tiger frames a man who offers the dread oath and comes to wed; in Ainkurunuru 261 the boar that has grazed the millet and sleeps on the rock slope frames a man the heroine suspects of fearing her father.
teaches: The fearless sleeping boar was a stock frame whose point turns on the man set beside it, matching the bold suitor in Natrinai and shaming the timid one in Ainkurunuru, so the same image can carry praise or an unspoken reproach.

note: Both are spoken by the woman about the pallor that the man's presence will remove: Kural 1265 wishes to see him and says the pallor will then leave; Ainkurunuru 263 says he has come and her beauty has come back.
teaches: The Sangam poem gives as an accomplished fact, in two verbs set side by side, what the couplet can only promise, showing the restored beauty as the very event of his arrival rather than its later result.

note: The two poems close on nearly the same words to the hill lord about the eyes of the woman he loves: in 264 they have yielded pallor, in 266 tears (பனி), after the friend owns their great modesty.
teaches: Read in order, the decade escalates the friend's case for marriage from pallor to weeping by changing one word, while the boar beside it changes from mating with its sow to fighting a tiger.

note: Both are Kapilar's: in Akananuru 248 a boar holding a narrow pass to guard its young is spared by a hunter who sees in it his own chief holding the path; in Ainkurunuru 265 a boar rears the young of a sow the tiger killed, beside a man who left his wife and son.
teaches: Kapilar's boar guarding its young is a model of protection that even the hunter honours as heroic, which makes the husband of Ainkurunuru 265 fail a standard that both the beast and the hunter keep.

note: Both set a boar with a striped young that has lost its mother beside a man who has left: in 265 the boar rears it after a tiger killed the sow, in 268 it sleeps with it on the peak.
teaches: Taken together the pair fixes the reading of the motherless young in 268 by the tiger-killed sow named in 265, and shows the decade using one creature's care twice, once against a husband and once against a lover.

note: Ainkurunuru 267 opens with the same boar formula as Natrinai 386 (சிறுகண் பன்றிப் பெருஞ்சின ஒருத்தல்); Natrinai's boar sleeps unafraid after raiding the millet, Ainkurunuru's drives off the bowmen to seize the hill rice, beside a man whose words are not to be trusted.
teaches: One formula line for the raiding boar served poets for opposite men, the suitor who swears and weds and the one who flatters without pledge, so the boar's daring is admired or suspected according to what the man goes on to do.
audit_text_issue: ainkurunuru:267 line 1 reads பறிப் for பன்றிப்

note: Both open on the earth a boar has ploughed: in 269 a wild reed rises there like a crop and the friend fears the lord will stay away; in 270 the hunters reap the first crop from it and the lord comes of himself.
teaches: The decade ends by answering the friend's fear on the same boar-tilled ground, where the field that bore only a wild reed now yields a harvest and his return, so the image tracks whether the love will bear fruit.

note: Purananuru 168 praises Kotran's hill, where hill people sow millet unploughed in the earth a boar has turned and feast on the first new grain; in Ainkurunuru 270 the hunters reap the first crop from the boar-ploughed slope and leave the hill bare.
teaches: The same unploughed tillage and first harvest is plenty and hospitality in the praise of a patron but, for lovers who met at the millet watch, the end of their season and a bare hill, so akam reads the hill's farming calendar as a calendar of meeting.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 270 line 2 repaired by rule.

note: Natrinai 168 and Ainkurunuru 273 share a formula: the young of the dull-headed female monkey feeding on the good hill and the girl called நின் நயந்து உறைவி; in Natrinai 168 the friend uses it to forbid his coming at midnight, in Ainkurunuru 273 to forbid his going away.
teaches: The same formula serves to stop the lover coming and to stop him leaving, which shows the double bind of secret love: the girl's life is staked both on the danger of his night visits and on his absence, and only marriage ends both.

note: In Kuruntokai 69 a widowed female monkey leaps from the ridge to her death and the friend begs the lover not to come at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 274 the male monkey carries his mate up the slope from the roaring tiger while the girl's lover has gone away.
teaches: Read together, the monkey couple names both fears of secret love: in Kuruntokai the girl would not survive losing him to the night path, in Ainkurunuru she is left by a man less faithful than the beast that shields its mate, so the danger lies as much in his leaving as in his coming.

note: Kural 1183 has the woman say he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; Ainkurunuru 278 says the lord gave a sickness never forgotten and took the beauty onlookers never tired of.
teaches: Valluvar keeps only the exchange as the woman's own complaint, while the Sangam poem sets it in an image of a bamboo springing back like a rod that has landed a fish, which shows the taking and the man's unharmed recoil that the couplet's bare bargain leaves out.

note: In Natrinai 334 the monkeys frolic with their male in the falls and the friend fears for the girl's life if the lover comes through the stormy night; in Ainkurunuru 279 the female monkey frolics with her mate and the friend warns that his coming will set the village gossiping.
teaches: Under the same image of monkeys at play with their mates, the friend has two separate reasons to keep the lover away, the night path's danger in Natrinai and the village tongue in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows that the creatures' open play stands for exactly the freedom secret love lacks on both counts.

note: In Ainkurunuru 103 the friend tells the mother that the shore lord has become fit for the girl and she for him; in Ainkurunuru 280 the friend reminds the hill lord that on hearing he would marry she told her mother.
teaches: The neythal decade stages the friend's disclosure to the mother, and Kapilar's poem shows its price: she spoke only on the strength of the man's word, so her standing at home now hangs on his keeping it.

note: Both count the girl's posting to the millet field as luck for the secret love: in Natrinai 134 the friend tells the girl that the mother herself sent her with the clapper to the field near the meeting place; in Ainkurunuru 281 the man blesses the parrots whose raids set her to guard.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show that the field watch which makes the day trysts possible is set up by agents who do not know what they serve, the mother by her order and the parrots by their raids, so the kalavu depends on the household's own ignorance.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 134 line 6 is a strong variant (ஏவினன் மன்னே நுந்தை, யாயும்), which changes who gives the order but not the point.

note: Both refuse the night visit on the hill path: Kuruntokai 141's girl would tell him she has been sent to drive parrots from the millet and that he should not come in the deep midnight when the tiger waits; Ainkurunuru 282's friend tells him not to come in the dark where tuskers roam.
teaches: Ainkurunuru 282 gives only the refusal, while Kuruntokai 141 adds the alternative the refusal implies, the millet field by day, so the pair shows that the night ban in kurinji is a redirection of the tryst to the guarded field, not a denial of it.

note: Both turn on the man's possible lie: in Kuruntokai 25 the girl says that if he denies his word she can do nothing, since only a heron watched; in Ainkurunuru 283 the friend says that even if he makes great promises and leaves, many women are caught in his net of lies.
teaches: The girl of Kuruntokai 25 treats his lie as her private helplessness with no witness, while the friend of Ainkurunuru 283 recasts it as his habit, a net that has caught many, so the friend's voice turns the heroine's fear into a public charge that can be used to press him.

note: Both look at the reaped millet field: in Natrinai 306 the friend, in the man's hearing, says the girl has been sent home and asks how he will come day after day to the bare stubble; in Ainkurunuru 284 the parrots keep coming to the stubble, unable to part from it.
teaches: Natrinai 306 assumes that the harvest ends the man's reason to come, but Ainkurunuru 284 shows creatures whose love keeps them at the empty field anyway, so the harvest cannot end such a love; it only leaves marriage as the way it can go on.

note: Both have the friend (for Parimelazhagar in the Kural) speak to the man about to part: Kural 1151 refuses his promise of a quick return, saying tell it to those who will be alive; Ainkurunuru 285 asks how he can part and leave her here with her bangles slipping.
teaches: The Kural states the friend's refusal as a bare threat to the girl's life, while the Sangam poem sets the same refusal in the girl's daily field life and names the visible sign, the slipping bangle, so the Kural's abstract 'those who will be alive' is shown as wasting already begun.

note: Both have the girl hold to the man's goodness while her pallor spreads: in Kural 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits yet pallor comes; in Ainkurunuru 286 she says he seems to have loved her without blemish yet takes her beauty.
teaches: In both the girl refuses to blame the man and lays the loss elsewhere, on the pallor as a cheat in the Kural and on his love itself in the Sangam poem, so the pair shows a fixed rule of her speech: the waste of her beauty is never his fault in her own mouth.

note: Both use the reaped millet stubble of the hill farmer: in Kuruntokai 133 the stubble cropped by parrots puts out leaves again in the rain, as the girl lives on after his first taking of her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 286 the stubble bears pods for his ever-yielding land while her own glow is taken.
teaches: The same stubble is a figure of the girl's own survival in Kuruntokai 133 but of the man's endless plenty in Ainkurunuru 286, set against her fading, so the image of renewal cuts both ways: what revives on his hills need not revive in her.

note: Both ask what return can be made to the small parrot of the millet field: in Natrinai 194 the friend asks it of the parrot that did not take the millet ears while they played with the hill lord; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man asks it of the parrots that eat the millet while the girl guards it.
teaches: The parrot is thanked in one poem for eating the crop and in the other for sparing it, opposite acts earning the same gratitude, which shows that what the lovers prize is not the bird's deed but whatever keeps the field watch going and hides what they do there.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 194 is marked uncertain.

note: Kural 101 says that help given unasked cannot be repaid by earth and heaven together; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man, knowing the good of the parrots' help, asks his heart what he can do in return.
teaches: The Kural's unrepayable help is a deliberate kindness, while the parrots helped without knowing or meaning it, so the lover's echo of the gratitude maxim stretches it to an unintended benefit and makes the debt even less payable, since the helpers cannot know they are owed.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 288 line 2 repaired from tamilvu.

note: Both have the parrots take the girl's sound for their own call: in Kuruntokai 291 the man says the parrots take her clapper's sweet call for one of their own and will not rise, so she weeps; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the parrots, taking her voice for a parrot's, come to the millet, so the elders may stop her guarding.
teaches: Kuruntokai 291 makes the image a lover's praise and a small vexation, while Ainkurunuru 289 follows it to its consequence in the household, the loss of the guard duty and so of the trysts, which turns the man's compliment into the friend's argument for marriage.

note: Both warn that the girl may lose the guard of the millet: in Akananuru 28 the friend, with the man nearby, warns that if she does not rise and scare the parrots her mother will send others; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the elders may stop her guarding because her own voice draws the parrots.
teaches: The threat to the field meetings comes in Akananuru 28 from the girl's neglect, which she could mend, and in Ainkurunuru 289 from her very voice, which she cannot, so the second friend can leave the man only one remedy, to marry her.

note: Both have the man in love rank a small favour of the beloved above the highest good: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep in her soft arms; Ainkurunuru 290 says parrots merely looked at and shooed by the hill girl are more fortunate than a just king.
teaches: The Kural sets union against heaven, while the Sangam poem sets far less, a glance and a shooing given to birds, against a righteous kingdom, so the pair shows the measure working at both ends: even the least share of her notice outweighs the highest worldly good.

note: Both give the man the same words for constancy: Kural 1125 உள்ளுவன் ... மறப்பறியேன், answering the friend who asks whether he remembers; Ainkurunuru 298 உள்ளுபு மறந்தறியேமே, said of a girl who shows him no grace.
teaches: The Kural's joke that he cannot remember what he never forgets answers a doubt about absence, while the Ainkurunuru sets the same claim against her coldness, so together they show the man's never-forgetting was the stock answer to both doubts the friend tests him with: will he stay away, and will he give up if she is unkind.

note: Both have the man say the blue water-lily (குவளை) cannot match the girl's eyes: Ainkurunuru 299 says the lily of her own hill spring can hardly open as her eyes do, and Kural 1114 that the lily, if it could see, would bow its head ashamed.
teaches: The Ainkurunuru states the defeat of the lily as a plain fact of the girl's own hill, and the Kural gives the lily sight and a modest bowed head, so the pair shows the Kural's conceit growing out of the akam habit of measuring the hill girl against her land's flowers, with the lily now made to act out her own modesty.

note: Both have the woman speak of her heart that has gone after the man: in Ainkurunuru 295 she wonders whether the heart that went with the hill man will come back or settle there; in Kural 1248 she calls her heart foolish for following the one who left, pining that he will not show grace.
teaches: The Kural judges the following heart a fool because the man has gone and withholds his grace, while the Ainkurunuru girl, with no doubt of him, only wonders whether her heart will return, so the pair shows that the same act of the heart going after the man is not folly in itself and is judged by how the man answers it.

note: Both have the friend bid the hill lord not come at midnight for fear of beasts: Ainkurunuru 296 in four lines, fearing a fierce beast; Akananuru 92 with a tiger striking an elephant, and then the offer that tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding the millet, where he may meet her by day (பகற்குறி, the colophon says, to press marriage).
teaches: Akananuru 92 spells out the day tryst at the millet field, which shows that the opening of Ainkurunuru 296, the millet the hill girl guards, is not idle scenery but the same unspoken offer, so the short poem's refusal of the night already points to where and when he may come.

note: Both turn on the girl's hand laid on the man's eyes: in Natrinai 28 the girl recalls how in the secret love he took her hand and pressed it to his eyes, then left her like a thief; in Ainkurunuru 293 the wife covers his eyes from behind in play and he says no one else lives in his heart.
teaches: In Natrinai 28 the hand on his eyes was his gesture of a promise that his leaving made false, while in Ainkurunuru 293 it is her game in the married bed that draws from him the vow of no other, so the pair shows the same touch losing its doubt once the promise of secret love has been kept in marriage.

note: Kural 1151 refuses any promise of quick return and asks only whether he is leaving; Ainkurunuru 302 grants that his work for wealth has its own right and argues only that the woman has an equal one.
teaches: Read together they show the friend's dissuasion in two registers, the couplet's flat ultimatum of death and the poem's balanced concession of rights, so the Kural's line is an extreme the Sangam friend reaches only after first admitting the claim of wealth.

note: Both use the elephant pair shrinking together in hunger on the scorched hill; in Akananuru 91 the friend uses it after he has gone to comfort the woman, in Ainkurunuru 305 before he goes to shame the man out of going.
teaches: The same image of the starving pair that will not part is turned on the man as reproach before the journey and on the woman as reassurance after it, so in the convention one karu image carries opposite arguments depending on whether the departure is still preventable.

note: Kural 64 makes the gruel stirred by children's small hands sweeter than amrita; Ainkurunuru 309 asks whether wealth gained across the waste is sweeter than an unborn son's smile.
teaches: The couplet's household ranking of children above every delicacy becomes, in the friend's mouth, a direct argument against the wealth journey, showing that the Kural's measure of sweetness was already a tool for weighing a husband's absence against his family.

note: In both the friend tells the man who has announced his journey that the woman's bangles will slip; Akananuru 271 wishes his work be capable (வல்வதாக) and asks if there is medicine for her, Ainkurunuru 310 asks whether he is capable (வல்லுவை) of parting.
teaches: Both friends turn வல், the capacity a man needs for his work, into the hardness that parting demands, so the pair shows the dissuasion convention attacking the hero's prized strength itself rather than his reasons for going.

note: Ainkurunuru 311 has the woman ask whether the man who crossed the forest will stay long (நீடுவர் கொல்); in Akananuru 69 the friend, by its colophon, comforts the woman who fears his delay with the answer that he will not stay long (நீடலர்) though he crossed the Mauryan cut.
teaches: The four-line poem gives only the woman's question and the long poem only the friend's answer, so together they show that the paalai exchange turned on a single verb of delay, asked in one mouth as a fear and returned in the other as a promise.

note: Both blessings are said by the woman to a thing of nature that governs her sight of the man who has left: the Kural blesses the moon on condition that it not set (படாஅதி வாழி மதி); Ainkurunuru 312 blesses the hill that has already hidden him (மறைத்த குன்றே).
teaches: The Kural's blessing is a bargain for sight, while the Sangam woman blesses the hill after it has hidden him, so her wish can only be for what the hill will do to him on the way, which shows the blessing turning from her own need to his safety.

note: In both the woman's heart has followed the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்; இறந்தோர் தேஎத்துச் சென்ற நெஞ்சம்); the Kural calls it a fool, Ainkurunuru 317 asks the friend why it is so slow to come back.
teaches: The Kural judges the heart's going as folly, but the Ainkurunuru woman takes the going for granted and worries about the heart's delay, so the same flight of the heart becomes, in the older poem, a second absence that mirrors the man's.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 is repaired; நீடிய பொருளே admits more than one construction.

note: Both state the same sign of separation on the same body part: the broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்; பணைநீங்கி) waste and the bangles slip once the partner is gone.
teaches: The Kural gives the slipping bangle as a plain effect of the partner's absence, while the Ainkurunuru woman names the departed men as those who killed her longing, so the poem shows the bodily sign being used as an accusation, which the couplet's general statement leaves out.

note: Both turn on the woman's own inability to forget (மறப்பறியேன்; மறவா நம்மே); the Kural asks what would become of her if she forgot, Ainkurunuru 319 asks whether he has forgotten her.
teaches: The Kural keeps the question inside her (remembering burns, forgetting would kill), while the Sangam poem turns the same constancy outward into a charge against him, so read together they show the two directions the claim 'I do not forget' could be pointed.

note: In both a woman left behind speaks of a man who crossed the hills where the silk-cotton blooms: Akananuru 185 compares the leafless ilavam in flower to the lamps of a great festival (பெருவிழா விளக்கம் போல), Ainkurunuru 320 compares its falling flowers to embers struck by thunder (உருமுப்படு கனலின்).
teaches: The same flowering tree on the paalai road is a festival of lamps in one woman's mouth and a thunderbolt's embers in the other's, so the silk-cotton was not a fixed sign of danger but a vehicle that swung with the charge each woman laid against her man, his iron will in one and the endless sickness he gave in the other.

note: Both are the woman's complaint that ends on almost the same closing line (கோடுயர் பிறங்கல் மலை இறந் தோரே; நிலையுயர் பிறங்கல் மலைஇறந் தோரே) after naming her wasted broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்) and slipping bangles.
teaches: The five-line decade poem is the bare frame of the thirteen-line Akananuru poem, the body's signs followed by the closing formula of the men who crossed the high hills, so the pair shows how a long paalai poem was built by filling the road between those two fixed ends with a scene.

note: The Kural's man says the fire she gives burns when he moves away from her (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம்); Ainkurunuru 322's man, far from her on the summer road, says the thought of her makes the burning path cool (தண்ணிய).
teaches: Held together they give opposite laws for distance: in the couplet absence from her is the source of heat, while in the desert poem absence is already given and her remembered presence is the only coolness, so whether she burns or cools depends on whether the man is measuring his desire or the land.

note: In 322 thinking of her turns a hot road cool; in 328 a road cooled by rain and flowers is hot because he has left her.
teaches: The two poems of one decade run the same switch in both directions, so the poet shows that paalai heat is set by her presence or absence in the man's mind and can override real rain as easily as real sun.

note: Akananuru 5's colophon has the man give up the journey (செலவழுங்கியது) at the sight of her tearful face before he sets out; in Ainkurunuru 330 he has already crossed the scorching forest (வந்தனம் ஆயினும்) when he calls off the journey (ஒழிகஇனிச் செலவே) thinking of her weeping eyes.
teaches: The pair shows that giving up the journey is not tied to a moment: the tears seen at the doorstep in Akananuru 5 and the tears only imagined halfway in Ainkurunuru 330 do the same work, so in this situation her grief, present or pictured, is what overrules the errand, not the danger of the road.

note: In Akananuru 19 the man reproaches a heart that neither stayed with her nor crosses the hills with him; in Ainkurunuru 329 he says the heart was taken by her and wonders whether it will come back with him.
teaches: Read together they show two accounts of the traveller's divided heart: the Akananuru man blames it for wavering between her and the road, while the Ainkurunuru man concedes it never left her, so the reproach of Akananuru 19 becomes in the short poem a plain admission that he travels heartless.

note: Both men, on the burning road, see the girl in sleep; Ainkurunuru 324 says he will surely see her (காண்குவென் மன்ற), while Akananuru 39 calls the dream false (வாய்அல் கனவின்) because it left his hand empty.
teaches: The short poem gives only the traveller's confidence in the dream, and the long one tells how it ends on waking, so together they show the road-dream as both his comfort and his torment, and explain why the returned man of Akananuru 39 can answer her charge of forgetting with it.

note: In Akananuru 197 the friend comforts the woman with the image of a tusker embracing his pregnant mate on the man's road; in Ainkurunuru 323 the man himself crosses a road where a red dog hunts for his craving pregnant mate.
teaches: The friend's reassurance rests on an assumption that the man will see such creatures and remember, and Ainkurunuru 323 shows it from his side: he does see the male caring for its mate and finds the girl's nature has come with him, so the comfort offered at home is confirmed by the road.

note: In Kuruntokai 285 the waiting woman asks where he can be, who crossed sky-high hills where a lone kite sits on the nyemai top; in Ainkurunuru 321 the man on such hills hears the hen kite call from the omai and says her nature never leaves him.
teaches: The same bare tree and kite are imagined by the woman and actually met by the man, and the pair answers her question from the other end of the road: where she fears he has forgotten her, the same scene brings her back to him.

note: The Kural's man says love is sweeter than toddy because merely thinking of it brings unfailing joy; in Ainkurunuru 325 the man says the scorching waste does not harm him because he has her nature as companion.
teaches: The couplet states that remembered love never fails to give joy, and the Ainkurunuru puts that claim to a hard test, the peopleless summer waste, where the memory works as a travelling companion (துணை), so the maxim gains a situation in which its truth is a matter of survival.
audit_text_issue: ainkurunuru:325 line 2 புகாவுண்ணாது is uncertain | Line 2 புகாவுண்ணாது is uncertain; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Both have the woman's foolish heart following the man who has left (Ainkurunuru: பேதை நெஞ்சம் பின்செல; Kural: பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு).
teaches: With the same words the couplet blames her own heart for going after an unkind man, while the Sangam wife lets the heart go and blames the man as harder than stone, so the following heart was an image that could lay the fault on either lover.

note: Akananuru 51's man tells his heart that wealth gained by parting is not worth leaving his wife's embrace; Ainkurunuru 337's wife says that for her man wealth is sweeter than the embrace.
teaches: The two poems weigh the same two goods, wealth and the embrace, and reach opposite verdicts according to who speaks: the man at home can still choose the embrace, while the wife whose man has gone can only infer that he chose wealth, so the akam tradition hands each verdict to the one who lives with it.

note: Akananuru 1's woman asks whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part (பிரியலம் என்ற சொல்) now that he has gone for gold; Ainkurunuru 336 says he embraced her as if he would never part (பிரியலர் போலப் புணர்ந்தோர்) and went for wealth.
teaches: Akananuru 1 rests the betrayal on a spoken vow, while the Ainkurunuru wife rests it on the embrace alone, so together they show that in paalai the embrace itself was read as a promise that the pursuit of wealth broke, with or without words.

note: In both the wife, parted from her man, speaks of the evening: the Kural asks the evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru 339 asks whether evening exists in the land he went to.
teaches: The couplet gives evening a hard partner of its own, and the Sangam wife supposes his land has no evening at all, so the pair shows the same assumption from two sides: evening is the hour that should force lovers together, and only an absent or hard-hearted partner escapes it.

note: In 332 the beasts fail to tell him that parting is cruel; in 333 the birds fail to tell him that they themselves live paired.
teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from the argument the beasts should have made by precept (parting is cruel) to the one the birds should have made by their own example (we live with our mates), so the wife tries both ways of restraining a man and puts each in a creature's mouth.

note: Every poem of the decade says the time has come (தான் வந்தன்றே); 350 says it is the time of which he assured them with sweet words (தேம்படு கிளவி ... தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
teaches: Read from 350 back to 341, the unnamed 'it' of the refrain turns out to be his promised date, so each spring sign in the decade is a clause of his oath being checked off, not a description of the season.

note: Akananuru 355 says spring has come of itself (செவ்விவேனில் தானே வந்தன்று) to a woman whose man is about to leave; the Ainkurunuru refrain says the same with தான் வந்தன்றே after he has gone.
teaches: The same formula serves first as the woman's argument against going, the season lovers spend in cool groves, and then as the proof that he went anyway, so 'it came of itself' carries the reproach that the season keeps its time unasked while the man does not.

note: Akananuru 355 says in spring lovers stay in the cool grove of dropping pollen and forget their rich homes (தண்பொழில் அல்கிக் காதலர் செழுமனை மறக்கும்); Ainkurunuru 345 says our fragrant cool grove (நம் மணங்கமழ் தண்பொழில்) is in bloom.
teaches: Akananuru 355 supplies the custom that the four-line poem leaves out: the flowering grove is where lovers spend spring together, so 'our grove blooms' is an empty place set for two, not a pleasant view.

note: In Natrinai 224 the red-eyed dark koel (செங் கண் இருங் குயில்) calls as if saying 'you who are joined, stay joined' before the man leaves; in Ainkurunuru 346 the same koel (செங்கண இருங்குயில்) cries after he has gone and not returned.
teaches: One bird in one spring is a plea against parting while the man is still at home and an announcement of his failure once he is away, so the koel's call has no fixed sense of its own and takes its meaning from the stage of the parting.

note: Natrinai 224 sets 'sweet spring has come' (இன்ப வேனிலும் வந்தன்று) beside 'those who assured us we will not part' (பிரியலம் என்று தெளித்தோர்); Ainkurunuru 350 ends with the time of which he assured them (தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே).
teaches: Natrinai uses தெளித்தல் for the man's sworn assurance in the very poem where spring arrives, which supports reading Ainkurunuru 350's தெளிக்கும் as his promise, and shows that spring's coming and the lover's oath were a fixed pair in paalai poetry.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 350 line 3 is a repaired reading.

note: In Akananuru 317 the man's quoted promise names the spring signs, the koel in the mango and the kongu and kuravam dropping flowers, and he arrives on time; in Ainkurunuru 350 the time of his assurance comes and he does not.
teaches: Akananuru 317 shows that the catalogue of spring flowers and birds was itself the wording of the man's promise, so the Ainkurunuru decade's list of the same signs is the promise read back to an absent man, and 317's ending is the one the decade is denied.
audit_text_issue: line 3 repaired from another source

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend calls the season of humming bees and a forest in bloom the medicine for the heroine's pallor (பசலை மருந்து); in Ainkurunuru 342 the bees revel on the flowering nunavam and he has not come.
teaches: The friend can call the flowering season a cure only because it guarantees his return; Ainkurunuru 342 shows the same flowering turning into the sickness once the season arrives without him, so the convention's comfort is only as good as the man's timekeeping.

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven for those who pine with their eyes on the day of return (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு); Ainkurunuru 350 is spoken on that day, the time he named, and he has not come.
teaches: The couplet measures the waiting before the fixed day as the long part, while the poem shows the fixed day arriving empty, so the Kural's pain has a limit that the Ainkurunuru woman has already passed, when waiting no longer has a date to count toward.
audit_text_issue: Line 3 is a repaired reading.

note: Ainkurunuru 355: he turned back from the wealth journey without blessing it; Akananuru 337: the heart once said 'let wealth stay there' (அவணதாகப் பொருள்) and came back alone, and now presses for a second journey.
teaches: Akananuru 337 supplies the sequel the Ainkurunuru decade leaves out: the return for love that 355 presents as final is, a season later, reopened by the same heart, so the turning back is one move in a recurring quarrel between wealth and the wife.

note: In Akananuru 97 the kuravam blooms (குரவுமலர்ந்து) in a spring when the man has not come and the woman cannot stop her tears; in Ainkurunuru 357 the kuravam's flowering is what makes the man give up his journey.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the spring flowers acting on both lovers at once: the same blossoming that tortures the waiting woman in Akananuru 97 is, in 357, what turns the man back, so the season's sign has power over him and fails only when he ignores it.

note: In Natrinai 43 a starving red dog kills a weary wild cow on the road the man is about to take; in Ainkurunuru 354 the red dog, with its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go on the road he has taken home.
teaches: The same predator of the waste kills on the outbound road and holds back on the homeward one, so the paalai poets set the beast's act to the direction of the journey: cruelty when the man leaves, restraint when he comes back to his wife.

note: Both use the formula விழுத்தொடை மறவர் வில் இட ... எழுத்துடை நடுகல்; in Akananuru 53 it is the stone on the outbound road the woman says he chose over her, in Ainkurunuru 352 a simile for an elephant on the road he did not call hard on his way back.
teaches: The one formula of the lettered hero-stone serves opposite arguments: in Akananuru 53 the woman reads the deadly road as proof he loves wealth more than her, while 352 makes the same road proof of love because he crossed it home without counting its danger.

note: In Kural 1170 the woman says her eyes would not swim in a flood of tears if they could go to him as her heart does; in Ainkurunuru 358 the eyes, which have become a flood however often they are wiped, will not let him stay away long.
teaches: The couplet makes the flood of tears a sign of the eyes' helplessness, bound to the house while the heart travels, whereas the Sangam poem turns that same flood into a power that pulls him back, so the tears are complaint in one and pledge of return in the other.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 358 line 4 உடிஅத்தெழு looks corrupt (perhaps உடைத்தெழு).

note: Ainkurunuru 360: the long burnt road was easy because he drove his chariot thinking of her; Akananuru 9: the returning man's heart outran even his sleepless chariot and has already reached her.
teaches: Read together the two returns show desire working on the journey in two stages: in 360 it shrinks the road the chariot must cover, and in Akananuru 9 it leaves the chariot behind altogether, so the heart arrives before the man does.

note: In Akananuru 99 the man leading the eloped girl through the waste likens the opening kongu buds to women's jewelled breasts and points to paathiri petals on the path; in Ainkurunuru 361 the girl wears a paathiri garland by the summer stream and her breasts and shoulders strike him harder than her eyes.
teaches: Akananuru 99 makes the waste's flowers stand for her body to coax her onward, while 361 has her wearing those same flowers and her body outdoing them, so the eloping man's praise moves from comparing the land to her to letting her eclipse it.

note: Kural 1085 finds death, the eye and the doe all in the young woman's look; Ainkurunuru 361 grants the eyes are fierce, then ranks her breasts fiercer and her shoulders fiercer still.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on the first sight puts all the deadliness in the look, and the Ainkurunuru poet answers that the eyes are only the first and mildest weapon, which shows the old akam poets could treat the same stricken lover as half joking where the couplet keeps him grave.

note: In Natrinai 144 the girl, with the man overhearing, says her heart frets now that she knows he comes alone by night over the forked paths (கவலை) where the tigress prowls; in Ainkurunuru 362 the same fear of the forked night path (கவலை) and its elephant is put to the man's face.
teaches: The overheard complaint of Natrinai 144 and the open question of 362 make the same plea, stop coming by night, in two registers, and holding them together shows that Ainkurunuru's direct-address decade turns the indirect device of the overhearer into plain speech without changing the situation.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 362 colophon thinai பாலை; the marker reads kurinji

note: Kural 1081: on first sight the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels; Ainkurunuru 363: the man tells the hunters' sister that what she calls freckles (சுணங்கு) his stricken heart calls a goddess (அணங்கு).
teaches: Where the couplet leaves the goddess as one of three guesses about the whole woman, 363 pins the striking power on one small mark she herself thinks a blemish, so the pair shows the anangu is not in her but in the gap between how she sees herself and how he is struck.

note: Both open with the friend's formula to the mother, அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை, answering her question why the girl has grown pale (பசந்தனள்); in Akananuru 48 the friend tells the whole story of the hunter who came asking after a tiger, in 366 she answers only that the kongu has flowered.
teaches: The shared formula shows these are two answers to one stock question: Akananuru 48 discloses the love by a full story and leaves the wise to infer the rest, while 366 compresses the same disclosure into one seasonal sign, so the reader learns how far the friend's hint could be shortened and still be understood.
audit_text_issue: ainkurunuru:366 line 5 is repaired.

note: In Akananuru 317 the man had promised to come back in the spring when the kongu and kuravam flower and the koel calls, and his arrival ends a pallor the mother had noticed; in Ainkurunuru 366 the friend tells the mother the girl's pallor is because the kongu has flowered.
teaches: Read through 317, the friend's excuse in 366 is no excuse at all: the kongu's flowering is the season a man promises to return by, so pointing the mother to the tree points her to an absent lover, and the pair shows a seasonal sign doing the work of a confession.
audit_text_issue: line 5 repaired from another edition

note: In Akananuru 48 the friend tells the foster mother of a youth with a flower garland and a chariot who stopped by the vengai slope and gazed at the girl; in Ainkurunuru 367 the friend tells the mother of the man who came near with his chariot wearing kongu and vengai flowers, and says the girl's life is joined to his name.
teaches: The same disclosure scene, chariot, flowered youth and vengai included, ends in Akananuru 48 with an inference left to the mother and in 367 with a flat verdict that the girl is already bound to him, which shows the friend's revelation could be pitched as a hint or as a fait accompli.

note: In Kural 1151 the friend tells the departing man to promise a quick return only to those who will still be alive; in Ainkurunuru 368 the friend invites him to stay and enjoy the cool summer with them if the girl is not to be ruined.
teaches: Both hold the girl's life against the journey, but the couplet does it by refusing his comfort and 368 by tempting him with the season's pleasure, so together they show the two strategies of the friend who would stop a departure, the bitter and the sweet, around the same threat.

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says she saw him on one day only and the gossip has spread like the snake seizing the moon; in Ainkurunuru 369 the friend tells the man that his tryst of yesterday (நெருநல்) is already louder in the town's mouth than the seasonal koel.
teaches: Both measure a single meeting against a public noise, the eclipse in the couplet and the koel's cry in 369, and holding them together shows the alar topic's fixed shape: the smaller and more recent the secret, the larger the natural event the gossip is said to outdo.
audit_text_issue: ainkurunuru:369 sense flagged uncertain by marker | Ainkurunuru 369's sense is flagged uncertain.

note: Both wish the wasteland the girl has crossed with her lover cool with rain or cloud, in the same frame (...ஆகுக ... போகிய சுரனே); Kuruntokai's speaker is the foster mother, Ainkurunuru's the mother.
teaches: Kuruntokai's wish asks only shade, sand and cloud for a frightened road, while Ainkurunuru adds that the girl judged the going to be the path of right, so the same blessing formula could also carry the household's grudging moral consent to the elopement.

note: 371 says the girl went having judged this the path of right (அறநெறி); 376 calls the fate that joined and sent her without right (அறனில் பால்).
teaches: One decade by one poet lets the mother both concede that her daughter chose rightly and curse the joining as wrong, so the dispute over whether elopement is அறம் is staged inside a single lament rather than between mother and girl.

note: Both mothers wish on the mother who bore the youth the same grief they feel (Natrinai: எம்போல் பெரு விதுப்புறுக; Ainkurunuru: நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் இடும்பை எய்துக).
teaches: Natrinai ties the wished grief to the sight of the girl's playmates at a festival, Ainkurunuru to every thought of the road, so the curse on the youth's mother was a set move whose point is to make the other mother feel exactly the speaker's own loss.

note: Akananuru 195's mother says the youth's mother will joyfully paint her walls for the couple's coming; Ainkurunuru 373's mother wishes that same woman grief.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the bereaved mother's view of the other house in its two moods, envy of the joy it awaits and a curse that it should share her grief, so the youth's mother is a fixed counter-figure of this lament.

note: Both mothers weep each time they see what the girl left (காண்தொறும்): Ainkurunuru the doll and the parrot she reared, Natrinai the courtyard, the playmates and the nochchi.
teaches: Ainkurunuru stops at the doubled grief of looking, while Natrinai turns from the same sight to declare the girl faultless, so the scene of the left belongings could lead either to bare lament or to the mother's acquittal of her daughter.

note: Ainkurunuru 377 says the girl left her ball, doll and pebbles to us; Akananuru 369 says the parrot will not drink and the doll gets no offering since she went.
teaches: In Akananuru the left things mourn with the household, while in Ainkurunuru they are a bequest the girl hands back with her childhood, so the same toys can be made grieving witnesses or the plain sign that childhood is over.

note: Both use the turn 'I do not grieve that she went; I grieve for...' (நோவேன் ... நோவல்): Akananuru 63 for the girl's night in a robbers' hamlet, Ainkurunuru 378 for the friend left behind.
teaches: The 'not this but that' turn of the mother's lament could redirect grief either to the girl's hardships on the road or, as in Ainkurunuru, to the companion at home, so the lament counts the friend's loss as a second wound of the elopement.

note: Akananuru 369's girl refused the rich wedding her kin were preparing (தமர்மணன் அயரவும் ஒல்லாள்); Ainkurunuru 379's mother asks whether going with him is sweeter than a good wedding among her companions.
teaches: Akananuru states the refusal of the home wedding as a grievance, and Ainkurunuru asks the question that refusal implies, whether the road was sweeter to the girl, so the mother's lament moves from blaming the choice to trying to imagine the girl's own preference.

note: Akananuru 263's mother says that had she known she would gladly have married the girl to him in her rich house; Ainkurunuru 380's mother says she was only mother in name and the playmates gave her away.
teaches: Read together the two show the mother grieving a lost office as much as a lost daughter: the giving of the bride that 263 wishes she had performed, 380 says was done behind her back by the girl's companions.

note: Akananuru 315's mother saw the girl's hair curl and breasts swell and blames herself for not guarding her; Ainkurunuru 374's mother says the girl's hair was not yet long enough to be knotted.
teaches: On one reading the two mothers read the same hair in opposite ways, as a sign of womanhood missed in Akananuru and as proof of childhood in Ainkurunuru, so the lament can either confess overlooked signs or deny that there were any.

note: Ainkurunuru 372 asks whether the girl thinks even of her mother (என்னும் உள்ளினள் கொல்லோ); Akananuru 383 says the girl never thought of the mother who raised her; gossip rises in both.
teaches: What Ainkurunuru leaves as an anxious question Akananuru settles as a charge, so the pair shows the mother's doubt about being remembered hardening, in the longer poem, into reproach.

note: Both have onlookers ask of the couple on the road யார்கொல் அளியர் தாமே; Kuruntokai leaves the question open over the rattling waste, Ainkurunuru answers it with the magandril pair.
teaches: The same onlookers' formula could end in fear for the pair (Kuruntokai's dangerous bamboo waste) or in a verdict that they are to be pitied only because they cannot be parted, so அளியர் held both pity and admiration.

note: Akananuru 321's foster mother wonders whether the girl will rest with her companion in a small hamlet (சீறூர்) or walk on into the night; Ainkurunuru 382 is told from the hamlet where they rested at nightfall (எல்லிடை அசைந்த ... சீறூர்).
teaches: What the foster mother can only imagine is answered from the hamlet itself, where strange women who have daughters feel her pain, so the grief of an elopement was pictured as reaching every house with a girl along the road.

note: Natrinai 362's eloping man tells the girl to play gathering velvet mites while he leans on a vengai on guard; Ainkurunuru 383 shows from outside the youth holding the maraam branch while she picks flowers for her doll.
teaches: Natrinai gives the man's own promise of guardianship and Ainkurunuru the onlooker's view of his delight in her child's play, so together they fix the eloping hero as an indulgent guardian of a girl still at play rather than a seducer.

note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving, pities the companions who will grieve at her ball and anklets; Ainkurunuru 384's girl, on the road, sends those companions word through brahmins that she went so her beauty might flourish.
teaches: The companions are the girl's first thought at both ends of the flight, pitied as she leaves and answered once she is away, and her message turns the pity into a justification that her going completes her mother's care.

note: 376's mother curses the fate that joined and sent the girl as without right (அறனில் பால்); 385's girl calls her mother without right (அறனில் யாய்) for keeping her at home.
teaches: In two adjoining decades by one poet each side of the elopement denies aram to the other, the mother blaming the fate that joined the lovers and the daughter blaming the mother's guard, so the dispute over whether the going was right is staged from both ends.

note: Akananuru 35's girl leaves the sky-touching walled house desolate (வான்தோய் இஞ்சி நன்னகர் புலம்ப); in Ainkurunuru 386 the mother is bewildered in the tall-walled good house (நெடுஞ்சுவர் நல்லில் மருண்ட).
teaches: The high wall that in Akananuru stands empty after the girl has slipped it becomes in Ainkurunuru the place where the mother is lost, so the house built to guard a daughter is shown to hold only the one left behind.

note: In both a searching woman asks brahmins on the waste road (அந்தணீர், அந்தணிர்) and they answer that they saw the girl (கண்டனம், கண்டனெம்); Kalittokai adds the sandal, pearl and lute argument and says the way never leaves aram.
teaches: The scene that Ainkurunuru leaves as a bare eyewitness report of the lover's tenderness was later expanded by Kalittokai into an argument that a daughter belongs to the man she follows, so the brahmins' reply grew from testimony into doctrine.

note: Kalittokai's brahmins tell the searching mother not to grieve for the girl who followed the man she chose; Ainkurunuru 388's travellers tell the searcher to rest out the noon heat and go on over the little hill to see the couple's road.
teaches: Wayside people meet the pursuer with two different answers, reasons to stop grieving in Kalittokai and directions to go on in Ainkurunuru, so the pursuit was not always treated as something to be talked out of.

note: Akananuru 17's foster mother asks whether her girl's small anklet-filled feet (சிலம்புஆர் சீறுடி) can walk the waterless waste; Ainkurunuru 389's searcher asks whether her anklet feet (அம்சிலம் படியே) kept pace with the youth who walked slowly.
teaches: The anklet foot is the searching woman's measure in both, but Akananuru weighs it against the road's hardship while Ainkurunuru, told the youth went slowly, weighs it against him, so the same worry could move from the danger of the way to the fitness of the match.

note: Natrinai 198 gives the foster mother's own words to those she meets in the waste, describing her daughter and blessing them; Ainkurunuru 390 gives the onlookers' reply to a woman who folds her hands to every good person and asks again and again.
teaches: Natrinai lets the searcher speak and Ainkurunuru shows how she looked to those she asked, wandering and worshipping strangers, so the two halves of the wayside exchange make up one recognised scene in which the onlookers' certainty answers her supplication.

note: Both reward the crow whose cawing brings a guest (விருந்துவரக் கரைந்த காக்கை; வரக்கரைந் தீமே): Kuruntokai's friend after the man has come, Ainkurunuru's speaker before the girl has.
teaches: Kuruntokai pays the crow afterwards and calls even seven bowls too little, while Ainkurunuru promises meat in a gold bowl in advance, so together they show the crow offering working as a bargain struck with the omen on either side of the homecoming.

note: 376 is the mother's curse on the fate without right (அறனில் பால்) that sent the girl; 393 describes her from outside as one who quarrelled with right and blamed it (அறம்புலந்து பழிக்கும்).
teaches: The curse the mother speaks in her own voice in decade 38 is named in decade 40 as a quarrel with அறம் that the daughter's return is meant to heal, so the poet frames the lament as a dispute with the moral order that the homecoming settles.

note: 376 calls the joining that sent the girl away a fate without right; 394 says the loveless right has after all shown grace (அன்பில் அறனும் அருளிற்று).
teaches: The same poet lets the verdict on அறம் turn with events, loveless when the girl left and gracious when she returns, so in these decades the moral order is judged by its outcome for the household rather than held fixed.

note: Both are the man's words to the girl at the end of the road as his own place comes into view (எம் சிறு நல் ஊரே; நம் மலைகெழு நாட்டே); Natrinai urges her on (ஏகுதி) because the day is ending, Ainkurunuru tells her to go slowly (மென்மெல ஏகுமதி) because the wasteland is behind them.
teaches: The same command to walk on means hurry in Natrinai and go slowly in Ainkurunuru, so the man's care at the journey's end is shaped by what threatens, the coming night or the danger just passed.

note: In both the man decks the eloping girl's hair with forest flowers, maraa in Akananuru 257 on the summer road, vengai in Ainkurunuru 396 at the edge of his town.
teaches: Akananuru's adorning happens on the march and admires how she walks, while Ainkurunuru's is a pause that lets her rest before she enters his town as a guest, so the flowers in her hair move from a token of the road to a preparation for her reception.

note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving by stealth, pities her companions (அளியரோ அளியர் என் ஆயத்தோர்) who will grieve at the ball and anklets she left; Ainkurunuru 397's speaker sends word ahead to her companions (என் ஆயத்தோர்க்கே) that she is coming.
teaches: The companions whose grief the girl foresaw as she slipped away are the first she sends a message to on the way back, so the playmates frame the elopement at both ends, its first cost and its first news.

note: 373 wishes on the youth's mother the grief of weeping at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் இடும்பை); 398's speaker says that she herself weeps so at every thought (நினைத்தொறும் கலிழும் என்னினும்) but the town is lonelier still.
teaches: Read together, the curse in 373 turns out to be the speaker's own condition, wished on the other mother, and in 398 the same grief is no longer used against anyone but set beside the town's loss while she blesses the road.

note: Akananuru 195's mother asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?); Ainkurunuru 399 proposes the answer: the anklet-removal in his house, the wedding in ours.
teaches: The question Akananuru leaves to the diviner Ainkurunuru settles by dividing the rites between the two houses, which shows that which house received the couple was a matter of standing that families negotiated, not only a mother's anxiety.

note: Akananuru 369's foster mother fears the girl had her anklets removed without honour in a poor stranger's hut (சிலம்புடன் கழீஇ); Ainkurunuru 399 concedes the anklet-removal to the youth's house but claims the wedding for the girl's own.
teaches: The anklet-removal that Akananuru dreads as a rite done without the family is in Ainkurunuru granted to the other house on condition of a proper wedding at home, so the girl's people could accept the lost rite once the honour of the wedding was kept.

note: Both say the lute is outdone by one's child: Kural 66 that only those who have not heard their children's prattle call the lute sweet; Ainkurunuru 410 that the bard's lute did not match the hour when the son rode on his father's chest.
teaches: The Kural's maxim has a scene behind it in which the lute is actually playing in the courtyard while the child plays, so the comparison was first a judgment between two pleasures heard together, and the child's worth lay in the whole family hour, not in speech alone.

note: Purananuru 188 says a rich man's days are fruitless without toddling children (குறுகுறு நடந்து); Ainkurunuru 403 shows a toddler (தளர்நடை) pulling a toy chariot and named after his grandfather.
teaches: Purananuru gives as general counsel that toddling children are what make a life worth having, and Ainkurunuru adds, through the grandfather's name the boy bears, that the toddler is valued also as the next link of a famous line.

note: Both call the wife who bore a son the lamp of the house in a mullai poem: Akananuru 184 குடிக்குவிளக்கு ஆகிய புதல்வற் பயந்த, Ainkurunuru 405 மனைக்குவிளக்காயினள் ... புதல்வன் தாயே.
teaches: Read together they show the lamp of the house was a fixed title of the mullai wife won by bearing a son: Akananuru grounds it in godlike chastity and fame, while Ainkurunuru turns the title back into a seen flame, the red light of a bowl lamp.

note: The same gesture, the husband holding his wife's small back (சிறுபுறம் கவையினன்) while she attends to their son: in Akananuru 26 after he had held off for fear of spilling her milk, in Ainkurunuru 404 while she nurses.
teaches: Akananuru 26 shows the back embrace as the husband's answer to a wife who has turned to the child after his coolness, so when the foster mother in 404 calls the same gesture good she approves the father's inclusion of himself in the mother and son, the very move that ended a sulk elsewhere.

note: 402 measures the couple's bed by the sweetness of bards plucking strings; 410 says the bard's lute could not match the joy once the son rode on his father's chest.
teaches: Within one decade the bard's music first serves as the measure of the couple's sweetness and then falls short of the family hour, so the poet ranks the joy of the child above the joy of the couple's union.

note: Both repeat இனிது மன்றஅவர் கிடக்கை; 401 says this world and heaven cannot easily obtain it, 409 says it is worth the whole of this world.
teaches: The same refrain carries two prices, above both worlds and equal to this one, so the foster mother's hyperbole is a varied formula of the decade rather than a fixed claim about the household's worth.

note: Kuruntokai's waiting woman says the men went for wealth without regard for youth (இளமை பாரார்); Ainkurunuru's returned hero says youth is sweet if spent together (இனிதுடன் கழிக்கின் இளமை).
teaches: The charge the abandoned woman makes in the rains is answered in the same season by the man come home, who adopts her measure of youth as his own, so the two poems stage the mullai argument over youth and wealth from both sides of the parting.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 415 line 4 அவர்ப் புணர்வு sits oddly in an address to மடந்தை.

note: The Naladiyar says the passing joy of youth is not found among the wise; the Ainkurunuru hero says youth spent together is sweet and the union is sweet now.
teaches: Both accept that youth passes, but the Naladiyar draws from that fact a duty to withhold delight, while the Sangam hero draws from it a reason to spend youth in shared pleasure, so the same premise yields opposite counsel in the old love poetry and the later ascetic quatrains.
audit_text_issue: line 4 அவர்ப் புணர்வு, third person in a speech to மடந்தை

note: In Kuruntokai the stag frisking with its sweet mate in the cool rain seems to taunt the waiting woman; in Ainkurunuru the hero shows his wife the beasts joined in delight, like us.
teaches: The paired beasts of the rainy scrub are one image read two ways: before the return they reproach the absent man through the woman's grief, after it they mirror the couple's reunion, so the image takes its sense from whether the speaker is still waiting.

note: The Kural's man says the bond between him and the girl is like that of body and life; the Ainkurunuru hero speaks of their faultless bond as lives mingled into one (உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய).
teaches: The Kural states the life-bond as a lover's private claim, while the Ainkurunuru hero, past a parting, finds it acted out by the scrub's mating beasts and makes the couple the measure of them, so the general likeness gains a witness in the season of return.

note: In Akananuru 134 the returning hero hushes his chariot so the stag and doe in union are not parted; in Ainkurunuru 414, now home, he bids his wife look at birds and beasts frisking in pairs.
teaches: On the road the hero shields the beasts' union as a sign of the one he is hurrying to, and once home he shows the paired creatures to his wife as a shared sight, so the mullai beasts move from his private token to the couple's common pleasure.

note: Both use the same pair of similes for the rain flowers: konrai like gold (பொன் என), kaayaa like sapphire (மணி என); Natrinai's returning hero urges his charioteer on, Ainkurunuru's promises to bring his wife to see the scrub.
teaches: The same jewelled konrai and kaayaa that make the returning man in Natrinai hurry home become, once he is home, a sight he promises to return to with his wife, so the formula's force changes from summons to leisure with the man's place in the journey.

note: Natrinai's hero, back from his work, blesses the cloud whose night rain fell on the town where he lay embraced with his wife; Ainkurunuru's says the rains mingled with the scrub and she embraced him.
teaches: Natrinai turns the coincidence of rain and embrace into thanks owed to the cloud, while Ainkurunuru sets the two side by side without comment, so together they show the returning hero crediting the season with the reunion it once threatened.

note: The Kural's man says an embrace no breeze can part is sweet to two who love; the Ainkurunuru hero asks if his wife, who held him close against her breasts (மாண்முலை அடைய முயங்கியோயே), is a woman of the sky.
teaches: The Kural names the close embrace as a pleasure common to all lovers, but the Ainkurunuru hero, after absence, finds the same embrace so beyond the human that he takes his own wife for a celestial, so the general sweetness is shown as wonder when it is regained.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 'வானம் பாடி' can be divided two ways.

note: In 424 the friend warns the man that his son will cry for the breast if he goes; in Akananuru 66 the crying son actually stops the man's chariot on the way to another wedding.
teaches: The friend's threat in Ainkurunuru 424 is the plan of which Akananuru 66 shows the working: the son as the one claim a departing husband cannot argue with was a recognised move, used against a journey for the king's work and against a journey to another woman alike.

note: In Natrinai 166 the husband himself tells his wife that their son has learnt to play and asks why he should part from her.
teaches: Natrinai gives the husband's own voice answering the friend's argument of Ainkurunuru 424, so the son as a reason to stay worked from both sides of the speech situation: urged on the man by the friend, and taken up by him unprompted.

note: In 426 the man has given up the king's hard task to stay with his wife; in Akananuru 214 the man in the camp says the war is their own duty (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while imagining her lonely rainy evening.
teaches: Held together, the poems show that the mullai husband's bond to the king's war was not fixed: one binds himself to it despite her loneliness, the other renounces it for her brow, so akam staged a real choice between royal service and the wife.

note: In 428 the rains, with the rainbow, halt the chariots and end the king's task; in Akananuru 84 the rains and the rainbow come but the angry king refuses tribute and moves his army on.
teaches: The convention that the rains end a campaign, which 428 takes for granted, is broken in Akananuru 84 by one king's anger, so the rainbow is a promise of return that only the king can keep or cancel.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 428 line 4 repaired.

note: In 426 the man has given up the king's war; in 429 he says he would go to it if the woman puts away her pallor.
teaches: Within one decade the poet sets a flat refusal of royal service beside a conditional consent to it whose condition, her pallor gone, is undone by the going itself, so 429 reads as a refusal phrased as a promise.

note: Both men give up a planned journey because of the woman; in 421 her shoulders 'block' the going, in Akananuru 5 her silent grieving and the son at her breast.
teaches: Ainkurunuru keeps only the outcome and one bodily sign of what Akananuru 5 unfolds as a scene of silent pleading, so the short form shows that the persuasion could be left wholly implied once the convention of the abandoned journey was known.

note: In Akananuru 254 the waiting wife watches the house dove fly with its mate while the man drives home; in 425 the man on the road hears the forest dove croon for its mate.
teaches: Together the poems place the paired dove at both ends of the return journey, in the wife's courtyard and on the husband's road, so the same creature serves as the sign by which each partner reads the other's longing.

note: Both dissuade the man from leaving, in the friend's voice on Parimelazhagar's reading of the couplet: the Kural argues from her survival, 423 from the rain already falling and her filled eyes.
teaches: The two show that the dissuasion of a departure had two set arguments, the season and her life, and the Kural keeps only the harsher second, while the Ainkurunuru friend leans on the order of the seasons that a man who leaves in the rains breaks.

note: Both set peacocks in their finery and the konrai-lovely forest of the rains before a waiting woman; Kar Narpathu's friend names the season the cure (மருந்து) for her pallor.
teaches: Kar Narpathu spells out that the season's beauty is a promise of return and so a cure, while Ainkurunuru only calls his road good for having it, so the decade's bare praise of the road is the same reassurance left unspoken.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 4 line 4 is a repaired misprint.

note: Both see the konrai as gold (Kuruntokai: பொன்செய் புனையிழை; Ainkurunuru: சுடுபொன் அன்ன கொன்றை); Kuruntokai's heroine refuses the forest's word that the rains have come, since he does not lie.
teaches: The gold konrai that Kuruntokai's woman must deny, because admitting the season means admitting a broken promise, is here worn by men on his road and praised, so the same flower could be held off as false witness or welcomed as the season's adornment of his way.
audit_text_issue: Line 5 of Kuruntokai 21 is a repaired reading; Ainkurunuru 432 is marked uncertain.

note: Kuruntokai's friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray shower for the kaar rains (வம்ப மாரியைக் காரென); Ainkurunuru calls the forest on his road one that has met the kaar rain (கார்ப்பெயற்கு எதிரிய).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that whether the forest's flowering marks the true kaar was itself what the waiting woman and her friend argued over, Kuruntokai explaining the signs away while Ainkurunuru accepts them.

note: Both put a doe with her frisking fawn on the rainy mullai road (Ainkurunuru: மறியுடை மான்பிணை; Akananuru: மறிஆடு மருங்கின் மடப்பிணை); in Akananuru the stag feeds and guards her and the returning man hurries his chariot home.
teaches: The image the waiting woman sets on his road without comment is, in Akananuru, the very sight that turns the man homeward, so the doe and fawn worked as a shared sign that the rains call the traveller back to wife and child.

note: Both list the flowers of the first rains (Ainkurunuru: தோன்றி, தளவம்; Natrinai: பிடவம், தளவம், கொன்றை, காயா); in Natrinai the returning man sees them and tells his charioteer the kaar has begun.
teaches: What the woman praises as the beauty of his road Natrinai shows from the other end, the man reading those same flowers as his deadline and driving hard, so her praise rests on a hope the hero's poem shows being kept.

note: Both men in the war camp turn on the wife's ignorance of their pain: Akananuru 304 says she does not know it (நந்நோய் தன்வயின் அறியாள்), Ainkurunuru 441 wishes she knew it (அவள் அறியினோ நன்றே).
teaches: Akananuru 304 spells out what the wife who does not know will think, that the man is without right or grace, so the bare wish of 441 is revealed as the soldier's answer to an imagined accusation of neglect.

note: Both set the home feast against the king's war: the couplet says let the king fight and win and let us feast at evening; 442 says if the king's war subsides she will receive guests in plenty.
teaches: The poem names whose feast the couplet's விருந்து is, the wife as hostess of guests and mother of a son, so the couplet's private wish is shown to be the restoration of a whole household that the king's war holds in suspense.

note: Both end on the same conditional of the camp: the king's elephants with tusk-rings split on enemy forts, and 'if the fierce king releases us' (வினைவிடப் பெறினே / முன்னுதல் பெறினே).
teaches: Akananuru 164 sets the fort-blunted tusks after a whole season scene and her regained beauty, while 444 keeps only the tusks and the sight of her, which shows the worn elephant is the paasarai situation's own sign of a war too long, not a seasonal ornament.

note: The same deep-voiced drum (தழங்குகுரல் முரசம்) sounds in both camps; in Akananuru 24 it keeps the sword-bearing army awake at night, in 448 the man meets sleeplessness thinking of her.
teaches: Read together, the drum that keeps the soldiers sleepless for the king's war is the same drum under which the man lies sleepless for his wife, so the camp's wakefulness is shown to be both duty and longing at once.

note: 449 has the chariot and horses ready on condition the king finishes his work (வேந்துவினை முடினே); Kar Narpathu 20 reports the king's work done (வேந்தன் வினையு முடிந்தன) and the road grown pleasant.
