teaches: The pair gives the two moments of the mullai return, the chariot readied in the camp while the king's work hangs, and the fulfilment when the work is done and the rain-cloud itself seems an army going home.

note: In Akananuru 214 the man in the rain-soaked camp says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while the king does not sleep; in Ainkurunuru 451 the wife says holding out in camp is the king's work (வேந்தனது தொழிலே), not her husband's.
teaches: On the same rainy-season campaign the soldier claims the war as his own duty and the wife assigns it wholly to the king, so the mullai situation is a dispute over where a man's obligation ends, and each side rests on a reading of whose war it is.
audit_text_issue: Akananuru 214's thurai gives the speech to தலைமகள, but the speaker is in the camp; the colophon is likely corrupt. | Akananuru 214 colophon says தலைமகள் though the speaker is in the camp; likely a slip for தலைமகன்.

note: Both open with frogs in every hollow (அவல்தோறு, அவல்தொறும்) and the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே/கின்றால் காலை; in Akananuru 364 the woman concludes that he in the king's camp does not think of us, in Ainkurunuru 453 that his chariot has set out toward us.
teaches: The same signs of the first rains, in nearly the same words, lead one wife to despair and another to expect the chariot, so the season's onset in mullai poetry is not itself a message: its meaning is decided by what the woman believes of the man.
audit_text_issue: 453 line 4 division is uncertain (marker flag). | 453 flagged uncertain sense

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty (தொல்கவின்) and the bangles slip; Ainkurunuru 455: the shoulders, their bangles loosened, have lost their old beauty (தொன்னலம்) just as the rains begin that stop the kings' war.
teaches: The couplet states the wasting of the shoulders as the general mark of separation; the Ainkurunuru poem times it to the rains that end the campaign, so the slipping bangle becomes evidence that he is overdue, not only that he is away.

note: Akananuru 24: in the last days of the cold rains, when the pakanrai opens, the man in the king's camp pictures his wife crossing the cold nights alone; Ainkurunuru 456: in the dewy cold season of pakanrai, the wife asks whether the men who promised to stay do not think of her.
teaches: Her question in 456, does he not think of us, is answered in Akananuru 24, where in the same pakanrai season he does think of her from the camp, so the pair shows that remembering runs both ways while neither lover can know it.

note: Kural 1231: thinking of him who went far, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers; Ainkurunuru 458: the rain-beaten kondrai flowers have come to resemble her eyes, which lost their beauty when he left.
teaches: The couplet's eyes lose a contest with flowers they once outshone; the Ainkurunuru poem reverses the direction, bringing the flowers down to the state of the eyes, so the wasted eyes become the measure the season is read by.

note: Kural 1265: once she has seen her husband to her eyes' fill the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave; Ainkurunuru 459: she asks whether she can embrace his chest so the pallor of her shoulders goes, while he is away with the king.
teaches: Both name the husband's presence as the cure for pallor, but the couplet makes the cure sight while the Ainkurunuru wife makes it embrace and doubts it is possible at all, because the king's war, not the man, decides when he comes.
audit_text_issue: Line 4 is a repaired reading.

note: In 451 the wife argues that endurance in the camp is the king's work, not her husband's; in 460 she admits the king does not weary of the camp and no message comes.
teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from argument to helplessness: the claim in 451 that the king alone should bear the camp turns in 460 into the recognition that the king's appetite for the camp is exactly what holds her husband there.
audit_text_issue: Line 1 of 460 and line 1 of 451 are repaired readings.

note: In both, the friend tells the waiting woman that the konrai bloomed foolishly, taking an unseasonal shower for the rains (Natrinai: கார் என்று அயர்ந்த ... மடவ; Ainkurunuru: காரென மயங்கிய பேதையம் கொன்றை).
teaches: Natrinai answers a question about the promised date by blaming both the mindless cloud and the flowers, while Ainkurunuru answers tears by blaming only the konrai and then vouching for the man, so the 'foolish flower' was a stock rebuttal the friend could aim at the calendar or at grief.

note: Kuruntokai's heroine herself refuses to believe the forest's konrai that says the rains have come, because he does not lie; Ainkurunuru's friend calls the same konrai deceived.
teaches: Read together, the two show that discrediting the konrai's sign was the shared way to keep the man's promise unbroken, whether the heroine did it out of trust in his word or the friend did it to stop her weeping.

note: Akananuru 364's heroine says the rains have begun and her lover in the fierce king's great camp, set on victory, does not think of them (நம்மும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 461's friend says the men of the victorious king's camp will not rest content having left her.
teaches: The same facts, the rains begun and the man held in a victorious king's camp, support despair in the heroine's mouth and assurance in the friend's, so the mullai situation was fixed and only the speaker decided its meaning.

note: Both open on striped frogs croaking and close the scene with the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே காலை.
teaches: The identical formula leads in Akananuru to an evening the heroine cannot swim through and in Ainkurunuru to a chariot arriving today, showing that the first-rain formula was a neutral hinge onto which either the dread of evening or the promise of return could be fastened.
audit_text_issue: ainkurunuru:468 line 4 is supplied from another source.

note: In Akananuru 164 the hero in camp says his wife could regain her beauty this season if only the fierce king would release him; in Ainkurunuru 467 the friend says the king is hurrying more than they are.
teaches: The hero's own speech shows the king as what holds him back, while the friend at home claims the king is more eager than the wives, so the friend's comfort is revealed as persuasion built on a report the camp itself contradicts.

note: Kar Narpathu 20's hero says the king's work is finished and the roads are pleasant; Ainkurunuru 466's friend says the king has released him after the great work and she is sure of his coming.
teaches: The hero announces the release as a fact on the road, while the friend can only infer it at home and stake her certainty on it, so the release from the king's work was the one event both ends of the mullai separation waited on.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 20 colophon reads வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகள், evidently for தலைமகன், since the speaker addresses the charioteer.

note: Kar Narpathu 12's friend takes the dark clouds rising on the right (ஏரும் வலம்) every day as a sign beyond doubt of his coming; Ainkurunuru 469's cloud rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு) to bring him.
teaches: Kar Narpathu treats the rightward rising cloud as evidence to be read, Ainkurunuru as an escort that brings the man and an occasion to go out and watch, so the omen of the right side could serve the friend both as proof and as a reason to act.

note: Both say the rain-season flowers have opened like eyes (கண்ணெனக் கருவிளை மலர; கண்மலர்போற் பூத்தன) as the friend's season sign.
teaches: In Kar Narpathu the eye-like flowers speak and announce the man's return, in Ainkurunuru they only mark a season he cannot forget, so the same flower simile let the friend present the hedge either as a messenger or as a calendar.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 9 line 1 உருவினை is probably a corruption of கருவிளை.

note: 471's heroine resents that the bard keeps coming (இன்னும் வருதி); in 477 the man tells the bard to stay a little as her comfort (உயவுத்துணை).
teaches: Read together, the bard's persistence that the wife takes for indifference turns out to be the man's own order, so the decade shows one act judged from both ends of the separation.
audit_text_issue: Ainkurunuru 471 line 4 is repaired from sangamtamil.com.

note: In 475 the heroine says the bard grieves for her more than his master does; in 480 the bard himself renounces his master over her tears.
teaches: The sympathy the wife reads in the bard's face becomes, by the decade's last poem, a spoken break with the patron, so the decade moves the go-between from the man's party to the woman's.

note: Natrinai 86 blesses the men as அறவர் for coming back before the season they named; Ainkurunuru 472 says the season has come and its makers feel no shame at their false word.
teaches: The named season works as a vow with a moral verdict either way: kept early it earns the title of righteous men, broken it is charged as shamelessness, so the return date was judged as truthfulness rather than as mere timing.

note: Both wives put to the bard a question about the evening of the herding land in the rains (Akananuru: மாலையும் உள்ளார் ஆயின் ... பாண; Ainkurunuru: மாலையும் உடைத்தோ ... பாண).
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives only the wife's accusing question and her name for him, loveless bard, while Akananuru tells it from the bard's side, who could not answer, played and prayed and went toward the man, so the pair shows the question was one the bard had no words for.

note: Both have the waiting woman put a question to or about evening: the Kural asks evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Ainkurunuru asks whether his land has this loveless evening at all.
teaches: The Kural explains the man's calm by a hard heart that evening shares, the Ainkurunuru by a land the evening may not reach, so the two give the waiting woman two answers to why he does not suffer the hour she suffers.

note: In 477 the man tells the bard to stay with his grieving wife (துனி மலி துயரமொடு) and promises his chariot; in Akananuru 314 the wife has asked the bard what will become of her, and the man arrives to end her துனிகொள் பருவரல்.
teaches: The man's instruction and promise in Ainkurunuru and the friend's welcome in Akananuru are two ends of one convention: the bard is posted with the wife to field her question, and the chariot's coming is what answers it.

note: In Akananuru 244 the bard's report of the wife's words makes the man yoke the horses at once, his work being done; in 479 the man, still kept away by the lands between, asks to hear her words again because they are sweet.
teaches: The same report of the wife's words could be a spur that ends the campaign or a comfort savoured while the man stays on, so the bard's message did different work depending on whether the man's task was finished.

note: In Purananuru 144 bards see a woman weeping over Pekan's neglect and rebuke him; in 475 the heroine says the bard wept over her wasting more than his master.
teaches: Puram shows the bard's pity for the neglected woman turned into a public rebuke of his patron, and akam shows the woman herself noticing that pity and setting it against her lord's coldness, so the bard's tears were a recognised charge against the man in both genres.

note: In Purananuru 145 Paranar asks as his only gift that Pekan ride to the grieving woman tonight; in 480 the bard, unheard, declares that he is no longer the man's bard.
teaches: Puram's bard spends his claim on the patron to win the woman's cause, while the Ainkurunuru bard, his plea having failed, gives up the claim itself, so the pair shows the patron bond as the bard's leverage and its renunciation as his last resort.

note: Both returning men order the goad (Ainkurunuru: முள் இட்டு ஊர்மதி; Natrinai: தீண்டா வை முள் தீண்டி), and Natrinai's order opens with the same half-line ஏமதி வலவ தேரே that Ainkurunuru 485 uses.
teaches: Natrinai adds that this goad has never before touched these horses, which shows what Ainkurunuru's bare order assumes: the goad's sting was the convention for an urgency greater than any the charioteer had known.

note: Both set the king's war against the home feast in the man's mouth: the Kural lets the king win and the man feast at evening with his wife; Ainkurunuru says one more day with the victorious king would be an age.
teaches: The Kural states the two duties as a calm pair of wishes, while the Sangam poem shows the strain inside that balance, since the king's victory is honoured in a line and then a single day of further service is weighed as an aeon.

note: Natrinai 81's man pictures his wife eager to prepare a feast for his coming (விருந்து அயர் விருப்பொடு); Ainkurunuru 482's man calls himself the great feast she will have (பெருவிருந்து).
teaches: Read together they show the word virundhu turning in the return poems from the meal the wife prepares to the husband himself as the guest she receives, so his homecoming is framed as the household's rite of hospitality.

note: 483's man drives so the woman may get back her beauty (தன்னலம் பெறவே); in 200 the friend sees the bangles tighten and the brow grow lovely now that the lord of the golden chariot has come.
teaches: The same anthology gives the restoring of beauty first as the returning man's purpose and then as a fact the friend watches on the woman's body, so nalam regained is the agreed proof, in mullai and neythal alike, that a separation is over.

note: Akananuru 144's man imagines his wife saying he does not even remember her hair bare of mullai (கதுப்பும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 484's man says himself that they have stayed long, forgetting her (நீடினம் நேரிழை மறந்தே).
teaches: The charge of forgetting that the longer poem puts in the waiting wife's mouth, the short poem has the husband confess unprompted, so the return poems treat the man's own guilt over the delay as the counterpart of her reproach and the hurried drive as his answer to it.

note: In both the returning man drives through the rain-season scrub where deer run startled; Natrinai 242 follows one stag that will not leave but searches for its scattered doe.
teaches: Ainkurunuru leaves the startled beasts as the land the chariot breaks through, while Natrinai singles out one stag seeking its mate, so the pair shows how the same stock scene becomes a mirror of the man's search for his wife only when one creature is given a lover's act.

note: Both praise the charioteer's wit with the same epithet (Ainkurunuru: மதியுடை வலவ; Kuruntokai: மதியுடை வல்லோய்): Ainkurunuru before the drive, Kuruntokai after it, for cutting a new road and bringing the chariot home today.
teaches: Ainkurunuru asks for the charioteer's skill and Kuruntokai thanks him for having used it, so the two show the charioteer as more than a driver: the returning man credits him with the judgement that ends the wife's suffering.

note: In Akananuru 74 the friend comforts the heroine that the man, seeing the rain-washed scrub, will think of her and say 'drive, charioteer of the strong chariot'; Ainkurunuru 488 is a returning man saying just that as the rains begin.
teaches: Akananuru 74 shows the waiting wife doubting the comfort that he will remember her at the rains, and Ainkurunuru 488 gives the very order the friend predicted, so the decade supplies the man's side of a promise that the akam comforting formula only foretells.

note: Both bid the charioteer drive fast at the evening of the rains, when swarms of bees hum at the fragrant mullai; Akananuru 204 frames it with the Pandya's victory camp and ends on the woman's shoulders.
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives the bee-and-mullai evening with only the girl's sorrowing heart for a goal, Akananuru wraps the same scene in a Pandya campaign, so the pair shows the king's war as an optional frame around a fixed core of season, hour and hurried drive.

note: Kar Narpathu's friend sees flowers bloom like the woman's eyes and hears them announce his return; in 492 the man sees peacock, mullai and deer as likenesses of her and comes home.
teaches: The same likening of the season's things to the woman works from both ends of the separation: for her the flowers that resemble her eyes are messengers of his return, while for him the creatures that resemble her are what sent him home, so the comparison is the bond that carries the promise across.

note: Akananuru 4's friend says the flowering land turns its back on loneliness (புலம்புபுறக் கொடுப்ப) as his chariot comes into view; 495's man says the scrub's loneliness has ended (புலம்பு தீர்ந்து) because he came.
teaches: What the friend in Akananuru offers as a sign that he is about to arrive, the man in 495 claims as his own doing, so the land's loneliness was read as the woman's own, ending at the same moment hers does.

note: Both have winged termites pouring from a red anthill (Purananuru: செம்புற்று ஈயல்; Ainkurunuru: நெடுஞ்செம் புற்றம் ஈயல்); Purananuru makes them the one-day life of kings who defied Vazhuthi.
teaches: The swarm of the first rains meant short-lived ruin in a war poem and food that ends the beasts' hunger in a love poem, and 497's war-loving lord stands between the two, come home from the kind of war in which other men were the termites.

note: In Akananuru 164 the man in the war camp says she would regain her old beauty in this season if only the king released him from his work (வேந்தன் வினைவிடப் பெறினே); 498 reports that the king left off his war (வேந்துதொழில் விட்டென) and her shoulders, bangles and eyes recovered.
teaches: Read together, the two poems give the conditional and its fulfilment of one plot, and show that in these mullai returns the woman's beauty hung on the king's campaign, not on the husband's will alone.

note: The Kural's woman says the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only once she has seen him to her eyes' fill; 498 says her shoulders have regained their beauty because he came.
teaches: The Kural states as the woman's own condition that only his presence cures the pallor, and 498 shows that condition met and observed from outside, item by item on her body, so the couplet's claim is confirmed as the accepted course of the return.

note: The Kural's woman says he went away with his resolve as companion (உள்ளம் துணையாக) and she lives only by longing for his return; 496's friend says he has come back to be the companion of her shoulders (தோள் துணையாக).
teaches: The word துணை marks the turn of the plot: the reproach that he chose his resolve as companion over her is answered on his return, when the companionship is given back to her as embrace, so the Kural's complaint is a stage the akam story expects to close.

note: In 357 the man sees the season-dressed forest himself and gives up the journey for wealth; in 499 he gives up his hard work because she would grieve if she saw the rain-dressed forest.
teaches: Ainkurunuru gives two reasons for the same turning back, the forest's beauty moving the man himself in the paalai decade and the forest's power to hurt her moving him in the mullai decade, so the season is at once his longing and his sense of her danger.

note: Both invocations, ascribed to Perundevanar, list Shiva by the same marks: the konrai garland and chaplet, the bull, the dark throat, the crescent, the matted hair. Akananuru 0 says Umai is joined to him (சேர்ந்தோள் உமையே); Purananuru 1 says the woman's form is one part of him that he can hide within himself.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two openings show each anthology choosing the god's form that suits its matter: the love anthology gives him a consort beside him, the outer anthology a body that holds the woman within it and shelters all lives.

note: Both are Mamoolanar's paalai poems that use Avi's Pothini: in 1 the woman fears the man has forgotten a vow fixed like Pothini's lac-set stone; in 61 the friend tells her he cannot stay away, forgetting her breast, as fine as Pothini.
teaches: One poet hands the same town to both sides of the separation, so Pothini is the woman's measure of the promise in one poem and the friend's measure of the man's longing in the other: the fear and its answer are built from one image.

note: Both speak in the woman's voice after a promise not to part is broken by his leaving: the Kural asks if the believer is at fault; Akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ).
teaches: The Kural turns the broken promise into a question of blame, while the Sangam heroine keeps it a question of memory; the poem shows a woman who will not yet say he broke his word, which the couplet's moral question has already assumed.
audit_text_issue: akananuru:1 line 5 recurs in akananuru:356 line 9.

note: Both are Kapilar's poems in which the friend presses the hill lord to marry: in 2 she still allows that he may come at night past the watchmen, under the vengai and the moon; in 12 she refuses night meetings outright and says the girl will not live if he comes.
teaches: Read in sequence they show the friend's pressure tightening from an ironic permission to a flat refusal, so the varaivu demand is a process with stages, not a single plea.

note: Both men speak to the heart that stands behind them (பின்நின்று): in 3 it drives him from behind toward wealth (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), in 19 it plans to stay behind with her (பின்நின்று ஒழியச் சூழ்ந்தனை).
teaches: The heart at the man's back is a fixed paalai figure that can push either way, toward the road or toward home, so in these poems the heart is not one side of the debate but the place where the debate happens.
audit_text_issue: Ak 3 line 18 repaired.

note: Both place a spot by the formula 'east of Uranthai' (உறந்தைக் குணாது): in Akananuru 4 the tall hill whose kanthal she smells of, in Purananuru 395 Pidavur, the patron Sathan's town.
teaches: The same coordinates serve a patron's address and a woman's fragrance, which shows that akam's landscape was drawn on the real map of Chola country that puram poets used for their patrons.

note: Both answer a man's announced departure for wealth: in Kural 1151 she says 'if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive'; in Akananuru 5 she says nothing, and he gives up the journey.
teaches: The Kural gives the refusal its sharpest words, and the Sangam poem shows the same refusal working without any: from the man's side, it is the unspoken sign and the withering garland on the child that stop him.

note: Both Paranar poems throw at the husband the same scandal, bathing with his beloved in the Kaveri flood (நீ வெய்யோளொடு), and both set it in Chola names: Thithan's Uranthai and Mathi's Kazhar. In 6 the wife speaks; in 226 the friend refuses him entry.
teaches: The repeated phrase and place-names show one marutham scandal reused by its poet from two speakers, so the bath in the Kaveri was a known situation that a hearer recognised from a few words.

note: Both use the formula of Thithan the great giver (மாவண் தித்தன்) and his paddy-rich Uranthai: Purananuru 352 likens the fine gifts offered for a girl, and refused, to Uranthai; Akananuru 6 sets the husband's riverside affair at Uranthai.
teaches: A single praise formula for a Chola chief served the puram poet as the measure of a refused bride-price and the akam poet as the stage of a husband's betrayal, which shows how much shared fame the two kinds of poem drew on.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:352 lines 2, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 16 are broken.

note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the foster mother after the girl's elopement: in 17 she sits at home picturing the girl's small feet on the waste; in 7 she has followed into the forest and is asking a doe and a hill girl for news.
teaches: Together they give the foster mother's grief two stages, imagination at home and pursuit on the road, and show that the poet built the udanpokku mother as a figure who moves through the story.

note: Both speak in the voice of the man returning from work to an evening at home: Kural 1268 wishes the king's war won so that he may feast with his wife at evening; Akananuru 9's work is done and his heart has gone ahead to her at the evening when calves come home.
teaches: The Kural names the evening the man looks forward to, and the Sangam poem fills it from the woman's side, her prayer at the lizard's chirp and the game of covered eyes, with his heart arriving before his chariot.

note: Both make the Chera port Thondi famous for its shore and its fragrance: Purananuru 48's bard calls it his own town, smelling of neythal, to direct another bard to its king; Akananuru 10's friend likens the girl's beauty to rich Thondi.
teaches: The friend values a girl in the terms a bard used for a king's town, so a woman's worth in akam could be stated in the public currency of puram praise, as a reason for open marriage rather than secret meeting.

note: Both praise the lord of Kodai (கோடைப் பொருநன் / கோடைப் பொருந) for giving elephants: Purananuru 205 says the bard's troupe never leaves him without elephants and chariots; Akananuru 13 says he gives to suppliants without limit, pausing only to tame a pit-caught elephant.
teaches: The friend in Akananuru 13 takes the very generosity that Purananuru 205 praises and makes it a ceiling: even wealth that large is not worth a winter apart, so puram praise becomes an akam argument against seeking wealth.

note: Both are mothers after an elopement: the mother in 15 ends by wishing hospitality on the man's town and acknowledging her daughter's resolve; the foster mother in 17 cannot get past the girl's small, tired feet.
teaches: Set together, the two mothers show that the udanpokku lament could close in blessing or in fear, and that the birth mother is the one given the larger acceptance of the daughter's choice.

note: Both are Kapilar's friend speaking to the hill lord about his night visits: in 18 she asks him to come by day instead, to the kanthal grove; in 12, by its colophon after day meetings have been stopped, she refuses the night as well and demands marriage.
teaches: The two poems show the friend's options closing one by one, night refused for day and then day lost to confinement, so the only path left is marriage, the end both poems are built toward.

note: Both join the town's gossip (கவ்வை, கௌவை) and the mother's response: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and the mother's words water to the woman's sickness; in Akananuru 20 the mother acts on the gossip and puts the girl under guard.
teaches: The Kural reads gossip and the mother as feeding love from within, while the Sangam poem shows their outward effect, confinement, and uses it to press the hidden lover to marry, so the couplet's paradox has a practical role in the akam plot.

note: Both are a man mid-road rebuking his heart for wanting to turn back; 21 holds the heart to its own choice and names the aim as making the house glad (மனைநக), 33 concedes never leaving would have been better and names the penalty as others' laughter (பிறர்நகு).
teaches: Read together they show the mid-road speech as a set argument with two stakes, the household's joy if he finishes and public ridicule if he quits, both expressed through laughter.

note: Kural 467 says to think before resolving and calls rethinking after resolve a lapse; in Akananuru 33 the man tells his heart it did not think then, and that to halt the work now would make him a thing others laugh at.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule against second thoughts applied by a lover to his own heart, and adds what the maxim omits: the resolved deed costs a wife left behind, and the man accepts that cost rather than the shame of turning back.

note: 23 is the wife at the end of the rains, seeing the promised season come without him; 24 is a man in the king's camp at the end of the cold rains, picturing his wife alone through the nights.
teaches: Set side by side in the anthology's order, the same season is seen from the empty house and from the sleepless camp, so each poem supplies the half of the separation the other cannot see.

note: Both describe the king's war camp at midnight with the long-tongued bright bell (நெடுநா ஒண்மணி) and the roaring drum; Mullaippattu's king lies awake thinking of the enemy while his queen waits, and Akananuru 24's soldier speaks of his wife alone at home.
teaches: The shared bell formula shows the midnight camp was a stock scene, and the two poems use it from different ranks: the idyll gives it to the king, the short poem to a man in his army whose wife waits like the idyll's queen.

note: Kural 1268 has a man serving in the king's war wish the king victory so that he may feast at home with his wife by evening; Akananuru 24 is such a man in the king's camp at the end of the rains, measuring the camp's sleepless night against his wife's lonely one.
teaches: The couplet states the soldier-husband's wish as a sentence; the poem gives the night that produces it, the blunted tusks, the drums and the cold rain, so the Kural's two clauses read as the end of a long vigil.

note: In 25 the falls on the hill sound like the sweet music of Thithiyan, lord of Pothiyil, victor in battle; in 36 Thithiyan is one of the seven kings crushed by Chezhiyan at Alankanam.
teaches: One chief serves in adjacent akam poems as a figure of glory and as one of the defeated, which shows the poets drew on a chief's fame and his fall alike as material for similes.

note: Both tell Nedunchezhiyan's one-man victory over seven kings at Alankanam in the same phrase, எழுவர் நல்வலம் அடங்க; Purananuru 76 praises it as unheard of, Akananuru 36 uses its victory shout to measure the noise of gossip about a husband's new wife.
teaches: The identical phrase in a praise poem and in a wife's complaint shows the battle had a fixed formula that akam poets lifted whole, so a private quarrel could borrow the loudest public event the audience knew.

note: Both show hero-stones by a stony cairn (பதுக்கை) crowned with peacock feathers (பீலி சூட்டி) for men who died over cattle; Purananuru 264 is the lament for one such fallen man, Akananuru 35 sees such stones only as worship on the road a runaway daughter took.
teaches: The puram poem tells who lies under the stone and who will miss him; the akam poem shows how the same stones looked to a mother who saw only their danger, so a hero's memorial became a mark of the perils of the wild road.

note: Purananuru 126 praises Malaiyaman Kari as lord of the Pennai country and giver to bards; Akananuru 35 likens a daughter's hair to the fine sand-ripples of the Pennai at Kari's ford.
teaches: A patron's river, praised in puram for the gifts it brings bards, became in akam a stock likeness of a girl's beauty, so a chief's fame lent its landscape to love poetry.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's frenzy-ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among Murugan's abodes, with red millet and blood scattered and the god called down (முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த), where seekers gain what they ask; Akananuru 22 describes the same rite and the heroine laughs that it was wasted on a stranger priest, since her lover was the cure.
teaches: The devotional idyll and the love poem share the rite's very words, but the akam poem limits its power: the god may come, yet the velan's diagnosis of a girl's sickness is wrong, so the rite's authority stops where secret love begins.

note: Kural 1323 asks whether any heaven equals sulking with one joined to you as water to earth; in Akananuru 26 the wife cannot sulk because her husband melted like ploughed red earth taking the rain.
teaches: The couplet makes the earth-and-water bond the reason sulking is sweet, while the poem uses the same image to end the sulk, which shows the likeness can either sustain lovers' quarrel or dissolve it, depending on who is melting.

note: In both a man back from the road answers his wife's charge that he forgot her: 29 says his body was held by shame to the work while his heart stayed with her, 39 offers a dream on the road in which he comforted her.
teaches: Two poets give the same answer in two forms, a division of body from heart and a dream, which shows that the reply to 'did you think of us' had to prove an inner presence the separation itself denied.

note: Both liken the beloved's coming to rain on those who live by it: the Kural states it as a rule of lovers' grace, Akananuru 42 makes it a drought broken at dawn over a whole countryside.
teaches: The Kural's two-line rain simile is the compressed form of a scene the Sangam poet builds at length, so the couplet's image carries the whole drought-and-tank picture behind it.

note: In 43 the man calls leaving a companion for wealth folly (மடமை) and pities those who do it; in 53 the heroine says her man left because his heart could not refuse the needy, a virtue she still reads as love of wealth over her.
teaches: Read together they show the paalai debate from both sides: the same departure is folly to one man and an unrefusable duty of giving to another, and the woman left behind refuses to call either grace.

note: Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and let us feast at home in the evening; Akananuru 44 opens with the king's work done and the tribute paid, and bids the chariot race home to sleep on her breast.
teaches: The Kural's couplet is the akam homecoming formula of the returning warrior reduced to its two clauses, the king's victory first and the household's evening second.
audit_text_issue: Colophon thinai of 44 is flagged (commentary gives பாலை).

note: Akananuru 44 records Pazhaiyan's fall in a war of many chiefs; Akananuru 186 uses Pazhaiyan's town Por on the Kaveri as a likeness for a bangle that will not be broken.
teaches: The same chief appears in one akam poem as a fallen man and in another as the owner of an unbreakable town, so akam poets drew on a chief's fame both before and after his fall.
audit_text_issue: Colophon thinai of 44 is flagged (commentary gives பாலை).

note: Both use Anni's cutting of Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai: 45 measures the gossip by the bards' clamour that day, 145 wishes on the foster mother's hand the fate of that felled tree.
teaches: One puram event served akam poets in two opposite ways, as a measure of noise and as a curse of destruction, which shows these battles were a shared stock of reference the audience was expected to know.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Both liken a woman's bangle to a rich king's town (Chezhiyan's Allur in 46, Pazhaiyan's Por in 186), one from the wife's side and one from the courtesan's.
teaches: The town-like bangle is a shared formula that both rivals in the marutham triangle could use, so the formula marks a woman's claim on the man, not which side she is on.

note: In both a cry of 'tiger' on the vengai slope brings men running: in 48 the girls' cry brings the young hunter who becomes the lover, in 52 a hill girl's cry for flowers brings the hill men with bows.
teaches: Together they show the vengai-plucking cry as a known custom of the hill, and 48 turns that public alarm into the private occasion of a first meeting that 52's heroine now wants kept secret.

note: Kural 1155 says if he leaves, union becomes hard (நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு); in 51 the man tells his heart that wealth is joined only by parting, and chooses to stay.
teaches: The same word புணர்வு carries both sides of one exchange: the Kural's woman counts what parting costs union, and the Sangam man counts what union costs wealth.

note: Kural 1138 says love breaks through secrecy into the public square whatever the lover's restraint; in 52 the heroine, her pallor already visible, still forbids her friend to name it even at the cost of her life.
teaches: The Kural's rule that love cannot be hidden is qualified by the Sangam heroine's will: the body discloses it, but the naming is still hers to refuse.

note: Kural 223 counts not saying 'I have nothing' and giving as the mark of the well-born; in 53 that very inability to refuse the needy is what drives the man away from the heroine.
teaches: The Kural's praise of giving has a cost the Kural does not count: in akam the generous man's virtue is the cause of the woman's abandonment.

note: Pannan of Sirukudi is praised in Purananuru 173 as the healer of hunger whose house feeds crowds; in Akananuru 54 his village's gooseberry gives the simile and he is called one who lives not for himself but for others.
teaches: An akam poet could fold a puram patron's reputation into one epithet inside a love poem, which shows how well-known Pannan's generosity was.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Akananuru 54 calls Pannan தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்.
teaches: The kaanchi poem's general ideal and the akam poem's praise of one patron use the same contrast of self and others, so the maxim was already a phrase of praise for real patrons.

note: Both tell of Cheralathan, ashamed of his back wound from the fight with Karikalan, sitting facing north to die; Purananuru 65 laments the king, Akananuru 55 turns to the noble men who died with him.
teaches: The akam poem keeps a detail the puram lament leaves out, the companions who followed the king into death, and uses it to measure a mother's wish that her life would follow her daughter.

note: Both use the battle at Venni: in 246 the uproar of Karikalan's victory measures the town's gossip, in 55 the defeated Chera's death measures a mother's grief.
teaches: One battle gave akam poets images from both sides, the victor's clamour for gossip and the loser's death for grief, so a puram event's meaning in akam depends on whose side the image is taken from.

note: Both name Chezhiyan's attack on Musiri, the Chera port: 149 has him seize an image there, 57 compares the wife's suffering to the wounded in that clamorous siege.
teaches: Two separate paalai poems witness the same Pandya assault on Musiri, which shows a single war entering the akam repertoire as a ready image of suffering and plunder.
audit_text_issue: Line count of 57 flagged (19 vs 18).

note: Purananuru 93 describes the rite of cutting with a sword the body of a king who died of sickness, so that he goes where battle-slain warriors go; Akananuru 61 opens with the saying behind that rite (blessed are those who die at others' hands, not seized by Death) as the reason a man leaves home.
teaches: Together they show the warrior's creed about a good death working at two scales: as a royal funeral rite in puram, and in akam as a proverb that sends an ordinary man away from his wife to strive.
audit_text_issue: 93 lines 2-11 are syntactically compressed. | 93 lines 2-11 are compressed. | purananuru:93 lines 2-11 are compressed; the rite reading is likely but the syntax is not certain

note: Both are the friend's comfort in paalai: in 61 even winning Pulli's Venkatam will not keep him, in 209 even going beyond Pulli's Venkatam he will not forget; both close by likening the heroine's beauty to a famous place (Pothini, the Kolli image).
teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served the paalai poets as the fixed northern limit of a man's absence, so different poets could promise his return by measuring it against the same frontier and the same kind of famous-place likeness.

note: Paranar in 62 and Kalladanar in 209 both liken the heroine to the image on Kolli that a god made: one in the lover's own memory after a failed tryst, the other in the friend's comfort during his absence.
teaches: The Kolli image was a shared likeness for a beauty that cannot be harmed or taken, used by a kurinji lover and a paalai friend alike, so the legend of the hill carried a fixed sense of untouchable loveliness.

note: Both are the returning man's words to his charioteer in mullai, and both set a pair of beasts going together (the stag and doe in 34, the bull and heifer in 64) beside his haste; 64 adds the cows' evening bells, which the wife hears alone.
teaches: The pairing shows the iraicchi tied to the speech situation rather than to one animal, and 64 develops it by making the herd's homecoming the very sound that hurts the woman, so the same image both promises his return and measures her waiting.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for giving the great feast without limit; Akananuru 65 likens the girls' joy at eloping to that of the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral.
teaches: The king's puram fame as a feeder of bards had become a proverbial measure of gladness, so an akam friend could express release from a watchful mother by the bards' delight at his court.

note: Kural 62 says evil will not touch for seven births those who have children free of blame; Akananuru 66 quotes a saying of the same kind (blameless sons bring fame here and a stainless next world) and finds it true when a toddler stops his father from marrying another wife.
teaches: The pair shows a maxim about a child's merit protecting the parent being tested in a household quarrel, where its proof is not the next world but a husband held at home, which shifts the rule from the father's destiny to the mother's marriage.

note: Lines 10 and 11 of 67 repeat lines 11 and 12 of 131 word for word (the hero-stones inscribed with names, crowned with peacock feathers, like a battle front with planted spears); in 67 the woman knows the road by report, in 131 the man refuses to take her along it.
teaches: The repeated couplet shows the hero-stone road as a fixed formula shared by poets, and the two poems turn it to opposite ends: hearsay that terrifies the woman left at home, and the man's reason for not taking her.

note: Both use nearly the same words for the Moriyar, whose chariots under sky-touching umbrellas cut a path through the rock with their wheels: in 69 that rock marks how far the man has gone, in Purananuru 175 the cutting's circle is a likeness for a patron's constancy.
teaches: The northern invaders' cut through the hills was a shared memory that akam used as a mark of distance and puram as an image of something fixed and open to all, showing one historical feature serving both kinds of poem.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Akananuru 69 says the man left for wealth wanting exactly that joy (ஈதல் இன்பம் வெஃகி), and the friend draws from it that he will not delay.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's joy of giving as the stated motive of the akam journey for wealth, so the separation the paalai poems lament is grounded in a virtue, and the friend can use that virtue as a promise of his return.

note: Akananuru 70 likens the town's silence after the wedding to the banyan Rama hushed at Kodi for his secret counsel; Purananuru 378 likens a bard's kin, putting on jewels the wrong way, to the monkeys who found Sita's jewels on the ground.
teaches: These are two early Tamil uses of the Rama story, both of minor episodes and both as similes, one akam and one puram, which shows the story was familiar enough to be drawn on for a passing likeness rather than told.

note: Kural 247 sets wealth and grace side by side as what this world and the next require; the man in Akananuru 75 quotes the saying that effort for wealth, not grace, is a man's task and refuses it, since nothing in this world can give back what parting wastes.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's balance of wealth and grace becomes a choice in a marriage, and the akam man qualifies the Kural's grant of this world to wealth by naming one thing in this world that wealth cannot restore.

note: In 45 the wife likens herself to Aathi Manthi, distraught after losing her husband; in 76 the courtesan tells the same legend and casts herself as the Kaveri that held the dancer, leaving the wife as Aathi Manthi.
teaches: The same legend serves the wife's lament and the courtesan's boast, which shows the akam poets reading a story from either side of a quarrel, and that the river's part could be claimed with pride.

note: Purananuru 172 praises Pittan, lord of the hard country, for his spear that wins hard battles and his great giving; Akananuru 77 names Pittan, Chera's warrior with unending toddy, and likens the woman's tearful eyes to the spear he raised against hostile kings.
teaches: The pair shows a chief's puram praise (his spear and his gifts) reused in akam, where his famous spear becomes the measure of the pain her eyes will cause, so the poet trusts listeners to know the patron's weapon.

note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

note: Both name Pulli's Venkatam: in 61 the friend says the man would not stay even for Venkatam with its festivals; in 83 the man says her virtues followed him past Venkatam regardless of distance.
teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served akam poets as the fixed far edge of the wealth journey, and they turned it both ways: a prize too small to hold the man, and a distance too short to stop the woman's pull.

note: Venkatam is Thiraiyan's hill of the victorious spear in 85 and lies in the land of Pulli, chief of the unlettered young men, in 83.
teaches: The same frontier hill is credited to two different lords by poets of one anthology, so Venkatam in akam is a border claimed by more than one chief, not a fixed realm.

note: In 44 the enemies pay their tribute and the man drives home; in 84 the king refuses the tribute offered and the man stays in the camp through the promised rains.
teaches: The mullai homecoming hangs on one puram act, the king's acceptance of tribute: taken, it frees the soldier, refused in anger, it holds him, so the woman's waiting is timed by a royal decision she never sees.

note: The foster mother in 89 sees the elopement road as a waste of marauders, slaughtered guards and failed rains; the lover in 99 calls the same kind of forest good and lovely, a temple town strewn with flowers.
teaches: The anthology gives the elopement road two incompatible descriptions from the two people with a stake in it, so the paalai landscape is a speaker's argument, made terrible by the one who loses the girl and beautiful by the one who takes her.

note: Kuttuvan's land is the measure of wealth in both: in Purananuru 343 a father refuses wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri as bride-price; in Akananuru 91 the man would not stay for Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, forgetting his wife.
teaches: Kuttuvan's riches stood in both books as the outer limit of wealth, and both poems use it to say a woman outweighs it: in puram the father refuses it for his daughter, in akam the husband refuses it for his wife.

note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola assembly at Uraiyur where justice stands unfailing; Akananuru 93 compares the man's hard-won treasure to the virtue-filled assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur.
teaches: The justice of Uraiyur's assembly, a praise theme in puram, was famous enough to serve an akam poet as a simile for something precious, so the court's moral fame had become a byword for worth itself.

note: Kural 524 says the fruit of gaining wealth is to be surrounded by kin; the man in 93 gives exactly this reason (ending the kin's ruin, feeding relatives, making strangers kin) for the journey that took him from his wife.
teaches: The Kural's purpose for wealth is the very reason the paalai hero gives for leaving, so the akam poem shows what the maxim costs in separation, and puts the return to the wife, not the kin, at the end.

note: In Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip manures her love-sickness and her mother's words water it; in Akananuru 95 the mother answers the gossiping women in her daughter's defence, and that trust is what the girl cannot face.
teaches: The Kural's couplet assumes a scolding mother whose words feed the love; the Sangam scene shows the harder case, where the mother's kindness against the town's gossip is what leaves the girl helpless, so the same two pressures can work through trust as well as blame.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veriyattu ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among the true places where Murugan comes to those who seek him; in Akananuru 98 the same rite, with kadambu, palm leaf and the god's great name praised, is a misreading of love-sickness by deluded women.
teaches: The same veriyattu rite is a real dwelling of the god in the devotional idyll and a comic error in the love poem, so the Sangam akam convention could treat Murugan's possession as a cover story without denying the god, who here might even cure her.

note: Kural 210 says that ruin is rare for one who does not stray into evil; the heroine of 101 quotes the same rule as an old proverb (நன்றுசெய் மருங்கில் தீதுஇல்) and asks whether it has turned false, since she did nothing hateful and is still left. On her reading the rule has failed.
teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's assurance was already an old proverb in the Sangam age, and that akam poetry was where it was tested: a blameless woman's abandonment is the counter-case the maxim does not answer.

note: Purananuru 158 names Ezhini among the seven dead givers, with his horse and sharp spear; Akananuru 105 names Ezhini of many spears with his horse, whose bowmen drive off cattle on the daughter's road. That both mean the same chief is likely but not certain.
teaches: The chief keeps the same epithets of horse and spear in both books, but the bard remembers him as a lost giver while the mother sees only his raiders on her daughter's road, so a patron's fame looked different from the path his men made dangerous.

note: Both marutham poems bring in Chezhiyan's wars: in 106 the courtesan wishes the wife would beat her own belly like the drum his bard beats at each victory; in 116 the friend says the gossip about the hero's river-play is louder than the shout at Koodal when Chezhiyan routed two kings.
teaches: Set side by side they show the Pandya's victories serving both parties to one marutham quarrel, the courtesan's curse and the wife's friend's reproach, so royal war was the common measure of household noise and anger whoever spoke.

note: Kural 551 judges the king who harasses his people and does wrong to be crueller than murderers; Akananuru 109 sets the murderers' road, with cairns over men shot though they carried nothing, in hills ruled by a king without aram (அறன்இல் வேந்தன்).
teaches: The Kural ranks the bad king against killers in the abstract, while the akam poet already draws the lawless realm and the murderous road as one landscape, so a lover's journey becomes the evidence of what a king without aram costs those who travel his land.

note: Kural 657 says the worthy prefer utter poverty to wealth gained under blame; the friend in Akananuru 112 says the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்), and so the hero should marry.
teaches: The same rule of the worthy, refusing any gain that brings blame, governs wealth in the Kural and love in the Akananuru, and the friend turns it from a counsel of going without into an argument for marriage, which removes the blame without removing the pleasure.

note: Same situation: a man held by the king's war who longs to be home at evening. Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and we will hold the evening feast with the household; in Akananuru 114 the war is done and the hero urges his charioteer to reach his wife before the evening's grief.
teaches: The couplet's two clauses, victory and then the evening at home, become in the poem a race against dusk, and the poem adds what the couplet leaves out: evening is the hour when the waiting wife suffers most, so his haste is to end her sorrow as much as to begin his feast.

note: Purananuru 233 is a bard's cry at the dawn news of Evvi's wounds, wishing it false; Akananuru 115 recalls the battle where Evvi fell and, on our reading, the bards breaking off and laying down the curved necks of their harps in worship.
teaches: The puram poem gives the bards' words at Evvi's fall and the akam poem their gesture, so together they show that his death was mourned with a known bardic rite that a love poet could cite as an image for seed pods on a road.
audit_text_issue: 233 marked uncertain; Akuthai's wheel (line 3 to 4) cannot be explained from the text. | 233 flagged uncertain

note: Purananuru 76 praises Chezhiyan, who alone defeated the seven who joined against him; Akananuru 116 recalls Chezhiyan at Koodal routing two great kings who rose together. The battles may not be the same.
teaches: Both poets make the Pandya's fame the defeat of an alliance, seven kings in the puram praise and two great kings in Paranar's simile, so one king against a coalition was the shape his fame took, whichever battle is meant.

note: Both are paalai laments over a daughter who eloped: in 105 the mother recalls the girl refusing milk from her nurses and caring nothing for the house's wealth; in 117 the foster mother recalls the girl refusing to let her wash her hair, which the lover now dresses.
teaches: Read together, the two laments divide the girl's upbringing between the women who raised her, the mother grieving through food and wealth and the foster mother through the hair she tended, and each measures the loss by a care the lover now takes over.
audit_text_issue: ak117's poet is not preserved.

note: In 118 the friend closes both trysts, fearing gossip by day and the tiger by night; in 112 she meets him at night, says he did wrong to come through the tiger's grove, and gives the moral ground for marriage.
teaches: Taken together they show the friend's case for marriage in two steps: 118 makes every meeting impossible without naming marriage, and 112 names it and supplies the reason a worthy man must accept, that the worthy want no pleasure that brings blame.

note: Both turn on Karikalan's victories: Purananuru 66 praises the king but sets above him the defeated king at Venni who, ashamed of a wound in the back, starved himself to death; Akananuru 125 likens the fleeing north wind to the nine kings who abandoned their umbrellas on the Vaakai field.
teaches: Read together they show the warrior code from both sides: the loser who dies of shame earns more praise than the victor, while the losers who run are proverbial for disgrace, so an akam poet could call a wind cowardly by naming Karikalan's battle.
audit_text_issue: Colophon thurai of 125 carries a stray '2' before தலைமகன்.

note: Both tell of Anni and Thithiyan's punnai tree: 145 has Anni felling the old punnai at the Kurukkai field, 126 has Anni, deaf to Evvi's counsel, coveting the punnai and dying in the fight.
teaches: The two poems give two halves of one story, the felling of the tree in 145 and the rejected counsel and death in 126, and each poet used only the half his speaker needed: a curse on the man who took a daughter, a warning to a stubborn heart.

note: Both name Cheralathan who drove off the sea-foe and cut the kadamba: in 127 his buried tribute is the measure of wealth the lover would refuse, in 347 the drum made after that victory is the measure of the town's loud gossip.
teaches: One king's campaign gave akam poets two different scales, its plunder for riches and its victory drum for noise, which shows how a puram deed was broken into separate stock comparisons.

note: Both are the man's words after first seeing the girl, about her eyes: the Kural says her look eats the life of those who see it; the Akananuru man tells the friends who rebuke him that they would not rebuke him if they had seen her look.
teaches: The Kural states the power of the look as a general truth, while the Akananuru puts it into a defence before the man's companions, showing that the couplet's claim first served as the hero's answer to rebuke (கழற்றெதிர்மறை).

note: Both describe the hero-stone of a man killed recovering cattle, crowned with peacock feather and inscribed with his name (பீலி சூட்டி, பெயர் பொறித்து); 264 mourns the dead man, 131 lines the road with such stones.
teaches: Purananuru 264 shows one stone as a single loss to the bards who depended on the man, and Akananuru 131 shows rows of them as the reason a lover will not travel, so the same memorial carried grief in puram and deterrence in akam.

note: In both a returning man in the rains spares mating creatures: in 4 he has tied his chariot bells so the bees paired in the flowers are not startled, in 134 he tells the charioteer to drive gently lest the stag and doe in union hear the chariot.
teaches: Placed side by side the two poems show a fixed mullai motif, the returning husband's gentleness toward paired creatures, that a poet could vary from bees to deer and from the man's own act to his order to the charioteer.

note: Both have the waiting girl say her pallor is like the peerkku flower (பீர்) and her bewilderment like Aathi Manthi's (பேதுற்று), alongside a siege simile for her state.
teaches: The repetition of three linked images in two poems by different poets shows that pallor, Aathi Manthi and a besieged town formed a ready set for the abandoned girl's lament.

note: Kazhuvul's Kamur appears in both: in 135 it is the town besieged by fourteen Velir, the image of her shaken heart; in 365 it is the place whose fragrant vengai the girl's hair recalls to the travelling man.
teaches: The same chieftain's town served one poet as a picture of ruin and another as a picture of fragrance, so akam poets drew on a place's whole fame, its war and its groves, and not on a single fixed meaning.

note: Both describe the rains that mark the promised return: in 4 the friend points to the rains to assure the girl he is coming; in 139 the rains are already over and he has not come.
teaches: Read in sequence the friend's argument from the season in 4 meets its test in 139, where the same signs, unanswered, turn from a promise into proof of delay.

note: Both are neythal poems in which the man answers his companion about a girl's eyes; in 130 she stands on Korkai's pearl-strewn harbour, in 140 she is a salt-merchant's daughter crying her wares in the street.
teaches: The same thurai is given to a girl of the rich harbour and to a salt-seller's daughter, and in 140 the man even compares himself to her father's ox, so the kalavu situation was open to heroines of trading families and drew its images from their work.

note: Both are Paranar's and both tell of Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili: in 208 the birds gather to shade the fallen man from the sun; in 148 the owl, ashamed, does not go out by day to see him.
teaches: Read together they show the legend had a second bird in it: the night owl that could not join the daylight shading, and the poet uses that one bird's shame as a reason for lovers to meet by night.
audit_text_issue: 208 lines 12 to 18 (Nannan and அகுதை கிளைதந்தாங்கு) are obscure.

note: In 142 the man Minjili killed at Nannan's Paazhi is Athikan, 'a protection to the birds' (புள்ளிற்கு ஏமம்); in 181 it is Aay Eyinan who falls to Minjili and a flock of birds hides the sun over him.
teaches: The epithet in 142 is explained by the scene in 181, but the name differs, so the bird-shade legend either belonged to one hero known by two names or moved between heroes of the Paazhi wars.
audit_text_issue: 142 lines 7 to 14 attach loosely to the sentence; marker flagged uncertain.

note: Both use the felling of the old punnai at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan: in 45 the gossip is louder than the bards' cheers that day; in 145 the foster mother curses her own hand to be cut down like that tree.
teaches: One puram event served the akam poets as a measure of two different things, public noise in one poem and deserved ruin in the other, so the war's fame had become a store of ready comparisons.

note: Purananuru 170 praises Pittan as soft to those who come in hope (நசைவர்க்கு மென்மை) and iron to enemies; Akananuru 143 calls him the giver of fine vessels to those who live by hope (நசையின் வாழ்நர்க்கு) and sets the woman's tears in a pool on his hill.
teaches: The akam poet takes from Pittan's fame the same formula of giving to the hopeful that the praise poem uses, which shows a patron's epithet passing whole between the two kinds of poetry.

note: In Purananuru 343 a father refuses suitors even if they bow and offer wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) like Muziri's, where ships bring gold for pepper; in Akananuru 149 the man refuses precious wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) even if easily won, beside Muziri where Yavana ships bring gold and take pepper.
teaches: Muziri's sea trade was the stock measure of the wealth a woman outweighs, used by the war poem for a father keeping his daughter and by the love poem for a husband keeping his wife.

note: Akananuru 152 names Aay as the one who gives to all who come, whether able or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்); Purananuru 134 says Aay is no trader in virtue who gives in this life for a return in the next.
teaches: Together they make Aay's giving unconditional on both sides, asking nothing of the receiver's skill and nothing of the next world, which neither poem says alone.

note: The man's maxim quoted in 151 is that the poor cannot support their dependants or laugh among their kin; Kural 1047 says poverty makes a man a stranger even to the mother who bore him.
teaches: The Kural states as a rule the claim the akam hero uses to justify leaving, and the poem shows what the rule costs when it is acted on: the wife says it leaves no room for grace.

note: Kural 760 says that for those who make bright wealth the other two (virtue and pleasure) come easily together; in Akananuru 155 the man says two things come from wealth, a life free of wrong and a wealth that never begs, and leaves.
teaches: The hero's version of the Kural's claim drops pleasure from the pair, and the poem makes that omission visible: the household pleasure is exactly what his errand for wealth suspends.

note: Both answer the man's announced departure: in Kural 1151 the reply (the friend's or the woman's) is a sharp refusal, tell your quick return to those who will survive; in Akananuru 143 the friend only reports the woman's tears at his 'small word', and the colophon says he stayed.
teaches: The same thurai had two answers, the Kural's barbed argument and the Sangam friend's report of tears, and the poem shows the second one succeeding, which the couplet's general statement cannot show.

note: In 149 the man says even easily won wealth is not worth her tears and stays; in 155 the man holds that virtue and independence both come only from wealth, and goes. On the plain reading they are incompatible verdicts on whether wealth justifies the parting.
teaches: The anthology sets the paalai argument on both sides in the men's own voices, so the case for going and the case for staying are each given their strongest form.

note: Both are a foster mother's lament after the girl has eloped across the desert; 153 blames the girl's trust in a hard man and fears for her soft feet, 145 turns the blame on the speaker's own hand that once beat her.
teaches: Together they give the two directions of the mother's grief in this thurai, outward to the girl's heedlessness and inward to her own harshness, both ending on the girl's tender body set against the road.

note: Both are the homecoming man's words to his charioteer, and both put a stag with twisted horns (திரிமருப்பு இரலை, இருதிரி மருப்பின் இரலை) by clear water (தெள்அறல்) caring for or resting with his mate, with the word ஏமுற.
teaches: Shared phrases across two poets show the stag with his mate is a fixed formula of this thurai, and in 34 ஏமுற is the man's own heart's ease while in 154 it is the beasts', so the formula passes the same rest from beast to man.

note: Kural 1157 has the woman say her slipping bangles already announce that the lord of the shore has left; in Akananuru 161 the friend tells the man the girl's tears show she has already understood his plan to go.
teaches: The poem turns the couplet's body-as-herald into an argument: the friend uses the tears that announce his going as the reason he should not go, so the sign the Kural records becomes a plea.

note: Both are the friend speaking to a man about to leave for the waste; 161 argues from the girl's tears, which already know, 179 from the dangers of the road and the girl's face.
teaches: Read together they show two tactics in the same office of dissuasion: one presents the departure as already a wound, the other as a risk set against a beauty left alone.

note: In 162 the man tells his heart of the midnight storm and the guarded house he braved to meet her; in 168 the friend tells such a man that the night path, with its tiger and darkness, must be given up.
teaches: The danger the lover counts as proof of his love is the very thing the friend uses to end the night meetings and press for marriage, so the same night risk carries opposite verdicts by speaker.

note: Both women, left alone, send a non-human messenger to the absent man: in 163 the cold north wind, in 170 the crab of the backwater.
teaches: The messenger is drawn from the poem's own season and land, the wind of the rains' end in one and the shore crab in the other, so even the convention of the go-between is fitted to its landscape.

note: Both are a man in the king's war camp telling his heart about his wife in the rains; in 164 he waits for the king to release him, in 174 he has turned away from further battle and she does not yet know he is coming.
teaches: Together they mark two moments of the same camp poem: the season of return arriving while duty holds him, and the moment he is free but her grief still runs ahead of the news.

note: In 166 the other woman mocks the husband's false oath so the wife's people hear; in 176 the wife's friend describes the other woman's public rage and refuses him the door.
teaches: Heard from both sides of the quarrel, the affair is fought through what the town hears: each woman's party uses the other's public display as its weapon against the husband.

note: In 167 the man, before leaving, pictures the ruined village where he would sleep and gives up the journey; in 169 a man who has already crossed many wastes pictures his wife grieving at evening.
teaches: The pair shows the road imagined from both ends of the decision: before setting out it is a desolation that keeps him home, after setting out it is the distance that makes her grief visible to him.

note: Akananuru 168 compares the roar of the waterfalls to the kitchen of Udhiyan, bound to the duty of giving; Purananuru 2 praises the Chera king who gave great food without limit to the armies of the war.
teaches: The akam poet can borrow the noise of Udhiyan's kitchen as a simile because his feeding was proverbial in puram praise, so a king's fame for food had become a stock measure of uproar.

note: In 172 the friend reproaches the hill-man for lovelessness to press him to marry; in 178 marriage is settled and the friend blesses the union, quoting his own words of devotion.
teaches: Read in sequence the friend's two speeches show the pressure for marriage and its answer, and her blessing in 178 quotes the very love she doubted in 172.

note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; in Akananuru 173 the man says that dharma and helping kin in ruin are not for those who sit at ease, and leaves to earn.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's premise about wealth working inside a marriage: it becomes the husband's reason for leaving and the friend's ground for comfort, and it shows the cost the maxim omits.

note: Akananuru 173 places the man's road on the gold-bearing slopes of Nannan of the swift chariot; Purananuru 151 names a patron as kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, whose hill was shut against poets.
teaches: Both books know Nannan by his chariot and his hill, but the puram poem remembers his line for a door shut against singers while the akam poem uses his range only for its gold and its danger, so the same name carries blame in one genre and mere geography in the other.

note: Both are the friend assuring the woman that the absent man will return; in 173 he will return because of his principle and his promise, in 177 because he will remember her body.
teaches: Side by side they show two grounds the friend can give for hope, his word and his desire, so the same office of comfort can rest on duty or on longing.

note: Akananuru 175 compares the lightning to the spear Chezhiyan raised after he won the battle at Alangaanam (ஆலங் கானத்து அமர்கடந்து); Purananuru 23 praises Nedunchezhiyan with the same phrase.
teaches: The identical phrase shows the victory at Alangaanam was already a formula, so an akam poet could use a celebrated battle to light up a love poem's rain clouds.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring word are at fault when the one who said 'do not fear' leaves; in Akananuru 175 the woman recalls his vows, the hand on her wrist and the promised season, which has now come.
teaches: The poem supplies the concrete pledge the couplet only names (a vow, a grasped wrist, a named season) and fixes the moment of testing at the arrival of the promised rains.

note: Akananuru 177 places a fertile mango grove on the Kaveri's north bank in the land of Pannan of the warrior anklets; Purananuru 173 praises Pannan of Sirukudi as the healer of hunger whose house rings with feeding.
teaches: If this is the same Pannan, akam uses the puram patron's land as a byword for fertile beauty, so a patron's renown for feeding becomes a measure of a woman's beauty.

note: Kural 1151, which Parimelazhagar gives to the friend, refuses to hear of a quick return; in Akananuru 179 the friend asks the departing man whether he can bear to live away while she is left alone.
teaches: The couplet compresses the friend's dissuasion into a threat of death, and the poem shows the fuller form of the same speech, arguing from the dangers of the road and the woman's beauty.

note: Akananuru 179 line 1 and Purananuru 151 line 2 are the same line (விண்தோய் சிமைய விறல்வரைக் கவாஅன்); in puram it is the slope of a patron's hill, in akam the slope of the dangerous waste.
teaches: The repeated line shows the poets shared formulas across akam and puram, and that the setting decides whether the same sky-touching slope means a patron's wealth or a lover's danger.

note: Both Paranar poems recall Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili with birds over the field: in 208 the birds shade the dead hero from the sun with their wings, in 181 a great flock dances thick in the sky and hides the sun's heat as he falls.
teaches: Read with 208, the bird flock in 181 is the known sign of Eyinan's death, the birds' honour to a fallen giver, so Paranar can use that public story as a mere measure of how thickly the Kaveri heaps its sand.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are flagged uncertain; 208 line 18 (அகுதை கிளைதந்தாங்கு) is obscure.

note: 262 tells the story of Anni Minjili, who refused food and white clothes after the Kosar blinded her father and was satisfied only when Thithiyan killed them; 196 names her in one line as the measure of the rival's gait.
teaches: 262 shows Anni Minjili's revenge as the lover's own surge of joy, while 196 turns the same woman into the wife's bitter picture of a triumphant rival, so one puram story served akam poets for opposite feelings.

note: Both Paranar marutham poems use Pazhaiyan, the Chola's warrior, lord of Por on the Kaveri: in 186 his town is the image of bangles never broken, in 326 his thrown spear is the image of a girl's eyes that never miss.
teaches: Together they show Paranar drawing on one patron's fame for women's power in the marutham quarrel, the fort for what holds and the spear for what strikes, so Pazhaiyan's name carried a known strength the audience could read at once.

note: Kural 1081 is the man's first sight: goddess, peahen or woman, his heart reels; in 198 he has already held her and still decides she is not a woman but the dread maiden of a mountain spring, having likened her coming to a peahen in cloud.
teaches: The couplet places the doubt at first sight and the commentators settle it in favour of a woman, but the poem keeps the same three terms after the union and settles them the other way, so the awe of the anangu was not only a first impression.

note: Same occasion reversed: in 182 Kapilar's friend tells the man who comes at night to come by day, for fear of the storm; in 148 Paranar's friend tells the man who comes by day to come at evening, for the girl's suffering through the long day.
teaches: Set side by side the two colophons show that the friend's ruling on when to meet is no fixed rule of kalavu but a reply to the present danger, and each poem names its own reason, the storm-struck night in one and the unbearable day in the other.

note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the mothers left after an elopement: in 189 the foster mother wanders the house and says the town has lost its treasure; in 195 the birth mother claims her years of care and asks the diviner which house the pair will reach first.
teaches: Read together the two mothers' griefs differ in kind: the foster mother mourns a public loss, while the birth mother, conceding she has no claim on the youth, turns grief into a practical question about the return, which shows the elopement already moving toward an accepted marriage.

note: In both the man refuses a journey his heart has resolved on: in 193 he grants the road is easy and names his wife's shoulders as the one thing he cannot leave; in 199 he lets the heart go alone and refuses even a king's restored wealth.
teaches: Taken together the two show the refusal hardening from a weighing of costs into a full split from his own heart, and 199 adds a puram measure of the wealth refused that 193 never names.

note: Both are the woman telling her friend that the rainy season he promised has come without him; the colophon files 183 under paalai and 194 under mullai.
teaches: The pair shows the colophon thinai following different cues for one situation: 183 is labelled by the road he crossed and 194 by the fields at home, though both speak from the waiting house in the rains.
audit_text_issue: 194 line 1 'வகைறை' looks like a misprint for வைகறை

note: Both are a friend comforting a woman whose man has crossed the desert, and both argue that no gain could keep him: 201 says not even the Chola rice country, 213 not even the world of the worthy with its nectar.
teaches: Side by side they show the friend's reassurance as a scale that can be pushed from an earthly kingdom to heaven, always measuring his love by what he would refuse rather than by any promise he made.

note: 204 says the wife's hair smells of the groves of Vaanan's Sirukudi; 117 compares the eloping girl's braided hair to the ripples of the stream north of Vaanan's Sirukudi.
teaches: Two poets use the same chief's village to praise a woman's hair, one by its scent and one by its waves, so Vaanan's Sirukudi had become a standing measure of hair rather than a single poet's image.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the man who said 'fear not' are at fault if he leaves; in 205 the woman names his oath 'we will not part' a lie and yet wishes his journey success.
teaches: The couplet treats the broken promise as a question of blame, while the poem shows the same woman blaming and blessing him at once, so the trust the Kural judges was not withdrawn when it was betrayed.

note: Both are Paranar's and both tell of Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili: 181 has a flock of birds cover the sun over the dead man; 208 has Nannan refuse to look on the field where the birds shade him.
teaches: Together they show the bird-shade legend was told with a witness who would not look, so the poet could use the same event for wonder in a journey poem and for a ruler's shame in a love poem.

note: 36 (Nakkirar) and 209 (Kalladanar) both measure gossip against the victory roar at Alankanam, where the Pandya Chezhiyan beat seven kings in a day.
teaches: Two poets reached for the same Pandya victory to size two different scandals, a husband's new marriage and a girl's secret love, which shows the battle's roar had become a set unit of public noise in akam.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori who ruled Kolli and Malaiyan who rode the horse Kaari side by side among the seven dead givers; Akananuru 209 says Kaari of Mullur killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
teaches: The bards' roll of the seven great givers sets a killer and his victim together as equals in generosity, and only the akam simile keeps the memory that one of them ended the other.

note: 226 names Mathi, lord of the fishermen, at the Kazhar ford where the Kaveri flooded; 211 names Mathi's stony ford and the gate of Venmani where Ezhini's teeth were set, and measures the gossip by the roar of its water.
teaches: Read together they show the akam poets drew their measures of public noise from the same Mathi's river country, one by a flood and the other by a war trophy, so a chief's ford could carry both his water and his fame.

note: Both answer a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell your quick return to those who will be alive then; 215 says wishing you a safe journey is for those who can bear to stay.
teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's refusal works in practice: the friend withholds the ritual farewell and fills the road with killers and vultures, so the threat of death the Kural only implies is made visible.

note: Purananuru 396 praises Ezhini Aathan of Vaattaaru as strength to the weak and kin to the kinless, in a land where the Kosar drink toddy; Akananuru 216 recalls the spear of the lord of Chelli, a Kosar town, pressed into Aathan Ezhini's chest.
teaches: If the two name the same chief, the patron the bard praised as a protector was remembered in akam only for his death wound, which a courtesan uses as a measure of how much she can hurt her rivals.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:396 lines 21-22 have a gap.

note: 202 counts the dangers of the lover's night path (thunder, snake, dark) to press for marriage; 218 counts the same dangers (tiger, night clefts) and moves the meeting to daytime instead.
teaches: Read in order they show the friend's two moves against the night meeting: first making the danger the women's suffering, then offering daylight, which trades his peril for the risk of the mother's knowing.

note: Both mothers recall feeding the girl milk at home, 219 coaxing her with 'your father's share too', 207 holding out milk with honey she refused, and both set it against the water of the desert road.
teaches: Two poets build the eloping daughter's mother around the same contrast of home milk and road water, so the feeding bowl was the stock emblem of the care the daughter left behind.

note: Both are Maruthan Ila Naganar's neythal poems naming Chellur: in 90 it is the town of the mighty god by the roaring sea, in 220 the place of the sacrifice of the axe-bearing tall one with its guarded pillar.
