teaches: The same poet ties Chellur's sanctity once to its god and once to a famous sacrifice, so for him the town was a sacred place whose guarded objects could stand for a girl kept from her lover.

note: Both use the Kazhar legend of Aathi Manthi and Attan Atthi; 222 names Maruthi, who restored the lover and entered the sea, 236 has Manthi searching town after town.
teaches: One legend served two speakers: the friend holds up Maruthi's fatal deed as a fame to win, the wife holds up Manthi's lament as her own shame, so the story was a shared stock the poets bent to opposite purposes.
audit_text_issue: 236 line 20 was repaired by splitting; 222 sense flagged as uncertain. | A236 line 5 இடைனில and line 10 உய்ர்த்தனென் look like misprints (இடைநில, உயிர்த்தனென்).

note: Both marutham poems reproach the husband for bathing in the Kaveri flood with the woman he desires (நீ வெய் யோளொடு), and both place it at Matthi's Kazhar near Thithan's Uranthai.
teaches: The shared phrase and places show that the bathing scandal at Kazhar was a set situation of marutham, which each poet then sharpened with a different puram comparison, a rout in 226 and a lost youth in 6.

note: Both measure gossip against a public spectacle: the Kural against the serpent swallowing the moon, the Akananuru against the shout at Katti's flight.
teaches: The Kural keeps the old akam habit of sizing a private scandal by a famous public event, but trades the historical rout for a cosmic eclipse, losing the political sting while keeping the scale.

note: Thazhumban's Unur stands as the measure of wealth in both, here as the region beyond which the lover's noisy departure is likened to Marungur's market, there as the town a girl's beauty is compared to.
teaches: A chieftain's town famous in puram praise was reused by akam poets as a ready scale of plenty, so a patron's fame circulated as a stock of comparison across the two kinds of poem.

note: Both set the absent man's wellbeing above the woman's pallor: the friend's blessing நோய்இலராக, the Kural's 'let my body pale, if he is well'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into the woman's own mouth a blessing that the Akananuru gives to the friend, showing how the anthology's go-between voice was absorbed into the single speaker of the later couplets.

note: Both refuse the promise of a quick return: the girl quotes his 'we will come right away' against the spring, the Kural says tell your quick return to those who will be alive.
teaches: Read together they show the same refusal of comfort in two registers, the Kural as a sharp retort before parting and the Akananuru as proof gathered afterwards from the season's signs.

note: In both the girl looks and bows her head; the Kural takes it as water poured into the bond, while here the bowed head with checked tears leaves the hero in pain.
teaches: The Kural fixes the bowed head as a sign of consent, but the Akananuru shows the same gesture as unreadable to the man at the moment it happens, so the maxim is a reading made after the fact.

note: Both give the man's reason for parting as the pursuit of glory or strength (நல்லிசை, உரன்), which takes his resolve as companion instead of her.
teaches: The friend's argument that glory is not for those who stay home is the very reason the Kural's woman lives on in longing, so the same heroic value comforts in one poem and wounds in the other.

note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.
audit_text_issue: Purananuru 2 line 23 றுஞ்சும் is a misprint for துஞ்சும். | Purananuru 2 names the patron only in its colophon; the poem itself names the feast.

note: Both have the returning man wish to finish the work and reach home for the evening; the Kural's evening feast at home is the poem's dusk arrival when the wife loosens her braid.
teaches: The Kural states as a wish what the mullai poem stages as a drive at dusk, showing that the evening return was the fixed goal of the man's speech in both traditions.

note: In both the evening comes with cold and brings the woman's sorrow to its height.
teaches: The Kural names the evening's chill and the swelling grief in two lines, while the Akananuru supplies the season's things, the north wind, the rain and the flowers, that make the evening cold, so the couplet presupposes the landscape.

note: Both are the friend's assurance that he will return; 231 grants that glory took him away, 237 says no rich town, not even Uranthai, will keep him from her.
teaches: Taken together the two comforts answer the two fears of the waiting woman, that his honour will keep him away and that pleasure will, and show the friend's arguments as a set repertoire.

note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.
audit_text_issue: 152 is flagged uncertain in sense, but the Nalli lines are clear.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: Both name former deeds as the cause of suffering: the woman's தொல்வினைப் பயன், the Naladiyar's fixed mark that cannot shrink or grow.
teaches: The Naladiyar draws from fixed former deeds the lesson that grief is useless, but the Akananuru woman names the same cause through streaming eyes and says she cannot bear it, so the explanation was available to akam speakers long before it was offered as a cure.

note: Both weigh wealth against the wife: in 265 she says he held wealth weightier than her; in 245 he imagines her saying wealth is dearer than life and refuses to go.
teaches: The same scale of wealth against the wife is read from both ends, and in 245 it is the wife's readiness to accept the man's reason that makes him unable to act on it, a turn the complaint of 265 cannot show.

note: Karikal's victory at Venni: Purananuru 66 praises the defeated king who starved himself facing north in shame at his back wound; 246 measures gossip against the victory shout at Azhundur.
teaches: The puram poet honours the loser of Venni above the victor while the akam poet borrows only the victor's roar, which shows how differently one battle served praise of honour and a scale for noise.

note: Both use the battle of Venni: 55 as Cheralathan's starving to death after his wound, 246 as Karikal's triumph.
teaches: Within one anthology the same battle supplies a mother's grief with the image of a death beyond comfort and a friend's scorn with the image of a deafening cheer, so akam poets picked a side of a public event to suit the speaker's mood.

note: Both are the friend refusing the husband after he bathed in the river with his woman, and both end 'the gossip is greater than the shout' (ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே) at a historical event.
teaches: The repeated frame shows that measuring marutham gossip by a public shout was a fixed form, and the poets made their point by which shout they chose: a Chola victory in 246, a rival's flight in 226.

note: Both name the rock-cut road the Moriyar's chariot wheels made: in the Purananuru the sun's disc standing over that pass is the image of the patron's daily charity; here the pass is the far road the lover crossed.
teaches: A northern dynasty's road through the southern hills was common knowledge to both kinds of poem, so the same landmark could stand for a patron's open-handedness and for the distance that keeps a lover away.

note: Both are the friend's comfort that he will return although he has passed the Moriyar's rock-cut road; 69 says he will not stay long, 251 that not even Nanda's wealth would keep him.
teaches: Put side by side the two comforts show that the Moriyar road had become the stock boundary of the far journey, and that 251 sharpens the assurance by setting against it the greatest wealth the poets knew.

note: 265's woman asks whether it is the Nandas' treasure hidden under the Ganges that he values more than her; 251's friend says he would not stay even if he got Nanda's wealth.
teaches: The Nandas' treasure is the same weight on the scale in both poems, but the woman fears it outweighs her and the friend swears it does not, so the comfort and the complaint are exact answers to each other.

note: Both are the friend's comfort that the man, gone past the Ayiri river, will come back because he will remember the woman's body (her thoyyil marks in 177, her face and look in 253).
teaches: Together they show the friend's argument from memory of the body as a set move, and 253 adds what 177 lacks, the woman's own fears of mother and town, which the remembered body is offered to outweigh.

note: Both measure gossip by a public shout over a royal victory, 253 at the Pandyan's Kudal after the Kongar were driven out, 246 at the Chola's Azhundur after Venni.
teaches: In paalai as in marutham the gossip-and-shout frame fits each speaker's land and dynasty, so the formula traveled across thinais while the king named changed with the poet.

note: Both show a lighthouse lamp on a tall tower that calls ships to the shore at night: the idyll as a sight of the port on the guide's road, the poem as the pilot's sign of landfall.
teaches: The idyll records the harbour light as a fact of the port; the akam poet turns the same light into the sure sign of a voyage's end and sets it against the woman's lack of any messenger, so a civic fixture became an emblem of return.

note: Both refuse the husband and measure the gossip by a public shout; 246 names a battle, 256 names an assembly's punishment of a man who falsely denied an affair.
teaches: The later poem bends the frame into a threat: the shout it chooses was raised against a man who swore 'I do not know her', exactly the denial the husband is making, so the comparison judges as well as measures.

note: Both are the man speaking to his heart about a night meeting and both name Nannan's fortress Paazhi.
teaches: Paazhi stands for a well-guarded prize in both of the man's speeches to his heart, rejoicing in 142 and despairing in 258, which shows that a chieftain's fortress had become the akam measure of a girl's inaccessibility.

note: 259's friend tells the girl to bear her mother's grief and go; in 55 the mother of an eloped girl says she cannot sleep and wishes her life had left with her daughter.
teaches: The friend names the mother's grief only as a weight the girl must carry away with her, while 55 shows from inside that the grief is a wish to die, so the anthology measures the cost the friend's counsel asks the girl to accept.

note: Both list the signs of dusk, with the anril calling or settling in the palmyra's inner frond (பெண்ணை அகமடல்) among them.
teaches: Kapilar's idyll uses the dusk catalogue as the moment the man promises marriage, while 260 uses the same signs to open a night of dread, so the formula of nightfall was shared and its turn at the end set its meaning.

note: 259 is the friend urging the girl to go now the season is right; 257 is the man on the road praising her walk through a summer waste.
teaches: Read in order the two poems show the elopement from its promised green season to the real summer road, and the man's praise of her walk answers the friend's request that she go with a steady mind.

note: Both are Paranar's and both use Anni Minili, whose father the Kosar blinded and whose vow Thithiyan fulfilled: in 196 the wife names the courtesan as one who carries herself like Minili; in 262 the lover's joy is like Minili's when her anger was released.
teaches: One poet draws on either half of the same local revenge story, the proud wrath in 196 and the relief after vengeance in 262, so the story was known well enough to be cited by a single name for a single mood.

note: Purananuru 142 (Paranar) praises Pekan as giving like rain that falls everywhere without choosing; Akananuru 262 (Paranar) gives Pekan's hill as கொண்டல் மாமலை, the rain-cloud hill whose drizzle wets the bushes, and lends its scent to the girl's voice.
teaches: The same poet's figure for Pekan's indiscriminate giving, rain, is carried into akam as the smell of his rain-soaked hill, showing a patron's praise-image reused as a lover's sensory measure.

note: Purananuru 233 is a lament that wishes false the dawn report of Evvi's many wounds; Akananuru 266 measures the gossip about the husband by the roar of the feast at Uraththur after Evvi's victory.
teaches: Evvi's name travels with loud public report in both books, a victory feast in akam and a death rumour in puram, so the akam poet uses his fame precisely as a gauge of how far news spreads.
audit_text_issue: 266 colophon reads தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது; the speaker is the wife, so தலைமகன் is likely a slip for தலைமகள்.

note: Purananuru 264 sets up a stone for a man who recovered cattle, crowned with red flowers tied with marral fibre and peacock feather and inscribed with his name; Akananuru 269 shows such stones on the road, names inscribed, washed, smeared with turmeric and crowned with red karanthai for men who held off the Mazhavar to recover cattle.
teaches: The puram poem gives the stone on the day of grief, when the bards still come not knowing; the akam poem shows the same rite kept up later on a travelled road, so together they show the hero-stone moving from mourning to a standing roadside cult.

note: Akananuru 270 names Kazhumalam as the town of Kuttuvan, the Chera, as a figure of beauty; Akananuru 44 tells how the Chola Senni took Kazhumalam after capturing Kanaiyan, and uses Senni's Azhumbil as its simile.
teaches: The same town appears as a Chera possession in one akam simile and as a Chola conquest in another, so the similes preserve a contested place under rival owners and are evidence for its history, not only ornament.

note: Purananuru 343, a maganmaruttal poem, has the father refuse his daughter even if suitors bow and give நலஞ்சால் விழுப்பொருள்; Akananuru 280 has the lover say she cannot be had even for நலம்சால் விழுப்பொருள் given by the shipload, and resolve to serve her fisherman father instead.
teaches: The near-identical phrase shows the akam suitor speaking inside the puram convention of the father who refuses wealth, and gives the convention's other side: where puram suitors bring siege, the akam lover answers the refusal with servitude.
audit_text_issue: 343 lines 2-6 show odd word division (மனைமறுக் குந்து, கரைசேர்க் குந்து), probably split -உந்து forms in the base text.

note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of a man who gives nothing to the needy to a beautiful woman growing old alone; the courtesan in Akananuru 276 likens her own beauty, if she fails to win the man, to the wealth of one who hoarded and never gave to those who asked.
teaches: The two verses run the same comparison in opposite directions, beauty as vehicle for hoarded wealth in the Kural and hoarded wealth as vehicle for beauty in the poem, which shows the pairing was a shared idea in which each term could explain the other.

note: Kural 1147 has the woman say her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water; in Akananuru 273 she says the sickness sprouted between her breasts, grew a trunk, spread branches of gossip and budded with scandal into a tree shading the world.
teaches: The Kural's two-line plant metaphor, gossip feeding the disease, is the seed of Avvaiyar's full tree, which adds the stages of growth and makes the scandal not only food for the love but its flowering.

note: In Kural 1236 the woman tells her friend that with bangles and shoulders slackening what hurts is hearing him called cruel; in Akananuru 267, when the friend says the oath-breaker has changed, the wife replies that he is not at fault and her shoulders, which let the bangles slip, are.
teaches: Same speaker, addressee and occasion: the Kural states the defence of the absent man as a feeling, and the poem shows its rhetorical move, turning the blame on her own body, so the couplet's restraint is seen as an argument with the friend.

note: Kural 1151 (the friend's words for Parimelazhagar) tells the departing man to promise his quick return to those who will still be alive; in Akananuru 271, the friend tells the departing man to prosper, but asks whether there is any medicine for the girl in the land where he will stay.
teaches: Both turn the farewell into a threat of her death, but the poem argues it through the road, whose nelli fruit revives dying travellers, so the couplet's bare warning is given a reason: the waste has remedies for strangers and none for her.

note: Both are a mother after her daughter's elopement: in 263 she says she would gladly have married the girl to the youth had she known; in 275 she recalls the girl's play and lisping speech and points onlookers to the sand house the girl left.
teaches: Read together they give the mother's two answers to the loss, regret that she was not asked and grief over the childhood left behind, so the elopement is a wound to her authority as well as to her love.

note: In 261 the man, back home, recalls the girl on the elopement road too shy to walk ahead of him, while a tiger roared and bowmen's drums sounded; in 275 the mother imagines her daughter on the bear-haunted hot road and is left with her sand house.
teaches: The same journey is seen from both ends: for the mother the road is only danger and loss, while the man remembers it as the girl's shyness and a slow camp in the wild, so the anthology lets each speaker hold the half the other cannot know.

note: Both set the man's road at the rock the Moriyar's wheels cut and arm him with a bow wound with a peacock's shed feather; in 69 the friend says he will not delay, in 281 the woman says he went without fear of breaking his word.
teaches: The same stock road and the same feathered bow serve one poet as a promise of return and another as proof of desertion, so the image fixed the distance while the speaker decided what the distance meant.

note: Purananuru 175 likens a patron's lasting charity to the rock-cut pass of the Moriyar's chariot wheels, a public way open to all; Akananuru 281 sends the lover over that same pass.
teaches: In praise poetry the Moriyar's cut road stands for something permanent and shared, while the akam poet uses it as the point past which a man is lost to one woman, so one piece of remembered history carried opposite values in the two kinds of poetry.

note: Both use the beaten drum (அறைபறை) for love exposed to the town while the man is away; in the Kural it is her own eyes, in 281 it is the gossip he left behind.
teaches: The Kural takes the stock drum of gossip and turns it on the woman's own eyes, so the pairing shows the couplet moving the blame for exposure from the town, as the Sangam poem has it, to her own body.

note: Kural 467 says to deliberate and then resolve, never resolve and then deliberate; the friend in 286 says the great weigh virtue, wealth and their own worth before carrying out what they intend.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule of deliberate action used as a lever in courtship: if the great think before they promise, a lover who swore cannot later plead haste, so the maxim becomes a way to bind a promise.

note: In 61 the friend tells the woman not to grieve gazing at the wall scored with the days; in 289 the man on the road imagines her looking at that wall.
teaches: The wall marked with the days of absence was known to both sides of the parting: the man can picture the very ritual the friend tries to stop, so his guilt in 289 rests on a convention the woman's side also names.

note: Purananuru 48 says Thondi smells of the neythal flowers blooming in its great backwater; Akananuru 290 says the woman's eyes were once like the great cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour.
teaches: Thondi's neythal was the town's own emblem in praise of its king, so when the akam poet says her eyes have lost that likeness he is measuring her pallor against a flower the audience knew as Thondi's pride.

note: Both are Mamoolanar's: in 61 the man would not stay even for Pulli's festive Venkadam; in 295 he has gone past Pulli's hill into the Vadugar country where the language changes.
teaches: Read together, the poet's Pulli's hill is the last familiar landmark: one poem stops at it as the measure of a great prize, the other goes beyond it to a land of strange speech, giving his geography of absence an inner and an outer edge.

note: Both are marutham poems in which the friend refuses the husband and compares the gossip about him to noise at Chezhiyan's Koodal; in 116 it is louder than the shout of the battlefield where he routed two kings, in 296 it is like the city's everyday clamour.
teaches: The akam poets measured scandal by the noise of the Pandya capital in war and in peace alike, so Koodal's fame worked as a ready scale for how far gossip had spread.

note: Purananuru 264 tells of a hero-stone newly set up with his name engraved and crowned with a peacock feather; Akananuru 297 shows such a stone grown old, its inscribed name passed unread by weary travellers.
teaches: The puram poem records the moment a name is carved to outlast death, and the akam poem shows the same kind of stone generations on with no one reading it, so the pair qualifies the promise of the engraved name.

note: Both use the wandering kodiyar troupe: in 301 their leaving empties a town's commons, and that emptiness is the heroine's evening; in 309 their going to Vaanavan is the model for the heroine's own journey after her man.
teaches: The same performers figure both sides of parting, the place left desolate and the traveller who will not count the forest long, so akam poets used the bards' life as a ready picture of both staying and going.

note: Akananuru 303 calls Paari the giver of hill-like elephants to any suppliant and makes his Parambu the place sparrows always return to at evening; Purananuru 108 says Paari never answers a suppliant with 'I will not come'.
teaches: The akam poet borrows the certainty of Paari's giving, famous from the puram poems, to make the sparrows' return seem certain, so that the heroine's disappointment is measured against a patron who never failed anyone.

note: Both open in the first rains with a stag, a doe and her fawn together; in 304 the hero sees them from the war camp and imagines his wife's reproach, in 314 the friend sees them as the hero comes home in time.
teaches: One scene of the deer family carries reproach while he is away and fulfilment when he returns, which shows that what a karu thing implies is fixed by the uri of the poem, not by the thing itself.

note: Both picture a public hall (பொதியில்) fallen to ruin, its pillar abandoned by its god; in Purananuru 52 it is the fate of lands the Pandya conquers, in Akananuru 307 a dove clings to it with its mate.
teaches: A ruined hall abandoned by its god was a stock picture of a conquered land, and the akam poet turns it round: even in that ruin a pair of birds keeps faith, which makes the hero's leaving harsher.

note: The same poet, Maruthan Ilanagan, praises Vazhuthi's war in Purananuru 52 and in Akananuru 312 likens lightning to the spear Vazhuthi raises against fleeing enemies.
teaches: One poet's war praise for a Pandya becomes, in his love poem, the measure of a storm's power, showing puram fame travelling into akam as a simile that its first hearers would recognise.

note: Both describe the waterless road where bowmen shoot travellers and birds feed on the dead; in Purananuru 3 suppliants brave it for the Pandya's gifts, in Akananuru 313 the husband crosses it for wealth.
teaches: The same death road is crossed for the same motive, gain, by the suppliant and by the husband; puram counts the crossing as praise of the patron, akam as the measure of what the wife fears.

note: Both are the friend telling the wife not to prolong her sulking: Kural 1302 says sulking is salt and too much spoils it; Akananuru 316 shows women who sulked too long left alone, poor and nursing hungry sons.
teaches: What the Kural calls spoiling by too much salt the Sangam friend spells out as the loss of fortune and household, so the couplet's measured image stands for a social and economic ruin, not only a lost pleasure.

note: Both are the friend turning back a man who comes at night by a beast-haunted hill path: in 308 she offers day meetings instead, in 318 she bans his visits and offers marriage.
teaches: Read in order, the two refusals show the stages of the friend's pressure: first moving the meeting to day, still within secret love, then closing the meetings so that marriage is the only road left.

note: Both are spoken to a man who announces his departure: Kural 1151 says tell me if you are not going, and keep your promise of a quick return for those who will still be alive; Akananuru 319's friend says go and get your wealth, since the girl cannot even say she will stay behind.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows why the friend speaks in this situation at all: the girl is too young and loving to answer him herself, which supports reading the couplet's 'tell me' as the friend speaking for her.

note: 326 likens the young woman's unerring eyes to the spear raised by Pazhaiyan, lord of Por and the Cholas' champion; 44 recalls the battle in which Pazhaiyan fell (பழையன் பட்டென) and Chenni avenged him.
teaches: Akam poets drew on both halves of one champion's story, his unfailing aim for a woman's dangerous eyes and his death for the scale of a war that keeps a husband from home, so the hero's fame served love poetry whole.

note: Both are marutham speeches by a courtesan meant for the hearing of others, and both stake her bangles on Chola martial formulas: 186 says the lord never broke her bangles, using Pazhaiyan's 'rain of arrows, cloud-dark shields' (மாரி அம்பின் மழைத்தோல்); 336 applies the same phrase to the Cholas and curses her bangles to break like the Aryans at Vallam.
teaches: The pair shows the courtesan's boast as a set form: her bangles stand for her hold on the man, and she guarantees them with the same Chola war formula, as a warrior swears by his king.

note: 338 wishes love to last like the Porai's Kolli; 209 tells how Kari killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras, who set a goddess image there.
teaches: Read with 209, the hero's figure of permanence is a hill that changed lords by a killing, so what the poet makes lasting is the hill itself, not any house that held it.

note: Purananuru 158 names Kolli as the hill Ori ruled, among seven givers now dead; Akananuru 338 calls Kolli the Porai's and makes it the measure of a love that must not perish.
teaches: The puram poem remembers Kolli by a dead patron and the akam poem by its new Chera master, so the hill a lover swears by already carries the record of a fallen lord.

note: Both name Thithiyan as lord of Pothiyil: 25 has his drums echoed in the waterfalls of the hills the absent man crossed; 322 makes his guarded, honey-hung peak the measure of how hard the girl is to reach.
teaches: One chief's hill serves two opposite uses, the distance a husband has gone and the closeness a lover cannot reach, which shows akam poets taking a puram place for its fit to the speaker's situation, not for its praise.

note: Both poems in this chapter name Thithiyan: 322 his war elephants and his guarded Pothiyil; 331 his daily court, his gifts to bards and the sword he drew against the Velir.
teaches: The same patron lends the frustrated lover his inaccessible hill and the abandoned wife his sword, so each speaker takes from a king's fame the face that matches her or his own trouble.

note: 85 names Thiraiyan's Venkatam hill on the road the husband crossed; 340 names Thiraiyan's flowery seaside town Pavaththiri as the measure of the girl's beauty.
teaches: The same chief furnishes a mountain for a paalai poem and a shore town for a neythal one, so a patron's domain was divided among the landscapes as the thinai required.

note: Same thurai: a man, his task done, urges his charioteer home. 34 drives by the stag that feeds and guards its doe; 334 by the breaking rains, hail and peacocks, and by the tribute won with the war drum.
teaches: Together they show the homecoming poem built in two ways: by a creature whose care mirrors the husband's intent (34), or by the season itself whose arrival is the pledge kept (334).

note: Both are night-tryst poems the lover overhears, and both close on the same formula, a tusker and his mate asleep on the plantain slope (வாழையஞ் சிலம்பிற் றுஞ்சும் / வாழையம் சிலம்பில் துஞ்சும்): in 328 he strokes a mate who has just calved, in 332 he lies down with her after killing a tiger.
teaches: A shared formula takes a different act each time to suit the speech: the calving mate presses toward married life in a poem of fear, the tiger-killing protector confirms the lover in a poem of praise.

note: Both are men arguing with hearts set on wealth, and both make the desert's killers the argument: in 327 the archers pity no victim and grieve only when they miss; in 337 the Mazhavar kill a starving messenger in case he has gold and leave scorning his rags.
teaches: Side by side they show the road weighing a man's life only by what he might carry, which is the very reckoning the heart is making when it trades her company for wealth.

note: Kural 1124: she is living to my life when with me and dying when she leaves; Akananuru 339 ends with love like the life's living and parting like dying, spoken by a husband as he sets out.
teaches: The Kural says it in courtship as praise; the poem puts the same claim in the mouth of a man choosing to leave, so the saying becomes the cost he knowingly pays, burning at both ends of the firebrand.

note: Kural 1122 calls the bond with the girl that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை ... நட்பு); 339 has the same word and image, friendship like life joined to the body (யாக்கைக்கு உயிர்இயைந் தன்ன நட்பின்).
teaches: The shared image and even the shared word நட்பு show the Kural's couplet as a distilled form of an akam figure that the poem still spends a scene of departure to earn.

note: Kural 247 grants that this world is not for those without wealth; Akananuru 335 opens by conceding that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, then gives up the journey for wealth anyway.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's premise about wealth in so many words yet refuses its practical pull, showing that the premise alone did not settle whether a husband should leave home to earn.

note: Kural 629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain; Akananuru 327 tells the heart that joy and grief come by turns like day and night, so it need not go seeking hardship for wealth.
teaches: The same doctrine of joy and grief in turn, which the Kural uses to teach calm under misfortune, becomes in the lover's mouth an argument for staying home rather than chasing gain.

note: Kural 81: all of keeping house is for receiving guests; in Akananuru 324 the attendants announce the husband's return by saying his wife will now have guests to feed too.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule from the inside of an absence: hospitality belonged to the couple, so a wife alone could not host, and the husband's return is announced as the return of guests.

note: Both are mullai poems in which the hero, his work done, tells the charioteer to drive fast through the rain-fed forest to his waiting wife.
teaches: Akananuru 34 grounds the hurry in an animal pair (the stag feeding and guarding his doe) while 344 grounds it in the clock, before evening falls, so the homecoming formula could be driven either by an emblem of care or by the promised hour.

note: Both are mullai homecomings after the task: in 344 the hero urges his charioteer; in 354 the attendants urge the hero, naming the victory and the cowherds' evening.
teaches: The pair shows the same return from both ends of command: the hero who orders speed in 344 is himself ordered by his men in 354, and both make the wife's pallor the thing his arrival cures.

note: Both poems by Mamoolanar use Cheralathan, who drove back the sea and cut the kadambu: 127 his tribute treasure, 347 his drum.
teaches: One poet drew two different measures from a single Chera victory, its plunder as the scale of the wealth the husband will not stay for and its drum as the scale of the gossip's noise, so akam borrowed puram events for value and for loudness alike.

note: Both paalai poems pass through the country of Ezhil hill: 345 recalls it as the hill sung by a poet given horses, 349 as Nannan's land where bards are given wealth unasked.
teaches: Read together they show that Ezhil hill was known through its patron's gifts to poets, so the absent husband's road ran through a landscape whose fame was generosity, sharpening the contrast with the man who left home to get wealth.

note: The Kural's woman has worn her fingers marking the days since he left; 351 names the marks drawn on the wall that she counts each day.
teaches: The couplet speaks only from the woman's side, while 351 puts the same tally marks in the returning man's mind, so the counting of days on the wall was a known practice that both partners could picture, not a private secret of the one who waits.

note: Both start from the coming of age: the Naladiyar's wise renounce early because grey hair will come; 353's hero refuses to leave his wife because the days pass like a dream and age is coming.
teaches: The same premise, that youth is short, yields opposite counsels, renunciation in the Naladiyar and staying in married love in 353, so impermanence was a shared starting point that the akam poets turned toward the household and the didactic poets away from it.

note: Both are spoken by the hero to his heart about the journey for wealth: 351 as he returns with it, 353 when the heart at home urges a second journey.
teaches: Placed in sequence the two show the pull of wealth outlasting its success: the heart that raced home in 351 is restless again in 353, and only the argument from age and the wife's virtue holds it back.

note: Both are the man at the king's war: the couplet wishes the king victory so that he may join his wife for the evening feast; in 354 the king has won and raised his flag, and the attendants urge the hero home before her pallor deepens.
teaches: The couplet's wish has two conditions, the king's victory and the evening at home, and 354 shows them met in order (the flag raised, the herds coming in at dusk), so the Kural's line compresses a whole mullai homecoming whose hinge is that the hero's private return waits on the public war.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Both are neythal poems in which the friend answers a lover's daytime visit at dusk: 350 asks him to stay and points to the town, 360 refuses the day meeting and sets a secret night one.
teaches: At the same hour the friend has two opposite tactics, drawing the lover openly toward the village in 350 and hiding him by night in 360, so the dusk scene of neythal could press either toward marriage or toward deeper secrecy.

note: Both open on the spring signs of new leaves and the koel calling in the mango and set them against the man's absence.
teaches: The same signs bring helpless lament in 341 ('there is no way through') and a planned reproach in 355 (we will go and quarrel with him), so the season's cue fixed the occasion but not the heroine's response.

note: Both make the man say that the sweetest thing is an embrace that lets nothing come between: in the Kural not even a breeze, in the poem not even a thread, at which she sulks.
teaches: The couplet states the delight as settled, while the poem quotes it as the argument the man lost to his heart's desire for wealth, so the Kural's claim is shown being tested and overruled inside the paalai situation.

note: Both are the hero's words to his heart under the same occasion (அல்ல குறி), both liken the girl to the treasure the old Velir guarded at Pazhi, and both turn on எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய்.
teaches: The repeated opening under one thurai shows a fixed formula for the spoiled night meeting, the Velir's hidden gold at Pazhi standing for the guarded girl, which 258 then ends in the heart's ruin and 372 in a run of similes for its swinging.

note: Pazhi is the Velir's god-guarded treasure city in 372 and the copper-walled fort Ilamperunchenni broke in 375.
teaches: One fort served akam poets for both halves of its story, as the byword for what cannot be reached and as the scene of a famous breach, so a puram place-name carried opposite meanings depending on which part of its history the speaker needed.

note: Kazhuvul's Kaamur is a place of blessed vengai fragrance in 365 and the town thrown into turmoil by the fourteen Velir in 135.
teaches: The same chieftain's town gives one poet the image of calm sweetness for the wife's hair and another the image of a besieged, shaken heart, showing that a puram name entered akam with its whole history, peace and siege alike, available for comparison.
audit_text_issue: akananuru:365 lines 7-8 hard to construe | 365 lines 7-8 are hard to construe. | Ak 365 lines 7-8 hard to construe.

note: Evvi is the unsparing giver (ஓம்பா ஈகை மாவேள் எவ்வி) in the Purananuru poem and the lord who gives toddy to the fishermen to end a brawl in 366.
teaches: The Purananuru names Evvi's giving as a title, while the akam simile shows it as a scene of keeping peace between farmers and salt-makers and makes his shade a measure of a woman's comfort, so a patron's fame for protection became an akam image of shelter.

note: Both use the figure of the ஓர்எயில் மன்னன, the chieftain of a single fort set against crowned kings: in 338 he will not give his daughter to them, in 373 he lies sleepless under their siege.
teaches: The kaanchi poem on a daughter refused to kings shows where the akam poet's image came from: the lone fort's siege was a known situation of puram, and the akam poet borrowed only its sleepless watch to picture the wife.

note: Both are a courtesan's words to the man, both liken his loss to the Kaveri seizing and hiding Atthi, and both end on the demand to give back her beauty and go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே).
teaches: Two poems sharing speaker, legend and closing line show that the Atthi story and the 'return my beauty' demand formed a stock courtesan's reproach, which each poet then fitted to a different king's town as the measure of her lost beauty.

note: Karikal is the victor of Venni in the Purananuru poem and the onlooker at Atthi's flood-dance at Kazhar in 376.
teaches: The conqueror praised in puram appears in akam only as a royal spectator who dates and places a love legend, so akam poets used a war king's fame as a frame for a story of loss rather than of victory.
audit_text_issue: 376 lines 1-2 are compressed.

note: The Kural says to give and live with renown (இசைபட) as the only gain; the poem names those who give with renown (இசைபடப் பெய்தல்) as the men who must sleep in ruined halls on the road to wealth.
teaches: The poem shows what the Kural's rule costs a married man: renown from giving needs wealth, and wealth needs the wasteland and separation, so the maxim's single profit is bought with the akam hero's loneliness.

note: Both say great wealth does not last: the Kural likens its coming and going to a crowd at a dance hall, the poem likens its passing to a night's dream.
teaches: The poem turns the Kural's general warning about wealth into a reason for a husband to stay home, using impermanence not to urge giving but to set the wife's embrace above a second journey for gain.

note: Both are a mother's words after the daughter's elopement; in 15 the mother prays that the town the girl reaches be rich and welcoming to strangers, in 369 the foster mother fears she has married in a poor one-cow hut.
teaches: Set side by side, the two laments show that imagining the daughter's new home was a set part of the eloped-daughter situation, and that the poets could make it either a blessing or a wound to family pride.

note: Both are the plea of the one left behind against a departure: the couplet says tell your quick return to those still alive; 387 asks him to say he will return, and then shows a road where great men turn back at a lizard's cry.
teaches: The couplet only doubts the traveller's promise; the poem shows why it is empty, since on that road a return depends on omens and beasts, not on the man's word.
audit_text_issue: Lines 4 to 8 and line 20 (சென்றோர் மன்னென இருக்கிற் போர்க்கே) are obscure as printed. | 387 lines 4 to 8 and the last line are syntactically unclear; marker flagged the sense uncertain. | Line 20 obscure; sense flagged uncertain.

note: Both are the man's account of a first sight, and both set a simple girl (பேதை) against eyes that make war (அமர்த்தன / அமர்த்தனள்).
teaches: The couplet's paradox of war-making eyes in an artless girl gets a cause in the poem: she glares because a stranger blocks her road and jokes about her body, so the 'deadly' look is her self-possession, and it ends in a smile.

note: Both speak of a lover who took a woman's beauty in exchange: the couplet's woman says he took grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor; the courtesan of 396 demands her beauty back before he goes.
teaches: Read together they show the claim that a lover owes back the beauty he took was not the wife's alone: the courtesan states it as a debt to be repaid, which the couplet's wife can only lament.
audit_text_issue: ak396 l.10 மார்புதரு கல்லாய் is uncertain.

note: Both are Paranar's courtesan poems, both end with the demand to give back her beauty and then go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே), and both use the Kaviri carrying off Aththi.
teaches: In 376 the river's seizing of Aththi is left without its tenor; 396 names it (I fear your wife will take you as the Kaviri hid Aththi), so the legend served Paranar as a fixed figure for the wife's lawful claim over the courtesan.

note: 208 tells how Aay Eyinan fell to Minjili at Paazhi and the birds shaded him; 396 says he died because he had promised 'fear not' to those Nannan drove from Punnadu.
teaches: 396 supplies the cause behind 208's famous death: Eyinan died keeping a promise of refuge, which is why a courtesan could cite him against a lover who broke an oath made before a god.

note: Kanaiyan appears in 44 as the chief captured by the Chola after Pazhaiyan fell, and in 386 as the patron shamed when Paanan broke his Aariya wrestler.
teaches: The akam poets used Kanaiyan only in defeat, once in capture and once in public shame, so his name had become a byword for humiliation before an onlooking crowd, which is exactly what the wife of 386 feels.

note: Puram 2 praises the Chera as வான வரம்பன், whose realm runs from the sea of sunrise to the sea of sunset; in 389 the husband goes beyond Vaana varamban's good land into tiger country.
teaches: The title that in puram means a king bounded only by the sky becomes in akam the edge of the safe world: the lover's journey is measured as going past a realm that claims to have no beyond.

note: Both are Mamoolanar's comfort poems: the man has gone beyond Pulli's good land (புல்லி நன்னாட்டு உம்பர்), where herders feed travellers, and he will not delay (நீடலர்).
teaches: Together they show a fixed comforting formula in which the herders' hospitality on Pulli's road is the reason the friend gives for the man's safety, so the same road scene doubles as evidence that he will come back.

note: In 391 the wife sees the tuft he dressed with athiral and mullai and remembers; in 393 the friend says he cannot stay away, having forgotten the sleep beside her hair dressed with blue lily and summer athiral.
teaches: The athiral in her hair is the shared token of the separation: for the wife it is proof of loss, while the friend turns the same token into proof that he must return.

note: Both are hill poems spoken at the night meeting with the lover listening, and both turn on the household's possession rite for Murugan.
teaches: The rite works two ways in the kurinji poems: in 382 its threat is news to hurry the lover, while in 388 the girl plans to use the diviner's own diagnosis to name the hunter, so the rite becomes the channel through which secret love is disclosed.

note: 394 invites the lover to eat milk rice in a mullai village home 'as your wife prepares it'; 384 shows the returned husband bringing a guest into such a home, where the wife receives him.
teaches: The friend's invitation in 394 pictures, as a reason to marry, the very scene 384 shows as marriage achieved: a mullai home where the wife serves guests.

note: Both foster mothers set the girl's flight against a festival at home: in 385 a festival is prepared and the girl says nothing; in 397 the youth will not take her in marriage at the house where the drum never dries.
teaches: Read together they show the elopement grieved as a refused home wedding, blamed in one poem on the girl's silence and in the other on the youth's haste.
audit_text_issue: 397 line 2 and 385 lines 6-7 are uncertain in this text. | Both verses are flagged uncertain; 397 line 2 is hard to construe.

note: Both anthology invocations show Shiva by his marks with the goddess beside him: Akananuru 0 sets Umai at his side on the bull; Kalittokai 1 has her keep the beat, measure and rhythm while he dances.
teaches: Each love anthology gives the god a partner suited to its form: the Akananuru, a book of spoken poems, seats her beside him, while the sung Kalittokai makes her the one who keeps time for his dance, so the consort's role follows the anthology's metre.

note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.
audit_text_issue: tirumanthiram:2733 reads கொடிகட்டி for கொடுகொட்டி; lines 2-3 are syntactically unclear | Tirumanthiram 2733 கொடிகட்டி / பாண்டுரங் are variant spellings of கொடுகொட்டி / பண்டரங்கம் | Tirumanthiram 2733 reads கொடிகட்டி for கொடுகொட்டி, and its lines 2 and 3 are syntactically unclear.

note: Kalittokai 2 calls the wife's chastity bright as the northern star (வடமீன் போல்) and sets her shoulders above wealth for suppliants; Purananuru 122 says Kari gives his land to brahmins and his tribute to bards and keeps as his own only the shoulders of his wife chaste as the northern star (வடமீன் புரையுங் கற்பின்).
teaches: The puram poem shows the patron's answer to the dilemma the akam friend poses: a giver can give everything away and still keep the wife's shoulders as his only possession, so generosity and staying home need not be traded off as the man in Kalittokai 2 supposes.

note: In both the man leaves because he cannot refuse those who ask; in Akananuru 53 the wife says this means he loves wealth more than her and rejects the friend's calling it grace; in Kalittokai 2 the friend herself argues that such leaving is not love and wins.
teaches: The same honourable motive is judged in opposite directions by the same two persons in different poems: the friend excuses it in one and refutes it in the other, so the giving motive was a debated case in akam, not a settled virtue.

note: Kural 1152 says that union, which once gave delight even at a glance, now carries the pain of fearing separation; Kalittokai 4 shows the woman reading his coming departure in caresses that exceed the usual.
teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: the fear spoils union because his tenderness itself has become the sign of leaving, so the more he gives the surer she is he will go.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

note: In Kalittokai 13 the man lists what the waste would do to her if she came; in 6 the woman answers such a list by asking for hardship as her companion.
teaches: Read together, the danger catalogue is a convention both lovers know how to answer: in 13 the friend discounts it as teasing, in 6 the woman turns it into the reason to go together, so the list deters no one.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so do at once what does; Kalittokai 8 says wealth is less stable than a lute, Fortune or a cruel king, so do not go after it.
teaches: From the same premise the two draw different conclusions: the Kural says to spend unstable wealth on lasting good, the love poem says not to leave love to seek it, so impermanence argued for staying home as well as for giving.

note: Both have a mother figure following an eloped girl and asking those on the road whether they saw her: in Akananuru 7 the foster mother asks a doe and a hill girl; in Kalittokai 9 the mother asks brahmin ascetics, who answer.
teaches: The Akananuru leaves the question unanswered on the empty road, while the Kalittokai brings in renouncers to answer it with a doctrine, so the later anthology turns the mother's lament into a debate the elopement wins.
audit_text_issue: Ak 7 flagged uncertain

note: In Akananuru 263 the mother says that had she known her daughter's mind she would have married her to the youth; in Kalittokai 9 the ascetics tell the mother that following the chosen man is the way of virtue.
teaches: What the Akananuru mother reaches only as regret, the Kalittokai states as a principle from outside the family: the girl's choice is rightful, so both books grant the eloping daughter the moral case against her parents.

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: Both use an elephant who gives food to his mate on the road the man took; in Kalittokai 11 the woman concludes that such a forest will bring him back; in Akananuru 59 the friend sets the same care against the men who do not remember (உள்ளார்).
teaches: One image of animal care is made to argue both for and against the absent man's faithfulness, so the force of the iraicchi depends on the speaker's purpose, not on the creature.

note: In Kalittokai 11 the woman infers that the man who saw a stag shade its doe will come home; in Akananuru 34 the man, having seen a stag feed and guard its doe, urges his charioteer home.
teaches: The woman's inference is borne out from the man's side in the other anthology: the creature's care on the road does turn the traveller homeward, so the iraicchi is a shared convention both lovers trust.

note: Both say death comes unseen and no one knows the last day; the Naladiyar concludes that one must lay up provisions of virtue in time, Kalittokai 12 that one must not let the days of embrace pass for wealth.
teaches: The same reminder of death is used to opposite ends: the Jain moralist spends the uncertain time on merit, the love poet on love, so the memento mori did not belong to renunciation alone.

note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; Kalittokai 14 puts the like saying (காதலார் எவன் செய்ப பொருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு) in the mouths of strangers and rejects it.
teaches: A maxim the Kural states as fact is quoted in the love poem as hostile outsiders' talk, so the wealth maxim was public wisdom that akam speakers could set against love and refuse.

note: Kural 113 says to give up at once gain made by leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Kalittokai 14 says wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next.
teaches: The Kural allows that unfair gain may bring good and asks for sacrifice anyway, while the love poem denies it brings good in either world, so the woman's argument is stronger than the ethics book's rule.

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband commands rain; Kalittokai 16 calls the woman the chaste one who gives rain to the world in drought and says virtue will not let her pale.
teaches: The power the Kural states as a marvel works in the love poem as an argument: a woman who can bring rain cannot be left to waste, so the belief served to bind husbands as well as to praise wives.

note: In Akananuru 5 the man says he gave up the journey because of his wife's silent, tearful sign; in Kalittokai 17 the friend says her own words, like medicine, made him give it up.
teaches: The same outcome is credited to whoever speaks the poem, the husband to the wife's mute grief and the friend to her own argument, so the given-up journey is a shared ending each voice claims.

note: In Akananuru 51 the man tells his heart that wealth won by parting is not worth having and he will stay and hold her; in Kalittokai 18 the woman tells him the same and adds that even sharing one cloth, the united live the only true life.
teaches: The case against the wealth journey is made from both sides, and the woman's version goes further by accepting poverty outright, which the man's version never has to face.

note: In 13 the man tells the woman that if she came the stones would blacken her lotus soles, the beasts' cries would startle her and the hot wind would wither her; in 20 the woman takes the same objections (her feet, no water, no shade, the heat) and denies that any of them weighs against going with him.
teaches: Held together the two poems stage both sides of one dispute: the man argues from her body's frailty, the woman from her life's shortness and the deer pair that cross together, so the paalaikkali treats the wife's right to share the road as a question it argues, not a given.

note: In Akananuru 133 the man once asked the woman whether she could come with him, then crossed alone the forest where the twisted-horned stag keeps his young doe; in Kalittokai 20 the woman asks to go and the man refuses, saying the forest is too hot, while she points to the stag and doe that go together.
teaches: The two poems give opposite men, one who invites idly and one who forbids, while the deer pair on the road answers both: whoever speaks, the creatures of the waste show the journey can be shared, so the stag and doe work as the paalai poets' standing proof against the lone journey.

note: The friend argues that wealth moves from one to another by former deeds (பழ வினை), so leaving to earn it is pointless; Kural 619 holds that even when fate denies, effort pays the wage of the body's labour.
teaches: The friend uses the doctrine of former deeds to keep the man home, while the Kural grants that doctrine only to deny that it excuses idleness, so the same belief about fate served the akam poets as an argument against striving and the moralist as one to be overruled.

note: In both the friend (for one Kural commentator) tells the man who announces his going that the woman will not survive him: 'tell your quick return to those who will be alive' and 'she will not live a blink without you'.
teaches: The couplet's bare refusal of comfort becomes in the kali an argued case: the friend first sets his two promises against each other and shows that wealth cannot be earned, and only then says the girl will not live, so the Kural's line reads as the last move of a dispute the long poem spells out.

note: Naladiyar 45 scorns men who praise teeth as jasmine buds, having seen fallen teeth in the burning ground; in Kalittokai 22 the woman asks the man who praised her teeth like jasmine buds whether he praised them falling out.
teaches: Both deflate the same compliment with the same decay, but to opposite ends: the ascetic uses the fallen teeth to free a man from desire, the wife uses them to bind him to her for life, so the image of the body's ruin cut both for and against staying with a woman.
audit_text_issue: Lines 5-8 and 19-22 hard.

note: In 14 the woman says his past praise of her shoulders, eyes, teeth, brow, hair and breasts has turned to estrangement; in 22 she asks whether he has praised the same teeth, hair and breasts as they will be when old.
teaches: The two poems run the same catalogue of praise through time: 14 looks back at praise already withdrawn, 22 looks ahead to the aged body, so together they make the lover's blazon a promise that covers the whole life of the body, which leaving for wealth would break.
audit_text_issue: 22 lines 5-8 and 19-22 are hard; sense uncertain

note: In both the woman tells her friend, before the man leaves, that she cannot survive his going: Kural 1155 asks her to stop it since union will be impossible once he goes, and Kalittokai 24 says her life has already gone with him.
teaches: The kali adds how she knows and why she yields: she learned of the journey from his sleep-talk and gives up her life to save his name from blame, so the couplet's plea to prevent the departure is shown coming from a woman who has already lost the chance to plead.
audit_text_issue: Line 11 of Kalittokai 24 is supplied from sangamtamil.com.

note: Kural 557: as the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of grace (அளி) is to those who live; Kalittokai 25: as is this world when the sky withholds rain, so is her beauty when his grace (அளி) is withdrawn.
teaches: The kali poet takes the moralist's image of rain and royal grace and applies it to a husband, so the man stands to his wife as a king to his realm and his leaving becomes a failure of rule, not only of love.

note: Kural 820 warns against the bond of those who are friendly at home and slander in the assembly; Kalittokai 25 compares her eyes, which shine while he is near and weep when he goes, to the bond of mean men who praise to the face and slander behind.
teaches: The friend turns the moralist's type of false friend into a figure for the woman's own body, whose eyes, bangles and brow publish her state once he leaves, so the danger the Kural sees in other people becomes, in love, the betrayal of the self by its own signs.

note: Purananuru 22 praises the Chera on campaign abroad, under whose white umbrella's shade the unarmed sleep safe while he does not sleep; Kalittokai 26 has the woman say her man guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade, praised by the world, while he lives in a stranger's land.
teaches: The akam woman quotes the very virtue the puram poet praises, shelter given abroad to all who seek it, and asks why it does not reach her, so the pairing shows the cost of the heroic ideal falling on the household the hero leaves.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the generous man to a fruit tree ripening in the town; Kalittokai 27 likens the riverbank trees flourishing in spring to the wealth of a man who gives without stint and lives by virtue.
teaches: The comparison runs one way in the Kural (wealth like a tree) and the other in the kali (trees like wealth), showing that the moral image had become common enough for a love poet to turn it round and use the giver's wealth to describe the season.

note: Kural 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm; Kalittokai 27 has spring encamp like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister let it in.
teaches: The Kural states the danger of a bad counsellor as a maxim, while the kali shows its outcome, the enemy camped inside the land, and uses that sight for spring's assault on a lonely woman, which shows the statecraft maxim already worked as a picture poets could borrow.

note: Kural 555: the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction wear away the wealth of the king who causes it; Kalittokai 34: her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed.
teaches: Read with the Kural, the woman's tears carry the threat the moralist gives to the subjects' tears, that they wear down the ruler who causes them, so her weeping is an accusation against the absent husband as well as a sign of grief.

note: Kural 788: friendship clears distress at once, as the hand of a man whose garment slips; Kalittokai 34: the lover has come on the promised day as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
teaches: Both use the hand that moves to the body without thought as the figure of help that needs no asking; the Kural gives it to friendship, the kali to a husband returning on the counted day, so the reflex image measures the ideal of timely help in both public and private bonds.

note: Kural 1257: the woman says she knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she longs for. Kalittokai 37: the girl says that, since he could not speak and she might not, she resolved (துணிதந்து) to do one shameless deed (நாண் இன்மை செய்தேன்), staging a fall into his arms.
teaches: The Kural makes the loss of shame something that happens to a woman when the lover acts, while Kapilar's girl chooses the shameless act herself because the man will not, and then praises him for the restraint that sends her home; held together they show that akam allows the heroine to set aside naanam as a tactic when the rules of speech leave both lovers mute.

note: Both use the simile of a poor man's youth (பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை, 38 line 15; the waste's trees in 10): poem 10 measures a withered landscape by it, poem 38 the girl's face drooping after a night of fear.
teaches: The paalai poet and Kapilar draw on one stock of moral similes, but Kapilar moves it from the land to the woman's body and pairs it with its opposite (the gracious man's wealth), so the girl's face becomes a landscape that his coming can drought or rain on, which is the kali form's way of turning a moral maxim into a lover's argument for marriage.

note: Kural 55: the wife who rises worshipping her husband, not a god, commands rain. Kalittokai 39: the girl, embraced by the man who saved her from the flood, could bring rain at need (line 6), and because hill women rise worshipping their husbands (கேள்வர்த் தொழுது எழலால்) the hunters' arrows do not miss.
teaches: The Kural's claim appears in the friend's disclosure as a belief the hill folk already hold, extended from rain to the whole hill economy and staked on a single premarital embrace, so the maxim on the wife's power was a shared folk conviction that the friend could use to argue the girl was already a faithful wife.

note: Kural 957: a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon. Kalittokai 41: if a falsehood appeared in the hill lord's truth it would be like fire appearing in the moon (திங்களுள் தீத் தோன்றியற்று).
teaches: The Kural uses the moon to say a noble man's fault cannot be hidden; the girls use it to say such a fault is impossible, so the same figure that warns the great serves in akam as a pledge of trust sung for the lover to overhear, binding him to live up to it.

note: Kural 428: not to fear what should be feared is folly, and to fear it is the work of the wise. Kalittokai 42 line 26: the friend checks her own reproach, saying he is not a lawless man who fears nothing that should be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சா அறன் இலி அல்லன்).
teaches: The Kural's prudence about danger is turned by the friend into a moral standard for a lover, where what should be feared is breaking a girl's heart, and failing it makes a man அறன் இலி; the pair shows the maxim already working as a test of character in love, not only in counsel.
audit_text_issue: Lines 11-22 and 25-32, including line 26, are flagged as absent from sangamtamil.com; the link depends on line 26.

note: Kural 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach. Kalittokai 43 lines 26-27: the lover is praised as one who, if he could not fill the want of one who told him of poverty, would give up his body (தன் மெய் துறப்பான்).
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is sung by the girls as a fact about one man to cure a girl's wasting, so the ethical maxim served in akam as the highest praise a lover could receive, and the praise itself works the cure before he comes.

note: Kural 980: greatness hides another's weakness, smallness tells only faults. Kalittokai 44: the girl hid the man's ungraciousness from her friend, the street and her companions, ashamed that others would blame him, and the friend calls this a nature rare even in a mother.
teaches: The Kural's mark of greatness is shown in the one wronged, a girl hiding her lover's fault, and the friend's report of it becomes a reproach, since the man learns that the greater one in the affair is she; the pair shows the maxim working as leverage in a love quarrel.

note: Kural 1112: the man scolds his heart for reeling at flowers, thinking her eyes resemble what many can see. Kalittokai 45: the friend asks whether he ruined the girl's eyes because they resembled the flowers of his hill's springs (மலர் ஏய்க்கும்). On one reading the claims are incompatible: the Kural's lover refuses the likeness as beneath her, Kalittokai's friend holds him to it as the motive of harm.
teaches: The flower comparison that the Kural's lover rejects to honour the girl is used by the friend against the man as an accusation, so the same convention of beauty can be denied as praise or pressed as a charge, depending on whether the lover or the friend wields it.

note: Kural 1192: the grace a lover shows the one who loves is like rain to those who live by it. Kalittokai 46: the girl longed for his grace like the bird that sings up to the sky for raindrops (துளி நசை ... அளி நசை), yet it was a stormy midnight (கனை பெயல் நடுநாள்) that kept him from the tryst.
teaches: The Kural's image of grace as rain is set in Kalittokai against real rain, which is what stopped the meeting, so the girl craves one rain while the other keeps it from her; the pairing shows the kali poet testing a stock equivalence against the weather of the kurinji night.

note: Kural 1133: the man says he once had shame and sound manliness and now has the palmyra horse. Kalittokai 47: the girl says a man of great strength and restraint has put off his manliness (தன் ஆண்தகை விட்டு) to tell her he cannot live without her.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's own account of losing his manliness, the threat behind the madal, while Kalittokai gives the girl's hearing of it, weighing whether to believe it and what consenting would cost her name, so the pair shows both sides of the same pressure in secret love.

note: Kuruntokai 3: the girl says her bond with the hill lord is larger than the earth, higher than the sky, deeper than the sea. Kalittokai 48: the friend tells the hill lord that the girl's grief, weighed, is greater than the hill whose bounds none knows (மலையினும் பெரிதே).
teaches: The same kurinji measure by immensity that the girl uses for her love the friend uses for its cost, so the pair shows that the size of the bond and the size of the grief at his absence are one quantity, and the friend can turn the heroine's boast into a charge against the man.

note: Both are the friend telling the hill lord not to come by night but by day (இரவின் வாரல் ... பகலும் பெறுவை; இரவின் வருதல் எவனோ? பகல்வரின்), and both open on a tusker after a fight with a tiger, wounded in Akananuru 308, dreaming and ashamed in Kalittokai 49.
teaches: Akananuru 308 turns the refusal into a full plan of the day tryst, while Kalittokai 49 builds a triple refrain that calls his love sweet and his coming bitter, so the pair shows the same convention used once as an invitation and once to separate the lover from his risk, with the tiger-fight's aftermath serving each as the danger of the night path.

note: Kural 1095: the man says she does not look at him directly but smiles with one eye narrowed. Kalittokai 51: the girl says the young man looked at her from the corner of his eye as if to kill and smiled (கடைக் கண்ணால் ... நகை கூட்டம் செய்தான்).
teaches: The Kural reads the sidelong smile as the girl's sign of consent, seen by the man; Kalittokai gives the same sign to the man, seen by the girl after she has lied for him, so the gesture of kurippu is not tied to one sex and seals a secret both have now chosen.

note: Purananuru 165 opens with those who wished to last in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து மன்னுதல் குறித்தோர்) and set up their fame; Kalittokai 54 ends with the girl wanting it said she acted from love, which in the unlasting world (மன்னா உலகத்து) is what lasts.
teaches: The akam heroine takes over the puram formula for lasting fame and applies it to a woman's choice of lover, so the Sangam ideal of a name that outlives one could be earned by love as well as by giving.

note: Kural 1117 asks whether a woman's face has spots as the moon does; Kalittokai 55 has the man make the same correction six times over (not the moon, for it has no stain; not the crescent, for it does not wane), reported by the girl.
teaches: The Kural's single corrected simile is shown in the Kalittokai as a wooing technique that the girl sees through, so the man's praise-by-correction is not only admiration but a calculated approach she names as such.

note: In Kural 1081 the man, first seeing her, cannot tell if she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Kalittokai 56 he asks if she is a craftsman's doll, a woman assembled from all women's best parts, or Death in a form it chose.
teaches: Both stage the first sight as a failure to classify the woman, but the Kalittokai adds Death and a girl too young to know her effect, so the Kural's bewilderment turns into a complaint that her beauty is a public danger no one has announced.

note: Kuruntokai 32 says appearing in the street on the palm-stem horse is blame (பழியே) for the man; Kalittokai 58 has the man say riding it will fix the blame on the girl (நீ படு பழியே).
teaches: On a defensible reading the two disagree about whom the madal shames, the rider or the woman, which shows the threat worked as leverage precisely because the disgrace could be made to fall on her household.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palm-stem horse; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the tusker-like warrior who threatens the mocked madal is truly without shame (நாண் இலன்).
teaches: The Kural gives the man's own confession that madal means the loss of shame and manliness; the Kalittokai gives the woman's side seeing that loss, and shows it is what persuades her that he will not stop.

note: Purananuru 12 asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma to take others' land so that it is painful to them (இன்னா ஆகப் பிறர் மண் கொண்டு) and do sweet things for his admirers; in Kalittokai 62 the girl asks whether forcing on others what pains them because it is sweet to oneself (தமக்கு இனிது என்று, வலிதின் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்வது) is good.
teaches: The same sweet-for-oneself, painful-for-others test is put to a conquering king and to a forceful lover, and in both the one questioned claims it as virtue (அறன்), so the Sangam poets judged seizure in war and in love by one moral rule.

note: Kural 316 says one must not do to another what one knows to be painful; in Kalittokai 62 the girl states that rule and the man answers that sweetness lies in the one who needs, and that seizing moon-faced women is virtue.
teaches: The Kalittokai lets the lover contest the Kural's rule with an argument from pleasure rather than ignore it, showing that the love poets knew the non-harm maxim and staged its failure under desire.

note: Kural 1102 says the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Kalittokai 60 the man tells the friend his only medicine is to see the girl's face, and there is no other.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as the man's private discovery after union; in the Kalittokai it is relayed by the friend as a plea before union, so the same conceit serves as an argument that obliges the girl to grant the cure.
audit_text_issue: lines 15-32 of kalittokai:60 are not in sangamtamil.com; the echo rests on lines 19-21

note: In Kalittokai 58 the man threatens madal to the girl herself; in 61 the friend reports the same threat, laughs at it as shameless, and still concludes they must act.
teaches: Read together they show where the madal threat lands: the girl too young to understand it in 58 cannot be moved by it, while the friend in 61 is, so the threat is effectively addressed to the household's guardians.

note: Kalittokai 67's three refrains say 'I would say I will sulk' (புலப்பேன் யான் என்பேன்மன்) and the heart says it will join him; Kural 1284 has the woman go to sulk and her heart go to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது).
teaches: The Kural's couplet is one turn of a song the Kalittokai performs three times with three different marks on the man's body, and the Kalittokai names the heart's act outright as treason (அறைபோகு), showing that the couplet's quiet split between woman and heart was heard as betrayal from within.

note: Kural 1254 says she used to call herself restrained (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்) but desire breaks out in public; Kalittokai 77 asks whether restraint (நிறை) is easy for one who lives with an enemy, her own heart.
teaches: The Kural blames desire in general for breaking restraint, while the Kalittokai wife places the failure in a precise moment, the sight of the unfaithful husband at her door, so the same loss of நிறை turns from a lover's confession into a wronged wife's helplessness against her own grievance.

note: Kural 1143 welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, because it gives as if already got what is not yet got; Kalittokai 76 ends that if the town has done what their kin would do at the wedding, nothing is left to do.
teaches: Both turn alar from shame into a kind of marriage, and together they show the two uses of the same claim: the Kural lover savours the gossip as a foretaste, while the Kalittokai friend uses it as an argument that the wedding is already public and must now follow.

note: Kural 1192 likens a lover's grace to the rain that sustains those who live by it; Kalittokai 71 likens the husband's once-a-year visit to a drizzle that cannot satisfy paddy withering for want of rain.
teaches: The Kural's rain stands for grace given in its season, and the Kalittokai shows the same image under neglect: a token visit is not rain but drizzle, so the wife measures grace by its sufficiency, a test the Kural's simile assumes but does not state.

note: Kural 580 praises those who, wanting a refinement worth loving, see poison poured and drink it; Kalittokai 74 calls the women who trust the husband's words though they see his graceless ways deluded, like those who eat poison knowing it kills.
teaches: Knowingly swallowing poison is a mark of courtesy in the Kural and a mark of delusion in the Kalittokai, so the same act is judged by whom it is done for: forbearance toward a friend is refinement, forbearance toward a faithless lover is folly.

note: Kural 1215 says what was seen awake was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet while it is seen; Kalittokai 68 says the husband's embrace is like wealth won in a dream, different on waking.
teaches: The Kural's lover levels waking and dream, both sweet while they last, but the Kalittokai wife uses the dream to name a possession that vanishes, so the dream simile can console a parted lover or indict an unfaithful husband depending on whether the absence is chosen.

note: Natrinai 250: the man came near his son practising walking with his little chariot in the street (தேர் நடைபயிற்றும்) and his wife shied away saying 'who are you?'; Kalittokai 81: the son practises walking with his chariot in the yard (கால் வல் தேர் கையின் இயக்க, நடை பயிற்றா) while husband and wife argue over him.
teaches: The Natrinai gives the husband's side in one recoil, while the Kalittokai stages the whole quarrel around the same toddling child, so together they show the son with his toy chariot as the standing occasion for the husband's return in marutham, and the wife's refusal as a scene both anthologies expected.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan clasping their son in the chariot street and gently asks if she is his mother too; in Kalittokai 82 the son's visits to the father's women, who adorn and kiss him, make the wife call for a stick.
teaches: The same encounter of the son with his father's women draws grace from one wife and fury from another, showing that marutham poets used it to test the wife's karpu: the Akananuru wife proves her dignity by kindness, the Kalittokai wife her love by jealousy.

note: Kuruntokai 359: the friend shows the bard the man embracing his son on the bed and the wife embracing his back; Kalittokai 75: when she quarrels, he hugs the son and feigns sleep (புதல்வன் புல்லிப் பொய் துயில் துஞ்சும்).
