teaches: Read together, the Kuruntokai's picture of a seemly household and the Kalittokai's account of the husband's tactic show that the son held in sleep was both the sign of reconciliation and the means of forcing it, and the wife in 75 knows it and yields anyway.

note: In Akananuru 66 the husband, on his way to a new wedding, lifts the crying son to his chest and gives up the wedding; in Kalittokai 79 the wife forbids him to take up the son, since the boy would wash off the other women's marks, and sends him back to them.
teaches: The husband's embrace of the son is the turning point of return in the Akananuru but is refused as a ruse in the Kalittokai, so the same gesture can end the husband's straying or be read by the wife as one more performance.

note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of matrons pouring water with petals and paddy and the bride curled in her new cloth (கோடிக் கலிங்கத்து ஒடுங்கினள்); Kalittokai 69 compares the swan pair to a brahmin circling the fire with his shy bride shrunk in her cloth (கலிங்கத்துள் ஒடுங்கிய).
teaches: The shy bride in her new cloth is a shared formula, but the rite around her differs: the Akananuru wedding has matrons, water and paddy and no fire, while the Kalittokai sets her beside a Veda-reciting priest circling the fire, so the two anthologies record two wedding rites in Tamil country.

note: Purananuru 92 says a son's prattle keeps no tune and makes no sense, yet moves fathers to grace; in Kalittokai 80 the mother hears the son's sweet 'attatta' but the father is away with other women.
teaches: The puram poet's comparison assumes a father present to be moved by the prattle, and the Kalittokai shows the house where he is not, so the grace the prattle should draw from the father falls to the mother and is mixed with pain.
audit_text_issue: Lines 1-3 are hard; the link does not rest on them.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife meets a courtesan cuddling her son in the chariot street and asks 'are you his mother too?'; in Kalittokai 84 the husband's women, the boy's 'mothers' (தாயர்), stop him in the street and load him with gifts, and the wife reads the shark ring as a message.
teaches: The two poems show that the son in the street was a fixed channel between wife and courtesan: the Akananuru wife disarms the rival by granting her a mother's place, while the Kalittokai wife finds that the same motherly gesture is used to send her a sign, so the courtesy of Akananuru 16 had a hostile counterpart.
audit_text_issue: Kalittokai 84 lines 10-41 are not in the sangamtamil.com text.

note: Purananuru 312 assigns bearing the son to the mother and making him worthy (சான்றோன் ஆக்குதல்) to the father; in Kalittokai 86 the mother herself teaches the son which of his father's qualities to copy and which to refuse.
teaches: Read together, they show the puram division of duties failing inside the house: when the father is the bad example, the mother takes over his task of forming the son, sorting his public virtues from his private fault, which the puram poem's neat allocation never anticipates.

note: Kural 70 says a son repays his father by making people ask what penance the father did; Kalittokai 86 has the mother wish the son to resemble the father in valour, justice and giving but not in leaving women.
teaches: The Kural assumes the father is the standard the son's goodness reflects back on, while the akam mother makes the son's goodness a correction of the father, so the same likeness that honours a father in the Kural reproaches him in the Kalittokai.
audit_text_issue: Kalittokai 86 lines 5 and 23 repaired.

note: In Kural 1259 the woman went to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him; in Kalittokai 87 the wife tells her heart that sulking at a shameless man is pointless and gives up her complaint.
teaches: Both wives abandon the sulk through the heart, but for opposite reasons: in the Kural the heart's desire overrides her, in the Kalittokai the heart concludes that a man without shame cannot be moved by sulking, so ending an oodal can be resignation as well as longing.
audit_text_issue: Lines 11, 12, 15 and 16 are not in sangamtamil.com.

note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that even if he wears a garland she accuses him of wearing it for another woman; in Kalittokai 88 the wife points to his faded garland, the pollen of other women's hair and the nail marks on him.
teaches: The Kural presents the wife's suspicion of a garland as groundless jealousy from the man's side, while the Kalittokai wife reads the same evidence correctly, so the couplet's comic complaint rests on an akam scene in which the garland really was a sign.

note: Kural 1325 has a faultless man delight in being kept from his beloved's arms; in Kalittokai 89 the husband says he has done no wrong (தீதோ இலேன்) and the wife calls the claim deceit and expects him to fall at her feet confessing.
teaches: The Kural builds the pleasure of oodal on the man's real innocence, while the Kalittokai shows the same plea of innocence as the stock defence of a straying husband, so the couplet's playful exclusion presupposes a faultlessness that akam wives treat as the thing in dispute.
audit_text_issue: Speaker division in Kalittokai 89 lines 10-11 is uncertain.

note: Kural 1260 asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in fire can say 'we will join and then sulk'; Kalittokai 90 ends with the wife asking whether women whose hearts cannot hold restraint (நிறை ஆற்றா நெஞ்சு) can say they will not bear his wrongs.
teaches: The Kalittokai gives the couplet's rhetorical question a full case: a detailed charge of a night visit, his dream defence and his plea, so that the wife's collapse comes after she has proved him guilty, showing that the melting heart of the Kural overrides evidence and not only pride.

note: In Kural 1288 the woman says his chest is to her as liquor is to drinkers, though it does shameful harm; Kalittokai 91 ends with the wife saying her heart melts when she sees him whatever wrong he does, so he need not try to please her.
teaches: The Kural states the compulsion as the woman's confession, while the Kalittokai draws its consequence for the man: because she always yields, he has no motive to behave, so the wife's helplessness becomes part of the reason the straying continues.

note: Paripadal 5 opens by hailing the spear that cut down Sur; in Kalittokai 93 one of the husband's 'goddesses' sang of the red-speared slayer of Sur with him on the hill through the rains.
teaches: The pair shows the Murugan hymn in two settings: in the Paripadal it is temple praise, while the Kalittokai places the same theme in a lovers' pastime on the hill in the rainy season, so devotional song at Murugan's hill was also an occasion for courtship that the wife can use as evidence.

note: In Akananuru 296 the friend refuses the man who bathed in the great Vaigai with a dark girl and comes home with his chest still wet; in Kalittokai 98 the man claims he only bathed in the Vaigai's new flood and the wife turns the flood itself into the courtesan.
teaches: The Akananuru records water play in the Vaigai as the plain occasion of an affair and its gossip, while the Kalittokai husband offers that same occasion as an innocent excuse and the wife answers by making the river a figure for the woman, so a known scene of straying becomes the material for the wife's metaphor.

note: Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade from the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, and that rain comes in the land of the just sceptre; Kalittokai 99 asks the husband, addressed as king, whether his wife fell outside the shade of the parasol he calls virtue's shade and the working of his sceptre.
teaches: The friend in the Kalittokai uses the same counsel a puram poet gave a king, that the parasol exists to shade those who suffer, and turns it on the household, showing that the akam poets could hold a husband to the standard of kingship and find him failing his nearest subject.

note: Kural 559 says that if the ruler bends justice the sky withholds rain; Kalittokai 99 praises the king for rains that come by his rightness and then asks whether his wife alone lies outside that rightness.
teaches: The Kural ties rain to the king's public justice only, while the Kalittokai grants the rain and still finds injustice at home, so the friend shows that the doctrine's measure of a ruler can be met in full while a wife is wronged.

note: Purananuru 55 wishes the Pandya the heat of the sun, the coolness of the moon and the giving of the rain; Kalittokai 100 praises the husband, as king, with the sun's harshness to foes, the moon's coolness to those under his parasol and the rain's giving, then says each praise is ruined by his wife's tears, bangles and pallor.
teaches: The akam friend takes the stock triad of royal praise found in the Purananuru and makes each term hostage to a woman's body, showing that the same encomium could be turned into a reproach by asking whether its subject meets it at home.

note: Kalittokai 101 says the herd girl's shoulders go to the one who seizes a bull that does not fear even a rutting tusker (கடாஅக் களிற்றினும் கண்ணஞ்சா ஏற்றை); Purananuru 342 says the chieftain's daughter's beauty is for fighters alone (பொருநர்க்கு அல்லது பிறர்க்கு ஆகாதே), her brothers threshing the battlefield with elephants for oxen.
teaches: Both give the girl only to proven courage, but the chieftain's family proves it in a war that uses elephants as threshing oxen, while the herders stage the proof on their own working animal inside a fenced pen, so the mullai contest is the puram bride-test turned from a siege that ruins the town into a bounded festival.

note: Purananuru 343: the father refuses even wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri humbly offered, and suitors' armies crowd the town; Kalittokai 103: the herd girls say they want no price (விலை வேண்டார்), only a man who will fall between the killer bull's horns as between their breasts.
teaches: Read together they show who sets the bride's terms: in the puram town the father refuses wealth and the girl becomes the cause of a war, while in the herders' song the girls voice the refusal themselves and name the one price they accept, so the mullai poem gives the woman the choice the puram poem leaves to her father and the kings.

note: Kalittokai 104 likens the pen strewn with gored men to the field where the five archers killed the hundred (நூற்றுவர் மடங்க... ஐவர் அட்ட பொரு களம்); Purananuru 2 praises the Chera who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five and fell on the field.
teaches: The Bharata war that Purananuru 2 treats as a dated occasion for one king's generosity is already, in Kalittokai, a stock picture of any heap of the fallen, used even for a village bull-catch, so the epic had passed from a remembered event into the common image store of the poets.

note: Kural 1150: the friend says the town raises the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant marriage if asked; Kalittokai 104: the friend tells the girl that her kin have gladly agreed to give her to the herder who leapt on the black bull, trampling on the heads of the town that raised the gossip (அலர் எடுத்த ஊராரை உச்சி மிதித்து).
teaches: The couplet hopes that the town's talk will move the lover to marry; the herders' poem shows a second way gossip ends, through the kin's public consent once the bull is taken, so in the mullai village it is the girl's family the gossip moves, and the wedding then silences the town.

note: Kural 1147: the sickness of love grows long with the town's gossip for manure and the mother's words for water; Kalittokai 105: the girl asks what joy equals this, that her mother beat her with a stick and the town made gossip linking her to the herder (யாய் என்னைக் கண் உடைக் கோலள் அலைத்ததற்கு... அலர் செய்துவிட்டது இவ் ஊர்).
teaches: The same two forces, the town's talk and the mother's harshness, feed a growing pain in the couplet but are welcomed as joy by the herd girl, because once the bond is public her marriage follows from the bull-catch; whether exposure hurts depends on whether an open road to marriage lies ahead.

note: Purananuru 278: the old mother, told her son fled, searches the field and rejoices more than at his birth to find him cut to pieces; Kalittokai 106: the herd girls sing that they will bind the bull-gored wounds against their breasts and that the tamer's blood on their curd-spotted shoulders is an ornament.
teaches: Akam takes over the puram pride in wounds taken facing the foe and moves it from the mother to the beloved: the wound that proves in Purananuru 278 that a son died well proves in Kalittokai 106 that a man is fit to be embraced, so the herd girls' desire is built on the warrior ethic.

note: In Kalittokai 107 the bull tosses the herder's mullai chaplet into the girl's hair by chance; in 115 she herself tied his chaplet in her hair and it fell before her mother; in both the kin then resolve to give her to him (அடை சூழ்ந்தார்).
teaches: The same outcome from accident in one poem and from the girl's own act in the other shows that among the herders the man's flowers in a girl's hair bind her however they got there: the kin read the first as a god's sign and the second as a fact to be ratified, and both end in betrothal.

note: Kural 1083: the man says he now knows Death, which has a woman's grace and big eyes that make war (பேரமர்க் கட்டு); Kalittokai 108: the man calls the girl the warrior who took up arms against his life, and mocks her trust in her mullai-bud teeth and battle eyes (பேர் அமர் உண் கண்ணும்), while she answers back and at last sets the tryst.
teaches: The couplet's lone confession of being slain by her eyes appears in the herders' poem as a line of banter that the girl hears, throws back and answers with a meeting place, which shows the conceit of the killing eye at work as courtship speech addressed to the woman, not only as the man's inner wonder.
audit_text_issue: Lines 20, 21, 46, 49 are hard; line 46 has a lost letter.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Kalittokai 109: the man watching the buttermilk girl reports that the town's wives, judging her fit to be an anangu to everyone (யார்க்கும் அணங்கு ஆதல் சான்றாள்), keep their husbands in and shut their doors when she comes.
teaches: Beside the couplet, the herders' poem shows that the word அணங்கு named a real danger, a beauty that strikes whoever sees it: what is one man's private bewilderment in the Kural becomes in Kalittokai a judgment the whole town shares and acts on by guarding its men.

note: Akananuru 180: while the girls play at sand houses, a man drives up, hangs a kuvalai wreath down her braid unasked, gazes and leaves, and the town starts talking; Kalittokai 111: a herder offers to build the girl's play-house, tie a garland in her hair and paint her breasts, and she refuses each, saying a girl who takes a stranger's flowers is a great fool (ஏதிலார் தந்த பூக் கொள்வாய்).
teaches: The herd girl's refusal states the rule the shore poem leaves unsaid, that a stranger's flowers in a girl's hair are a claim on her; that rule is why the silent wreath of Akananuru 180 sets the town talking, and why the herd girl answers the same offer by asking her friend to tell her parents.

note: Akananuru 86 presents the rite (sand spread under the pandal, தருமணல் ஞெமிரி; the matrons' blessing of chastity; the kin giving the bride, தமர்தர) as the start of the marriage; in Kalittokai 114 the girl, seeing her kin prepare a wedding with sand spread low (தரு மணல் தாழப் பெய்து), says she knows only the one union she made among her play-house companions and that two weddings are against the nature of herd girls. On this reading the rite that makes a marriage in 86 makes none in 114.
teaches: Held together, the two show that akam could place the binding moment of marriage either in the kin's sand-strewn rite or before it in the secret union, so the same ceremony that founds a wife's chastity in Akananuru 86 would, given to another man, be a forbidden second marriage for the herd girl.
audit_text_issue: kalittokai:114 has lacunae at lines 2 and 18; lines 7-13 and 16-21 are absent from one source, and lines 1-2 do not fit

note: Kural 1229 says that when evening spreads the whole town is bewildered and suffers; Kalittokai 118's refrain says evening torments those parted but cannot dim (கடிகல்லாய்) the beauty, sweet speech and smile of lovers who are together.
teaches: Read beside the poem, the couplet's 'the whole town suffers' shows itself as the lonely woman's projection, since the kali poem insists evening harms only the parted, so the grief belongs to separation and not to the hour.

note: Kural 1221 tells the hour it is not evening but the time that eats the lives of the wedded; Kalittokai 119, after a long catalogue of dusk, says those who call it evening are deluded, not knowing it is the hour that unwraps women's lives.
teaches: The couplet compresses into one address the argument the kali poem builds through fifteen lines of homing birds, closing flowers and lit fires, so the Kural's 'not evening but a killing hour' is a summary of an established neythal rebuttal rather than a fresh conceit.

note: Both close on the same half-line, மாலை என்மனார் மயங்கியோரே; Kuruntokai 234 says that for the lonely even dawn and day are evening, Kalittokai 119 says that evening is really the hour that undoes women's lives.
teaches: The shared closing formula was a set rebuttal that could be turned two ways: the short poem stretches evening over the whole day, the long one narrows it to a killing hour, so 'those who call it evening are deluded' was a commonplace the poets argued with, not one poet's phrase.

note: Kural 1224: in the lover's absence evening comes like enemies to a killing field; Kalittokai 120 makes evening a hunter aiming at a deer, a mocker of the beaten, a man pushing a spear into a burn, and Death grinning with the crescent as its tooth.
teaches: The poem unfolds the couplet's single image of evening as executioner into a series of cruelties each aimed at someone already wounded, which shows that the Kural's 'like enemies' means an attack on the defenceless, not just a hostile arrival.

note: Both use the reign of a weak ruler (மெல்லியான் பருவம்) for nightfall: in 129 the confused dark comes like the weak reign after a just king; in 120 the cruel evening vanishes as the enemy of a weak reign is driven off when a good king appears, the lover's return.
teaches: The same poet places one political figure at both ends of the night, darkness arriving as misrule after a just king and lifting when a rightful king returns, so in these poems the absent lover stands in the place of the king and his coming restores order, not only pleasure.

note: Kural 1246 tells the heart its anger is false, since it cannot stay angry on seeing the man who ends quarrels by union; Kalittokai 122 has the woman, chided for sulking, say she knows he keeps other women, yet when he tends her a little her shameless heart melts and is calmed.
teaches: The kali poem supplies the setting the couplet leaves out, a friend mocking her sulks as causeless, so the Kural's confession that the heart's anger is false turns out to answer that reproach: she knows his fault fully, and her heart still gives way.

note: Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for following the man who left while lamenting his lack of grace; Kalittokai 123 asks the simple heart (மட நெஞ்சே) that went to him at night whether it saw, embraced or knew him, and pities it for tossing like the backwater tide.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's 'you go after him' looks like as an event, the heart's nightly journey met by three questions it cannot answer, so the Kural's rebuke of the foolish heart is the end of a scene in which the heart keeps coming back empty.

note: Kural 1235: the friend says the shoulders, bangles gone and old beauty faded, declare the cruel man's cruelty; Kalittokai 124: the friend tells the man the woman hid her pain even from her, but her pale forehead, wasted shoulders and streaming eyes could not hide it.
teaches: Together they show the body as a witness that overrides the woman's own silence: the poem adds that she tried to keep the pain even from her closest friend, so what the couplet calls the shoulders 'declaring' is a betrayal of her will to conceal, which the friend then turns against the man.

note: Kural 293: do not lie about what your own heart knows, for after the lie your heart burns you; Kalittokai 125 opens with the maxim that those who think no one saw may hide what their heart knows, but no witness is closer than the heart, and then charges the lover.
teaches: The akam friend turns the ethical maxim into a weapon of courtship: the Kural's inner witness, a general law of truthfulness, becomes the ground on which she charges a lover with knowing his own neglect, so the doctrine of conscience was already available to love poetry as rhetoric.

note: Kural 1218: when I sleep he is on my shoulder, when I wake he runs into my heart; Kalittokai 126: the friend says the woman, thinking of him, believes him on her shoulder (தோள் மேலாய்), embraces him as if awake, finds nothing and knows it was a dream.
teaches: The poem tells the couplet's moment from outside and counts its cost: what the Kural's woman offers as a defence of her lover (he never leaves me) the friend reports as the last of three daily delusions ending in grief, so the shoulder-dream is comfort in the first person and harm in the third.

note: Kural 1157: the bangles slipping past her wrist announce that the lord of the shore has left; Kalittokai 127: the friend tells the lord of the shore that her bangles slip (இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த) and asks him to give grace as the wave shelters the adumbu creeper.
teaches: The couplet has the bangles accuse the man to the woman herself; the poem has the friend carry the same evidence to the man's face and pair it with a remedy, so the slipping bangle moves from private proof of desertion to an argument for his return.

note: Kural 1213: my life lasts because I see in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Kalittokai 128: the woman tells of a dream in which she quarrelled with the man and he bowed at her feet, and says her life held at the brink hoping he would come awake too.
teaches: The poem shows the mechanism the couplet only asserts: the dream keeps her alive by letting her act out the quarrel and his submission and by feeding the hope of a real coming, so the Kural's 'my life lasts' rests on both satisfaction and expectation.

note: Kuruntokai 30 calls the dream of the lover's embrace a lying dream (பொய்க்கனா) that deceived her and left her wasted; Kalittokai 128 says the dream in which he came kept her life from going, in hope he may come awake. On a plain reading one treats the dream as deceit, the other as ground for hope.
teaches: The same dream of the lover is judged a cruel lie in one poem and the thing that keeps the woman alive in the other, so akam poets held no single view of dreams and used the dream's truth or falseness to mark whether hope survived.

note: Kural 1222 asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Kalittokai 129 asks the sea, the anril on the palmyra and the little flute in turn whether, like her, they have someone who loved and left them.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's question as one move in a round of addresses to sea, bird and music, so the Kural's single address to evening reads as a compressed survival of a sung form in which each sound of nightfall is asked whether it too was abandoned.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds at morning and blooms at evening; Kalittokai 130: as the great backwater flowers close at evening, her heart closes in ruin (அழிவொடு கூம்பும்).
teaches: The two invert one flower image: the couplet makes the evening sickness bloom, the poem makes the heart shut with the evening flowers, so love's pain at dusk could be figured as opening or as closing, and the Kural's paradox depends on reversing the shore's ordinary evening closure.

note: Kural 1154: if the man who said 'do not fear' leaves, is the fault in those who trusted his word; Kalittokai 132: the friend asks the man whether the woman's pallor and lost beauty are not the fruit of his 'do not fear' (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு) and 'trust me' (தெளி) at their secret meetings.
teaches: The couplet's question of who bears the fault is answered in the poem by the friend, who reads each reassurance as the direct cause of a named loss, so the Kural's moral question has a speech situation behind it in which the promise is handed back to the man as a debt.

note: Kalittokai 133 defines அறிவு as bearing the words of fools (பேதையார் சொல் நோன்றல்) and பொறை as bearing with those who do not cherish you; Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths.
teaches: The same act is filed under different virtues: the kali friend calls forbearance toward fools wisdom and keeps patience for those who neglect you, while the Kural calls it strength, so this forbearance had no fixed place yet in the lists of virtues, standing under wisdom in one and strength in the other.

note: Kalittokai 133: justice (முறை) is taking life without favour (கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்); Kural 541: justice is to examine, show favour to no one (கண்ணோடாது) and act after weighing.
teaches: Both define justice with the same word கண்ணோடாது, but the love poem gives its harshest form, taking life, in a list meant to shame a lover, so the definition of முறை as unbending punishment was common coin a friend could quote, and the Kural's procedural version tempers a stock definition centred on the death sentence.

note: Kural 1164: the sea of love is there but there is no raft of safety to cross it; Kalittokai 134: her grief ends as a man whose ship broke in a shoreless sea is saved by a raft the waves bring, the lovers hastening home. One says no raft exists, the other that the sea itself brings one.
teaches: The two use the same sea and raft with opposite outcomes, which shows that in love the raft is not something the sufferer can find for herself: the couplet's woman has none, and in the poem it arrives only with the beloved's return.

note: Kalittokai 135's friend tells the shore lord that abandoning the girl would lie as a great fault on his lineage (குடிமைக் கண் பெரியது ஓர் குற்றம்); Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out high like the spot on the moon.
teaches: The couplet's rule that high birth makes a fault more visible is what gives the friend's threat its force: she aims at his lineage rather than his love because a lord's desertion, unlike a commoner's, would be seen by all, so the maxim is already a working argument in akam persuasion.

note: Kalittokai 136 likens the girl's joy at each meeting to a gambler's winning throw and her grief at his leaving to the loss of a stake; Kural 932 says the gambler gains one and loses a hundred.
teaches: Read with the couplet's arithmetic of the dice, the friend's simile becomes a warning: a secret love that runs on wins and losses must end in ruin on balance, which is why she ends by telling him to take the girl in marriage and stop the game.

note: Kalittokai 137 says his gentleness burns her worse than fire (தீயினும் கடிது); Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, while love's sickness burns when the lover is away.
teaches: The couplet states as a single paradox what the kali poem reaches through three graded steps (word above bow, kindness above enmity, gentleness above fire), so the Kural's compressed contrast between fire and love was the end point of an argued rhetoric the longer form still displays.

note: Kalittokai 138's madal rider sings that grief and the palmyra horse are what she gave (படரும் பனை ஈன்ற மாவும் நல்கியவை); in Kural 1135 the man says the girl gave him the madal and evening's anguish.
teaches: Both men list the madal among the woman's gifts, so the convention made the beloved the author of the lover's public shame; the kali poem adds the outcome the couplet leaves open, her coming in grace, which shows the gift was meant to be returned.

note: Kalittokai 139 calls the horse she gave a shelter (ஏமம்) against the army of love; Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard (ஏமம்) and no strength but the madal.
teaches: Both use the same word ஏமம் for an act of humiliation, and the kali poem shows how the safeguard works: it is spoken to the worthies whose duty is to treat another's pain as their own, so the madal protects by putting the assembly under obligation.

note: Kalittokai 139's rider swims the sea of love with the madal as his raft (மடல் புணையா நீந்துவேன்); Kural 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: Where the couplet's flood sweeps away the raft of shame, the kali lover takes the shameful act itself as his raft, so the two together show the madal as what is left when shame has failed: a raft made of the loss of one.

note: Kalittokai 140's rider complains that the town sees his sickness and does not soften (கண்டும் கண்ணோடாது இவ் ஊர்); Kural 576 says those who have eyes and do not turn them kindly are like trees fixed in the soil.
teaches: The madal rider appeals to the civic virtue the Kural names கண்ணோட்டம், so the madal is shown to work through the town's duty of kindly regard, and the town that will not soften is, by the Kural's measure, as insensible as a tree.

note: Kalittokai 141's rider says she made him, who rides the war horse in battle, ride the madal to the common; in Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The couplet's before-and-after inventory is spelled out in the kali poem as three lost ranks (warrior, protector, orator), which shows that the manliness the Kural says is lost is a public standing, not only a private virtue.
audit_text_issue: Lines 11-12 are obscure, as the marker says; the link does not depend on them.

note: Kalittokai 142's girl, once laughing with hidden teeth, now laughs aloud and weeps so all hear and sings her love to the worthies; Kural 1138 says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks secrecy and comes into the open.
teaches: The couplet states as a law what the kali poem stages as a scene with an audience and a song, and shows the price: once love breaks into the open, the woman faces two pains, love and gossip (காமமும் கௌவையும்), where the couplet names only the first.

note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.
audit_text_issue: 143 lines 10-13 are obscure, as the marker notes.

note: Kalittokai 144's girl says that when she opens her eyes to seize him he runs and hides in her heart; Kural 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
teaches: The same fancy of the lover fleeing into the heart on waking appears in both, but the kali poem frames it as a madwoman's complaint to the sea, so what the couplet offers as consolation (he never leaves her) is also a sign of her derangement.

note: Kalittokai 145's woman begs the sun not to set and speaks of bearing evening's enmity (மாலைப் பகை); Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what enmity (பகை) to evening.
teaches: The couplet's riddle about why evening is hostile is answered in the kali poem by an action: she asks the sun to stay and hopes the man will come at dawn over the sea, so the hours are enemies or friends according to when the parted can expect his return.

note: Kalittokai 146's woman says that if she told her pain to the night that puts many to sleep (பலர்த் துயிற்றும் யாமம்), it would not sleep; Kural 1168 says the night that puts all beings to sleep has no companion but her.
teaches: Both make the night, the one who puts all to sleep, the only wakeful companion of the deserted woman; the kali poem goes further and threatens to keep the night itself awake with her song, turning the couplet's pity for the night into her power over it.

note: Kural 1137 says nothing is worthier than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the madal; Kalittokai 147's woman, maddened in the street, begs Kama's arrows so that the man will come riding the palmyra horse.
teaches: The kali woman keeps the rule the couplet praises, she does not mount the madal, but she gets around it by wishing the madal on him, so the restriction on women survives even in the most extreme akam scene and shapes the form her desire takes.

note: Kalittokai 148 calls evening a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; in Kural 1226 the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband was still with her.
teaches: The couplet records the discovery and the kali poem the double nature behind it: the same hour is a raft and a suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for lovers together and a sickness for the parted, which is why she learned its cruelty only after he left.

note: Kalittokai 149's friend warns that failing those who helped in want will strike the doer even in his descendants; Kural 110 says one who kills a good done to him has no escape.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's gravest moral rule to a lover's delay, so the woman who gave herself in secret is counted as a benefactor, and his failure to marry her becomes ingratitude, the one wrong with no escape.
audit_text_issue: Lines 7 and 11 are repaired readings.

note: Purananuru 34 quotes dharma that there is expiation for many crimes but none for those who kill a benefit; Kalittokai 149's friend says ingratitude to helpers will not spare a man, however good his sword.
teaches: The rule the puram poet uses to praise a king's gifts to bards is turned in the akam poem against a lover, which shows the ethic of gratitude ran across both halves of Sangam poetry and could bind a man's private love as tightly as a patron's duty.

note: In Kalittokai 16 virtue itself runs to block the man's venture for wealth; in Kalittokai 150 the friend says he left 'giving up virtue' (அறம் துறந்து) and still assures the woman that he will not prove false.
teaches: In 16 virtue is the force that keeps him home, while in 150 the friend grants that he broke virtue by going and yet trusts his word, so the two poems split the man's duty into staying (அறம்) and keeping faith (not being பொய்), which can come apart.

note: Kuruntokai 0 knows Murugan by his lotus-red feet, the spear that split the mountain and the cock banner, and says his guarding keeps the world safe; Thiruppugazh 323 names the same spear that pierced Krauncha, the cock banner and the golden anklet feet, and asks for release from desire.
teaches: The same three marks of Murugan pass from a guarantee of the whole world's safety in the oldest invocation to one devotee's plea for rescue from his own lust, so the iconography stayed fixed while the god's protection moved from the world to the self.

note: In both the man praises the woman he has just joined by addressing a creature of the flowers: Kuruntokai 2 asks the bee whether any flower is more fragrant than her hair; Kural 1111 tells the anicham it is soft but she is softer.
teaches: Valluvar keeps the Sangam device of praise through an apostrophe to nature but changes the sense judged, from smell to touch, and drops the witness: the Kuruntokai man asks the bee for evidence, the Kural man simply declares the verdict.

note: Both have the woman in separation with eyes that cannot sleep; Kuruntokai 5 uses the sleeplessness to ask whether this is love-sickness, Kural 1179 says the eyes do not sleep when he is away nor when he comes.
teaches: The Sangam woman learns from sleepless eyes that she is in love, while the Kural woman, past that discovery, finds the sleeplessness survives even his return, so the couplet assumes and goes beyond the moment the older poem records.

note: Both set the sleeping world against the one woman awake in separation; Kuruntokai 6 leaves her alone awake under the dead night, Kural 1168 makes the night itself her companion, pitied for having no one else.
teaches: The Kural turns the bare Sangam contrast of a sleeping world and one waking woman into a conceit in which the night shares her vigil, so the couplet adds a companion, even a mocked one, to a solitude the older poem leaves complete.

note: In Kuruntokai 7 onlookers see anklets still on the eloping girl's soft feet; in Akananuru 321 the foster mother says the girl took off her pebble-filled anklets for fear her mother would hear, before crossing the bamboo hills.
teaches: Together they show the anklet as the sign of an unwed girl read from two sides: at home its sound must be silenced for her to escape, while on the road strangers recognise from it, still on her feet, that the pair are lovers in flight rather than a married couple.

note: Kural 906 says men who fear their wife's shoulders are worthless even if they live like gods; in Kuruntokai 8 the other woman mocks the man for doing his son's mother's bidding like a mirror image, and on the akam reading this obedience is the household holding him, which the poem does not condemn.
teaches: Read together they show that the conduct the Kural brands as a man's vice appears in akam only as the other woman's spiteful jibe, so the ethical charge of wife-obedience and the love poem's victory of the wife are the same act seen from opposite sides.

note: Both open with யாயாகியளே and both have the friend tell how the wife hides her husband's cruelty (கொடுமை) out of shame; in 9 she wilts like an unworn flower, in 10 she comes as leader of the festival yet ashamed.
teaches: Placed together the two poets show the wife's concealment as a set karpu situation with two costs: it wastes her body in private and shames her in public, and in each case it is the friend, not the wife, who breaks the silence.

note: Kural 1248 has the woman call her heart a fool for running after the man who left; in Kuruntokai 11 the woman herself bids her heart rise and follow him even past the land of the Vadugar, since staying here cannot be survived.
teaches: The heart that the Kural woman scolds for following is the one the Sangam woman sends out on purpose, so the same impulse is folly in the Kural's chapter and the only means of survival in Maamulanar's poem.

note: In both the woman says her lover gave her sickness and pallor: Kuruntokai 13 says plainly he gave the sickness and pallor fills her eyes; Kural 1183 says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange.
teaches: The Kural turns Kapilar's single complaint of a gift into an exchange with two sides, naming what was taken (சாயல், நாண்) as well as what was given, so the pair show the 'he gave me pallor' formula growing into an account of loss.

note: Kuruntokai 15 measures the lovers' fidelity by the good word of the Kosar of Nalur given under the old banyan; Akananuru 113 calls the Kosar many-speared guards who never swerve from friendship even in bad times.
teaches: Akananuru 113 supplies the reputation the Kuruntokai simile depends on: the Kosar were known for keeping faith in adversity, so the foster mother vindicates the eloped girl's bond by the standard of a war band's unbreakable loyalty, not by its feeling.

note: Both are the man speaking of the madal: Kuruntokai 17 lists as a general rule what men do when love hardens (ride the palm horse, wear erukku, become a street spectacle); Kural 1133 says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal.
teaches: The Kuruntokai poem supplies the public ritual (the erukku garland, the mocking street) that the Kural compresses into a single inventory of loss, and the Kural adds what the older poem leaves unstated: that taking up the madal costs a man his shame and manliness.

note: Kuruntokai 18 says her love hangs on her small life like a great jackfruit on a small stalk; Kural 1163 says love and shame hang from the two ends of a carrying pole that is her life.
teaches: Both picture love as a weight hanging from life, but the Kural adds shame as a counterweight, so the Sangam image of a stalk about to snap under one load becomes in the couplet a pole balanced between two loads that will snap either way.

note: Purananuru 233 refuses to believe the dawn news that Evvi, leader of the bards' families, lies with spear wounds in his chest; Kuruntokai 19 compares the man's grieving heart to the flowerless heads of the bards impoverished by Evvi's loss.
teaches: The puram lament gives the moment of the news, and Paranar's simile gives its aftermath, bards going bare-headed without flowers, so the pair show a patron's death becoming a recognised mourning custom that akam could borrow to measure a lover's estrangement.

note: In Akananuru 43 the man who stays calls those who leave their companion for wealth fools (மடமையோர்); in Kuruntokai 20 the woman left behind grants the leavers the name of the wise (உரவோர்) and claims folly (மடவம்) for those who stay.
teaches: The paalai debate is fought over the same pair of words, wise and foolish: the staying man pins folly on the leavers, while the abandoned woman lets them keep wisdom and takes folly as the side of love, so who names whom foolish depends on who was left.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Purananuru 216 he says his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar calls himself 'the foolish Chola's'; in Kuruntokai 20 his heroine says let the leavers be wise and let us be fools.
teaches: The same king, in puram and in akam, gives the name of folly to loyalty that prudence would abandon, his friend's in the one and the waiting woman's in the other, so the akam poem's irony has a model in the king's own creed of friendship.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend points to the bloomed konrai that has made the forest lovely as proof that the season of his return has come. Kuruntokai 21: the woman says that even if the konrai forest declares the rains, she will not believe it, since he does not lie.
teaches: The same konrai sign is proof of his return in the friend's mouth and a sign the woman refuses in her own, so the season argument of the mullai poems could be turned around: faith in his word can deny the season rather than read it.

note: Kuruntokai 25: the only witness of the secret union was a heron watching for fish. Kuruntokai 26: against the lover's possible denial, the friend says even the male monkey of the hill knows that cruel man.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the lack of a human witness to kalavu as a standing fear, answered by pointing to the land's own creatures: the woman doubts that the heron saw anything, while the friend insists that the monkey knows.
audit_text_issue: Kuruntokai 26 occasion uncertain

note: Kural 1189: the woman says let her body turn pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is well. Kuruntokai 27: her beauty, of use neither to her nor to him, is left for pallor to eat, like milk spilt on the ground.
teaches: The Kural lets the woman accept pallor as a price paid for his welfare, while the Kuruntokai poet counts it pure waste, a yield that reaches no one, so the same pallor in absence is read as sacrifice in one and as loss with no gain in the other.

note: Kural 1168: the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, for it has no companion but her. Kuruntokai 28: she wants to strike, butt or cry out at the town that sleeps unaware of her pain.
teaches: Both set one sleepless woman against a sleeping world, but the Kural turns the loneliness into pity for the night, while the Sangam poem turns it into rage at the town, which shows that the same isolation could be voiced as tender complaint or as a wish to wake everyone.

note: Kural 1229: when evening spreads, the whole town is bewildered and suffers (on the reading that the town shares her pain). Kuruntokai 28: the town sleeps, not knowing her grief.
teaches: On that reading the Kural imagines the town grieving with the lovesick woman, while Kuruntokai 28 has the town sleep through her grief, so whether the community shares a private sorrow is answered both ways in the love poetry.

note: Kural 660: making wealth by deceit and feeling safe is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. Kuruntokai 29: the heart, passing over good counsel, is like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain, plunged into a flood it cannot hold.
teaches: In both the unfired pot is ruined by what it is made to hold, so the image locates the fault in the vessel rather than the water: wealth got by fraud undoes its keeper as desire taken in against counsel undoes the heart.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 30: a lying dream of his embrace deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed, alone.
teaches: The Kural blames waking in the abstract, while the Kuruntokai poem shows the very moment, the hand on the empty bed, so the couplet's complaint gains a scene and the scene gains a name for its cause.

note: Kural 1218: in sleep he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart. Kuruntokai 30: on waking from the dream she finds only the empty bed and calls herself alone and pitiable.
teaches: The Kural consoles the dreamer that waking only moves the lover inward, while the Kuruntokai woman finds no such refuge and is left alone, so the two disagree on whether the waking after a love dream is a loss or a passage into the heart.

note: Akananuru 236 likens the heroine to Aathimanthi, who wept from land to land and town to town asking 'have you not seen Aattan Atthi?', the dancer the flood took. Kuruntokai 31, by Aathimanthiyaar, has a woman of the dancing ground search festival and dance for the chief who is a man of the dancing ground.
teaches: Read with Paranar's simile, the unnamed 'man of the dancing ground' in Kuruntokai 31 is the lost dancer of the legend, and the poem gives in the first person the search the Akananuru turns into a stock comparison for a woman maddened by loss.

note: Akananuru 222 tells how Aathimanthi, after the Kaveri seized Aattan Atthi, searched in bewilderment until Maruthi showed her the lover and entered the sea. Kuruntokai 31 is the woman's own voice at the stage where she finds him nowhere.
teaches: Together the two poems order the story: Kuruntokai 31 stands in the middle of the search, 'nowhere do I see him', and the Akananuru supplies the end that the short poem never reaches, so the legend outlived the poet's own lament.

note: Kural 1131: for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse. Kuruntokai 32: to ride the madal in the street is shame, and to live apart is shame too.
teaches: The same lover's threat is a safeguard in the Kural and a disgrace in the Kuruntokai, which only weighs it as the lesser of two shames, so the madal was argued both as the lover's last strength and as an equal dishonour to living on without her.

note: Kural 1227: love-sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening. Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is a lie.
teaches: The Kural gives love a daily clock with evening as its worst hour, while the Kuruntokai lover says true love cannot tell the hours apart, so the two set the convention of the evening's pain against the claim that real longing knows no time.

note: Akananuru 376: the courtesan asks the lord to give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai. Kuruntokai 34: the friend calls the wife's bright brow lovely as Kuttuvan's Maranthai.
teaches: The same Chera port is the standard of beauty for a wedded girl and for a courtesan, so the akam poets used Maranthai's fame as a neutral measure of a woman's nalam whatever her standing.

note: Purananuru 71: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not rout the allied kings he may be parted from his wide-eyed wife. Kuruntokai 36: the lover swore a vanjinam that he would not leave her.
teaches: Separation from the beloved is the penalty the king stakes on his battle vow and the very thing the lover's vow forswears, so the akam vow borrows the puram form and the friend's trust in it rests on the warrior's honour that a vanjinam is never broken.

note: Akananuru 59: the friend tells the wasting heroine that on the road the man took a tusker bends a tall yaa tree to feed its young mate, and the poem ends on 'the road he went'. Kuruntokai 37 gives the same tusker easing its mate's hunger on the yaa and the same close, 'the road he went'.
teaches: The long poem spends its lines on her lost beauty, a Mal simile and his forgetting before reaching the tusker and the road, so Kuruntokai 37 shows the consolation reduced to its working parts: a promise of his love, the creature's care as proof, and the road.

note: Kalittokai 11: the woman says the man himself told her that in the burning forest the tusker lets his mate drink the little muddy water first, the dove fans its tired mate and the stag shades the doe, so he will return. Kuruntokai 37: the friend gives one tusker stripping the yaa for his mate.
teaches: The later Kalittokai multiplies the single tusker into three caring males and puts the inference in the heroine's own mouth, which shows the comforting iraicchi of porul 5.35 growing from the friend's one proof into a catalogue the heroine argues from.

note: Akananuru 45: the lover crossed a summer forest where the dried pods of the uzhunjil rattle like the drums of a dancing ground. Kuruntokai 39: they say his road is the hard waste where the wind makes the dried uzhinjil pods rattle.
teaches: The rattling uzhinjil pods are a fixed sign by which a waiting woman pictures the man's road; the Akananuru makes the sound a dance drum, while Kuruntokai 39 keeps it as hearsay ('they say'), showing that the woman's knowledge of the waste is report, not sight.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life. Kuruntokai 40: the man says their mothers, fathers and they themselves were strangers, yet their loving hearts have mingled like rain in red earth.
teaches: Both men declare an inseparable bond, but the Kuruntokai first denies any tie of kin, so the union it praises is made between strangers and inseparable only after mingling, which the Kural's body-and-life image, a pair joined from birth, does not show.

note: Naladiyar 125 says the bond (தொடர்பு) with small men wanes (தேயுமே) of itself like the moon while friendship with the great grows; Kuruntokai 42 asks the hill lord whether our bond (எம் தொடர்பும்) will wane (தேயுமோ) even if desire ends.
teaches: The same two words, bond and waning, show the friend putting the lover to the Naladiyar's test of character: a bond that wanes once its first cause, desire, is spent marks the small man, so her question demands that he prove himself one of the great.

note: Kural 1151 has the woman (or her friend) speak at once: if you are not leaving, tell me; your quick return, tell those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 43 says neither spoke: she thought he would not go, he thought she would not bear it.
teaches: The couplet is the sentence whose absence Avvaiyar's poem mourns: set beside it, the poem shows a parting that happened because pride on both sides kept that sentence unsaid, so the Kural's bluntness reads as the cure for the silence that undid the Kuruntokai pair.

note: In Akananuru 7 the foster mother, following her eloped daughter into the waste, cannot catch up and questions a hill girl she meets; in Kuruntokai 44 her legs are worn out, her eyes dimmed from looking, and the others she sees are more than the stars.
teaches: Together they give the search its course: the long poem is its middle, where the nurse still questions each stranger in hope, and the four-line poem is its end, where every face has proved to be someone else's and the looking itself has cost her sight.

note: Kural 1222: the woman tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed as hers. Kuruntokai 46 asks whether the sad evening (புன்கண் மாலை) is absent in the land where he has gone.
teaches: Both women make the evening's sorrow a test of the absent man: the couplet asks whether the evening's partner is as hard as hers, the poem asks whether he has any evening at all, and its sparrows settling with their young supply what the couplet leaves out, that evening is when every creature with a home returns to it.

note: Kural 1119: the man tells the moon that if it would resemble her face it must not appear for many to see. Kuruntokai 47: the friend tells the long white moon it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
teaches: Both speakers wish the moon would not shine for others, for opposite reasons: the Kural's lover wants her face kept to himself, the Kuruntokai friend wants the meeting kept from watchers, so the moon's openness, which the couplet turns into a compliment, is in the older poem the danger that ends secret love.

note: Kural 1315: the man says they will not part in this birth, and her eyes fill with tears. Kuruntokai 49: the woman asks that even when this life turns into the next he be her husband.
teaches: The couplet's joke rests on a wish it never states, that the bond reach past this birth; Kuruntokai 49 is that wish in the woman's own mouth, so the pair shows why 'in this birth' wounds her: she had asked for the next one too.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness and her bright bangles slip. Kuruntokai 50: the shoulders he embraced have wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, adorned with loneliness.
teaches: The couplet names the wasted shoulder and slipping bangle as the sign of separation; the poem shows what the sign was used to say, setting it against his town's ford adorned with flowers, so the body's loss becomes an accusation of a place that still flourishes.

note: Kural 1143: the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not welcome, since it is like having what he has not yet obtained. Kuruntokai 51: the friend says the gossiping town too speaks of the girl with him, and her mother and father favour him.
teaches: The couplet values gossip as a foretaste of a union not yet had; the poem shows the next step, when talk that pairs the lovers joins the parents' consent, so the gossip the Kural's lover enjoys in fancy becomes one of the voices that brings the marriage about.

note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

note: Kural 447: who can ruin those who keep companions that rebuke them? Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking companions (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்) that it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread past bearing.
teaches: The Kural makes the rebuking companion a ruler's best protection; the lover grants the rebuke its good intent and shows where it stops, since love has spread like butter on hot rock before any word could check it, so the ethic of correction meets its limit at kaamam.

note: Kural 1199: though the one she longs for gives no grace (நல்கார்), even word of him is sweet to her ears. Kuruntokai 60: even if her lover does not grace her (நல்கார்) or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
teaches: Both women claim sweetness from a lover who gives none, with the same verb; Paranar's simile of the cripple licking his empty palm beneath the honeycomb shows what the couplet's maxim hides, that this sweetness is tasted only in imagination, a pleasure that is also the measure of what is withheld.

note: Purananuru 189 concludes that the use of wealth is giving, since king and hunter alike eat one measure; Kuruntokai 63's heart argues the same, that there is no giving and enjoying for the penniless, to drive the man to work.
teaches: The puram maxim that wealth exists to be given becomes, in the akam poem, the very reason a man leaves his wife, so the pair shows the giver's ethic carrying a private cost the praise poem never counts.

note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; the heart in Kuruntokai 63 states that premise, and the man answers it only by asking whether she can come along.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the poem shows the Kural's blunt premise as a voice inside a lover's head that he can neither refute nor obey, so the maxim's truth is granted and its price is made visible in the separation.

note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feeding and guarding its doe and hurries home; in Kuruntokai 65 the waiting woman sees the stag back with its mate in the rains while her man does not come.
teaches: The same sign of the stag with its mate is read from both ends of the separation: for the man it is a spur to return, for the woman it is evidence against him, so the iraicchi's force depends on who is watching.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend points to the bloomed konrai as the season and the cure of pallor; Kuruntokai 66's friend calls the bloomed konrai foolish, fooled by stray rain, and denies that the season has come.
teaches: The friend's comfort can use the konrai either way, as proof the promised season is here or as a false sign to be dismissed, which shows that the consolation lies in the friend's argument and not in the flower itself.

note: Perunkoppendu in Purananuru 246 refuses a widow's life and chooses the pyre; the female monkey in Kuruntokai 69, unable to bear widowhood (கைம்மை உய்யா), leaves her young with kin and leaps to her death.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram queen's refusal of widowhood and gives it to a creature of the hill, making the girl's not outliving her lover a law of nature for the night-visitor to weigh, not a royal vow.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but this woman is the cure of the sickness she gives; Kuruntokai 71: if medicine, she is medicine; if treasure, she is treasure.
teaches: The man's claim that she is his medicine is the same in both, but the poem adds treasure (வைப்பு), so under its paalai colophon the cure-paradox of the couplet becomes an argument against leaving to seek wealth.

note: Both are the man's speech under paalai about leaving for wealth: 63 asks his heart whether she can come along on the work; 71 calls her both medicine and laid-up treasure.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two give the man's full answer to the case for earning: 63 asks how wealth helps if it takes him from her, and 71 says she is already the treasure, so the journey has no object.

note: Kural 1084: the eyes of this artless girl devour the life of those who see them; Kuruntokai 72: the eyes of the girl scaring sparrows from the millet have, like arrows, made him sick for all to see.
teaches: The poem places the couplet's paradox, the simple girl with killing eyes, in her actual work of chasing small birds off the hill millet, and adds what the couplet lacks: the wound is public, known to everyone.

note: Akananuru 113 praises the Kosar who never swerve from friendship even in bad times, with unswerving plans (திரிபில் சூழ்ச்சி); Kuruntokai 73 holds up the Kosar of the single word, who cut down Nannan's mango, as the model of hard-eyed scheming (வன்கண் சூழ்ச்சி).
teaches: The Kosar's fame was for a kept word carried out by planning, and akam poets drew on it two ways, as loyalty in one poem and as ruthless resolve in the other, so the same people supplied both the virtue and the hard edge of a sworn word.

note: Akananuru 265: the woman asks whether the wealth her man went for is as great as the Nandas' treasure hidden at Pataliputra; Kuruntokai 75: the woman wishes the bearer of news of her lover's return to win Pataliputra rich in gold.
teaches: Pataliputra's gold was the akam measure of the greatest wealth, and the two women price it against love from opposite sides: one doubts it outweighs her, the other would give it for word of his coming.

note: Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts the woman is hearing him called cruel; Kuruntokai 77: there is no fault in him, or if any, it is that her soft shoulders proved easy to leave.
teaches: Both women defend the absent man with their wasted shoulders as the evidence, but the poem goes further than the couplet by moving the blame onto those shoulders, while its desert of dead travellers' cairns lets the reproach stand unspoken.

note: Purananuru 230: while Ezhini lived, the herds rested in the forest unguarded and safe; Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan tells the wife to guard her husband like the great herds at Ezhini's war front.
teaches: The courtesan's taunt rests on Ezhini's puram fame as the protector of herds, so she casts herself as the cattle-raider and the husband as plunder that only a war-chief's watch could keep, using the heroic guard to mock a household one.

note: Both use the saying 'eating one's own in one's own house': Kural 1107 for the joy of the beloved's embrace, Kuruntokai 83 for jackfruit hanging sweet on the lover's own hill as the mother announces he will come.
teaches: The pair shows the phrase was a common measure of untroubled, owned pleasure; the Kural applies it to union itself, while the Kuruntokai friend lays it on the lover's land at the moment marriage is promised, so the image belongs to the settled household rather than to secret love.

note: In Kural 1168 the woman says the night that lulls every creature to sleep has only her for company; in Kuruntokai 86 she asks at midnight whether anyone else hears the cow's bell.
teaches: The Kural asserts that she alone is awake; the Kuruntokai poem tests the claim with a question and finds one other wakeful thing, a lonely cow whose bell rings with her, so the solitude the Kural states is shown as a search for a companion.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has paled, no one says he left her. Kuruntokai 87: the god destroys the false, my lover is not false, yet my brow has paled.
teaches: Read together they show why the blame lands on her body: in the Kuruntokai the woman herself clears him before the avenging god, so the only visible sign of the wrong is her pallor, which is exactly the one-sided verdict the Kural's woman complains of.

note: Both compare a hill girl to the figure carved on Kolli's western face; 89 calls Kolli Porayan's, 100 calls it Ori's.
teaches: The same carved figure serves two poets as the measure of a girl's innocence while the hill is credited to different lords, the Chera Porayan and the archer Ori, so the simile was fixed to the place and outlived the change of its master.
audit_text_issue: 89 is flagged uncertain by the marker.

note: Avvaiyar's Purananuru 97 warns Anji's enemies that his worn swords, spears and elephants prove resistance is hopeless; her Kuruntokai 91 makes the night terror of a frontier town fearing Anji the measure of a wife's sleepless marriage.
teaches: The same poet supplies both sides of Anji's war: the puram poem speaks for the conqueror's threat, the akam poem borrows the sleeplessness of the threatened town, showing that the fear puram praise produces was available to akam as an image of domestic misery.

note: Kural 1222 asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 92 at sunset watches birds hurry home with food for their young.
teaches: The Kural guesses that the evening suffers from a cruel partner like hers; the Kuruntokai's dusk answers that every creature in it is hurrying home to its own, so the hard-heartedness is her man's alone and not the hour's.

note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering where there is no lover who knows you suffer; Kuruntokai 93: what is sulking worth when love is gone; do not speak against him, he is mother and father to us.
teaches: The Kural gives the reasoning that sulking needs a lover who will notice; the Kuruntokai wife draws the conclusion in her own case and adds the reason she cannot quarrel, her total dependence on him, so the maxim is shown ending in silence rather than in oodal.

note: Kural 1088: my might, feared in battle, broke before her bright brow; Kuruntokai 95: her grace like water quenched my strength like fire.
teaches: The Kural reports the man's defeat as a wonder of scale, so great a strength and so small a brow; the Kuruntokai explains it by kind, water putting out fire, so his strength was not outmatched but met by its natural undoing.

note: On the Kural reading where gossip feeds love and keeps it from drooping, Kuruntokai 97 disagrees: the secret turned to talk in the square is one of four things scattered apart, with her beauty lost and the man in his own town.
teaches: The man in the Kural can welcome gossip as fuel for love, while the woman in the Kuruntokai counts it among her losses, so the pair shows that rumour's value in the akam world depends on which lover bears it.

note: Both have the man set the gods' world against lying in the beloved's arms: the Kural asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter, Kuruntokai 101 puts earth and heaven together on one pan of a balance against a single day of embrace.
teaches: The Kural's open question about heaven has an older Sangam answer: the poet had already weighed both worlds together against one day and found them light, so the couplet's question reads as an allusion to that verdict rather than a doubt.

note: Both put the woman in the same bind, nearly in the same words (உள்ளின் உள்ளம் வேமே; உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்): remembering burns her and not remembering is impossible.
teaches: The Kural keeps Avvaiyar's bind and drops her last line, the charge that the man is not noble, so set side by side they show the couplet turning a complaint against him into a pure description of her state.

note: In Akananuru 122 the house cock and the owl that eats house rats are among the night's watchers that keep the secret lover away; in Kuruntokai 107 the wife curses the cock for ending her sleep beside her husband and wishes it prey to the wildcat that hunts house rats.
teaches: Held together they show that marriage did not free the lovers' night from its old enemy: the cock that guarded the house against the secret lover still cuts short the wedded night, and the wife's curse sends it to the very rat-hunters of the courtship poem.

note: Both make the woman's pain open with the evening: the Kural's sickness buds at dawn and blooms at evening, and in Kuruntokai 108 the jasmine opens red in the sunset as the cows go home and she says she will not survive.
teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for the sickness rests on a real mullai sight that Kuruntokai 108 shows, the jasmine opening at red dusk as the herds return, so the couplet's conceit is that scene folded into the body of the woman who watches it.

note: In Kuruntokai 111 the friend wishes the hill man would come and expose the household that believes the diviner's word about Murugan; in Akananuru 22 the girl, embraced by her lover on the very night of the rite, laughs (நக்கனென்) at the offering wasted on a stranger priest.
teaches: The laugh the friend in Kuruntokai 111 hopes for is the laugh the girl of Akananuru 22 actually has, so together they show the veriyattu rite was framed in akam as a comic error waiting for the lover's arrival to undo it.

note: Both hang the woman between love and shame: the Kural has the two hung from a carrying pole that is her life, Kuruntokai 112 names the town's talk as the fear and pictures her as a branch an elephant has snapped that still hangs by its fibre.
teaches: Kuruntokai 112 gives the Kural's evenly balanced pole a cause and a breaking point: the weight on shame's side is the town's gossip, and the balance is already a break held only by a strand, which the couplet's still image does not show.

note: Both tie the slipping bangles to the absence of the lord of the shore (துறைவன்): in the Kural they announce his leaving to the town; in Kuruntokai 117 the friend says let him stay away, smaller bangles can be bought from the sellers.
teaches: The same sign of wasting is grief in the woman's mouth and a weapon in the friend's: Kuruntokai 117 shows the slipping bangle could be turned into mockery meant to shame the man, which the Kural's lament never does.

note: In the Kural the woman pities the evening as a fellow sufferer and asks if its mate is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 118 the evening is loveless (நாரில்) and the birds and beasts that settle in loneliness are company she gets no comfort from.
teaches: Read together they show two answers to the same hour: the Kural's woman finds a companion in the grieving evening, while the Sangam woman finds the whole world, beasts and gatekeepers included, going home around her, so the evening isolates rather than consoles.

note: Both have the man say that his strength has been broken by a young girl: the Kural by her bright forehead alone, though foes in battle feared him; Kuruntokai 119 by the likeness of a hatchling snake felling a wild elephant.
teaches: Kuruntokai 119 supplies the image behind the Kural's paradox of the mighty man undone by a forehead: the elephant brought down by a hatchling snake, a picture of poison not strength, which explains why the couplet's warrior has no defence.

note: Both by the poet of the paalai (Perunkadungo): the man calls the waste harsh (இன்னா, Kuruntokai 124; கடுமைய காடு, Kalittokai 6) and the woman's side answers him.
teaches: The same poet gives the same plea two answers: in the short poem the friend argues the house alone is as harsh as the forest, a reason for him to stay, while the long poem has the woman draw the next step, that hardship shared on the road is her only joy, so the argument from equal harm leads straight to the demand to go with him.

note: Both say the fragrant cool rain-season laughs with mullai buds for bright teeth (முல்லை ... இலங்கெயிறு ... நறுந்தண் கார் ... நகும்); in Kar Narpathu 14 the friend reads the laugh as proof he will come quickly, in Kuruntokai 126 the woman hears it mocking her: where are they?
teaches: The later poet took the older line almost word for word and reversed what it means: the same laughing season is a sign of his return to the friend who comforts and a jeer at the deserted woman, which shows that the image itself carries no fixed mood and the speaker's place in the situation decides it.

note: Both use the same half-line, திண்டேர்ப் பொறையன் தொண்டி: Akananuru 60 makes the girl's bangle as fine as Poraiyan's Thondi; Kuruntokai 128 makes the girl the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, longed for by a wingless heron on the eastern sea.
teaches: Poraiyan's Thondi served the love poets as a stock measure of the desirable, but they could aim it two ways: as a measure of the girl's worth that the man must win by marriage, or, set against the eastern sea, as a measure of how far out of reach she is.

note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Kuruntokai 129 he tells his comrade, 'friend of poets', that a girl's brow has bound him like a new-caught elephant; in Purananuru 216, fasting to death, he tells doubters his poet-friend, whom he has never seen, will surely come.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices turn on the same bond of male friendship: in the love poem the comrade is the one he confides his captivity to, in the death poem the friend's coming is the proof of his worth, so the paangan of akam convention is, for this poet, a role he filled with a real friendship of poets.

note: Both quote a saying about men's work: 'work is life to men' (வினையே ஆடவர்க்கு உயிரே, Kuruntokai 135) and 'effort, not grace, is men's wealth' (அருள் அன்று ஆக ஆள்வினை ஆடவர் பொருள், Akananuru 75); in both the man does not leave.
teaches: The maxim that a man's life or wealth is his work was common enough to be quoted, yet in both poems it is quoted only to be overruled: the Akananuru hero weighs it against beauty that cannot be given back, and the Kuruntokai friend completes it with its other half, that men are women's life, so the love poets used the work ethic as the premise they argue against.

note: Kural 1151 (the friend or the woman to the man): if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the woman he himself said men are women's life, so he will hold back.
teaches: The couplet states as a threat what the Kuruntokai friend leaves the man to infer from his own words: if men are the women's life, then his going kills her and any promise of a quick return is addressed to the dead, which is why the friend can be sure he will stay.

note: Kural 1227 (the woman) calls love a sickness that buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 136 (the man) says love is neither a spirit nor a disease and does not swell and subside, but has its season like an elephant's musth when it finds one to look on.
teaches: The two agree that love keeps time but disagree on what kind of thing it is: the Kural's woman makes it a disease with a daily clock inside her, the Kuruntokai's man denies it is a sickness at all and makes it a latent season set off from outside by sight, so whether love is illness depends on whether one is waiting or seeing.

note: In Akananuru 279 the man leaves because men who stay at their wife's breast cannot bear to see friends in want and kin in distress; in Kuruntokai 137 the man swears that if he ever leaves his wife, may suppliants stop coming to him.
teaches: The same value, being the one the needy come to, drives the man out of the house in the Akananuru and binds him to it in the Kuruntokai, where losing the suppliants is the curse for leaving, so the puram duty to give could be argued on either side of the akam choice to go or stay.

note: Kuruntokai 140: the woman asks how the gossiping town came to know the grief she bore in silence; Kural 1180: the woman says it is not hard for the town to learn the secret of those whose eyes beat it out like a drum.
teaches: The Kural answers the Kuruntokai woman's question: she kept silent, but her eyes told the town, so the gossip she resents is her own grief made public by her body, not betrayal by anyone else.

note: Akananuru 18 has the same thurai, the night-comer told to come by day: the friend tells the hill lord the night ford is deadly and he may meet the girl by day in the kaanthal grove. Kuruntokai 141 gives the refusal to the heroine, who only reports her mother's errand to the millet field.
teaches: Held together they show the one message in two voices: the friend may name the day meeting outright, while the heroine can offer it only by passing on her mother's errand, so the day tryst comes through indirection exactly where the speaker's freedom is narrowest.

note: Naladiyar 2: wealth stays level with no one but turns like a cart wheel, so share it the day it comes. Kuruntokai 143 uses the wealth that does not stay with a generous man as the image of pallor that will pass.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues from wealth's instability to giving, and the love poem had already fused the two into one image, the giver whose wealth leaves him, and turned that ethical commonplace into a promise that sorrow too is the kind of thing that leaves.

note: Kural 331 calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for lasting. Kuruntokai 143's friend says impermanence alone is permanent, and draws hope from it.
teaches: The Kural uses impermanence to rebuke attachment, but the friend of the love poem applies the same truth to grief, showing that the doctrine was a two-edged tool: what cannot last includes the pallor of longing, so it consoles as readily as it warns.

note: Kural 1168: the night that puts all living things to sleep is pitiable, having no companion but her. Kuruntokai 145: the long night here has only sleepers who will not talk with the sleepless.
teaches: Both women stay awake while everyone sleeps, but the Kural turns her loneliness into a mock pity for the night, while the Kuruntokai blames the sleeping village; together they show that the wakeful heroine's complaint can fall on the night or on the people, and that the couplet's wit grows from the poem's social grievance.

note: 146: the friend asks whether 'those who unite the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்ப்போர்) have come, staffs in hand. 156: the hero asks the Brahmin with his staff whether his learning holds a medicine 'that unites the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்க்கும்).
teaches: The same phrase names the go-between's office from both sides of kalavu: in the friend's mouth the uniters arrive as joyful elders of a marriage embassy, while the hero doubts that a Brahmin's book can unite anyone, so the phrase shows that union was expected from social go-betweens, not from learning.

note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover met in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 147: the hero says the dream, as if it had brought her, rouses him from sweet sleep.
teaches: The Kural's woman blames waking and spares the dream; the Kuruntokai's man blames the dream itself for ending his sleep, so set together they show that the dream meeting was felt as both gift and cheat, and that the blame shifts with which side of it the lover dwells on.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend shows the bloomed konrai and the dancing peacocks and calls the season medicine for the pallor. Kuruntokai 148: the friend denies that the konrai and kurundham mean the rains, and the heroine asks if she is dreaming.
teaches: The friend's proof from the season only works before the season is spent; once the konrai has bloomed and he has not come, the same flower proves his breach, so the comforter must deny the season and the heroine turns the argument against her.

note: Kural 1134: the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (the man speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty is a small sand dam that holds as long as it can and gives way when the sweet flood presses (the woman speaks).
teaches: Both picture desire as a flood against shame, but for the man shame is a raft that is swept away with him on it, and for the woman it is a dam that holds the water back, so the shared image is divided by gender: his shame rides the flood, hers resists it.

note: Kural 1251: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame (the woman speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty struggled long, held as long as it could and now gives way.
teaches: The Kural states the collapse of restraint as a single blow of an axe, while the Kuruntokai gives it duration and fellowship, a modesty that 'suffered with us' long before giving way, which shows the couplet compressing a process the older poem tells as a struggle.
