note: Kural 1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near. Kuruntokai 150: the woman says the pain swells when she thinks of his chest and vanishes when she embraces it.
teaches: The Kural's man finds the paradoxical fire in the woman, but the Kuruntokai heroine finds the same sickness in herself and sets it off by memory, not distance, so the pair shows that the burning-and-cooling belongs to both lovers and that thinking of the absent one is itself the burning.

note: 151: on the hill path a hen whose mate fell to a hawk keeps calling, and the hero decides leaving her would be the end of youth. 154: in the waste a hen whose cock has gone to find food calls in loneliness, and the heroine asks how men learn to part.
teaches: The same carrier, a hen calling for an absent mate on the road, works from both sides of the separation: in the hero's mouth it is the reason he stays, in the heroine's it is the reproach to a man who went anyway, so one native image can hold both the decision and its blame.

note: Akananuru 337: the hero reminds his heart, which presses for another journey, that once it found parting no joy, said 'let wealth stay where it is' and came back alone through the robbers' waste. Kuruntokai 151: the hero refuses the hill path, saying going would end his youth.
teaches: Kuruntokai 151 gives the moment of refusal, and Akananuru 337 shows that such a refusal does not settle anything: the heart that once turned back is urging the road again, so the decision not to leave is a choice that must be remade, not a resolution.

note: 141: the heroine asks the friend to tell the lover not to come in the deep night, when the tiger lies in wait on the slope. 153: her heart, once afraid of an owl or a monkey in the yard, now goes along the slope to him in the dense dark night.
teaches: The dangers of the night slope are the argument she uses to keep him away, yet her own heart travels that road without fear, so the pairing shows the night-danger plea as care for him rather than prudence she lives by.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart where it goes seeking, since the lover lives within it. Kuruntokai 153: her heart, once timid, now goes along the night slope to him without tiring.
teaches: The Kural mocks the heart's going out as needless because he is already within, while the Kuruntokai heroine marvels at the same going as courage, so the pairing shows the couplet's wit resting on an older picture of the heart as a traveller on the lover's road.

note: Kuruntokai 156: the lovesick hero asks the Brahmin whether his unwritten learning holds a medicine to unite the parted. Kural 1102: the man says other illnesses have other cures, but this woman is herself the cure for her sickness.
teaches: The couplet reads as the answer to the Kuruntokai hero's question: no learned remedy exists, because only the woman herself cures the sickness she causes, so the pair turns the hero's doubt of the Brahmin's lore into the Kural's general rule of love's medicine.

note: Kar Narpathu 10: as thunder roars and the bull bellows back, the swift chariot comes with the sound of a forest stream. Kuruntokai 155: the evening of the season has come, but not the word that his chariot with its ringing bells is on its way.
teaches: The venba lets the sound of the chariot arrive with the season, but the Kuruntokai keeps season and chariot apart and has the heroine wait first for the report of it, which shows the chariot-sound of mullai as a promise the older poem could leave unkept.

note: Kar Narpathu 17: on the high rock-ledged hill the thunder crushes snakes and the sky, thick with dark, shows the season; the friend reads it as his return. Kuruntokai 158: the heroine asks the cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes dead on the tall slope, whether it has no pity on lone women.
teaches: The same storm with its snake-killing thunder is a sign of comfort when the friend reads it as the promised season and a terror when the lone heroine faces it at night, so the image carries whatever the speaker's situation gives it rather than a fixed meaning.

note: Akananuru 305: on cold north-wind midnights a single anril on the palm cries in grief, and the heroine asks how she can live while he is away for wealth. Kuruntokai 160: at hushed midnight in the cold north wind the anril cries with its hen from their nest, and he does not come.
teaches: The anril's midnight cry in the north wind is shared, but the Akananuru bird is alone and mirrors her, while the Kuruntokai bird is with its mate and shows what she lacks; together they show that the anril, bird of the unparted, can serve as either likeness or contrast to the waiting woman.
audit_text_issue: Akananuru 305 line 5 supplied from a commentary edition.

note: Akananuru 17: the foster mother remembers how the girl, tired after ball and jacks, would lie in her arms, and wonders how her small feet will manage the waste. Kuruntokai 144: the foster mother remembers the girl's play in the backwater and the waves and sees her gone over the gravel to the far mountains.
teaches: Both foster mothers measure the elopement by the girl's play, but the Akananuru measures it on the body (tired feet, sweat), while the Kuruntokai measures it on the map, from sea shore through waste to mountain, so the pair shows the sevili's lament working through both the body and the landscapes the girl crosses.

note: Kural 1090 says liquor delights only one who drinks it while love delights at a look; in Kuruntokai 165 the man, having only seen her hair and grace, says the sight came on his desire like toddy on top of joy.
teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's claim that love works by sight alone but denies the contrast with liquor: for the man who has looked, seeing acts exactly like a second drink, so the couplet's rule holds while its comparison is turned around.

note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse; in Kuruntokai 173 he mounts it with shame killed (நாணட்டு) and says the town will name her fault.
teaches: The Kural counts only what the madal costs the rider, his shame; the poem names what it is for, turning his public shame into her blame on the town's tongue, which is the pressure that makes the threat work on her kin.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 163 she asks the sea who has hurt it, since she hears it crying at midnight.
teaches: Both women treat a natural thing as a fellow sufferer, but the poem shows how the projection is built: she knows the sea grieves because she herself is awake to hear it, so the sympathy is evidence of her sleeplessness rather than a fancy.

note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth and the other world not for those without grace; Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves for wealth, in this world wealth alone is wealth and grace has no one.
teaches: The heroine grants the Kural's premise about this world in its own words (இவ்வுலகத்து) and drops its consolation: with no other world in view, the couplet's balance of wealth and grace collapses into a world where grace has no owner.

note: In Akananuru 75 the man quotes the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth and declines to follow it; in Kuruntokai 174 the woman, whose man did follow it, concludes that wealth alone is wealth and grace belongs to no one.
teaches: Together they show the wealth-over-grace maxim as a live argument of the paalai poems argued from both ends: the man can refuse it out of love, and the woman, when he does not, turns it from a rule of conduct into a bitter verdict on the whole world.

note: In Kural 1148 the woman says hoping to quench love with gossip is like quenching fire with ghee; in Kuruntokai 175 she refuses to tell everyone she is not grieving and asks what the gossip matters.
teaches: The Kural's woman answers the town with an argument that talk only feeds love, while the poem's woman refuses the remedy the friend proposes, public denial, so the pair separates two defences against gossip: rebutting its power and declining to perform the concealment that would silence it.

note: Naladiyar 363 calls a wife who does not enter the kitchen at dawn a disease and one who does not serve what she cooked a demon; Kuruntokai 167 shows a young wife, smoke in her kohl eyes, cooking and serving with delight at her husband's praise. On the Naladiyar's reading the act is a duty enforced by threat; on the poem's it is the wife's own joy.
teaches: The same kitchen duty that the ethics book defines by the horror of its failure is shown in the Sangam poem as freely chosen pleasure, so the pair shows the domestic norm seen from the husband's fear and from the wife's satisfaction.

note: Both poems are by Kachchippettu Nannakaiyar and both ask about the man who left (துறந்தோர்): in 172 the woman at evening asks whether he is happy being alone; in 180 the friend asks whether he has grown hard in the land he went to.
teaches: Read together, the poet's two questions mark the turn of a long absence: the first still imagines him as lonely as she is, the second fears his heart has changed, so the doubt moves from his comfort to his constancy.

note: Kuruntokai 182: the lover asks whether throwing off his great shame (பெருநாண் நீக்கி) and riding the palm horse through the street will win her after the messenger failed; Kural 1132: body and life will mount the palm horse once shame is put aside (நாணினை நீக்கி).
teaches: The Kural states the madal threat as a general law of the unbearable, while the Kuruntokai shows its occasion (a failed go-between) and counts its price in other men's mockery, so the Kural's 'putting shame aside' is a public cost the hero weighs, not a private loss.
audit_text_issue: line 6 variant reading

note: Kuruntokai 184: the hero tells his companions his heart is caught in the net of the fisher girl's eyes; Kural 1084: the man says the artless girl's eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them.
teaches: Both men describe a first sight as the girl's eyes acting on them, but the Kuruntokai draws the weapon from her own people's trade (the fishermen's fine net), showing that the Kural's abstract killing gaze was, in the older poetry, given a landscape and a craft.

note: Kuruntokai 185: the girl asks what use it is to tell him she has wasted because of him; Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts her is hearing him called cruel.
teaches: Both heroines decline to blame the man for their wasting body, but for opposite reasons: the Kural's woman defends him, the Kuruntokai's expects no answer from a man as unmoved as the rock under the beaten kaanthal, so the same refusal can be loyalty or despair.

note: Kuruntokai 187: he is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts; Kural 1291: she asks her heart why it is not hers when his heart stays with him.
teaches: Kapilar gives the image and the Kural the argument of one complaint: the man's heart keeps to itself like stone while hers goes over to him, and together they show the heroine's quarrel is with her own heart's softness more than with his hardness.

note: Kuruntokai 188: evening has come, aiming at her beauty, when the mullai has budded and he has not come; Kural 1221: she tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the lives of wives.
teaches: The Kuruntokai shows why the evening attacks: it arrives with the season he promised to return by, so its hostility is the broken promise made visible, which the Kural's address to the evening leaves unstated.

note: Kuruntokai 190: at midnight in the storm she hears the cattle stall's one bell ring with every step of the bull; Kural 1168: the night that puts all beings to sleep has her alone for company.
teaches: The Kural's claim that she alone keeps the night company is proved in the Kuruntokai by what she hears: only a wakeful listener counts the bull's every step by its bell, so the single sound measures the sleepless solitude the couplet asserts.

note: Kuruntokai 192 and Akananuru 97: the friend says do not grieve (இனையல், ஆழேல்), and the heroine answers that she cannot stop weeping when the koel calls in the flowering mango.
teaches: The same reply to the same comfort shows the spring koel in the mango was a fixed answer in the heroine's mouth: the long Akananuru spends its lines on the dangers of his road, while the Kuruntokai replaces them with the gesture of stroking flowerless hair, so the short form puts the proof in her body rather than in the landscape.

note: Kuruntokai 196: the husband who once called neem sweet now calls the cool spring water of Pari's Parambu hot and brackish; Purananuru 176: the poet regrets the days lost like people who scorned the clear spring of Parambu because it was in their own town.
teaches: Read with the Purananuru, the friend's choice of Parambu's water carries its proverbial lesson: the sweetest thing is scorned when it is near, so she diagnoses the husband's turning as contempt bred by having the wife at home.

note: Kuruntokai 199: the lover tells his heart his love-sickness will last on into the other world; Kural 1315: he told her they would not part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
teaches: The Kural's joke works only because Paranar's belief was the convention: love was expected to outlast this birth, so a lover who promised only 'this birth' had set a limit the older poem's lover would not accept.

note: Kuruntokai 200: surely he has forgotten, but we do not forget; Kural 1207: what would become of her if she forgot, when she knows no forgetting and remembering burns.
teaches: The Kural keeps forgetting inside the woman, as a danger she cannot afford, while Avvaiyar turns it outward as a charge against the man, proven by the rains that came on time, so the same refusal to forget can be self-torment or an accusation.

note: Kuruntokai 183: the wife wonders whether he will see the stag parted from its doe; Akananuru 34: the hero, seeing a stag feed and guard its doe, bids his chariot hurry home.
teaches: The pair shows the stag and doe of the scrub working from both ends of a separation: the waiting wife hopes he will see a parted pair and feel her loss, while the returning hero is moved by a pair together, so the same creatures carry absence for her and return for him.

note: Kuruntokai 202 sets the nerunji's flower, sweet to the eye, before its thorn as the lover's kindness before his cruelty; Kural 1120 uses only the nerunji fruit, the thorn, to say how soft things feel to her feet.
teaches: Both poets know the nerunji as a plant that pleases first and pricks after; the couplet takes only the prick to praise a woman's delicacy, while the Sangam poem uses the order of flower and thorn to tell the history of a love, so the same plant can measure a body or a story.

note: Kuruntokai 204: the companion says love is neither a spirit nor a disease but a feast always new; 206: the hero says love brings unbearable grief and warns the wise to keep away.
teaches: Read together, the two poems are the two sides of the companion's rebuke and the hero's answer: the friend outside love calls it a light pleasure, and the man inside it calls it a pain the wise should flee, so the anthology lets each speaker's place decide what love is.

note: Kuruntokai 206 tells the wise to keep from love because the woman is too sweet, her words like ambrosia; Naladiyar 41 tells men to turn from desire because the admired body is a frail bag the crows would tear.
teaches: The same counsel, keep away from love, rests on opposite judgments of the beloved: the Sangam lover flees because she is ambrosia and the pain is love's own, the Jain moralist because she is carrion under skin, so the later ethic keeps the advice and reverses its reason.

note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover is going; look here, the pallor is spreading on my body. Kuruntokai 205 asks how the pallor on her forehead knew so soon, when the shore lord has only now driven away.
teaches: The couplet's two pointing words make his going and her paling one instant; the Kuruntokai poem has the same instant but turns it into a question to the pallor itself, and supplies the scene the couplet leaves out, the white chariot rising like swans and the sea spray on its wheels.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 207: he left without telling her, thinking that if he spoke, going would become hard, and she heard of it from others.
teaches: The couplet's demand to be told assumes the parting is spoken; the Kuruntokai man knows the power of that speech so well that he avoids it, so the heroine is denied even the chance to answer him that the Kural's speaker uses.

note: Purananuru 150: Nalli, unnamed, roasts fat in his forest for a starving poet and gives him his own chain. Kuruntokai 210: the friend prices the meal owed to the crow that called a guest in the ghee of the herds of Nalli's forest.
teaches: Holding the two together shows why Nalli's forest is the measure in the love poem: he was remembered as the host who fed a stranger in the woods unasked, so the friend, repaying a bird for bringing a guest, reaches for the most famous hospitality she knows and still calls it too little.

note: Kuruntokai 213: the friend says he has deep love, since on his road the stag goes hungry and stands as shade for its young. Akananuru 59: the friend says on his road the bull elephant bends a tree so its mate can eat, yet those men do not remember her.
teaches: The same device, a beast caring for its own on the road the man took, is used for opposite ends: in Kuruntokai the friend makes it proof that he will come back, in the Akananuru she makes it the reproach that he does not, so the image does not carry its comfort in itself but takes it from the speaker's verdict.

note: Akananuru 34: the returning man sees a stag feed its doe and guard her sleep and bids his charioteer hurry home. Kuruntokai 213: the friend says that on his road, they say, the stag starves to shelter its young, so he has deep love.
teaches: The friend's comfort in Kuruntokai is a prediction that the man will see the beasts' care and be moved; Akananuru 34 shows that very sight working on the man himself, so the two poems give the two ends of one iraicchi, the promise at home and its fulfilment on the road.

note: Kar Narpathu 1: the friend says the man who promised to come when the rain hung low can hardly fail to come now that the clouds roar and pour. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the great cloud pours, thunders and flashes with no pity, aimed at her life.
teaches: The rain of the promised season is the same sign in both, but the friend reads it as his oath falling due and the heroine as the deadline passing on her; set side by side, the poems show the rainy season carries both senses at once, and the speaker decides which is heard.

note: Kar Narpathu 3: the friend, showing her own distress, says the wind, hail and thundering sky act as if all aimed at one lone woman. Kuruntokai 216: the heroine says the thundering cloud flashes with her life as its aim.
teaches: The complaint that the storm is aimed at her is the heroine's own in the older poem, and in the later venba the friend speaks it for her about 'one woman', so the charge against the rain had become a formula that could be handed from the sufferer to her companion.
audit_text_issue: Kar Narpathu 3 line 3 has a recorded variant (இழித்தெழுங் தோங்கும்). | Kar Narpathu 3 line 3 has printed variants (@ இழித்தெழுங் தோங்கும்).

note: Kural 1209: her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of one who said they were not separate. Kuruntokai 218: he, like life to her life, who could not bear a parting even a blink long, can now forget her and stay away, and she will still think of him.
teaches: The couplet names the wound as the broken claim of oneness; the Kuruntokai poem gives the claim its measure, not a blink apart, and adds what the woman does with the wound, vows, omens and thought, so the poem shows the couplet's dying as a life kept busy with ritual.

note: Kural 1255: the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to those sick with love. Kuruntokai 219: her restraint has gone far and her mind urges her to go to him, but she holds back for fear he will ask 'who are you?'
teaches: The couplet says the lovesick cannot know the pride of not following; the Kuruntokai heroine, lovesick, still stays, held back not by pride but by fear of being met as a stranger, so the poem shows a restraint that survives the loss of honour and the couplet's claim is too absolute.
audit_text_issue: Line 7 of Kuruntokai 219 is restored from Swaminatha Aiyar's text and its sense is unsettled.

note: Kural 1227: this sickness buds in the morning, swells through the day and blossoms in the evening. Kuruntokai 220: in the evening the jasmine opens its small buds like a wild cat smiling, and the man who left for wealth has not come.
teaches: The couplet makes a flower's day the shape of love-sickness; the Kuruntokai poem shows the real flower, the mullai opening its buds at dusk in the season he named, at the moment her grief opens, so the metaphor rests on the evening flowering of the jasmine land.

note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend says they are sure he will come quickly, since the rain cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its bright teeth. Kuruntokai 220: the jasmine buds open like a wild cat smiling, the evening is here, and he has not come.
teaches: Both poems read the opening jasmine as a smile with teeth, but in the friend's venba it is the season laughing in welcome and in the heroine's Kuruntokai poem it is a wild cat's grin, so the one image turns from promise to mockery once the day of return has passed.

note: In Akananuru 274 the returning man says her town lies in the rainy scrub where a lone herdsman stands in the drizzle with his lambs; in Kuruntokai 221 the waiting woman sees the goatherd with his lambs crowned with mullai buds and says the man has not come.
teaches: The herdsman of the mullai scrub is the season's witness from both sides: on the man's road he marks the way home, at the woman's door he wears the proof that the promised season has come without the man, so one figure serves as sign of return or of broken promise.

note: Kural 1122: the man says the bond between him and the girl is that of body and life; in Kuruntokai 222 the man says she takes the head of the raft when he does, the tail when he does, and would follow him into the current.
teaches: The couplet names the inseparability as a metaphor, and the poem shows how a lover knows it: she mirrors his every movement in play and would follow him into danger, so the body-and-life bond is proved by action before it is stated.

note: Purananuru 34 states that there is no expiation for killing a benefit and binds the poet to praise the king who fed the bards; Kuruntokai 225 makes a king who forgets, once enthroned, the help he had in ruin the type of ingratitude the lover must not imitate.
teaches: The puram poem casts the king as the benefactor to whom gratitude is owed, while the akam friend can cite the king who forgets his helpers as a familiar figure, so the same norm of gratitude was also turned against kings, and borrowed to bind a lover to marriage.

note: Kural 110: there is escape for every other killing of good, none for one who kills a benefit; in Kuruntokai 225 the friend promises the girl's hair to the man only if he does not forget kindness as an enthroned king does.
teaches: The Kural's absolute rule becomes a condition of marriage in the poem: the friend uses ingratitude, the one unpardonable fault, to define in advance what deserting the girl would be.

note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart whom it goes to seek when the lover is inside it; Kuruntokai 228: though he left for a far country, he is near to her heart.
teaches: The same indwelling is used two ways: the couplet makes it a reason to scold the restless heart, while the poem makes it a consolation that cancels the distance, so the lover in the heart can either rebuke longing or quiet it.

note: Kuruntokai 40 marvels that two whose mothers, fathers and selves were strangers have hearts mixed like rain in red earth; Kuruntokai 229 marvels that two who fought as children under their nurses' eyes have been joined in marriage, and credits fate (பால்).
teaches: The anthology explains a match both between strangers and between childhood neighbours, and in each case puts the cause outside the families: loving hearts mixing on their own in 40, fate's apportioning in 229, so union by kin arrangement is the case neither poem celebrates.

note: Kural 1247: the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both; Kuruntokai 231: neglected by the man in her own town, she says her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like a loosed arrow.
teaches: The couplet presents a choice still open between desire and shame, while the poem shows it already made and past recall, desire having killed shame on its own, so the Kural's dilemma is the moment before the poem's confession.
audit_text_issue: line 6 கணியிற் where the sense wants கணையின் 'arrow'

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftover (மிச்சில்) needs sowing at all; Kuruntokai 233 praises her father's town where the leftover (மிச்சில்) of rice poured out for the great is shared with all without limit.
teaches: The love poet measures a bride's family by the very household ethic the Kural states, even with its word for the leftover, so the hospitality rule was already a mark of a good marriage before it was a maxim about prosperity.

note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 234: for those without a partner the dawn and the day are evening too.
teaches: The couplet keeps evening as the climax of a daily growth, while the poem refuses any such gradation and makes every hour evening, so on one reading the parted woman has no easier morning at all, which the Kural's flower image allows.

note: Kural 1183: the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor in exchange; Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the man that if he means to leave he must first give back the beauty he has consumed.
teaches: The couplet records the exchange as done, and the poem turns the same commercial idea into a demand for repayment that cannot be met, which makes it an argument that he must stay.

note: Kural 1108: an embrace so close not even the wind can part it is sweet to two who desire each other; Kuruntokai 237: the man far away says he cannot count what now stands between their embrace, groves where tigers roar.
teaches: Read together, the measure of separation is the same embrace the couplet praises: where once not even a breeze passed between them, now forests and tigers do, so the poem's distance is felt as a gap inside the embrace.
audit_text_issue: Kuruntokai 237 line 2 repaired; lines 1-3 compressed

note: In Akananuru 60 the friend warns the hero not to crush the bangle of a girl fine as Porayan's Tondi; in Kuruntokai 238 the friend tells the lord of the fields to give back a beauty that was like Tondi and go.
teaches: Both friends price the girl's beauty by the Chera port of Tondi, one before harm, as a warning, and one after, as a demand for restitution, so the town's fame served as the standard of a beauty that can be damaged and must be repaid.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders lose their old beauty and her bangles slip; Kuruntokai 239: her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there shame left to give up?
teaches: The couplet lists the slipping bangles as a sign of grief, while the poem draws from the same sign a conclusion: since the body has already told, modesty has nothing left to hide, so the wasting licenses the woman to speak out.

note: Kuruntokai 234 says that for those without a partner every hour is evening; Kuruntokai 240 shows one evening's work, as the north wind blows and his hill sinks from view like a ship.
teaches: Together they show why evening is the worst hour: in 234 it is a state that swallows all hours, in 240 it is the moment the last visible trace of him, his hill, is taken away, so the evening's pain is the loss of sight of him.

note: Kural 1171: the woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her and brought on the sickness; Kuruntokai 241: she bears her desire, while her eyes, which saw the hill man, weep out of their own intimacy.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes as the cause that now complains, while the poem excuses them as loyal intimates of the man, so the same weeping eyes can be charged as culprits or honoured as the part of her that keeps faith with what it saw.

note: Kural 1207: she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns; Kuruntokai 243: she resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep.
teaches: The poem tries the remedy the couplet says is impossible, a vow not to remember, and the very need to vow it confirms the couplet: remembering keeps her awake and forgetting cannot be chosen, only resolved.

note: Kural 1188: people say she has grown pale, and no one says he left her; Kuruntokai 245: worse than her lost beauty would be his unkindness becoming known to many.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women want opposite things from the town: the couplet's woman resents that the blame falls on her body and not on him, the poem's woman dreads exactly that blame reaching him, so the lover can either demand that the fault be named or shield it at her own cost.

note: Kural 791: nothing is as ruinous as befriending without inquiry, for once formed a friendship cannot be left; Kuruntokai 247: the friend says she knew then that the man's friendship is flawless, fruitful, righteous and a raft for kin.
teaches: The Kural's test of friendship is meant to come before the bond, but in secret love the bond comes first, so the friend's knowing it to be flawless arrives after the fact and has to argue, in the Kural's own terms of fruit and kin, that the inquiry would have passed.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 250: the man tells his charioteer to drive the swift horses before evening comes, for her distress.
teaches: The couplet names evening as the feast the returning man looks to; the poem shows why it is a deadline as well as a reward: evening is the hour the stag is with its mate and the hour she suffers most alone, so he must beat it.

note: Kuruntokai 65: the stag that drank the clear water among the hard pebbles frisks with its sweet mate, as if mocking the woman who waits; Kuruntokai 250: the stag that drank the water of the pebbled hollow frisks with its mate as the man hurries home.
teaches: The anthology uses one sight from both ends of the separation: to the waiting woman the frisking pair is a taunt, to the returning man it is a spur, so the same iraicchi accuses the absence on one side and hastens its end on the other.

note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray rain for the season and flowering; Kuruntokai 251: the friend calls the peacocks foolish for dancing to a stray cloud's thunder, and explains the cloud is only emptying its old water.
teaches: Together they show the friend's consolation as an argument about evidence, not a denial of rain: in 66 the flowers misread the rain, in 251 the cloud's thunder is given a cause of its own, so the friend separates rain from season, the very distinction the man's promise rests on.

note: Kural 1286: when she sees him she sees no fault, when she does not see him she sees only faults; Kuruntokai 252: urged by her friend to reproach him, she says the worthy cannot speak blame to a face.
teaches: The couplet presents her silence before him as a blindness of love; the poem's woman sees the fault plainly and calls him crooked, yet keeps silent by a rule of the noble, so the same silence can be read as love's blindness or as chosen restraint.

note: Akananuru 59: on the road for wealth an elephant bends a yaa tree so its young mate can eat, yet the man forgets her; Kuruntokai 255: on that road the elephant strips the yaa tree to feed its whole hungry herd, and the men went to fulfil their duty.
teaches: The same road-sign is turned two ways by the friend: feeding one mate in Akananuru 59 shames the man who forgets his wife, while feeding the whole herd in Kuruntokai 255 matches the man's duty to his household, so the friend can use the elephant to reproach the journey or to justify it.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Kuruntokai 256: before he could say he would return when the work was done, her weeping eyes blocked his chariot.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's spoken refusal of the promise of a quick return; the poem shows that refusal made without words, before the promise is spoken, and records that it worked: the chariot stopped.

note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders have lost their fullness and the bangles slip; Kuruntokai 260: the bangled shoulders are filling out again, read with heron and bush as a sign he will return.
teaches: The couplet makes the shoulders a record of his absence; the poem reads them forward as an omen of his return, so the body that registers separation is also consulted to foretell its end.
audit_text_issue: Kuruntokai 260 line 7 (கன்றி லோரா விலங்கிய) does not construe.

note: In Akananuru 292 the girl dreads the stranger velan's rite and the kid's killing because she would be ashamed; in Kuruntokai 263 the friend protests that the same rite praises strange gods that cure nothing and brands the girl as possessed.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the veri rite wounding the secret love from both sides: to the girl it threatens exposure, and to the friend it threatens a false name, possession, for a love she insists is blameless.

note: Kural 804: the wise welcome the unasked acts of old friends; Kuruntokai 265 likens the kaanthal bud opening to the bee to duty-knowing men opening to the worthy they have long known, then shows the man ashamed and ready to act once told.
teaches: The Kural's ethic of intimacy is used in the poem as a simile for nature and then as a forecast of the lover's conduct, so the old-friendship rule becomes the friend's evidence that he will marry without being pressed.

note: Kural 335 says that, because death stops the tongue unannounced, good deeds must be rushed to; the man of Kuruntokai 267 argues from Death's crooked, daily taking that those who know it do not leave their women to go after work and wealth.
teaches: The same awareness of death leads to opposite conduct: the Kural spends the short life on merit done in haste, the lover on staying with her and refusing the journey, so impermanence by itself does not decide between duty and love.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my wife and feast the evening; Kuruntokai 270: his work done, the man lies on her hair and bids the rain pour.
teaches: The couplet's wish is the poem's fulfilled state: the evening feast he pictured while the king's work held him is given its weather and its pillow, and the rain he dreaded on campaign becomes a blessing once he is home.

note: Both poems use the same line, செய்வினை முடித்த செம்மல் உள்ளம், for the man whose task is done: in 270 he says it of himself, already with her in the rain; in 275 the friend imagines it of him as she listens for a bell at dusk.
teaches: The formula is the hinge of the mullai return seen from both sides of the door: the friend's hopeful projection in 275 is exactly what the man claims in 270, so the waiting and the arrival are framed by one satisfied heart.

note: In 280 the man would give up even half a day of life after a single day's union; in 271 the woman says one day's union has become a disease lasting very many days.
teaches: The same single day of union is priced in opposite currencies: the man offers the rest of his life for it, and the woman, who has had it, pays in many days of wasting, so the two speakers measure the secret love by different costs.

note: Kural 1269: for those who wait for the day of return, one day passes like seven; Kuruntokai 271: one day of union has turned into very many days of sickness.
teaches: The couplet stretches the waiting days, the poem multiplies the one day of joy into a long illness, so the woman's suffering is measured not only by slow time but by a debt that a single meeting keeps collecting.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Kuruntokai 272 likens her eyes to the bloody arrow her brothers drew from a stag near a doe parted from its herd.
teaches: The poem stages the couplet's three-way question as one hunt: doe, killing shaft and eye stand together, and because the shaft belongs to her brothers, the deadliness of her look is also the threat of her kin to the suitor.

note: In 262 the friend says the girl has chosen to drink elephant-footprint water with him in a far country; in 274 the man says the cruel forest will be sweet if he goes holding her.
teaches: The claim that the beloved's company sweetens the desert is made for the girl by the friend and by the man for himself, so the elopement rests on a premise both lovers hold, voiced by different speakers.
audit_text_issue: Kuruntokai 274 line 8 variant முயங்கினம் / உள்கினம்

note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating without favour and acting after judgement toward everyone; in Kuruntokai 276 the lover thinks of taking his case to the just king's court and at once asks what would become of her.
teaches: The lover's question shows where the Kural's impartial justice stops: a harm done without intent by an innocent girl is real but cannot be judged, so the just court is imagined only to be abandoned.

note: Kural 1124: she is to him as life when present and as death when she goes; Kuruntokai 280: for one day's union he would not want half a day of life after.
teaches: The couplet equates her presence with life, the poem goes further and trades the rest of life for one day of her, so the man's praise of love moves from equation to sacrifice.

note: Kuruntokai 283 reports the man's maxim that the life of those who have nothing is more shameful even than begging, and he leaves for wealth; Kural 1064 says the worth that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for the world to hold. On the reading that 283 ranks poverty below begging, the two rank the same states in opposite order.
teaches: The Kural makes the destitute man who refuses to beg the height of dignity, while the akam hero's maxim makes destitution itself the deepest shame, so the poems show that the urge to go for wealth rested on a ranking of poverty and begging the Kural explicitly reverses.

note: Kural 1103: the man asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; Kuruntokai 288: the woman asks whether the world of the gods is sweeter even than the hurt that comes from kin because of her lover.
teaches: The couplet weighs heaven against the joy of love, the poem weighs it against love's pain, so the woman's claim is the stronger: not only the embrace but even the suffering it brings outweighs the gods' world.

note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now seem to announce the parting; Kuruntokai 299: the woman's shoulders gain beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves, after the tryst on the shore.
teaches: The couplet gives the swelling and the wasting as public evidence that others read, while the poem gives them as the woman's own bewildered discovery, tied to the day her eyes saw him and her ears heard him, so the same bodily sign is both the town's proof and her private record.

note: Kural 1130: he lives joyfully in her heart, while the town says he is unloving and lives apart; Kuruntokai 289: she grieves for him out in the rain, and the clamouring town grieves for her more.
teaches: In both the woman's thought goes out to the absent man while the town's goes to her plight, but the town's verdict differs, blame in the Kural and pity in the poem, so the town's talk in akam is not fixed as hostile gossip and can be her chorus.
audit_text_issue: Line 8 prints இவ் வழங்கல், most likely a split of இவ்வழுங்கல் (இவ் + அழுங்கல்). | 289.6 'பட்ட மாரி படாஅக் கண்ணும்' is hard to construe | Line 6 of 289 obscure.

note: Akananuru 45, told to bear up, the woman answers with the dangers of his road, the gossip and her own coming madness like Aathi Manthi's; Kuruntokai 290 answers the same counsel ('bear your love') by saying she will waste away like foam on a rock.
teaches: The two poems answer the same counsel to endure in opposite registers, one with public ruin and a famous madness, the other with a silent dissolving, which shows that the heroine's refusal of endurance could be voiced as loud breakdown or as quiet vanishing.

note: Kuruntokai 73 (Paranar) tells of the Kosar who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango and drove him from his land; Kuruntokai 292 (Paranar) tells of Nannan killing a girl who ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refusing eighty-one elephants and her weight in gold.
teaches: Read together, Paranar's two poems hold both halves of one tale, the cruelty over a fruit and the tree's later felling, and each friend uses a different half: one as a model of hard scheming, the other as the type of cruelty to curse a watchful mother with.

note: Purananuru 233 names Akuthai as the strong one whose elephants never ran short for those who came for gifts; Kuruntokai 298 recalls the young she-elephants Akuthai's father gave to singing women and likens the lover's long waiting to that gift.
teaches: The puram lament knows the house of Akuthai only as givers of elephants, and the akam friend turns that known generosity into a figure for a lover's patience, so a patron's fame for gifts served akam as a ready image of an act that waits on a return.

note: In Kuruntokai 300 the man says he would not leave her even for the sea-ringed world; in Kuruntokai 288 the woman says even the hurt love brings is sweeter than the world of the gods.
teaches: The man measures his love against earthly rule and the woman against heaven, so the two speakers of kalavu each renounce the highest good of their own sphere, kingship for him, the gods' world for her.

note: Kural 1179 says her eyes do not sleep when he fails to come nor when he comes; in Kuruntokai 301 he does not come, and the bell of a chariot that is not there rings in her ear at midnight while her eyes give up sleep.
teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's 'when he does not come' still keeps the eyes open: the ear makes his chariot out of the night, so absence is lived as an arrival that never quite happens.

note: Kural 1205 rebukes the man for barring her from his heart while he keeps coming into hers; in Kuruntokai 302 the man likewise comes only into her heart at midnight, and she asks whether fear of gossip keeps him away.
teaches: Together they give two verdicts on the same phantom visit: the couplet calls it shameless trespass, the poem excuses it as fear of the town, so whether his absence is a fault depends on the reason the heroine allows him.

note: Kural 1150 says the town is raising the very gossip they want, since it will bring the lover round; in Kuruntokai 302 the gossip that calls the pair inseparable is what she fears has kept him away. On this reading the same talk helps in one and harms in the other.
teaches: The pair shows alar cutting both ways in secret love: the talk the Kural's speaker welcomes as a lever toward marriage can, as the poem fears, frighten a lover into staying away altogether.

note: Kural 1171 says the eyes showed him and so she came to see an unending sickness; Kuruntokai 305 opens with the bright fire of love that the eyes brought and follows it to a sickness no one can stop.
teaches: The couplet blames the eyes and stops at 'unending'; the poem carries the same sickness to its end in the dunghill cocks' fight that only death stops, so 'unending' is shown to mean ending only in death.

note: In Akananuru 91 the friend points to the elephant that shrinks together with its hungry mate on the scorched road as proof that the man still loves; in Kuruntokai 307 the heroine points to a tusker that fells a tree to feed its weary mate as proof that he has forgotten.
teaches: The same iraicchi of the tusker's care on the wasteland serves the friend as comfort and the heroine as reproach, so the device's sense is fixed by who is speaking and what she wants, not by the beast.

note: Kural 1288 tells the thief that his chest is to her as toddy is to drinkers, though it does them shameful harm; Kuruntokai 309 says the women are like the neythal that blooms again in the field it was weeded from, though he does them many unkind things.
teaches: Both say she cannot leave him though he harms her, but the Kural calls the bond an addiction while the poem calls it rootedness in his own field, so the pair shows the same dependence judged as weakness and as loyalty.

note: Kural 1222 asks the dim evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 310 sees the sky dazed like herself at day's end and then says she may yet live if someone will carry word to him.
teaches: The couplet stops at fellow-feeling with the evening; the poem turns that fellow-feeling into a need for a messenger, so the evening lament is shown as the point where the heroine starts to seek a go-between.

note: Kuruntokai 212 has the friend say the shore lord's chariot comes, bells ringing, only to be seen and goes back leaving shame; in Kuruntokai 311 the chariot that would not stop was seen by the whole troop of flower-gathering girls, and the heroine asks how the gossip can end.
teaches: Read together, the chariot that the friend in 212 calls mere display is in 311 the very evidence the gossip rests on, so the lover's conspicuous visits are both his courtship and the cause of the alar.

note: Kapilar praises Malaiyan in Purananuru 123 as giving more chariots than the raindrops on the heights of Mullur; in Kuruntokai 312, also Kapilar's, the girl comes at midnight filling Malaiyan's Mullur forest with her fragrance.
teaches: The same poet uses his patron's hill both as the measure of a king's countless gifts and as the secret ground of a tryst, which shows a court poet setting his love scenes inside the land he praised in puram.

note: Kural 1271 has the man tell the girl that though she hides it, her eyes go beyond her control and speak; in Kuruntokai 312 the man marvels that by dawn she is wholly one of her kin again, face unmoved. On the poem's reading her concealment holds.
teaches: The pair sets two views of the girl's secret side by side: the Kural's man reads it in her eyes, Kapilar's man admires a disguise he cannot see through, so concealment in kalavu is both a failure and an art.

note: Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the lord of the shore is knotted and settled, hard to untie; Kuruntokai 304 says the friendship made with the lord of the shore has brought enmity.
teaches: Held together they show why 304's grief is so sharp: the bond that 313 praises as impossible to untie is the same bond that, once it brings hostility, cannot be undone either.

note: Kural 791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since for the faithful there is no leaving once the friendship is made; Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the shore lord is tied and settled, hard to untie.
teaches: The heroine states as her settled joy the very fact the Kural gives as the reason for caution, so the pair shows that love's bond is the friendship the ethics book warns about, entered without the inquiry it prescribes.

note: Kar Narpathu 12 has the friend say that his coming is certain, shown beyond doubt by the dark clouds that rise every day; in Kuruntokai 314 the full rain cloud flashes lightning at evening and the heroine says he still does not come. On this reading the sign the friend calls certain has failed.
teaches: Set beside the Kar Narpathu's confident friend, the poem shows the other side of the season-sign: the cloud that is offered as proof of return becomes, when he does not come, the measure of his broken word.

note: Kuruntokai 202 compares the lover to the nerunji, which first gives a sweet flower and then thorns; Kuruntokai 315 makes the man the sun and her shoulders the nerunji that turns to it.
teaches: One weed of poor ground carries two opposite lessons in the same anthology, its turning to the sun as her dependence and its later thorns as his change, so the heroine's image in 315 already holds the pain that 202 states.

note: Kural 1288 addresses the lover as thief whose chest is like toddy that harms; Kuruntokai 318 calls the man thief too, but also the one bound by his oath and the raft who must carry her across.
teaches: The Kural's 'thief' names only the sweet harm, while the poem turns the same title into a claim: whoever stole is bound to restore, so the word becomes the ground of her demand for marriage.

note: Kural 1221 says the hour is not evening but a spear that eats the life of the wedded; in Kuruntokai 319 the rain-evening comes as the stag and the elephant take shelter with their mates, and she asks what will become of her life if he does not come.
teaches: The poem shows why the evening kills: it is the hour when every creature goes to its mate, so the Kural's bare claim that evening eats life gets its cause in the paired beasts the heroine watches.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on one day only, yet the talk has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; Kuruntokai 320 says they have not even the blame of laughing together one day, yet the town spreads gossip.
teaches: The Kural concedes one meeting behind the talk while the poem denies even that, so the pair shows the gossip of kalavu needing ever less fact, until in 320 it rests on nothing but the town's cruelty.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether heaven is sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; in Kuruntokai 323 the man calls every other day chaff and counts as lived only the days spent sleeping on her shoulders.
teaches: The couplet ranks the embrace above heaven's pleasure; the poem turns the same ranking on time itself, so the pair shows the claim growing from a comparison of joys into a measure of which days of a life count as lived.

note: Kural 1192 says a lover's grace to those who love is like rain to those who live by it; Kuruntokai 327's man has learned to withhold grace from those who live only if he is gracious (நல்கின் வாழும்), and water reaches her as a flood from his hill.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's rain of grace is shown in reverse: the one who lives by it is denied it, and the water that does come down from the lover's hill is muddy and destroys, so dependence on grace is seen from the side of its failure.

note: Purananuru 151 refuses the young Vicchi lord the poet's embrace because of a door shut against singers; Kuruntokai 328 measures gossip by the uproar of Kurumbur when bards saw the Vicchiyar chief stand like a tiger against the kings.
teaches: The Vicchi house is remembered by singers in two ways at once, its war-cry loud enough to be an akam poet's yardstick for noise and its door shut against bards in puram, so the pair shows that a chief's fame for valour could circulate apart from, and despite, his name for giving.

note: In Kural 1167 the woman swims love's flood without seeing a shore and at midnight is the only one awake; in Kuruntokai 329 she cannot sleep in midnight's thick dark, thinking of the man on the desert road.
teaches: The couplet gives the midnight wakefulness as a bare state; the poem gives it a content, the road he took buried under fallen iluppai flowers, so the pair shows the sleepless mind of separation travelling the absent man's road.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 330 she asks whether the sorrowful evening (புன்கண் மாலை) and its loneliness exist at all in the land he went to.
teaches: Both make the evening testify against the absent man, but in opposite ways: the couplet makes it a fellow sufferer, the poem imagines a land without it, which would explain why he stays away, so the pair shows the evening serving as companion and as accusation.

note: In Kuruntokai 63 the man's heart argues that work for wealth must be pressed because the penniless can neither give nor enjoy; in 331 the friend says he goes for wealth he rates above them (நம்மினுஞ் சிறந்த).
teaches: The same journey for wealth is a duty in the man's reckoning and a ranking of the women below gold in the friend's, so the pair shows that the paalai departure is argued from both houses and that neither side's account mentions the other's.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman tells her friend to prevent the departure of the one fit for her, since once he goes union is hard; in Kuruntokai 334 she tells her friend that if he leaves, what they lose is only their one life.
teaches: Both speak to the friend before a parting, but the couplet asks for help to stop it while the poem asks for none and names the price, her life, so the pair shows the same plea in two moods, one still bargaining and one already resigned.

note: In Kural 1081 the man cannot tell whether she is an anangu, a peahen or a woman; in Kuruntokai 337 he is sure she is an anangu (அணங்கென) and adds that she herself does not know it.
teaches: The couplet's bewilderment is about what she is; the poem moves it to the gap between her power and her ignorance of it, the one-sided love of kaikkilai, so the pair shows the anangu figure turning from a lover's confusion into an observation about a girl not yet aware of herself.

note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feed and guard its doe and hurries his chariot home; in Kuruntokai 338 the friend sets a stag resting with its doe at evening beside the news that the victorious chariot has come.
teaches: The stag with its doe is the spur to return in the man's mouth and the sign that the return has happened in the friend's, so the pair shows one iraicchi working at both ends of the journey, as motive and as fulfilment.

note: In Kuruntokai 65 the stag back with its mate in the rains mocks the waiting woman because her man has not come; in 338 the same pairing at evening comes with the chariot that ends her pallor. On the waiting woman's reading in 65 the sign is false; in 338 it is kept.
teaches: The same image of the stag beside its mate is read as a reproach when the man fails the season and as a promise kept when he arrives, so the pair shows that the iraicchi carries no fixed sense apart from whether the man returns.

note: In Kural 1249 the woman asks her heart whom it goes seeking, since the lover is within it; in Kuruntokai 340 her heart, where he dwells, can settle on neither side and sways like a kandal with ebb and tide.
teaches: The couplet treats the heart's going out to him as an absurdity to point out; the poem's rooted kandal, bent out by the ebb and back by the flood, makes the same divided heart a rhythm she cannot stop, so the paradox becomes a condition rather than an error.

note: The line ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ closes the friend's memory of how he won the girl in 176 and stands in 325 after the heroine admits she herself told him to go.
teaches: The same cry for the lost support carries blame of the man in the friend's poem and self-reproach in the heroine's, so the pair shows a formula line taking its charge from who speaks it and what precedes it.

note: In Akananuru 54 the returning man sees the milch herd hurrying home at dusk to the calves with the cowherds behind and wants to reach his wife and son; in Kuruntokai 344 the waiting woman sees the cows with dripping udders leave the herd for the village at dusk and says only the fortunate see their lovers return.
teaches: The same dusk image of cows hurrying home to their calves is the man's cue to return when he speaks and the woman's reproach when she speaks, so the herd's homing is a fixed sign of the duty to come home that each side reads against the other.

note: In Akananuru 110 a stranger asks the bathing girls if he may eat with them and stay in their noisy fishing hamlet, and they turn him away; in Kuruntokai 345 the friend herself asks the man whether staying with his chariot at their small town by the great water would be a fault.
teaches: The night's stay in the fishing hamlet is the neythal courtship's measure of trust: asked for by the stranger at the start and refused, it is offered by the friend once the love is known, so who proposes the stay marks how far the affair has gone.

note: In Kuruntokai 236 the friend tells the lord of the shore to give back the beauty he consumed before he leaves; in Kuruntokai 349 the woman answers such a proposal by saying that demanding back what was given is worse than losing one's life.
teaches: The demand to return her beauty, which the friend can make as a just claim, the woman herself refuses because it treats her love as a loan, so the same claim is fair in a friend's mouth and shameful in the giver's, by the code that a gift is not taken back.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should at once do what lasts; in Kuruntokai 350 the friend calls the wealth for which the man left நிலையாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, and regrets they did not stop him.
teaches: The ethicist's premise that wealth does not stay becomes in akam an argument against the journey itself: the Kural spends unstable wealth on lasting good, while the friend counts the lasting thing given up as the woman's company, so the same premise judges the pursuit of wealth from the household's side.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the woman the town raises the very gossip they want, since the lover will grant marriage when asked; in Kuruntokai 351 the friend tells the girl to rejoice because their kin have declared the marriage, and asks whether the gossiping town is still the same.
teaches: The couplet hopes the town's gossip will force the marriage, and the poem shows the end of that hope: once the kin declare the marriage, the talk that pressed for it has nothing left to say, so the gossip served its purpose and the friend can mock it.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not left; Kuruntokai 352: the woman says she knew the reality of the small dull evening only when she could not see him.
teaches: The couplet states the late discovery of evening's pain as a bare fact, and the poem gives the sign through which she learned it, the creature that leaves its day-tree lonely at dusk, so the knowledge the Kural reports is shown arising from a scene in which the hour itself repeats the parting.

note: Both foster mothers ask யாங்கு வல்லுநள்கொல் தானே of a girl who refused milk held up in a fine vessel at home: Akananuru 105 follows the question with the raiders' road of Ezhini's bowmen, Kuruntokai 356 with the scalding muddy water she must gulp.
teaches: The shared formula of the refused milk and 'how will she manage' is a stock frame of the foster mother's lament, and the two poems show its slot filled differently: the long poem measures the girl's leaving by the road's dangers, the short one by what she must now drink, so the same frame can carry either fear or tenderness.

note: Kural 1261: the woman's fingers are worn from marking the days since he left; Kuruntokai 358: the friend speaks to the woman who scores lines and clings to the wall, and points to the mullai buds as the season he promised.
teaches: The couplet gives the counting of days only as the woman's wasting, while the poem lets the friend answer it with a sign outside the wall, the season's buds, so the count the Kural leaves open is closed by the promised season and becomes ground for comfort.
audit_text_issue: kuruntokai:358 line 7 repaired; syntax hard, but the link rests on lines 2-4.

note: In Akananuru 26 the wife turns to their son and the husband, saying he too loves the child, embraces her back and weeps; in Kuruntokai 359 the friend tells the bard that the man embraced his son and the son's mother embraced the man's back.
teaches: In both reconciliations the son carries the embrace between husband and wife, and with the roles reversed (in one the husband clasps the wife's back, in the other the wife the husband's), so the akam poets made the child the agreed route back into a marriage after estrangement.

note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs because during the velan's midnight rite her lover slipped past the guards and his embrace cured her; in Kuruntokai 360 the girl, while the velan misreads her sickness, prays that the lover not come at night.
teaches: The two girls in the same veri situation take opposite views of the lover's night visit, one as the cure that mocks the rite and the other as a danger worse than the rite's misdiagnosis, so the veri scene could be turned either to triumph or to selfless restraint.

note: In Akananuru 98 the girl tells her friend that the mother does not know her ache is eased only on the hill lord's chest, while the velan's rite goes on; in Kuruntokai 362 the friend puts that same claim to the velan as a question: will his chest eat the offering?
teaches: The pair shows the step from private knowledge to disclosure: what the girl can only say to her friend in the long poem, the friend turns into a riddle spoken at the rite itself, so the mockery of the diviner is the means by which the secret reaches the mother.

note: Kural 1151's friend refuses comfort with an ultimatum about who will still be alive when he returns; Kuruntokai 363's friend asks whether crossing the waste is sweet when even the bull there stays by its doe.
teaches: The same dissuasion of a man about to leave is made by threat in the couplet and by the example of the road's own creatures in the poem, so the pair shows the friend has two arguments, death of the one left and the shame of being less faithful than a beast.

note: Both are courtesans answering, within hearing of the wife's side, the wife's talk against them: in Akananuru 76 she vows to hold him as the Kaveri took Atti; in Kuruntokai 364 she points to the coming thunangai festival where eyes clash.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the concubine's convention of answering slander not with denial but with a public contest announced in advance, a river's seizure or a festival's rivalry, so the household quarrel is moved out into the town's open spaces.

note: In Kuruntokai 229 onlookers see destiny (பால்) at work in two who fought as children and are now joined; in 366 the friend invokes the same destiny before any outcome to refuse to judge the man.
teaches: Destiny serves after the fact as the onlookers' explanation and before the fact as the friend's argument for consent, so the pair shows the akam idea of பால் doing persuasive work, not only describing what happened.
audit_text_issue: 366.5-6 'உள்ளகை பழுத கண்ணள்' is hard to construe; line 3 repaired from another edition

note: In 369 the friend calls the paalai road pleasant, its pods rattling like anklets, and urges the girl to go; in 378 the foster mother, after the girl has gone, can only pray that the same road's sun and bare paths be cooled.
teaches: The one elopement road is a promise to the girl's accomplice and a danger to the woman who raised her, so the pair shows the akam books dividing a single event between voices who cannot both be right about the land.

note: Purananuru 3 tells the Pandya that even if the earth shifts his word must not; Kuruntokai 373's friend says that even if the earth shifts and fire and water change places, the lovers' bond suffers no harm from gossip.
teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram formula for a king's unbreakable word and gives it to a secret love, so the pair shows that the lovers' bond was claimed in the language of royal oath, and that a pledge, not a feeling, is what kalavu asks to be trusted.

note: In Akananuru 122 the girl lists the town, mother, guards, dogs, moon and owl that keep watch, and complains that when all sleep he does not come; in Kuruntokai 375 the friend says it is better he does not come, since the guards beat their drum all night against the tiger.
teaches: The same sleepless watch is used to reproach the lover for missing his chance and to wish him away from it, so the pair shows that the catalogue of obstacles is addressed to the man in both directions, and that its real end is to make the night visit impossible and marriage necessary.

note: Kural 1104's man asks where she found a fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near; Kuruntokai 376's man says she is cool in summer and warm in the cold season.
teaches: Both men praise her as a reversal of temperature, but the couplet makes it depend on his distance and the poem on the season, so together they show the convention of the beloved as a climate of her own, which the Kural turns inward into the lover's desire.

note: In Akananuru 283 the friend, arranging the elopement, wishes rain to fall on the forest and cool it so the road is sweet; in Kuruntokai 378 the foster mother, after the girl has gone, prays the sun not burn and cool clouds hang over the waste.
teaches: The same wish for a cooled desert passes from the accomplice who sends the girl to the woman who has lost her, so the pair shows the foster mother's grief taking the form of blessing, joining in the elopement she did not choose.

note: In Akananuru 84 the man in the king's war camp sees the drum-voiced rain-clouds and thinks of his wife in her small village; in Kuruntokai 380 the waiting women hear the cloud roar like the drums kings beat in victory while the lover stays far away.
teaches: Read together, the simile in the women's mouth names the cause the man's poem shows from inside, the king's campaign, so the rains are the same drum to both and the season of war and the season of waiting are one.

note: In 381 the friend says the girl's wasting and pallor are the only fruit of having laughed with the shore lord; in 401 the girl says that even laughing play with the shore lord has been forbidden.
teaches: Read together the two neythal poems show laughter with the shore lord as the whole of kalavu at its smallest unit: one laugh costs the girl her beauty in 381, and in 401 the household guards against exactly that, so the forbidding is the town's answer to the danger the friend names.
audit_text_issue: Kuruntokai 401 line 6 division uncertain (ஐதே)

note: In 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking the untimely rain for the season; in 382 the friend says the rain itself is untimely, since if it were the season the man would have come.
teaches: The friend's comfort moves from blaming the tree to denying the season: in 66 nature is fooled by false rain, in 382 the man's promise is made the test of what the rain is, so his word outranks the calendar of flowers.

note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not yet left; in 386 the woman knew evening only as the festival hour of jewelled women and did not know its sorrow wide as the earth.
teaches: The poem fills in what the couplet's woman did know of evening before: the public festival hour of the women's gathering, so the Kural's 'I did not know' is the reversal of a known, shared evening into a private sorrow.

note: Kural 1167: the woman swims the fierce flood of desire and sees no shore, and at midnight only she is awake; in 387 she swims across the evening to reach the night as its bank, and finds the night's flood larger than the sea.
teaches: The couplet's shoreless flood gets its hours in the poem: the evening is the first water and the night a second, larger one, so the shore the Kural's woman cannot see is the bank of evening that only opens onto the night.

note: In Akananuru 253 gossip is louder than the cheering at Kudal when the green-jewelled Pandiyan drove out the Kongar; in Kuruntokai 393 gossip is louder than the Kongar's shout when the green-jewelled Pandiyan's general Athikan fell at Vaakai.
teaches: The Pandiyan's wars with the Kongar gave akam poets their yardstick for gossip from both outcomes, his victory cheer at Kudal and the enemy's cry over his fallen general, so the measure was the loudest noise of a known war whichever side made it.

note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why the girl will not drink milk and has paled, and the friend tells her of the young hunter; in Kuruntokai 396 the foster mother, after the girl has gone with her man, recalls that she would not drink her milk or take up her ball.
teaches: The same symptom, refused milk, stands at two points of one story: in Akananuru 48 it is a question the friend answers in time to open the way to marriage, in Kuruntokai 396 a clue the foster mother reads only after the elopement, so the akam poets used it as the sign that decides whether disclosure or udanpokku follows.

note: Kural 1187: she lay in his embrace and turned aside, and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up; in 399 pallor is moss on the village well that parts where he touches and spreads where he lets go.
teaches: The couplet's instant hyperbole is given a mechanism by the poem: pallor is a surface like well-moss that closes the moment the hand lifts, so the Kural's 'at that very moment' is not exaggeration but what anyone at a village well has seen.

note: Kural 1146: gossip about one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; in 395 the woman says no one frees her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, nor even tells her not to fear.
teaches: The eclipse served both as a spectacle everyone sees and as a rite in which everyone rushes to help: the Kural takes the first sense for gossip, the poem the second for rescue, and the woman's complaint is that her eclipse draws the town's eyes but none of its help.

note: In Akananuru 34 the man, his work done, bids the charioteer drive fast so that his wife may regain her beauty; in Kuruntokai 400 the man thanks the charioteer who cut a new way across the gravel and brought the chariot home to the wife in pain.
teaches: The two poems are the command and the thanks of one homeward drive: Akananuru 34 asks for speed, Kuruntokai 400 credits the charioteer with the resolve and the shortcut, so the driver is shown sharing the husband's care for the wife and earns praise for it.

note: In 7 onlookers on the road ask who the pitiable bowman and his anklet-wearing girl are, setting out into the wilds; in 390 onlookers tell the man, mate of the young she-elephant, to stop for the night because of the frontier guards' drum.
teaches: The onlookers of udanpokku move from pity to protection: in 7 they only wonder at the couple, in 390 they name the danger of the road at nightfall and halt them, so the kandor are not only witnesses of the elopement but its guardians on the way.

note: Natrinai 0 builds the discus-bearer's body from the cosmos: earth his feet, sea his garment, sky his body, the quarters his hands, moon and sun his eyes; Tirumanthiram 2774 gives Shiva the same map, space his body, the eight directions his hands, the three lights his three eyes, as he dances.
teaches: The body made of sky, quarters and heavenly lights is a frame older than either sect: the Sangam invocation fills it for the discus-bearer as a fact the Veda reports, and Tirumular fills it for Shiva and sets it dancing with a third eye of fire, so the image passed between gods while its parts stayed fixed.

note: Natrinai 1's heroine calls her man sweeter the longer one knows him (நீடுதோறு இனியர்) and the bond of the noble lofty; Kural 783 says the companionship of people of character delights the more it is practised, as a book does the more it is studied.
teaches: The heroine uses the Kural's rule about friendship with the noble as the premise of a love argument, reasoning from his character that he cannot leave her, so a maxim about good company served in akam as evidence against a report of parting.

note: Both use the formula of the world that cannot do without water (நீர் இன்று அமையா உலகம், நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு): Kural 20 as the first step of an argument that all conduct depends on rain, Natrinai 1 as the measure of how she cannot live without him.
teaches: The same clause is a step in Valluvar's proof about rain and a simile of a woman's dependence in Kapilar, which shows it was a common saying both drew on, apt to the akam poet for a lover's need as it was to the moralist for the world's.

note: Natrinai 2's onlookers see the elopement road as a wasteland where a tiger cub with blood on its mouth eyes deer at evening, and call the youth's heart crueler than thunder; in Natrinai 9 the eloping man describes the road as cool groves of koels and mango buds where she may linger in the shade and make sand dolls.
teaches: Read together, the two poems give the same udanpokku road two natures by speaker, a tiger's evening for the bystanders and a spring garden for the lover, so the danger of paalai is a judgment the voices make and not only a fact of the land.

note: Both are Perumpathumanar's onlookers on an eloping pair: in Kuruntokai 7 they ask who these good, pitiable people are, the bowman and the girl with anklets still on, heading into the bamboo wilds; in Natrinai 2 they say the youth's heart is crueler than mountain-shaking thunder.
teaches: The same poet lets the onlookers pity both runaways in one poem and in the other lay the whole blame on the man who leads her into the tiger's country, so the kandor voice was a place to judge the hero, not only to witness the pair.

note: Both are a man answering a heart that urges a journey for wealth: in Natrinai 3 he recalls thinking of her at lamp-lighting time on the edge of the wasteland on an earlier journey; in Natrinai 16 he sets out the dilemma that wealth and union cannot both be had and gives up the journey.
teaches: The same refusal is reached once by memory and once by argument: Natrinai 3 calls her sweet as a finished task, putting the journey's goal already at home, and Natrinai 16 states the reason as a rule that wealth leaves no trace, so the decision is held both as felt experience and as reasoned principle.

note: Both concern the town's gossip about a secret love: Kural 1143's man asks whether gossip the whole town knows is not good for him, since it is like having what he has not yet got; Natrinai 4's friend fears that gossip reaching the mother will end the meetings and asks whether the man will take them to his own town.
teaches: The gossip that the Kural's man welcomes as a foretaste of union is, for the women of Natrinai 4, the danger that ends their meetings, which they can only turn into pressure to marry, so the worth of alar in the secret stage depends on who bears its cost.

note: Both name வல்வில் ஓரி: Purananuru 152 shows the hunter whose single arrow kills an elephant, a tiger, a stag, a boar and an iguana, and who feeds the bard venison; in Natrinai 6 the girl's hair smells of Ori's forest, where the ripe fruit of the kumizh falls as food for young deer.
teaches: The love poet takes from the hunter-patron's fame only his forest's scent and plenty, a place where the very deer his bow kills feed unharmed, so akam borrowed a puram name for the bounty of a land and left its violence behind.

note: Both are the man at first sight of the girl: Kural 1081 asks whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, his heart reeling; Natrinai 8 asks whose daughter she is, blesses her father and wishes on her mother the fortune of Thondi.
teaches: Valluvar's man asks what she is and the Natrinai man whose she is, his first words going to her parents, so the Sangam poem shows the couplet's stunned wonder already turning toward the kin and the marriage that will need them.

note: Natrinai 8 places in Poraiyan's Thondi neythal flowers that look like eyes; in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that beauty.
teaches: The Thondi neythal and a woman's eyes were a fixed pair that ran both ways, the flower measured by eyes in a man's first praise and the eyes by the flower in a woman's grief at separation, so one token marked beauty found and beauty lost at two stages of love.

note: Kuruntokai 7's onlookers see anklets still on the eloping girl's feet; in Natrinai 12 the friend tells how the girl, hiding herself at dawn, slipped off her pebble-filled anklets and left her striped ball before going.
teaches: Together they show the anklet as the mark of an unmarried girl, read by strangers on the road in one poem and taken off by the girl herself in secret in the other, so the eloping girl performs alone at dawn the change of state that a wedding would have made in public.

note: Both are about restraint that can no longer keep love hidden: Kural 1254's woman says she used to think herself restrained but her love now breaks out in public; Natrinai 15's friend tells the man they have let go even their long modesty and the town may gossip.
teaches: The Kural records the loss of restraint as an inner confession, while Natrinai 15 makes the same loss a threat spoken to the man, likened to a mother forced to give her child to a demon, so the collapse of naanam also served as a lever to force marriage.

note: Both hold that wealth does not stay: Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance and goes as it disperses; Natrinai 16 says wealth vanishes like the trail of a fish in a pond.
teaches: The Kural uses wealth's impermanence to counsel detachment, while the Natrinai man uses it to choose his wife's gaze over a journey, so the same doctrine served an argument for staying at home in love as well as one for letting go.

note: Both rank modesty above life: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for it but never shame for life; Natrinai 17's girl says she almost forgot the modesty dearer than life when her mother spoke softly.
teaches: The Kural states the ranking as a firm rule, and the Natrinai girl who holds it nearly breaks it not under threat but under a mother's tenderness, so the poem shows the rule's weak point to be a kindness the maxim does not foresee.

note: Both answer a lover's departure by saying she will not live until he returns: Kural 1151 says to tell his quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 19's friend says go, knowing well she will not live the few days till you come.
teaches: The couplet's bitter refusal of comfort appears in Natrinai 19 inside a friend's demand for marriage in the secret stage, so the claim that she will die before he returns worked in kalavu as pressure to marry and not only as grief.

note: Both are a wife's sulk at the husband's straying, fixed on his chest: Kural 1311 refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes; Natrinai 20 describes the girl who slept on the lord's chest and walked off at dawn with crushed earring and withered garland.
