teaches: The Kural states the wife's charge in general terms, and Natrinai 20 shows the single scene behind such a charge, the rival's disordered body read as proof and blessed in irony, so the couplet's reproach rests on a convention of reading the other woman's appearance as evidence.

note: Both are by Maruthan Ilanaganar on the same occasion (the man, his work done, speaks to his charioteer): in Akananuru 34 a stag feeds and guards his doe, in Natrinai 21 a forest cock scratches out its morning food and looks to its hen, and both close the image on the same word, பெருந்தகை / பெருந்தகு.
teaches: Holding the two together shows one poet keeping a fixed frame for this thurai, a male creature's noble care for its mate seen from the speeding chariot, and changing only the creature, so the iraicchi of the homecoming was a reusable device rather than a chance sight.

note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.
audit_text_issue: 23 line 3 (இடிப்பு மெய்யது ஒன்று உடைத்தே) is hard. | Natrinai 23 line 3 (இடிப்பு மெய்யது ஒன்று உடைத்தே) is hard. | Natrinai 23 line 3 is hard. | Natrinai line 3 hard

note: Both rest on the maxim that work is what men are: in Kuruntokai 135 the friend adds that men are the life of the women at home and concludes that he will put off going; in Natrinai 24 the woman adds nothing and praises her friend for consenting to his going. On the plain reading the two conclusions are incompatible.
teaches: The pair shows that the saying about men and work was common ground each speaker could turn either way, toward consenting to the parting or toward stopping it, so the maxim settled nothing and each poem's argument lies in what it adds to it.

note: Both are by Peri Saathanar and both name the man as the one who chased parrots from the millet with them (கிளி கடிந்து ... நம்மொடு; கிள்ளை நம்மொடு கடிந்தோன்): in Natrinai 25 he leaves without finding a chance to speak, and in Akananuru 242 the mother, not knowing this same man came in love, calls the velan.
teaches: Read together, the poet's one formula marks two stages of a single courtship, the silent visitor at the millet field whose plea the friend carries and the unseen cause of the sickness the mother misreads, so the parrot-chasing stranger is what separates the friend's knowledge from the mother's ignorance.

note: Natrinai 32's friend ends with the saying that the great take a friend after inquiry and do not inquire after befriending, and that once accepted it is hard to undo; Kural 791 says nothing brings ruin like befriending without inquiry, since there is no leaving once the bond is formed.
teaches: The Kural's rule and its reason, inquire first because a formed bond cannot be left, already serve in the Natrinai as a proverb a friend applies to a girl choosing a lover, so the ethics of friendship framed the irrevocability of a love match before Valluvar set them apart in his book on polity.

note: In Akananuru 242 the friend calls the velan ignorant (அறியா வேலன்) for finding Murugan's seizure in the girl; in Natrinai 34 the friend addresses Murugan himself, who knows the sickness is not his yet comes to the veri at the velan's call, and calls the god a fool.
teaches: Together they show the friend's scorn for the veri rite moving up from the priest to the god: where one poem blames only the diviner's ignorance, the other makes the god complicit, since he knows the truth and comes anyway.

note: Both liken a woman's beauty to Kuttuvan's harbour town Maranthai: in Akananuru 376 the deserted courtesan asks the man to give back her Maranthai-like beauty before he goes; in Natrinai 35 the friend, the day after the wedding, asks whether the wife's Maranthai-like beauty has slackened though he has not left her side.
teaches: The same city-simile measures a beauty the man must answer for in both, but the pair shows it waning for opposite reasons, the courtesan's because he left and the new wife's while he stays, so the Natrinai places the loss in love itself rather than in absence.

note: Purananuru 72 has Neduncheliyan vow to rout the kings who mocked him and seize them together with their drums (முரசமொடு); Natrinai 39 names Cheliyan as the one who took the drums and crossed the foes' guarded walls (முரசு கொண்டு ஓம்பு அரண் கடந்த) and likens the girl's shoulders to his Koodal. The Natrinai does not say which Cheliyan; the drum-taking matches.
teaches: The pair shows a king's battle vow hardened into a stock epithet inside a love simile and turned on the lover: the city of the king who took walled forts becomes the measure of shoulders that overpower the man, so puram conquest lends akam its language of love's assault.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a household is for caring for guests; Natrinai 41's friend says men suffer far off in the waste because they want the household where the wife cooks for a night guest.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes, in the friend's mouth, a reason for the separation itself: if the house exists for the guest, then the husband's absence earning for it is the rule at work, so the Kural's praise of hospitality is shown to carry the cost the wife bears in paalai.

note: Kural 1151, in Parimelazhagar's reading the friend's words: if you are not leaving tell me, your quick return tell those who will be alive. Natrinai 43: the friend tells the departing man his going is joy to him and ruin to her.
teaches: Both friends answer an announced departure by saying she will not survive it, but the poem adds the grounds the couplet leaves out: the man once said 'fear not', so his leaving is a broken pledge of protection, which explains why the couplet treats talk of a quick return as worthless.

note: Kural 1094: when I look she looks down, when I do not she looks and softly smiles. Natrinai 44: after bathing she gave him an unaimed look and a smile and went home, and now, confined, he asks his heart whether she knows.
teaches: The couplet treats the averted look and smile as a sign the man can read with confidence; the poem shows the same sign after the girl has been shut in, when there is no second meeting to confirm it, and the reading collapses into doubt, so the Kural's reading of hints depends on continued access to her.
audit_text_issue: Line 9 is a repaired reading.

note: Naladiyar 16: the fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the garland leaves at the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise. Natrinai 46: pleasure and youth pass like an arrow's shadow, so the man should not leave her for wealth.
teaches: The two start from the same premise, the speed with which youth passes, and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar says renounce its pleasure, the Sangam friend says spend it in love and despise wealth instead, which shows that impermanence was an argument both renouncers and lovers used, and settles nothing by itself.

note: Kural 333: wealth does not stay, so when you get it do at once what stays. Natrinai 46 calls the wealth the man leaves for மன்னாப் பொருள், wealth that does not last.
teaches: Both call wealth impermanent, but the Kural still tells a man to get it and convert it into lasting good, while the friend uses its impermanence to argue against going after it at all, which shows the couplet's maxim leaving room for the very journey the akam poem condemns.

note: Akananuru 242: with the man listening, the friend tells the girl the mother has called the velan, and the man should come and hold her before the goat is killed. Natrinai 47: with the man listening, the friend asks whether she may tell him that the mother's Murugu rite cannot help the girl's pallor.
teaches: In the same overheard situation the Akananuru friend names the cure outright while the Natrinai friend only asks whether she may speak and lets a bereaved elephant show the loss to come, so the pair shows how much directness the overheard speech allowed: the remedy stated, or the danger shown and the remedy left for him to supply.

note: Kural 508: one who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble without end. Natrinai 50: the friend failed to guard the girl because she trusted the man without seeing, taking his smallness for greatness.
teaches: The couplet is a rule for a king choosing men; the friend applies the same failure to herself in the household and names its cause, a public reputation (even his enemies admire him) taken in place of examination, so the pair shows the akam go-between bound by the same duty of testing the Kural lays on the king.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 50 flagged uncertain in sense

note: Akananuru 292: the girl, afraid of the veri rite, blames the hill lord, where a sling stone flung at an elephant scatters vengai blossom and lodges in a jackfruit. Natrinai 51: the girl, facing the veri rite, names the hill lord where a killer tusker broke the young jackfruit among vengai with strewn flowers.
teaches: Two poets give the girl facing the velan the same hill emblem, a blow among vengai blossom that strikes a jackfruit, which shows it was a stock figure for the harm the unmarried lover does and supports reading the broken young jackfruit of Natrinai 51 as a hidden comparison rather than scenery.

note: Purananuru 152: Ori, met as a hunter in the wilds, gives a strange troupe meat, toddy, gold and gems unasked. Natrinai 52: even wealth equal to the giving of Ori, lord of the Mazhavar, would be slight against his wife's embrace.
teaches: The puram poem shows Ori's giving as so lavish it reached strangers in the wilderness, and the akam poem takes exactly that giving as the upper limit of what a man could hope to gain and still sets it below love, so the pair shows a patron's fame serving akam poets as a fixed measure of wealth.

note: Kural 616: effort produces prosperity and its lack ushers in poverty. Natrinai 52: the heart set on ஆள்வினை is loveless, and wealth made by toil is a slight thing.
teaches: The Kural makes effort the source of fortune and the duty of a man; the husband of Natrinai 52 calls the heart that obeys that duty loveless and declares its fruit slight, so read together they show that the ethics of ஆள்வினை and the akam of the home make incompatible claims on the same man.

note: Kural 1102: medicine for a disease is something other than it, but for the sickness this woman gives, she herself is the cure. Natrinai 53: the mother prescribes the stream water from the lover's hill as medicine for the girl's shivering.
teaches: The couplet states as a paradox that the cause of love-sickness is its only cure; the poem shows the mother unknowingly obeying it, sending the girl to water that comes from the lover's own hill, and the friend reports it so that the man listening learns he is the medicine and must come to marry.

note: Kural 1226: she did not know evening brings sickness while he who wed her had not left. Natrinai 54: the small dull evening is deeply lonely, she tells a heron going home to its kin, and begs it to carry her plight to him.
teaches: The couplet says evening hurts only when he is gone; the poem shows why, through the heron that at evening flies home to its flock, so the hour that sends every creature to its kin is the hour that marks her lack, and her plea that the bird delay its homing for her is the couplet's sickness acted out.

note: Purananuru 108: in Pari's Parambu the firebrand a hill woman lights is sandalwood, its smoke reaching the vengai. Natrinai 55: the friend explains the bees on the girl by pointing to a burning sandalwood firebrand.
teaches: The puram poem records that hill households burned sandal as ordinary firewood, which is what makes the friend's lie in Natrinai 55 credible to the mother: the girl could smell of sandal from the hearth, so the trick depends on a fact of hill life the puram poet praises as the land's wealth.

note: Kural 1293: heart, do you follow him as you please because the ruined have no friends? Natrinai 56: has my heart stayed with him to return together, or has it seen my lost beauty and left me as a stranger?
teaches: The couplet gives only the bitter answer, that the heart deserts her as fair-weather friends desert the ruined; the poem holds that answer beside a kinder one, that the heart is loyally waiting with him, so the Kural's accusation is shown to be one horn of a doubt the woman cannot settle.
audit_text_issue: line 6 vowel sign restored; the poem breaks off at தலைமணந்த

note: Akananuru 2: a monkey drunk on fallen jackfruit wine sleeps content; the friend says if beasts find unplanned joy so easily, the hill lord's planned joy should not be hard. Natrinai 57: a monkey steals milk from a sleeping wild cow, and the friend ends on the coming harvest that will shut the girl in.
teaches: Both friends press the hill lord to marry with a monkey of his own slopes, but Akananuru 2 draws the moral aloud while Natrinai 57 leaves the monkey's seized moment unexplained beside the girl's closing one, so the pair shows the same urging done once by open comparison and once by hidden comparison.

note: Akananuru 34: the returning man bids his charioteer hurry past a stag that feeds and guards its doe. Natrinai 59: the returning man tells his charioteer of the land where a hunter comes home with his catch and revels at ease.
teaches: Both returning husbands read their own homecoming in a figure of the road, and the figures differ: the stag shows the care he will give, the hunter the ease he will take, so the pair shows the mullai homecoming imagined both as tending and as rest.

note: In Natrinai 80 the man says there is no medicine but the girl for his sickness; in Natrinai 64 the deserted woman says that even if he comes he is no medicine for her sickness.
teaches: Read together, the two poems show the anthology using one figure, the beloved as the only cure, at both ends of secret love: the pursuing man asserts it and the abandoned woman revokes it, so the claim holds only while hope does.

note: Both have the man say that the woman herself is the only cure for the sickness she causes; the Kural states it as a paradox of medicine, Natrinai 80 says it to his own heart so that the friend who keeps him off will hear.
teaches: The couplet's general paradox becomes in the older poem a lever in a negotiation: by declaring the girl his only medicine where her guardian can overhear, the rejected man turns a private conceit into a claim on the friend's pity.

note: In both the woman tells her friend that the man's departure must be stopped because union after he goes will be hard; Natrinai 79 rehearses the words she might say and asks by what means to stop him.
teaches: The Kural gives the friend a reason to act, while the Natrinai woman supplies the argument she would use, that rejoining after parting makes another parting harder, and then doubts any words will work; the poem shows the couplet's advice as a thing she has already tried in her head.

note: Both are the friend's speech to a man about to leave: Kural 1151 says tell me only if you are not going, and tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 71 grants the woman may let him go and asks whether he can stroke her eyes and leave.
teaches: The couplet argues from the woman's death, the Natrinai friend from the man's own tenderness at the moment of leave-taking, so the two show the dissuasion speech had two separate levers, her survival and his ability to bear the parting.

note: Natrinai 71 opens by calling wealth impermanent (மன்னாப் பொருள்) to keep the man at home; Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should do at once what lasts.
teaches: The same premise, that wealth does not last, yields opposite advice: the Kural tells a man to seek and spend it on what endures, the friend uses it to argue he should not seek it at all, which shows nilaiyaamai served the akam poets as a rhetorical weapon before it was a doctrine.

note: Both are the friend speaking to the woman while the man overhears, about the town's gossip; in Kural 1150 the gossip is welcome because it will push him to marry, in Natrinai 72 his anxiety about gossip is read as a sign his love is drying up.
teaches: In the same speech situation the friend can treat gossip as an ally or as a threat depending on how the man reacts to it, so the pair shows that alar works on the lover's resolve, not on the woman's name.

note: Both concern the woman's indifferent glance in early love: Kural 1099 says looking at each other like strangers is found only in lovers; in Natrinai 75 the rejected man says her glance that does not look has wounded him like a hunter's arrow.
teaches: The look the Kural's observer reads as proof of love is, to the man who receives it, a fatal wound, so the pair shows the same sign read from outside as a disguise and from inside as a refusal.

note: Both have the wife alone at evening hearing the cowherds' flutes; Kural 1228 calls the flute the messenger of evening and a killing weapon, Natrinai 69 sets the flutes and cow bells among the evening's signs and says that if such an evening came where he is, he could not stay at his work.
teaches: The couplet makes the evening's music a weapon only against her, while the Natrinai wife imagines it falling on him too and so excuses his absence by supposing his land has no such evenings, turning the same lament into a defence of his love.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is, since their own steadfastness is the best guard; in Natrinai 68 the friend says shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for the household.
teaches: Both reject confinement, but the Kural does so for the wife because her virtue makes it needless, while the Natrinai girls reject it for the unmarried daughter because it blocks a love headed for marriage, so the same verdict rests on opposite views of what the woman's will is for.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Malaiyan who rode Kaari and won great battles among the seven givers; in Natrinai 77 Kapilar likens the relief the girl's look once gave the lover to Malaiyan riding his horse into enemy land, breaking forts and breathing out his weariness.
teaches: The puram poem keeps Malaiyan as a rider and giver in a public roll, while the akam poem takes the same rider at the private moment after the raid, his sigh of relief, so akam used the king's fame for the feeling of a finished deed rather than for the deed.

note: Kural 1268 wishes the king victory so that the man may join his wife and keep an evening feast for guests; Natrinai 81 is that moment reached: the king has quelled the enemy and the man hurries home to a wife whose grief was her longing to host guests.
teaches: Held together they show that the soldier's picture of home was a feast for guests, voiced as a wish before victory in the Kural and as a race home after it in the Natrinai, which adds that the wife's sorrow was her inability to host alone, so hospitality is a couple's act that war suspends.

note: In Kural 1082 the man is struck by her answering look as by a goddess with an army; in Natrinai 82 the man says he cannot bear to look at her form, which strikes his eyes like Valli joined with Murugan.
teaches: The Kural puts the wound in her returned glance, the Natrinai in his own looking at her beauty, and only the Natrinai can name the goddess as the hill's own Valli, so the divine attack of the Kural's abstract couplet is, in the older poem, a local deity of the land where the love happens.

note: In Kuruntokai 153 the girl's heart, which once took fright when the hill owl hooted, now goes out through the dark night toward him; in Natrinai 83 the friend begs the owl at the town ghat not to sound its fearful cry while they wait awake for him.
teaches: The owl's cry is the standard measure of the night tryst's fear, and the pair shows it split between two roles: love has carried the girl's heart past that fear, while the friend, who manages the meeting, still has to buy the owl's silence with offerings.

note: Kural 81 says that all of keeping a home and guarding its goods is for caring for guests and doing good; Natrinai 84 says the man leaves his wife for the waste because he cannot live a home life that fails to relieve those who come begging.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the cost of the Kural's rule: if a household exists to give, a household without wealth fails its purpose, so the very ideal that defines home life is what sends the husband away from home and leaves the wife to grieve.

note: In Kuruntokai 21 the woman refuses to believe the konrai's sign of the rains because he does not lie; in Natrinai 86 the friend calls the men righteous because they came back before the season they had named.
teaches: The Kuruntokai woman's faith that he keeps his word is a wager, and the Natrinai shows the wager won, with the kept promise named as அறவர், virtue, so truthfulness about the season is what the akam poets count as a husband's righteousness.

note: In Natrinai 86 the friend reads the flowers of the late dew and early summer as true signs that the man came before his season; in Natrinai 99 she calls the rainy-season flowers foolish, blooming for a rain that is not the season, because he has not come.
teaches: Read together they show that the friend's reading of the season's signs follows the man's conduct, not the signs themselves: when he keeps time the flowers are witnesses, when he does not they are fools, so the season in akam is an argument made for the woman's sake.

note: In Kuruntokai 201 a bat that has eaten sweet mango gulps sour nelli and hangs from the bamboo, in a poem of good news that the hill lord will come; in Natrinai 87 a bat hanging asleep on a mango only dreams of the sour nelli of a far forest, and her day of longing passes like that dream.
teaches: The same bat, mango and sour nelli carry fulfilment or its absence according to whether the bat eats or only dreams, matching the good news of Kuruntokai 201 and the empty day of Natrinai 87, so the poets varied one fixed image by a single verb to change its sense.

note: Kural 620 says those who toil on without flagging see fate's back; in Natrinai 88 the friend tells the girl not to be stricken as though by their own old deeds but to rise, go and speak to the man.
teaches: The Kural states for the man of affairs that effort overturns fate, and the Natrinai shows the same refusal of fate in a girl's friend inside a secret love, where the effort is speech to the man, so the rule had a domestic use, and the friend's action is an answer to the household's fatalism.

note: Kural 1222 pities the sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) evening and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed (வன்கண்ணது) as hers; Natrinai 89 calls the evening sad (புன்கண் மாலை) but makes it the ally of the hard-hearted (வன்கணாளர்) who do not come. On this reading the evening is a fellow victim in one and an accomplice in the other.
teaches: The same two words, புன்கண் and வன்கண், are distributed differently: the Kural gives the evening its own hard partner and so makes it a sister in grief, while the Natrinai joins the evening to her own hard man, so the woman's view of the hour turns on whether she sees it as abandoned or as sent.

note: Both open with உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி, the friend asking whether the men who crossed the waste will not think of them; Kuruntokai 16 answers with a lizard calling to its mate, Natrinai 92 with a tusker winning water for its mate and calf.
teaches: The formula comes with its answer, a male creature caring for its mate on the road the man has taken, and the pair shows that answer sharpened: a lizard's call only reminds, while a tusker that provides and then moves on mirrors the man who left to provide, so the friend's comfort lies in the likeness.

note: Kural 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse; in Natrinai 94 the woman herself says that speaking out desire suits a man while womanhood makes her hold it in, and asks what kind of man he is not to know.
teaches: The Kural's praise of the woman's silence becomes in the Natrinai a grievance spoken by the woman under that rule, aimed at the man who is free to speak and does not, so the restraint the couplet admires is shown from inside as a constraint she resents.

note: Kural 1185 is built on the pointing words உவக்காண், இவக்காண்: look there, he goes; look here, the pallor spreads. Natrinai 96 points with இதுவே, உதுவே, அதுவே to the places where she met him, and ends on the pallor.
teaches: Both make pallor out of pointing, but the Kural points across the distance of a departure seen as it happens, while the Natrinai friend walks back through the places of meeting before an overhearing man, so pallor comes in one from the sight of leaving and in the other from memory of place, used to press for marriage.

note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend says the konrai is foolish to bloom for a stray rain before the promised season; in Natrinai 99 the friend, answering the woman's own question, says the cloud itself forgot itself and the pidavam, konrai and kodal bloomed because they are foolish.
teaches: The Natrinai takes the Kuruntokai's single foolish tree and widens the folly to the sky and to three flowers, and places it as the answer to the woman's doubt, so the consolation grows from a remark about one tree into a whole season declared mistaken.

note: Purananuru 123 makes chariot-giving Malaiyan's mark, chariots given sober outnumbering the raindrops on Mullur; Natrinai 100 names him only as தேர் வண் மலையன் and borrows his musicians' drum to measure a frightened husband's trembling.
teaches: The akam poet can name Malaiyan by the epithet the puram poems established and rely on his fame being known, and turns it to mockery: the drum of a great giver's festivals throbs for a man afraid of his wife, so puram glory serves akam as a scale for comic smallness.

note: Both are the man struck by the girl's look and both find a doe in it: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Natrinai 101 says the shore hamlet was sweet to live in before he saw her deer-like look.
teaches: The couplet says what the look contains, the doe beside Death; the Natrinai man shows what Death in it did, measuring the wound as the loss of his home's sweetness from the day he saw her.

note: In both the heroine sends the hill lord word that she has been set to guard the millet against parrots: in Kuruntokai 141 through the friend, with a warning not to come at midnight, in Natrinai 102 through a parrot itself.
teaches: The millet-guard message was a fixed kalavu signal meaning she can be met by day, and Natrinai turns the crop's enemy into its carrier, so the bird she is posted to chase becomes the go-between she bribes with the crop.

note: Both put a drought-starved animal couple on the man's road for wealth: in Akananuru 91 the friend cites the elephant shrinking beside his hungry mate to assure the wife of his love; in Natrinai 103 the man himself sees the male wild dog grieving for his starving mate.
teaches: The image the friend offers the wife as reassurance is the one the man meets as self-reproach on the road, so the pair shows the same iraicchi working from both ends of the separation, comfort at home and conscience in the waste.

note: Akananuru 91 says the man would not stay away even if he gained Kuttuvan's rich Kudanadu; in Natrinai 105 the man's heart, midway on the road, turns back to her hair, fragrant as the kuvalai of Kuttuvan's western hill.
teaches: What the friend in Akananuru 91 asserts from outside, that Kuttuvan's whole land would not hold him, Natrinai 105 shows from inside his heart, where Kuttuvan's country survives only as a measure of her fragrance.

note: Both have the woman's heart following the man who has left; Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for going after him, Natrinai 107 says the heart that went has the good share and she who stayed has the pain.
teaches: The same split between a heart that follows and a self left behind is judged in opposite ways: Valluvar's woman despises the following heart, the Natrinai woman envies it, because she is the one left to bear the town's gossip.

note: Both are the separated woman at evening in a pastoral scene: in Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; in Natrinai 109 she stands alone like a cow tied by the head in a dripping shed.
teaches: The pastoral evening gives the Kural woman a sound that attacks her and the Natrinai woman a posture she shares, so the mullai hour wounds in one from outside and in the other makes her one of its own tethered creatures.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife as one who lives within the means of the man who took her; Natrinai 110 shows a spoilt girl who once refused honeyed milk now eating only at alternate meals in her husband's poor house, refusing her rich father's food.
teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's rule costs and how strange it looks to her own family, who ask where she learned it, so living within his means appears as a change of person rather than a skill.

note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for the great food he gave at the war of the hundred and the five; Natrinai 113 likens the heroine's sob to the ambal pipe the musicians blow on the hushed field after Udhiyan's loud battle.
teaches: Where the praise poem remembers Udhiyan's war for its feeding of the armies, the love poet remembers its aftermath, the silent field and the mourning pipe, so akam took from the same king's fame the grief that puram praise leaves out.

note: Both paalai poems use Udhiyan Cheral's great occasions as similes: Akananuru 233 compares the crowded hills of the man's road to the ghouls gathered at Udhiyan's great feast; Natrinai 113 compares the left wife's sob to the pipe blown after Udhiyan's battle.
teaches: Held together they show akam poets dividing one king's famous scenes between the two halves of separation, his feast for the harsh road the man crosses and his battlefield's lament for the woman he leaves.

note: Both have the friend fearing the man's night path, where storms strike down snakes on the hill; Akananuru 182 tells him directly to come by day, Natrinai 114 speaks to the heroine within his hearing and adds the thunder-killed tusker and his grieving mate.
teaches: The pair shows the two routes of the same warning: the direct plea in Akananuru 182, and in Natrinai 114 the overheard speech that lets the friend show him, through the she-elephant, what his death would leave behind without telling him what to do.

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are men who would give their lives for fame; Natrinai 115 says the absent lover, of great love, would not stay away even for endless fame.
teaches: On one defensible reading the two rank the same goods in opposite order, puram putting fame above life and akam putting love above fame, so the friend's comfort works only by overturning the heroic scale the puram poem praises.

note: Both are the friend comforting the wife with the same formula, that the man has very great love (பெரும்பேர் அன்பினர், மிகப் பேர் அன்பினர்) and would not stay even if he gained something: Kuttuvan's land in Akananuru 91, endless fame in Natrinai 115.
teaches: The comfort is a fixed frame whose slot each poet fills with the highest prize of the puram world, land in one and fame in the other, so the formula is a measure of love against the goods of war.

note: Both are the deserted woman facing the town's gossip: in Kural 1149 she asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her; in Natrinai 116 the bond has burst like a fallen jackfruit yet the women still keep up their talk of her.
teaches: In the Kural his leaving cancels the shame of the gossip, while in Natrinai the gossip outlives the bond it was about, so the pair shows two answers to the same abandonment: indifference to talk or bearing talk about a love that is already gone.

note: Both are the woman's love-sickness at evening in separation: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds at morning, grows through the day and blooms at evening; Natrinai 117 sets her evening on the shore, where the neythal closes and birds go home together while he does not think of her.
teaches: Set beside the shore's evening, where the neythal shuts, the couplet's sickness that blooms at evening reads as the one flower that opens when the others close, and the poem supplies the scene the couplet compresses into a single growth.

note: Kural 90 says a guest withers when the host's face changes; in Natrinai 120 the man brings a guest into the house because his sulking wife will not show an angry face to a guest and he will see her smile.
teaches: The rule of the welcoming face that the Kural lays on the host becomes, in the poem, the husband's lever against the wife's sulk, so the guest is both the object of hospitality and the akam go-between (வாயில்) that ends an oodal.

note: Kural 1268 has the man wish that the king fight and win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer reports that the king has let them go and drives him home to the wife preparing the evening feast for guests.
teaches: The couplet is a wish spoken while the war still holds him, the Natrinai poem the same wish granted and on the road, so together they show the full arc of the mullai return, and that the king's release and the evening guest-feast were the fixed terms of it.

note: In both a man returning from work passes a deer pair: in Akananuru 34 he himself sees the stag feed and guard his doe and urges the charioteer on; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer points to the doe resting with her stag to calm him.
teaches: The same deer pair works as a spur when the hero reads it and as a sedative when the charioteer offers it, so the mullai image carries a promise of home whose force depends on who in the chariot speaks.

note: In Kural 1155 the woman asks her friend, if she would guard her, to stop the man's departure; in Natrinai 124 the friend does exactly that, telling the man not to go and pointing to the season.
teaches: The Kural gives only the request, while the Natrinai shows the friend carrying it out, adding the rainy-season argument and the anril image, so the couplet's appeal is revealed as the opening move of a known scene in which the friend speaks for the woman to the man.

note: Naladiyar 16 says the fleeting pleasures of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling its garland, are not found among the wise; Natrinai 126 says no wealth surpasses youth and that love must be taken in youth because wealth cannot buy it later.
teaches: Both start from the shortness of youth and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar to refuse youth's pleasure, the Natrinai hero to refuse wealth for its sake, so the same premise of impermanence served the akam poets as an argument for love and the didactic poets as one against it.

note: Both are poems in which the hero stops his heart from leaving; 126 argues that youth is worth more than wealth, 137 sets before the heart the tusker who breaks a tree to feed his mate in the drought.
teaches: The same thurai (செலவு அழுங்குதல்) is won once by reasoning and once by an animal example from the very road to be travelled, so the anthology shows two ways a hero could argue himself out of leaving: a calculation of value, or the shame of being harder than a beast.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 129 mocks as a great joke the man who says he will go and that we will live on at home until he returns.
teaches: Both turn the man's promise of return into a question of whether she will survive to see it, but the Natrinai supplies what the couplet leaves out, the midnight thunder she must hear alone, so the Kural's bitter one-liner has behind it a scene in which the waiting itself is the threat.

note: Kural 1168 has the sleepless woman say the night, which puts all creatures to sleep, has only her for company; Natrinai 132 begins with the great town asleep but fills the house with the cold wind, a trembling dog, guards by the bed and watchmen ringing the bell.
teaches: The couplet's solitude of the one waker is qualified by a poem in which others do wake, but only to keep her in, so the sleepless night of the guarded girl is not loneliness but confinement.

note: In Kural 1236 the woman, bangles slipping, is hurt when her friend calls the man cruel; in Natrinai 133, with the same slipping bangles, the friend says he will not cause them suffering, and the word gives the woman a little relief.
teaches: Held together they show the friend's two possible speeches and the woman's response to each, blame wounds her and defence of him comforts her, yet the Natrinai measures that comfort as a smith's sprinkle on a furnace, small and passing.

note: Kural 1157 says the bangles slipping past the wrist spread the news that the lord of the shore has left; in Natrinai 136 the father fits the girl with golden bangles that cannot slip, which hide the blame of her shoulders.
teaches: If, as the Kural says, slipping bangles are the body's gossip, the Natrinai shows that gossip could be silenced by a tight bangle, so the sign of separation was something a household could conceal, though only the lover could cure what it signified.

note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on only one day yet the gossip spread like the eclipse; Natrinai 138 says that their meeting at the ford was once known only to their eyes and asks whether the whole festive town does not know it today.
teaches: The Kural compresses into an eclipse the leap from one private sight to public talk that the Natrinai spreads over a remembered garland and a dancing town, and the Natrinai's overhearing hero shows the complaint was spoken to push him toward marriage.

note: Kural 211 asks what the world can give back to the rain, whose obligation seeks no return; in Natrinai 139 the hero blesses the rain cloud as his helper for the night rain that fell while he lay with his wife.
teaches: The Kural's rain serves the world and gets nothing back, while the Natrinai hero answers its private help with a blessing, so the poem shows the one return a person could make to the rain and turns the rain's public good into a favour done to two people.

note: In Kural 1102 the man says every disease has a cure other than itself, but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Natrinai 140 the refused man tells his heart there is no other medicine for the sickness he has.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox from the side of a man already united with her, the Natrinai from the side of a man refused, so the same claim that she alone is the cure is a joke in fulfilment and a sentence of endless pursuit in refusal.

note: In 122 the friend warns that the millet will be guarded and the mother frowns on the girl's secret doings; in 134 the mother herself sends the girl to drive parrots from the millet on the hill where the lover set his sign.
teaches: Millet-guarding is both the cover and the clock of the secret love: the same parental order that sends the girl to the field makes the meeting possible, and its ending, which 122 foresees, closes it, so the hill harvest sets the term within which the man must marry.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 134 line 6 differs strongly from sangamtamil.com; the poem is marked uncertain.

note: In Akananuru 91 the friend comforts the waiting woman with the elephant who in the drought shrinks together with his hungry mate; in Natrinai 137 the hero shames his own heart with the tusker who breaks an omai tree to feed his young mate.
teaches: The drought elephant that keeps faith with its mate is used by the friend to assure the woman that the man still loves her and by the man to accuse himself of leaving, so the image's single sense, even beasts do not desert their mates, could be turned to comfort or to reproach.

note: Both compare a woman's hair to the bright ripples (அறல்) of a named river: the Arisil by Killi's Ambar in Natrinai 141, the forest stream north of Vaanan's Sirukudi in Akananuru 117.
teaches: The one simile marks the two ends of the girl's story: in Natrinai 141 the river-dark hair is what keeps the lover from leaving her, and in Akananuru 117 it is the mother's last picture of the daughter who left with him, dressed now by his hands.

note: Kural 84: the goddess of fortune dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face. Natrinai 142 sets the wife who rejoices at a guest even at night in a woodland of unfailing plenty (பொய்யா யாணர்).
teaches: The poem gives the couplet's householder a face and a hour: the glad host is the waiting wife, her welcome extends even to guests who arrive after dark, and the plenty the Kural promises is already the landscape the returning husband drives through.

note: Akananuru 165: onlookers see the mother after the elopement rest under the nochchi the girl touched and embrace her doll. Natrinai 143: the mother herself weeps at the playmates and the nochchi and confesses she noticed the scent of the girl's hair and said nothing.
teaches: Held together, the two give the mother's grief from outside and from inside: what onlookers see as pure loss, her own words show to include guilt, since she read the signs in the girl's hair, heard the gossip, and chose silence.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother asks whether the hair she once combed and the girl would not let her wash now falls loose, dressed with her lover's flowers; in Natrinai 143 the mother recalls telling the girl her hair smelled fragrant.
teaches: Both mothers read the daughter's love in her hair, one before the flight and one after: the fragrance the mother let pass in Natrinai 143 is the lover's flowers that Akananuru 117 imagines on the road, so the hair is the household's evidence of a bond it could see but not stop.

note: Kuruntokai 17: when love hardens, men ride the palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as flowers and are jeered in the street. Natrinai 146 addresses such a rider in his erukku chaplet and promises that kind people will gather and offer him shade like a just king's umbrella.
teaches: The street that mocks the madal rider in Kuruntokai 17 is also the street that pities him in Natrinai 146; set side by side they show that the ride works by public feeling, ridicule and compassion together, which is what presses the girl's people to yield.

note: In Akananuru 28 the friend warns that if the girl will not scare the parrots her mother will send others to guard the millet and the lover will be out of reach. In Natrinai 147 the parrots have taken the millet, the mother questions her, her denial gives her away, and her going to the field is over.
teaches: The two friends' speeches are the before and after of one plot: the warning of Akananuru 28 comes true in Natrinai 147, and the second poem shows how, through the girl's own guilty denial rather than through the parrots.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 148 ends, after the man has gone for his work, with 'I will not grieve, friend; may his journey prosper'.
teaches: On the same departure for work the two voices take incompatible stands, the couplet refusing all comfort as if the going were a death, the poem blessing the journey; the iraicchi of the tiger hunting for its mate shows how the friend's comfort turns the one stance into the other.

note: Kural 1147: the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness. In Natrinai 149 the street women spread the gossip, the mother beats the girl with a cane, and she resolves to leave with the shore lord.
teaches: The couplet says that gossip and the mother's scolding feed the love they mean to kill; the poem shows what that fed love finally does, turning the same two pressures, the street's finger at the nose and the mother's cane, into the reason for elopement.

note: Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, helpless evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is false. Natrinai 152's lover tells the hours exactly: the sun as it dims gave him loneliness, and the night with the andril's call gave him helplessness.
teaches: On one reading the claims are incompatible: Kuruntokai 32 makes losing track of the hours the proof of true love, while Natrinai 152 gives a lover whose love is real precisely because each hour is known by its own fresh pain, so knowing the clock is no sign of coolness.

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the palmyra horse that lovers ride. Natrinai 152: love gave him the madal, the erukku gave him gossip, the sun gave loneliness, night gave helplessness.
teaches: The couplet records one exchange, virtues lost for a madal; the poem turns it into a chain of gifts in which each thing hands on the next harm, so the madal is not the end of the loss but the first link of a day-long sequence.

note: Kural 338: the bond of body and life is like a bird that flies off leaving its nest alone. Natrinai 153: her heart has gone after him and her body, left behind, lives on by eating, like the lone man guarding a ruined town.
teaches: The poem shows the couplet's departure without the death: the heart flies off as the life does in the Kural, yet the body stays, sustained only to keep watch over its own emptiness, so separation in love is a death the body is made to outlive.

note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman. Natrinai 155: at their second meeting he asks her aloud whether she is the goddess of the sea or of the backwater, and she answers with a smile and tears.
teaches: The couplet leaves the man's doubt as a question in his head; the poem puts the same question to the girl and lets her answer it, since a smile and tears are a woman's reply, not a goddess's, so the doubt is settled by her response.

note: In Akananuru 118 the friend fears gossip if the hero comes by day and fears the tiger still more if he comes alone at midnight, and says the girl has stopped the millet songs. In Natrinai 156 the friend refuses the night tryst and asks him to come by day, since they will guard the millet for many days.
teaches: The two friends weigh the same choice of day or night and decide it by the millet: while the girls still guard the field, as in Natrinai 156, the day offers a safe meeting place, and once the guarding has stopped, as in Akananuru 118, day and night are both closed and only marriage is left.

note: In Kuruntokai 14 the man wishes that once he wins the girl the town would know it and many in the street would call him the good woman's husband. In Natrinai 159 the friend asks him to let his chariot lodge in the fishing hamlet so that it wakes in uproar.
teaches: Both treat the town's knowing as the way to marriage, but from opposite sides: the man in Kuruntokai 14 wishes for it after winning her, while the friend in Natrinai 159 demands it now as the means of winning her, using the hamlet's noise as pressure.

note: Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking friends it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread like butter melting on a hot rock. Natrinai 160: he tells his rebuker that he knew good sense, shame and conduct better than him, before he saw her eyes.
teaches: These are two answers to the same rebuke: one grants that the friends' aim is good and says no one can carry it out, the other says the friend's lesson is one he already knew best, so together they show the rebuke fails not for lack of knowledge but because sight of her has overridden it.

note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the madal. Natrinai 160: shame, decency and good conduct he knew better than his friend, before he saw her.
teaches: The couplet says the virtues were possessed and are now gone; the poem says they are still known, better than the rebuker knows them, and simply no longer govern him, so love takes away their rule, not the knowledge of them.

note: Both returning men, speaking to the charioteer, picture the wife with the same words, the freckle-waisted woman who deceives their son (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும், திதலை அல்குல்); Akananuru 54 fills it with her promising the moon milk for a gold tali, Natrinai 161 with her pointing out strangers to the boy.
teaches: The shared phrase shows that soothing the son with a fiction was a fixed mullai picture of the home a returning man imagines, and the two fillings show where the poet's freedom lay: in choosing the fiction, a coaxed moon or a stranger passed off as the father.

note: Both men are going home with the task done; in 161 he wonders whether the omen birds have already told her, in 169 he speaks to the house lizard and asks it to chirp for her.
teaches: Together they show the returning husband imagining the omen from her side and then trying to work it from his own, so the signs she watches for become signs he wishes he could send.

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; in Natrinai 166 a husband says that seeing his wife he is like those settled in virtue, and gives that and his son's first play as reasons he will not leave.
teaches: The poem shows the Kural's claim used as an argument against the paalai journey: a husband offers the household's settled virtue as his answer to the pull of wealth abroad, which makes the maxim a reason to stay.

note: In Akananuru 66 the sight of his small son stops a husband on his way to a second wedding; in Natrinai 166 the husband himself names his son's first games as one reason he will not leave.
teaches: Read together, the son is the akam poets' anchor of the husband to the house, named by the man himself in 166 and working against his intent in 66, so in both the wife's fear is answered by the child rather than by her own claim on him.

note: Purananuru 127 praises Aay, whose bards led away his elephants and whose palace stood bare from giving; Natrinai 167 makes the rattle of the chariots bards won at Aay's feast the sound of a heron's cry on the shore of the man whose bard the friend turns away.
teaches: The pairing shows an akam friend borrowing Aay's puram fame as the measure of a generous patron, so the bard who in puram goes home rich is in akam the go-between sent home empty: one profession seen from the giver's hall and from the wronged wife's door.

note: In Akananuru 72 the girl says the man who came through the midnight rain with only a spear for company (எஃகு துணையாக) is not cruel and the fault is hers; in Natrinai 168 the friend asks the man who comes at midnight with his spear for company (எஃகு துணை ஆக) whether that can be called good conduct. The same act is blameless in one and a failure of conduct in the other.
teaches: The same lone midnight journey is innocent to the girl and faulty to the friend, which shows the night tryst was judged by who spoke: the girl takes the blame on herself, while the friend's charge is her lever toward marriage.

note: In Akananuru 351 the returning man pictures the lizard chirping at her ear as she worships the omen birds; in Natrinai 169 he speaks to the lizard on the long wall and asks whether it will chirp to end her worry.
teaches: Together they show the house lizard as an oracle both ends of the separation rely on: she listens for it at home, and he, on the road, begs it to speak for him.

note: Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan for chariots given more freely than the raindrops on the peak of Mullur; Natrinai 170 recalls Malaiyan's single spear routing the many Aryans at Mullur, as the image of wives helpless before one rival.
teaches: Held together they show a chieftain's fame had two faces, giving and lone valour, and the akam poet chose the war face because the household's problem was one woman beating many: akam borrowed from puram exactly the facet its situation needed.

note: In Akananuru 388 the girl would ask the mother's velan whether his god goes hunting on a deer's track with a bloody arrow; in Natrinai 173 the friend asks whether saying that the hill lord caused the sickness would wrong Murugan.
teaches: Both turn the veri rite's diagnosis against itself by slipping the real cause, the hill man, into a question about the god, which shows that disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிலை) had a recognised form: a mock-pious question put within the lover's hearing.

note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her man's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 174 the wife, told she should be well now that he is back and never leaves her side, says he gave his chest to another woman and an embrace is worth nothing without love.
teaches: The Kural grounds the refusal in shared possession; the poem grounds it in absent love even when he is wholly present, so the pair separates two grievances the oodal chapters run together: that he is shared, and that he is there without love.
audit_text_issue: natrinai 174.9 'வீழாக் கொள்கை வீழ்ந்த கொண்டி' is compressed and uncertain

note: Kural 1147 says love's sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Natrinai 175 shows a mother who has never met the man, believing the hamlet women's petty talk, glaring at the girl's pale body at midnight.
teaches: The poem supplies the order the couplet only implies: the gossip reaches the mother first and her watch follows from it, so she acts on hearsay about a man she does not know, which is why her words feed the sickness instead of curing it.

note: Kural 1276: the woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking hold the hardship to come and the thought of his lack of love; in Natrinai 177 the girl tells her friend she reads his going in his being more tender than before, along with his spear wiped and his shield decked.
teaches: The couplet names one sign, excess tenderness; the poem shows it read together with the readied weapons, so the Kural's inference is the abstract of a scene in which caress and war gear together give the man away.

note: In Akananuru 17 the foster mother remembers her girl tiring at a little ball play and lying in her arms, and asks whether those feet can walk the waste; in Natrinai 179 the nurse recalls the girl sobbing and refusing milk over a creeper the cow ate, and hears she has crossed the waste smiling.
teaches: Both measure the elopement by remembered childish frailty, but 179 ends on the girl's smile, so the pair shows the nurse's lament with two endings: fear for a frail child in 17, and in 179 bewilderment that a child who wept at a small loss left without grief.

note: Both use the punnai felled in the war of Anni and Thithiyan as a simile: in Akananuru 145 the foster mother wishes on her own hand the ruin of that tree; in Natrinai 180 the friend fears she will be ruined like it in the quarrel of husband and wife.
teaches: Read together, the felled guardian tree was a stock figure of ruin, and 180 draws from it what 145 does not need, the tree's innocence: it is the bystander destroyed because two powers fought over it, which is the go-between's place in a marriage quarrel.

note: Both men measure the girl by a divine figure on Kolli: in 185 the figure-like girl has plotted his death; in 192 thinking of her figure-like beauty makes the beast-haunted path safe.
teaches: Read together, the Kolli image proves double-edged: the same god-made beauty is a killing power when the girl or her friend refuses him and a protecting charm when she fears for him, so its force depends on which way her favour runs.

note: The figure painted by a god on the western face of Porayan's Kolli measures the girl in both; in the Kuruntokai the friend uses it, in Natrinai 185 the lover.
teaches: The friend uses the Kolli figure to plead that so innocent a girl can bring no harm to the town, while the lover uses the same figure to say she is killing him; the shared image shows the figure stood for a beauty both harmless in itself and dangerous to the one who sees it.

note: Both compare the girl's beauty to Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan: Natrinai 190 at its height, which the lover's heart rejoiced in; Kuruntokai 258 as it wastes under gossip.
teaches: Held together, the two poems use Azhisi's rich town as a fixed standard of the girl's beauty and show both ends of it, the lover's delight and the friend's report of its ruin, so that one patron's town served the poets as a measure of beauty gained and lost.

note: The neythal of Thondi stands for the girl's eyes in both: in 195 the flower cut by reapers tossing in water, in Akananuru 290 the flower whose sapphire beauty has turned to gold.
teaches: The pair shows that Thondi's neythal was a set measure for the beloved's eyes, and that two poets spoiled it in two ways: by tears, the cut flower tossing in water, and by pallor, the blue turned to gold.

note: In both the separated woman speaks to the moon about the man who is gone: the Kural asks it not to set so she may see him; Natrinai 196 asks it to show where he hides.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one blessing and plea a scene the Natrinai poem argues at length: the moon sees all worlds, so its silence is a witness's lie and its waning the punishment, which shows how much reasoning lies behind the Kural's single request.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 196 is marked uncertain.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother says the girl did not think of the nochchi or her playmates when she left; in Natrinai 184 the mother cannot bear to see the nochchi and the terrace where the girl played.
teaches: The pair shows the same household shrub on both sides of the elopement: forgotten by the daughter who has gone, and unbearable to the mother who stays, so the left-behind play things measure how unequal the parting is.

note: Kural 212 says wealth earned by effort exists to do good to the worthy; in Natrinai 186 the wife says her husband crossed the waste for wealth with a heart that strives for others.
teaches: The wife in the poem defends a painful separation with the Kural's ethic of earning in order to give, so the household rule appears here as the reason that made the paalai journey honourable in her eyes.

note: Kural 211: duty seeks no return, and the world makes none to the rain. Natrinai 194: the friend asks what return (கைம்மாறு) they can make to the elephant and the parrot.
teaches: The friend applies the Kural's word for repayment to beasts who helped without meaning to, the parrot that raided the millet and so kept the girls in the field, so her mock gratitude turns the rule of unrepayable benefit into a teasing way of announcing that the meetings are over.

note: Both poems call on the potter of the town: Purananuru 228 to make the burial urn for a dead Chola king; Natrinai 200 as the crier who proclaims festivals, asked to proclaim the bard a liar.
teaches: Taken together, the potter appears as the town's public servant for both its funerals and its festivals, and the friend's commission parodies the solemn address to him by making the crier's voice carry a domestic quarrel.

note: Both use the same formula line (செவ் வேர்ப் பலவின் பயம் கெழு கொல்லி) and the god-made image on Kolli that does not decay: in Natrinai 201 the man says the girl stays in his heart like that image under storm and earthquake; in Akananuru 209 the friend says the absent man cannot forget her beauty, which is like that image.
teaches: The Kolli image lends its one property, that it does not perish, to the lover's memory in one poem and to the woman's beauty in the other, and both times it answers a doubter (the rebuking companion, the weeping girl), so the image worked as a stock guarantee that a bond will last.

note: Both are elopement poems that see the flowering trees of the wasteland as the lamps of a town festival: kongam like Karthigai lamps in Natrinai 202, silk-cotton like a festive town's oil lamps in Akananuru 17.
teaches: The eloping man offers the festival-lit forest to the girl as something homely and beautiful, while the foster mother left behind sees the same lights on a waterless road her girl's little feet must cross, so one image of the paalai road comforts or terrifies according to who speaks.

note: In both the friend, with the man listening, reads the mother's look at harvest time: in Akananuru 302 the mother keeps the girl home and stares at her body; in Natrinai 206 the father sends her to guard the millet while the mother wishes the wedding vengai would flower and looks at her face.
teaches: Together the two show the ripe millet as the moment when the parents read their daughter either as a field guard or as a bride, and the friend in both turns the mother's silent look into the deadline that should make the listening man ask for marriage.

note: In Natrinai 208 the friend says the great rain's voice seems to seek out parted lovers and bring them home; in Natrinai 214 the woman hears the rain's voice as flashing and roaring in mockery of her grief, because he has not come.
teaches: The monsoon thunder is the same sign of the promised season in both, but the friend before the parting reads it as a power that fetches the man and the wife after the deadline reads it as a jeer, so the rain's meaning in paalai depends on whether the promise is still ahead or already broken.

note: Natrinai 210 defines the wealth of the worthy as gentleness that fears the distress of those who depend on one; in Natrinai 214 the man leaves his wife, whose bangles slip from grief, to win wealth because fame, pleasure and giving need it.
teaches: By 210's definition the departing man of 214 is pursuing the wrong wealth, since the distress of a dependant is exactly what true wealth fears to cause, so the anthology holds the akam parting for wealth and a moral critique of it side by side.

note: Natrinai 210 says grand speech and harsh riding are not wealth, only the fruit of deeds, and the wealth of the worthy is a gentle-eyed nature; Kural 241 says the wealth of grace is the wealth of wealths, since the base also hold goods.
teaches: The friend aims the Kural's general ranking of wealths at a particular rich husband who has hurt his wife, and narrows grace to fear of the dependant's distress, so the maxim is shown at work as a rebuke inside a marriage.

note: Kural 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute and lute sweet; in Natrinai 212 the bards tune their strings on the road while at home the child's sweet voice asking to be held made the mother anxious each time.
teaches: The child's voice that the Kural ranks above music becomes, while the father is away, a reminder of his absence, so the couplet's household joy assumes the father is present to hear it.

note: Kural 613 says the pride of generosity rests on effort; the man of Natrinai 214 leaves saying fame, pleasure and giving do not come to those who sit idle.
teaches: The akam poem shows the Kural's rule as a departing husband's stock reason, quoted by the wife he leaves and then mocked by the thunder, so the maxim that giving needs effort was already common speech, and the poem counts what it costs the one left behind.

note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress at once, like the hand of one whose garment slips; the other woman of Natrinai 216 says her lovers do not help her sorrow as the hand helps a hurt eye, yet the town they live in is still sweet.
teaches: The parathai admits her lovers fail the Kural's test of friendship, the hand's unthinking help, and still finds their mere presence in town enough, so the pair shows love surviving a failure that by the Kural's measure would end a friendship.

note: In Kural 1260 the woman says those whose hearts melt like fat in fire cannot say they will join and then hold out in a sulk; in Natrinai 217 the wife says that though the man is very sweet she will brood and sulk, since making him feel it drives off her loneliness.
teaches: The Kural woman doubts that a loving heart can keep a sulk, while the Natrinai wife resolves to keep one precisely because she loves him and wants the long loneliness to end, so the two disagree on whether the sulk is weakness overcome or a strategy of love.

note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; in Natrinai 218 the girl, past the promised season, lists the evening's creatures, the bats going home, the cock calling his mate, the owl, and asks if she must hear the andril alone.
teaches: The Kural woman makes evening a fellow sufferer, while the Natrinai girl finds every creature of the evening paired or going home, so the same projection onto nightfall can give companionship or prove isolation, and the unmarried girl gets only the second.

note: In Kural 1188 the woman says people speak of her pallor but none says he left her; in Natrinai 219 the girl says she will not blame him though pallor spreads and she dies, since he and she joined of their own accord.
teaches: The Kural woman complains that blame falls on her skin and not on him, while the Natrinai girl takes the pallor as her own because the union was her own choice, so the pair shows how a self-chosen secret union changes who can be blamed for the suffering.

note: Kuruntokai 17 says men whose love hardens ride a palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as a garland and become a spectacle in the street; in Natrinai 220 small boys with erukku garlands and a horse that does not eat roam the street with the man.
teaches: Kuruntokai 17 states the madal as a lover's desperate public act, and Natrinai 220 shows children copying its very costume as a street game, so the madal was familiar enough to be play, and the lover uses the children's ease against the adults' censure.

note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting (ஒப்புரவு) lives and others are counted among the dead; in Natrinai 220 the lover says the townspeople, if they knew ஒப்புரவு, would side with him and tell him not to be a stranger to the girl.
teaches: The lover appeals to the Kural's civic duty of fellow-feeling to claim the town's support for a love match it is condemning, so the pair shows ஒப்புரவு invoked against the town's own idea of propriety.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win, and let me join my home and keep the evening feast. Natrinai 221: the work done, the man bids the charioteer hurry to the wife who loves to host guests and the son who now calls him.
teaches: The Kural states the soldier's wish to trade the king's war for the evening feast at home in two lines; the Natrinai scene fills that home with a hospitable wife and a child just learning to walk and call him father, so the 'feast' of the couplet is shown to be a whole household's welcome, not only the wife's.

note: Akananuru 374: campaign over, the man bids the chariot go through the morning rains so the slender wife may receive him as a guest. Natrinai 221: the man bids the charioteer go so he may hear his small son's first call to him.
teaches: Both homecoming speeches to the charioteer turn on விருந்து, but the Akananuru makes the returning husband the guest his wife receives, while the Natrinai makes the wife the one who loves receiving guests and adds the son, so the convention could place the hero either as guest or as master of a hospitable house.

note: Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word? Natrinai 224: what can I say now to those who assured me 'we will not part' and set off for the waste?
teaches: The Kural poses as a moral question who is at fault when an assurance is broken; the Natrinai woman, using the same verb of assuring (தெளித்த), cannot even ask it aloud and lets the budding kuravu and the koel's 'stay joined' do the accusing, so the broken word is judged by the season instead of by her.

note: Purananuru 184: a king who takes his due like an elephant fed balls of paddy keeps the land rich, but one who grabs is like an elephant loosed in the field. Natrinai 226: kings do not take gold that ruins the land's wealth, yet her lover does not know the measure of the wealth he seeks.
teaches: The counsel that a king must take tribute without ruining its source had become a proverb a wife could quote, and Natrinai 226 turns it on the household: a husband who leaves to make wealth regardless of her life is the elephant loose in the field.

note: Kuruntokai 258: the friend says talk has risen on seeing the beauty, like Azhisi's Arkkadu, of this girl wasting. Natrinai 227: the friend says the man's grace has become talk as loud as the streets of the Cholas' Arkkadu.
teaches: In two speeches of the same kind, a friend telling the man that gossip has risen, the one town Arkkadu stands once for the girl's endangered beauty and once for the noise of the gossip itself, so a famous town was a measure akam poets could set against either side of the alar.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 229: so go, finish the work, but do not linger, for the north wind has come.
teaches: Faced with the same announcement of departure, the Kural's speaker refuses any promise of a quick return as useless to the dying, while the Natrinai friend bargains for exactly that promise and binds it to a season already arrived, so two stances to a leaving husband stand side by side: refusal by death, and consent with a deadline.

note: Purananuru 133: go and see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain. Natrinai 237: the rain clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered for suppliants.
teaches: The puram poet likens Ay's giving to rain, and the akam poet turns it round and likens the rain clouds to Ay's gift elephants, so the patron's bounty and the monsoon were interchangeable images and the friend can offer the season as a promise as sure as a great giver's word.

note: Kar Narpathu 12: his coming is certain; every day the dark clouds, like elephants anointed with oil, rise on the right. Natrinai 237: look, the clouds rise like the elephants Andiran gathered.
teaches: Both friends point a pining woman to clouds that rise like elephants as proof of the season's return, but Kar Narpathu's anointed elephants and the rising on the right make the cloud an omen, while Natrinai's patron's elephants make it a gift laid up for those who wait, so the same image could reassure by augury or by the ethic of giving.

note: Kuruntokai 158: the woman asks the storm cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes on the slopes and can shake the Himalaya, whether it has no pity for women without a companion. Natrinai 238: the woman tells the season's cloud that its coming is not like the noble, and its thunder that dulls the snakes' hoods is not sweet even to a hard heart.
teaches: Both women rebuke the thundering cloud of the season, but the Kuruntokai shames it by its might, while the Natrinai holds it to the conduct of the noble (சான்றோர்), so the reproach to the absent man is voiced in one through power misused and in the other through manners breached.

note: Kural 1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that not even a breeze can part. Natrinai 240: even the closest embrace is such that sleep comes between, yet the forest road stands like a mountain.
teaches: The Kural makes the gapless embrace the ideal of union; the Natrinai lover admits that even such an embrace is parted by sleep, and that admission is what lets his heart argue for leaving, so the ideal of perfect closeness becomes, in the man's mouth, a reason that union is already imperfect.

note: Both open with the same words, உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி: in Kuruntokai 16 the woman pictures the kalli waste he crossed, a lizard calling its mate with a sound like thieves testing arrows; in Natrinai 241 she pictures her own surroundings, the reed flowering in the north wind and the dewy midnight.
teaches: Read together, the formula question can be answered from either end of the separation, the dangers of his road or the season at her door, so 'do they not think of us' is a frame into which the poet sets whichever world the woman imagines, and the choice of world is the poem's real statement.

note: Kural 754 says wealth rightly gained yields virtue and pleasure, placing wealth below and in service of aram; Natrinai 243's woman says that if parting for wealth in such a season is men's nature, wealth must be dearer than aram itself. On the plain reading men's conduct, as she sees it, contradicts the Kural's ordering.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's ordering of virtue over wealth being turned into an accusation from inside the household: the woman accepts the scale but finds that men's going inverts it, so the ethical rule became a weapon in the akam speaker's mouth.

note: The same question, யாரையோ, is asked in both: in 245 the shore lord, struck at first sight, asks the girl 'who are you?'; in 250 the wife, estranged, asks her husband 'who are you?' as he comes to embrace their son.
teaches: Holding the two together traces the question across the whole course of akam love, from the wonder of a stranger at first meeting to a wife's pretended non-recognition in sulking, so the same words that began the bond are later used to deny it.

note: In Natrinai 246 the friend reassures the woman with a lizard chirping on the lucky side, a koel on the house's nochchi and the season's flowers; in Kar Narpathu 12 she calls his coming certain because the dark clouds rise every day on the right.
teaches: The pair shows that the friend's reassurance in the rains rested on reading omens, the right side being lucky in both, and that the rainy season itself was read as one more omen of return, which is why Natrinai 246 can end its certainty as a question.

note: Kural 1102 has the man say that this jewelled girl is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes; Natrinai 247's friend tells the man that for the girl's pallor there is no medicine other than him.
teaches: Read together, the cure that is also the cause belongs to both lovers, and the Natrinai shows the claim used as pressure: what the man says of her in delight, the friend turns back on him as an argument that only marriage can treat the girl's sickness.

note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking untimely rain for the season the man named; in Natrinai 248 she calls the thunder false and refuses to be fooled like the young peafowl who dance at it.
teaches: The pair shows a fixed move of the friend's, denying the season by calling some creature of the land deceived, and in Natrinai 248 the move turns inward, since she speaks of herself as the one who will not be fooled, so the device is an argument about belief, not about weather.

note: In Kar Narpathu 1 the friend says that with the sky roaring and pouring, the man who said 'we will come' can hardly fail to come now; in Natrinai 248 the friend says the same roar is false thunder and not the promised season. On the plain reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what the rain shows.
teaches: Set side by side, the same evidence serves the friend either way: when the season must mean his return she affirms it, and when his absence would make him a liar she denies it, so the season's sign was something the friend argued about rather than read off.

note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan secretly embracing her son in the chariot street; in Natrinai 250 the husband goes to embrace the son in the street and the wife, taking it otherwise, shies away.
teaches: Read together, the small son in the street is where the marriage's suspicions are read from both sides, another woman betraying herself by loving him and the husband being refused because of what his embrace carries, so the child who should join the parents becomes the evidence between them.

note: Kural 616 says effort brings prosperity and its absence brings want; Natrinai 252 states the same as the man's resolve (no rare wealth for those who stay) and then shows the planned work blocked by the woman's beauty.
teaches: The pair shows the maxim of effort accepted in full by the lover and yet not acted on, so the Natrinai marks the limit of the Kural's rule: it decides nothing while something dearer than prosperity stands in the way.

note: Both are by Kapilar: in Purananuru 109 the kings besieging Paari's Parambu, with its jackfruit and its springs, cannot take it by force, but bards who come singing will be given it; in Natrinai 253 the girl, grown beautiful and hard to reach, is like Paari's jackfruit hill closed in by rain.
teaches: Read with the puram poem, the akam simile carries its argument: Parambu yields not to siege but to those who come asking, so the friend's comparison tells the man that the girl will not be had by stealth but only by asking for her in marriage.

note: In Purananuru 337 a girl courted by kings is hard to see, like the cold spring of Paari's Parambu, shut in the house while her brothers fight the suitors; in Natrinai 253 the girl, guarded like Paari's hill, is hard to reach for her secret lover.
teaches: The pair shows Parambu as the standard image of the guarded marriageable girl in both akam and puram, and sets two kinds of suitor against the same closed house: kings who would take her by war and a lover who must now stop coming by night.
audit_text_issue: purananuru:337 line 4 is a lacuna and lines 3 and 13 are obscure; the link does not depend on them.

note: Both are the girl's fear for the man on the hill path at midnight in rain: Akananuru 72 lists the path's dangers (a tiger that killed an elephant, a snake's gem, crocodiles) and ends by blaming herself; Natrinai 255 lists ghouls, a tiger that fought a tusker, the snake searching for its gem and thunder, and ends by wishing he would not come.
teaches: Read together, the same catalogue of night dangers leads to two different conclusions, self-blame for drawing him out and the wish that he stay away, so the poets used the fixed list as a premise and placed the girl's character in what she concludes from it.

note: Kuruntokai 375 says it is good if he does not come today because the millet has ripened and the night watchmen beat their drum at midnight; Natrinai 255 says the same, வாரார்ஆயினோ நன்றுமன், because of ghouls, a tiger, a snake and thunder on his path.
teaches: The two give the same wish two different reasons, discovery by the watchmen and death on the path, so the wish that he not come is a set response whose grounds range from the secret to his life, and Natrinai 255 shows the graver one.

note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 256 is the man telling his grieving wife that he has given up going, through the burnt forest and even through the cool forest of the rains.
