teaches: Read together, the Natrinai supplies the one answer the Kural's speaker would accept, a plain 'I am not going', and shows that to be believed it had to renounce the pleasant season as well as the harsh one, since a man who stays only while the road is burnt will go when it rains.

note: In both the stag (இரலை) with his young doe is shown to the reader in the rains: in 242 he stands searching for her when the herd scatters, and the returning man hurries; in 256 he rests holding her in the shade, and the man gives up going.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the iraicchi's sense fixed while the man's act changes: the stag keeping to his doe stands for the man's duty to his wife both when he hurries home and when he declines to leave.

note: In 255 the girl fears the midnight path for him and wishes he would not come; in 257 the friend tells the man himself that she knows fierce beasts roam the path and he still comes at midnight, and presses marriage.
teaches: The pair shows one danger serving two speakers: the girl's private fear in 255 becomes in the friend's mouth in 257 a lever on the man, so the convention of the dangerous path is both a feeling and an argument for marriage.

note: In 251 the speaker begs the millet to ripen late so the girl's days in the field may last; in 259 the millet heads have ripened like the sea drawing back, and the friend asks what they will do.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two poems are the before and after of one threat, making the millet's ripening the clock of the secret love: the harvest that ends the field season also ends the meetings unless the man marries.

note: Both use the marutham buffalo as ullurai for the straying husband: in Akananuru 46 it breaks its tether at night, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; in Natrinai 260 it has grazed the red lilies, tired of the lotus, and sleeps on the sand away from the field.
teaches: Read together, the one creature carries different stages of the husband's straying, the breaking out in Akananuru 46 and the surfeit and sleeping elsewhere in Natrinai 260, so the buffalo ullurai was a fixed vehicle whose actions the poets chose to fit the moment of the quarrel.

note: Kural 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words; Natrinai 262's man, seeing his wife already wasting, ends on 'hard indeed is the shame of having nothing' (இன்மையது இளிவே).
teaches: The Natrinai shows what Valluvar's shame of poverty weighs against in a man's life: it is the one argument strong enough to set beside a wife's midnight suffering, so the couplet's social fear turns out to be the engine of the paalai parting.

note: Both are the man arguing with his heart over leaving his wife for wealth; in Akananuru 199 he refuses even riches like the land Narmudi Cheral won back, in Natrinai 262 he ends on the unbearable shame of poverty, which on the plain reading tips him toward going.
teaches: Read together they show that the debate with the heart had no fixed outcome in the tradition: the same scene of the wife's shoulders could close either way, and what decides each poem is the argument the poet places last.

note: Both are neythal poems about a man who will not marry: in 263 an old lame stork brings sea fish to his pregnant hen in the field, in 272 a red-beaked sea crow searches the backwater for fish for his hen heavy with young on the sand.
teaches: Two poets put the same act, a male shore bird feeding its pregnant mate, beside the same complaint, so the provider bird was a conventional reproach that let the women shame an unmarried lover without naming his fault.

note: Both are Paranar's, both the man speaking to his heart after meeting the girl: in Akananuru 152 her shoulders are like the plumage of the joyous peacock on the Ezhil hill of Nannan, lord of Paaram; in Natrinai 265 her hair is like the plumage of the joyous peacock (கலி மயில் கலாவத்து) on Ori's Kolli, and Paaram, guarded by Minjili, is another of her measures.
teaches: The pair shows Paranar keeping one formula, a chief's hill peacock, for the girl and changing only the chief, and Akananuru 152 supplies the Paaram-Nannan link that makes sense of the elliptic 265: her beauty is ranked among the guarded possessions of the hill chiefs.

note: Akananuru 208, also Paranar's man speaking to his heart after union, tells of Minjili's war at Paazhi and ends on her hair fragrant as the flowers of Ori's Kolli; Natrinai 265 names Minjili guarding Paaram and Ori's Kolli in its run of comparisons for her hair.
teaches: The longer poem tells the war story behind the names that the short one only lists, so Natrinai 265's Minjili is not a decorative name but the victor of a battle Paranar's audience knew, and the girl is measured against fame won in war.

note: Both are, on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural, the friend trying to stop the man's departure: Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 269 sets before him his son climbing down his chest and his wife's eyes on his face.
teaches: The pair shows two opposite tactics for one thurai, the Kural's friend making the woman's death the stake and the Natrinai's friend making the man's own pleasures at home the stake, so the couplet's threat is one option among the friend's arguments, not the only one.

note: Both are Paranar's and both use Nannan's cruelty to a woman as a measure: Kuruntokai 292 curses the mother to go to hell like Nannan who killed a girl for eating a fruit; Natrinai 270 tells the husband his cruelty is worse than Nannan's to a woman's hair.
teaches: Holding them together shows that Paranar made one king's notorious offence against a woman into a standing scale for cruelty in love, turned in one poem on a guarding mother and in the other on a straying husband.

note: Both are about a mother whose daughter has eloped: Akananuru 165, seen by onlookers, has a calf drinking at the buffalo in the old town, the playmates mourning and the mother crying 'let my life end'; Natrinai 271, in the mother's own voice, has a buffalo calf asleep on the dung of the house, the playmates going home at evening and her curse on Death for not taking her.
teaches: The two poems share an inventory for the house a daughter has left (the buffalo calf beside its mother, the girl's playmates, the mother's wish to die), which shows these were the fixed signs of that grief and lets the calf safe beside its dam be read as the daughter who did not stay.
audit_text_issue: Akananuru 165 line 3 (எந்த) is unclear and the editions differ on its line count (13 against 12).

note: Both are neythal poems of a girl neglected by the lord of the shore with the sea crow and its 'lovely hen' (காமர் பேடை, காமர் பெடை): in Akananuru 170 the small sea crow rests with its mate while she is alone at midnight, in Natrinai 272 the crow fishes for its pregnant mate while the man is not kind.
teaches: The pair shows the shore crow with its mate measuring the man's neglect in two ways, by companionship in the one and by provision in the other, so the bird's pairing was a flexible yardstick for whatever the girl lacks.

note: Both have the friend speak to the girl while the man overhears about the mother who, not knowing the cause, will bring the velan to hold a veri; in Akananuru 242 the friend says they should go to him before the goat is offered, in Natrinai 273 the poem ends on her trembling heart.
teaches: Together they show the announced veri as a set lever on the overhearing man, the false diagnosis that will expose the secret, and Akananuru 242 states the remedy, his embrace before the sacrifice, that Natrinai 273 leaves him to supply.

note: Both carry the thurai of the friend disputing the season of his return: in Kuruntokai 66 the konrai are foolish to take the untimely rain for his season; in Natrinai 274 the rain has come and she asks whether the man who invited the girl along the rain-washed hills has those words now.
teaches: The pair shows two ways to deny the season: Kuruntokai 66 blames the trees and so keeps faith in his promise, while Natrinai 274 sets his own old words against the rain and so doubts him, so the same thurai could comfort or accuse.

note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the bee, knower of flowers, whether any is more fragrant than her hair; in Natrinai 277 the woman curses the bee for sucking the yellow peeram but not her yellow pallor, because it has no scent, and asks it to carry word to her man.
teaches: Akam's bee is a judge of scent, and the pair shows the limit of that office: it can testify to a beloved's beauty in union but cannot be made to carry the scentless pallor of separation, which is why the girl's appeal to it fails.

note: Both have the girl, with no human messenger, beg a creature to go to her man: in Akananuru 170 the crab, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Natrinai 277 the bee, after she scolds it.
teaches: Together they show the creature-messenger as the last resort of a girl who cannot speak openly, and Natrinai 277 adds the grievance that the creature has its own pleasures to prefer, so the appeal is also a complaint that even the messenger neglects her.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a house is for tending guests; in Natrinai 280 the wife, urged not to sulk at her philandering husband, says she cannot even sulk because her house, like the Velir's Kunrur, is never free of feasting guests.
teaches: The Natrinai shows the Kural's household duty turned into a weapon in love: hospitality is a reason no one can fault, so the wife uses it to refuse both the sulk and the husband, and the virtue becomes the frame of her pride.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die half done; in Natrinai 284 the man's own reason says the same, that leaving work unfinished brings ignorance and disgrace, while his heart urges him home.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's maxim on unfinished work already living inside an akam man as the voice of his reason, and the Natrinai adds what the maxim leaves out: obeying it costs a body torn like a rope between two tuskers.

note: Natrinai 284 has the man's body as an old rope pulled at both ends by two tuskers, heart against reason; Kural 1163 has the woman's life as a carrying pole with love and shame hung at its two ends, in a body that cannot bear them.
teaches: Set side by side, the two show one figure, a load-bearing cord or pole strained between two claims, serving both the man's conflict of love against duty and the woman's of love against shame, so the tradition pictured a lover's divided mind as a physical strain whatever the second claim was.

note: Kapilar in Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan of Mullur for chariots given while sober, more than the raindrops on Mullur's heights; Kapilar in Natrinai 291 measures a girl's ruined beauty by the herd-owners whose cattle the king of Mullur drove off at nightfall on his horse.
teaches: Read together, the same poet's two Mullur poems show the giving king's other face: the wealth praised in puram as countless gifts came partly from night raids on herds, and akam borrows the raid from the side of those who lost everything.

note: The bereaved mother in Natrinai 293 wishes that the young man's mother may suffer great anguish like hers (எம்போல் பெரு விதுப்புறுகமாதோ); the mourner of Purananuru 291 wishes the same on the king (என்போற் பெருவிதுப்பு உறுக) whose garland sent the man to his death.
teaches: The shared curse formula shows that akam treated a daughter's elopement as a bereavement in the full puram sense: the mother speaks in the words a mourner uses over a warrior's body, aimed at the one who caused the loss.

note: Paranar in Purananuru 348 compares a girl to rich Unur of truthful Thazhumban and pictures suitors' chariots in every shade and elephants tied at every place for her; Paranar in Natrinai 300, with strangers' marriage offers in the colophon, has a chariot set at the gate as her bride-price and likens the lover to Unur's begging elephant at the kitchen.
teaches: Holding the two Paranar poems together shows him using Thazhumban's Unur for the same occasion, a girl besieged by suitors with chariots and elephants: in puram the siege threatens the town, in akam the friend turns it into a goad to make the hidden lover ask for her before others do.

note: In Akananuru 242 the mother calls the diviner not knowing that the man who chased parrots from the millet with them came to the girl in love; in Natrinai 288 the friend fears the diviner will say the girl went to scare small parrots from the millet and Vel seized her.
teaches: Natrinai 288 puts in the diviner's own verdict the very scene Akananuru 242 says the mother does not know, so the pair shows the veri's error lying not in the facts but in the agent: it finds the right place, the millet field, and names the god instead of the man.

note: Natrinai 289's woman says her lover would not shift from his word even if the earth shifted, though the promised rains have come without him; Kural 1154's woman asks whether any fault lies with those who believed the assuring words of one who then left.
teaches: On the plain reading the two women answer the same broken promise in incompatible ways, one keeping her faith in his word intact and blaming only her unpitied state, the other turning the promise into a charge against him, which marks out the range a waiting woman's speech could take.

note: Kural 1156: if he is hard enough to speak of leaving, the hope of his grace is vain; Natrinai 296: told he will go, the woman asks what will become of her, since he leaves with a heart set on work even in the season when the kondrai blooms and the parted grieve.
teaches: Kural 1156 finds the man's hardness in the announcement itself, and Natrinai 296 adds a second measure the couplet does not give, the timing: to leave in the very season made for grieving apart shows a heart given wholly to work.

note: Kural 1102: the jewelled woman is herself the cure of the sickness she causes; Natrinai 294: at the wedding, the friend says the man's chest has become both the sickness and the joy, as the sky bore both fire and wind.
teaches: The couplet states the paradox as the lover's private discovery in secret union, while Natrinai 294 has the friend confirm it at the wedding, so the pair shows the same claim moving from a lover's wonder to a public fact once marriage makes the cause of the sickness its lawful cure.

note: In Natrinai 284 the man already away hears heart and reason argue and fears his body will snap like a rope; in Natrinai 298 the man about to go tells his heart it cannot hold both the hills and her shoulders, and he stays.
teaches: Read as a pair, the two poems show the same divided man before and after the journey begins: before it, the heart can still win and the journey is dropped, but once the work is under way reason rules and only the body is left to break.

note: Both set a sleepless woman against a night in which everyone else sleeps: Kural 1168 says the night that lulls all creatures has only her for company; in Natrinai 303 the hamlet has fallen silent and only the paired anril cries.
teaches: The couplet's lonely vigil turns out, in the Natrinai scene, to have one other waker, a bird that has its mate, so her sleeplessness is measured against a pairing she lacks, and her question is whether he lies awake too.

note: Both make pallor the immediate price of the lover's absence: Kural 1187 says it came the moment she turned in his embrace; Natrinai 304 says beauty joins her when he joins and pallor wrecks it when he parts.
teaches: The couplet records the speed of the pallor; the Natrinai woman draws the moral that the same chest is joy and harm at once, like the hand that plays to the asunam and then kills it.

note: Both are the friend's warning, heard by the man, that the millet field is ending and the girl will be confined: in 313 the crop has just reached reaping time; in 306 the reaping is done and the field is bare stubble.
teaches: Read together they show the harvest working as a clock for the secret love, with the friend's message moving from 'soon' to 'now' as the millet goes from ripe ear to stubble.

note: Both describe the reaped millet field as a broken stalk-head stubble in nearly the same words (பொறை இறுத்த கோல் தலை இருவி; குலவுப்பொறை யிறுத்த கோல்தலை மருவி), and both picture the man finding it empty and sad (பைதல்; பைதலன்).
teaches: The shared formula shows that the reaped field was a fixed sign of the closed meeting-place: Natrinai's friend uses it as a threat to make him ask for the girl, while Akananuru's friend imagines him already standing there grieving.
audit_text_issue: Akananuru 38 line 13 மருவி is probably இருவி, and line 15 ஐ.தேங்கு is corrupt.

note: Both are the moment the man announces departure: in Kural 1151 she answers with a sharp demand, tell me if you are not going; in Natrinai 308 she can neither ask nor stop him and only presses against his chest.
teaches: The Kural gives the woman a defiant sentence to stop the journey, while Natrinai shows wordless grief doing what the sentence could not, since it is her silence that melts his resolve.

note: Both start from the same premise, that youth passes and does not return; Naladiyar 11 concludes that the wise renounce desire from childhood; Natrinai 314 uses it to condemn the man who left an embrace for wealth.
teaches: The same commonplace of fleeting youth served opposite ends: for the akam woman it is a reason to spend youth in love now, for the didactic poet a reason to give love up, so the ascetic use of the maxim takes over an argument love poetry had already made.

note: Both argue from an unknown lifespan against putting something off: Naladiyar 19 says do not defer good deeds because the wind may drop the unripe fruit; Natrinai 314 says no one knows the measure of a life, yet he left her for later gain.
teaches: The pairing shows that 'do not defer, life is short' was a shared argument whose object changed with the genre, virtue in the Naladiyar and love in the Natrinai, where wealth-seeking is the deferral blamed.

note: Both are the friend's comfort that the rain is false: in Kuruntokai 66 the konrai is foolish for taking stray rain for the season 'before the season comes' (பருவம் வாரா அளவை); in Natrinai 316 the cloud itself is foolish for pouring 'before he comes' (வரல் வாரா அளவை).
teaches: Natrinai moves the foolishness from the flowers that believe the rain to the cloud that sends it, so the consolation could discredit the season at either end, the sign or its source.

note: Both are the same midnight on the guarded shore: in 303 the woman lies awake while the hamlet sleeps and asks whether he knows; in 319 the man, kept away by the watch, lies awake while even the fish sleep.
teaches: Set side by side, 319 answers the question in 303: he is awake too, and the anthology places the same sleepless midnight on both sides of the guard that separates them.

note: Purananuru 158 lists Ori of Kolli and Malaiyan who rode Kaari side by side among the seven great givers; Natrinai 320 remembers the street where Ori was killed and Kaari entered as a byword for a stricken town.
teaches: The bards' canon of seven generous patrons hides that two of them were enemies, one killing the other, and the love poem shows that killing had become a proverb for a town in panic.

note: Natrinai 327's girl stakes her life on the belief that the noble do not fail in what they owe; Kural 990 says that if the worthy declined in worth the earth could not bear its load.
teaches: The Kural makes the failure of the worthy a cosmic impossibility, while the Natrinai girl turns the same belief into a private wager on one man, so the pair shows what the maxim costs when a single life rests on someone being counted among the worthy.

note: Both have a woman awake at midnight with a love too great to get past: the Kural's flood with no shore and only herself awake, Natrinai 335's great love with no one to clear it while moon, surf, wind, anril and lute keep the night going.
teaches: The couplet's 'only I am here at midnight' is filled in by the older poem with a crowd of sounds and scents that will not stop, showing that the woman's solitude is not silence but a shore night that keeps working on her.

note: Vaanan's Sirukudi, its fields and groves, is the vehicle for the wife in both: her hair smells like its groves in Akananuru 204, her bangles are as precious as the town in Natrinai 340.
teaches: Held together, the two show one patron's fertile town used as the standard of a wife's worth from both sides of a marriage: the faithful husband hurries home to a beauty like Sirukudi, and the wronged wife names the same town to measure what her husband has taken.

note: In both a bear digs into a snake-haunted termite mound on the path: in 325 on the wasteland road the man would take for wealth, in 336 on the hill path he takes to the night meeting.
teaches: The same bear tearing open the snake's mound marks the danger of the road away from her and of the road to her, so in the anthology the friend's fear attaches to the man's going whichever way he goes.

note: Natrinai 52 has the man refuse the 'life of living apart' (பிரிந்து உறை வாழ்க்கை) for his wife's athiral-and-paathiri scented hair; Natrinai 337 has the friend say that wealth-makers by custom live apart (பிரிந்து உறை மரபின) and forgo that same scented hair.
teaches: The shared phrase and the same flowers show the choice put in fixed terms, and the pair tempers the friend's complaint: what she calls a custom set when the world was made, the man of Natrinai 52 does turn down, so it is a choice and not a law.

note: Natrinai 66 is the mother at home picturing her eloped daughter on the hot track; Natrinai 324 is the man or onlookers on the track picturing the mother at home.
teaches: Each poem imagines the other end of the elopement: the mother sees only her daughter's eyes red with suffering, while those beside the girl see her running as at play and give their pity to the mother, so each grief misjudges what the other side sees.

note: In Natrinai 34 the friend tells Murugan he knows the sickness is not his affliction; in Natrinai 322 she tells the girl, within the man's hearing, that the velan has called it a spirit's work.
teaches: Together the two show the friend undoing the velan's diagnosis before two different audiences, the god himself and the hidden lover, and only the second can end the rite, by marrying the girl.

note: Both are cold-season war-camp poems that end on the same turn, யாமே ... பாசறையேமே: in Akananuru 24 the man pictures his wife swimming alone through the long cold nights (தமியள் நீந்தி); in Natrinai 341 he pictures her well companioned at play and calls himself the one without company (துணை இலேம் தமியேம்).
teaches: With the frame and the closing words the same, the pair shows that the camp poem could place the loneliness on either side, so whether the wife pines or the soldier envies her company was the poet's choice and not something the convention fixed.
audit_text_issue: Natrinai 341 lines 1-5 are obscure; the companion may be a child at play, but the contrast of துணை holds either way.

note: Kural 1222's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Natrinai 343's woman asks whether there is no such evening in the land where her lover went.
teaches: Both turn the woman's grief into a question about where evening reaches, but the Natrinai grounds it in a village dusk of cows, offerings and a crow going home to its kin, so the couplet's bare question gains the scene that makes the absent man's freedom from evening seem unnatural.

note: Purananuru 158 names Ori as the one who ruled Kolli (கொல்லி ஆண்ட வல்வில் ஓரியும்) among the seven givers now dead; Natrinai 346 measures the wife's fragrant hair by the kulavi of the great cool Kolli of Porayan.
teaches: Set beside the elegy that names Ori as Kolli's dead lord, the love poem's passing epithet shows the hill in the Chera Porayan's hands, so the pair records that Kolli changed masters after Ori, which neither poem states.

note: Kural 1168's woman says the night that puts every creature to sleep has only her as companion; Natrinai 348's woman lies sleepless while moon, festival town and paired bees all rejoice, and asks whether the world fights her or she the world.
teaches: The couplet makes the sleepless woman the night's one companion in a sleeping world, while the Natrinai wakes the whole world in celebration around her, so the same sleeplessness becomes either a bond with the dark or a quarrel with everything else.

note: Purananuru 281 has women guard a wounded warrior from ghouls with neem, music, mustard seed and incense; Natrinai 349's man likens himself, ever behind the fisher girl, to the ghoul that hovers by men gravely wounded on the battlefield.
teaches: Read with the warding rite, the lover's simile casts him as the very presence a household drives from its wounded with neem and smoke, so his self-portrait as tireless follower carries his knowledge that he is the unwanted one at her door.

note: In Natrinai 68 the friend wishes someone would bow and tell the mother that shutting young girls in the house is neither right nor good for it; in 351 she tells the mother herself that the confinement has made the girl paler, that worshipping gods will not help, and that guarding the millet field would restore her.
teaches: Together they show the friend's case against the girl's confinement in two stages: a wished-for argument from what is proper, then her own direct plea that adds the evidence of pallor the mother has misread and a cure that quietly returns the girl to her lover's field.

note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the girl, the man overhearing, that the town is raising the very gossip they want; in Natrinai 354 the friend tells the man to his face that his friendship has become gossip as loud as the salt traders' din.
teaches: The pair shows the friend aiming the same town gossip toward marriage from two sides: told to the girl in his hearing it is the talk they hoped for, told to the man directly it is a public noise that shames his friendship.

note: Kural 580 says that those who want a refinement worth loving will drink poison they see poured; Natrinai 355's friend says the very refined (நனி நாகரிகர்) drink even poison if old friends give it, and asks the man to be kind to the girl by கண் ஓடி.
teaches: Valluvar files the poison saying under கண்ணோட்டம; the Natrinai quotes it and then asks for exactly that kindly regard, so the pairing shows the courtesy ideal of the chapter on statecraft working in love poetry as the friend's lever to bind a man to a girl who has no one else.

note: Purananuru 67 asks the swan, flying from the ford of Kumari to the northern mountain, to stop at the Chola king's palace with the poet's name; Natrinai 356 likens the man's toiling heart to the swan that grazes the southern sea and carries food to its chicks on the Himalaya.
teaches: Both send the swan between the southern sea and the northern mountain, but puram makes it a messenger to a king while akam makes its tireless feeding flight the lover's own heart, so the long-flight swan served as a go-between in one genre and as the self in the other.

note: Kural 1207's woman says she does not know forgetting and that even remembering burns; Natrinai 357's woman says the remembered day of play with the man has scarred her heart and will not fade, and on that she says she can bear the delay.
teaches: In both, memory cannot be shed, but the couplet makes it a burn and a danger, while the Natrinai makes one remembered day the scar on which the woman rests her claim to endure, so the same unfading memory is wound in one and support in the other.

note: Kuruntokai 87's woman meets the belief that the old god of the common destroys the false by saying her lord is not false at all, though her brow pales; Natrinai 358's woman grants that he swore and stays away and goes to make offerings so that the god will not harm him.
teaches: Together they show the belief that the oath-god punishes the perjured lover pressing on the woman in two moves, first denial that he is false and then propitiation on the oath-breaker's behalf, so the one he wronged becomes his protector before the god.

note: In Kuruntokai 214 the hill girl has been given a great leaf skirt and garland and the whole town is thrown into uproar; in Natrinai 359 the friend, holding the man's gift of leaves, fears the mother if they wear it and hurting him if they return it.
teaches: Read together, the leaf skirt shows itself as a public sign of courtship: the Natrinai gives the friend's dilemma before it is worn, and the Kuruntokai gives what follows the wearing, the town's uproar, which is just what the friend feared.

note: Kural 1311's woman refuses the philanderer's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 360 the friend, or on the colophon's second reading the wife in oodal, refuses him at the door and pictures yesterday's women left like a doll after the festival.
teaches: Both refuse the straying husband, but the couplet objects that he is shared, while the Natrinai shows how he uses and discards each courtesan, so the wife's scorn reaches past her own wrong to the rivals he abandons.

note: Both poems close on the same formula for the waiting wife, விருந்து அயர் விருப்பினள் with திருந்துஇழை: in 361 the friend reports it as the wife's state once the chariot is home; in 374 the returning husband imagines it on the road, joined to வருந்தும், her suffering.
teaches: The same line serves as the end of waiting in one poem and as the husband's picture of waiting in the other, so the wish to feast guests was a fixed sign of the wife who keeps the house ready, and whether it is joy or grief depends only on whether the chariot has arrived.

note: The eloping man in Natrinai 362 vows that if a fight comes he will not fear and will drive it off, but if her kin come he will hide (நுமர் வரின் மறைகுவென்); Pattinathar's antadhi verse 922 gives the hero the same two conditions, hill men he will make food for kites, but if they are her kin he will hide (உமராயின் மறைகுவனே).
teaches: Pattinathar kept not only the eloping lover's boast but its exact limit, courage against strangers and concealment before her family, which shows the devotional kovai inherited the Sangam udanpokku speech as a fixed thurai with its own logic, since striking her kin would undo the marriage the flight is meant to make.

note: Kural 1228 has the waiting woman say the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Natrinai 364's heroine says the herdsmen's kondrai flutes and the cattle bells at evening will take her life if they come with the rain after the named season has passed.
teaches: The couplet's flute that kills is given its setting by the Natrinai poem, cows driven home, bells that never knew thunder and the season he named already gone, which shows why a sweet pastoral sound became deadly: it marks the homecoming hour, and the season promise turns it into proof that he has not come.

note: In 371 the returning hero tells his charioteer that the rain has begun toward where she lives, that she has begun to burn and the herdsmen have begun their flutes; in 364 the heroine herself says the herdsmen's flutes in the rainy evening will take her life.
teaches: Held together, the two poems show the man's guess on the road matching what the woman says at home almost sound for sound, so the herdsmen's evening flute was a shared code in mullai by which each partner knew the other's hour, and the hero's haste is grounded in knowing exactly how that evening falls on her.

note: Kural 1137 holds that nothing is nobler than a woman who suffers a sea of desire yet does not ride the madal, that is, does not make her love public; in Natrinai 365 the friend proposes that they slip the mother's watch, go to the common in daylight before everyone and ask the way to his town to rebuke him.
teaches: The couplet makes the woman's silence a virtue, but the Natrinai friend uses the threat of breaking it, a daylight public walk being the woman's form of the madal, as a lever on the overhearing hero, so the restraint the Kural praises was also a weapon that worked only while it might be dropped.

note: In Akananuru 167 the man tells his heart, which is pressing him to leave for wealth, that after a sweet night with his wife in the tall house he would lie sleepless in a ruined village hall, and gives up the journey; in Natrinai 366 he tells his heart that whoever leaves her washed, flower-tied hair and soft bed in the north wind that shakes the sparrow's nest is a fool.
teaches: The two give the same refusal two arguments: Akananuru 167 sets the home against the terror of the road, while Natrinai 366 never reaches the road and argues from the season alone, a cold wind that even a bird's home must withstand, so the stay-at-home decision could rest either on fear or on a general law of the world (உலகியல்).

note: In 367 the friend tells the heroine that the young men have come wearing a garland of mullai and blue lily and that her man will surely come today; in 361 the friend reports that he himself and his young men are wearing mullai as his chariot reaches the house.
teaches: Read in sequence the two poems show that the mullai garland was the badge of the returning party, worn first by the retinue as a herald and then by the master on arrival, so the friend could promise the return from the young men's flowers before any chariot was seen.

note: Kural 1251 has the woman say love's axe breaks the door of restraint (நிறை) barred with shame; Natrinai 369's heroine, left unmarried while he seeks wealth, says she cannot swim across a love that breaks her restraint (நிறை அடு காமம்) like the Ganga in flood breaking dams.
teaches: Both name the same loss, restraint broken by love, but the Kural's image is a single blow to a closed door while the Natrinai's is a flood from the Himalaya that keeps coming each evening, so the poem adds what the couplet lacks: that the breaking recurs at a fixed hour and the woman's question is endurance, how to swim, not resistance.

note: In 370 the husband recalls his wife in the lying-in room, smeared with ghee and mustard, newly called 'old woman' after bearing a son, and finds her shy smile the sweetest thing; in 380 the friend says the wife's ghee-soiled clothes, milk-wet breasts and smell of new birth make her no match for the jewelled women he visits.
teaches: The same marks of motherhood are the husband's proof of tenderness in one poem and the wife's side's proof of his desertion in the other, which shows that the marutham quarrel is fought over what a mother's body means, and that the husband's memory in 370 is an answer to exactly the charge 380 makes.

note: Kural 1268 has the man, held by the king's war, wish that the king win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast for guests; Natrinai 374's man, returning from his work, asks travellers about the wife who longs to feast guests yet weeps.
teaches: The couplet gives the feast for guests as the man's own goal after duty, while the Natrinai poem puts the same wish in the wife and shows it unfulfilled in her tears, so the household's guest-feast was the shared picture of reunion that each partner ascribed to the other.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily and carrying a bow, coming to the swing by the asoka and the harvested millet field and finding them deserted; in Natrinai 376 she tells the parrots to tell the man with the garland and bow who appears by the asoka that the mother still guards even the empty field.
teaches: Together they show the harvested millet field as the clock of the kalavu plot: once the crop is cut the daytime meeting place is gone, and the friend's two messages, where our village is in Akananuru 38 and the guard that stays on the empty field in Natrinai 376, both push the man to come openly as a suitor.
audit_text_issue: akananuru:38 line 15 ஐ.தேங்கு looks corrupt.

note: In Kural 1133 the turned-away man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the madal that lovers ride; in Natrinai 377 the turned-away man, speaking for the friend to hear, asks whether riding the madal and praising the girl through lands and towns will not kill him like a disease.
teaches: The Kural states what the madal costs the man, his shame, while the Natrinai shows what it would do, carry her beauty's praise through every town, so the threat works on the friend because his loss of shame would become the girl's public exposure.

note: Kural 791 says nothing is as ruinous as making a friend without inquiry, since the devoted cannot leave once the bond is made; Natrinai 378 ends with the friend (or the heroine) calling her sleepless nights and the neighbours' gossip the measure of the bond made without inquiry (நாடாது இயைந்த நண்பு) with the lord of the shore.
teaches: The akam poem applies the ethics book's rule for choosing friends to a love made at a girl's sand-house, and its suffering shows the second half of the couplet at work, that she cannot leave the bond once made, so the maxim on friendship was available as a verdict on unwise love.

note: Purananuru 101: Avvai tells her heart that Athiyaman's gift, late or soon, is as sure as the food an elephant holds between its tusks. Natrinai 381 (also Avvaiyar): the rain has settled in like Neduman Anji's seat from which he keeps giving chariots.
teaches: The same poet who in puram counts on Anji's giving as something that never fails makes that unfailing giving the image of a rain a waiting woman cannot bear, so the patron's plenty is a blessing to the bard and a torment to the lover depending on who receives it.

note: Kural 1161: she would hide this pain, but it wells up like spring water when drawn. Natrinai 382: at evening she must hide her grief even if her life goes.
teaches: The couplet gives the woman's wish to hide her pain without a reason and says it fails; the Natrinai woman supplies the reason, that the slander of his enemies would shame him, so concealment in separation is shown to be a duty to his name and not only her modesty.

note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but the sickness this jewelled woman causes she alone cures. Natrinai 384: eloping, the man calls her the one who was the medicine when he suffered after casting off shame.
teaches: The Kural's paradox that the woman is the cure for the sickness she causes becomes in Natrinai 384 the eloping man's reason for taking her across the waste: he now carries his medicine with him, so the couplet's moment of union is extended into the whole journey of udanpokku.

note: Akananuru 175: the clouds flash more often than the spear Chezhiyan raised after his victory at Alankanam; the time he set for return has come. Natrinai 387: the cloud flashes like swords drawn in Chezhiyan's camp at Alankanam; he will come.
teaches: In both poems the lightning of the promised rains is measured by the weapons of Chezhiyan's victory at Alankanam, spoken once by the waiting woman and once by her friend, so the battle had become a stock sign of the season of return and could serve either as complaint (the time is here) or as comfort (he will come).

note: Akananuru 91: even if he won Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, he would not stay there forgetting her beauty. Natrinai 391: who would leave for wealth even to win Nannan's Ezhil hill, and make her eyes weep?
teaches: The friend's comfort had a fixed shape, a famous chief's rich land weighed against the woman's beauty or tears, and the pair shows its two stages: in the Akananuru the man has already gone and will not linger, in the Natrinai the journey is only announced and will not be made at all.

note: Akananuru 376: the courtesan tells the lord to give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai, and then go. Natrinai 395: the friend tells the shore lord to give back the girl's beauty, which is like Maanthai on the sea, and go.
teaches: The same formula, beauty likened to a Chera town and demanded back before he leaves, is spoken by a discarded courtesan in the Akananuru and by the friend of an unmarried girl here, so the restitution formula belonged to the speech of any woman wronged by the man, and in the friend's mouth it becomes a demand for marriage.

note: Kuruntokai 49 (Ammuvanar): even when this life changes to the next, may you be my husband and I the one close to your heart. Natrinai 397 (Ammuvanar): I do not fear death, but I fear that in another birth I may forget my lover.
teaches: The same poet gives the hope and the fear of the same belief: in Kuruntokai 49 rebirth is a chance to be joined again, in Natrinai 397 it is the risk of forgetting, so for these women the next birth mattered only as it kept or lost the present love.

note: Purananuru 39: because justice stands firm and unfailing in the Chola court at Uranthai, justice is not this king's own fame. Natrinai 400: like justice that never fails in the Uranthai court of the warlike Cholas, he knows no failing in her heart.
teaches: The puram poet says Uranthai's justice is too settled to count as any one king's merit, and the courtesan borrows exactly that settledness for her lover's place in her heart, so an inherited institution, not a person's virtue, was the akam poet's measure of a love that cannot change.
